title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > How we picked
text:
The rules were simple. A tool had to move data into an Azure service or an Azure-hosted lake, and its own pages had to say how you buy it. We read Microsoft's documentation first, then looked at outside tools that name an Azure source or target.

If we couldn't source a tool from a primary page, it's out. The order is not a ranking. Entries for other vendors list limits from their own pages, and that includes each Microsoft service.

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Which Azure ETL tools fit where your data lands
text:
Where the data lands removes half the list at once.

One term you'll see a lot is change data capture (CDC), which means reading a database's own change log instead of re-reading whole tables, so a copy stays fresh without hammering the source.

The same ETL guide lists Fabric Data Factory first for pipelines and Azure Data Factory for "hybrid and non-Fabric scenarios". That's the split this page follows.

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 Azure ETL tools
text: Eleven tools, three groups, starting with the Microsoft services.

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 Azure ETL tools > Microsoft services
text:
**1. Fabric Data Factory: copy jobs into OneLake**

At a glance

- Kind: Microsoft's software-as-a-service (SaaS) data movement inside Microsoft Fabric
- Billing: Fabric capacity units (CUs). Copy job meters are 1.5 CU-hours for a full copy and 3 CU-hours for an incremental copy, per the copy job pricing page (checked Oct 2026)
- Entry price: Microsoft's Fabric pricing page lists F2 (2 capacity units) at $262.80 a month, pay as you go (checked Oct 2026)

Microsoft's compare page says Fabric Data Factory is "the next generation of Azure Data Factory" and uses OneLake, Fabric's built-in data lake. A Copy job moves data on a schedule, and you don't have to build a pipeline. Per Microsoft's data movement guide, it can do a full copy, an incremental copy using a watermark column, or CDC replication.

Where it fits

- The data movement guide says to use a Copy job for raw (bronze) data, because it handles scheduling, column mapping and incremental loads without pipelines.
- Per Microsoft's Copy job connector page, it supports append, overwrite, upsert and a history-keeping mode called SCD Type 2 (in preview). It also runs behind firewalls through a gateway (checked Oct 2026).
- The same connector page (last updated 2026-09-16) lists Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, MongoDB, Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Salesforce and Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 among the sources and destinations for a Copy job.
- Microsoft says CDC in copy jobs "enables automated replication of changed data (including inserted, updated, and deleted records)" from a source to a destination, so deletes are carried over on the supported connectors.
- Microsoft's compare page says approximately 90% of the activities in Azure Data Factory are already available in Fabric Data Factory, and that billing has "no charges for external or pipeline activities, only activity runs and pipeline data movement" on top of the capacity (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 Azure ETL tools > Microsoft services (part 2)
text:
- CDC replication is Preview and covers Azure SQL, SQL Server, Oracle and a few more, but not PostgreSQL, MySQL or MongoDB, per Microsoft's connector page (checked Oct 2026).
- SSIS runtimes and managed virtual networks are "To be determined" in Fabric, per the compare page (checked Oct 2026). The same page lists the SSIS activity, Synapse Notebook and Spark job definition activities as not available (N/A) in Fabric Data Factory, though ADF has them.
- Incremental copy meters at 3 CU hours against 1.5 for a full copy, and Microsoft says the 3 CU hours rate applies to the initial full load in incremental mode as well as the later runs, per its Copy job pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- On the connector page, SCD Type 2 in Copy job "is currently in preview", and it is not supported yet when you run CDC replication from Oracle sources (checked Oct 2026).
- Microsoft's Copy job pricing page says consumption rates "are subject to change at any time." (checked Oct 2026)

**2. Azure Data Factory: hybrid pipelines and SSIS**

At a glance

- Kind: Microsoft's platform-as-a-service (PaaS) pipeline service
- Billing: $1 per 1,000 activity runs and $0.25 per data integration unit (DIU) hour for copying (East US, US dollars), per Microsoft's pricing page (checked Oct 2026)
- Data flows: $0.274 per vCore-hour with an 8 vCore minimum, on Microsoft's live page (checked Oct 2026)

ADF is, in Microsoft's words, a managed cloud service for hybrid ETL, ELT and data integration. It runs copies, data flows and SQL Server Integration Services (SSIS) packages. A self-hosted runtime reaches data on your own network.

Where it fits

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 Azure ETL tools > Microsoft services (part 3)
text:
- It has a self-hosted runtime for on-premises data and runs SSIS packages. Microsoft's compare page lists the SSIS activity as available in ADF and N/A in Fabric Data Factory, and Azure-SSIS integration runtimes as "To be determined" in Fabric (checked Oct 2026).
- Microsoft's pricing page shows the meters, and Microsoft's retail price feed lists a one-year reservation for data flows at $1,795, about $0.205 per vCore-hour by our arithmetic (checked Oct 2026).
- Integration runtime charges on the pricing page are "prorated by the minute and rounded up", so you pay by the minute rather than by the hour (checked Oct 2026).
- Microsoft's change data capture page says native CDC in mapping data flow uses the database's own change capture with "no timestamp or ID columns" needed, and that "Pipelines in ADF are batch only, but the CDC resource can run continuously." (checked Oct 2026)
- Its Iceberg format page describes an Iceberg sink in the Copy activity (IcebergSink) that writes to Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- Microsoft says, "If you're new to data integration, start with Fabric Data Factory," on the Azure Data Factory Iceberg format page, and new Fabric features "aren't backported to Azure Data Factory or Azure Synapse pipelines," per the compare page (checked Oct 2026).
- Native CDC covers SAP, Azure SQL, SQL Server, Cosmos DB and Snowflake. On the CDC page, MySQL and PostgreSQL appear only under auto incremental extraction, where "the incremental column is required to identify the changes," and, per the pricing page, the CDC resource is billed at General Purpose rates for four cores during the public preview of CDC (checked Oct 2026).
- The Iceberg format page lists Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 as the only connector and shows no catalog setting and no update, delete or merge setting (checked Oct 2026).
- Data flows have an 8 vCore minimum and also bill for the managed disk and blob storage they use. Copying data out of an Azure datacenter adds a separate outbound transfer line, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- The pricing page FAQ says an inactive pipeline, one with zero runs in a month, is charged after one month of zero runs (checked Oct 2026).
- Text copies of the pricing page show "$-" until the rates load, so check your region's numbers yourself.

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 Azure ETL tools > Microsoft services (part 4)
text:
**3. Fabric mirroring: free, read-only copies of databases**

At a glance

- Kind: managed replication into OneLake, not a general ETL tool
- Sources listed: Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Database for MySQL (preview), SQL Server, Oracle, Snowflake and more, per the mirroring overview (checked Oct 2026)
- Billing: replication compute is free, and storage is free up to 1 TB per capacity unit you buy, per the mirroring overview (checked Oct 2026)

Mirroring keeps copying a database into OneLake as Delta tables, an open table format built on Parquet files. Microsoft says changes "can be published as fast as every 15 seconds," a figure we did not test (checked Oct 2026). Its data movement guide calls mirroring the simplest choice for processed (gold) data you only need to report on.

Where it fits

- Microsoft's docs describe setup as a connection and a table choice, with no pipelines to build or schedule. We did not try it.
- Background replication compute "is free and doesn't consume capacity," per Microsoft's overview (checked Oct 2026).
- The overview also says the free storage allowance is one terabyte for every capacity unit you buy, so an F64 capacity gets 64 free terabytes used only for mirroring (checked Oct 2026).
- The overview table lists database mirroring for Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure SQL Database, Oracle, Google BigQuery, SAP, Snowflake and SQL Server, metadata mirroring for Azure Databricks, and an open mirroring option.
- Microsoft's OneLake page says Delta Lake tables now include virtual Iceberg metadata, so Iceberg readers can open them, and that generating the metadata can take between 5 seconds and 2 minutes (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 Azure ETL tools > Microsoft services (part 5)
text:
- A running Fabric capacity is required, and storage beyond the free limit is billed, per the mirroring overview (checked Oct 2026).
- Mirroring writes to "a single, read-only destination in OneLake," per the data movement guide, and Microsoft's comparison table shows no custom scheduling or table and column management for it (checked Oct 2026).
- On SQL Server 2016 to 2022, a schema change makes mirroring fail until you disable and re-enable CDC on that table, per Microsoft's SQL Server limitations page (checked Oct 2026).
- SQL Server mirroring copies up to 1,000 tables and does not replicate tables above that limit, per the same page. Microsoft's Azure PostgreSQL mirroring limitations page sets the same 1,000-table cap and allows one Fabric item per database (checked Oct 2026).
- On Azure Database for PostgreSQL, DDL changes and TRUNCATE TABLE on mirrored tables are not supported, and stopping mirroring and starting it again reseeds all the tables, per the Azure PostgreSQL limitations page (checked Oct 2026).
- The same PostgreSQL page says columns of several data types, including inet, json, jsonb and xml, cannot be mirrored, and views, materialized views and partitioned tables are not supported (checked Oct 2026).

Before you rely on it, check how fresh your tables stay under load, because Microsoft's refresh figure is not a guarantee.

**4. Azure Synapse pipelines: teams already in a Synapse workspace**

At a glance

- Kind: the pipeline feature inside Azure Synapse Analytics
- Sources: Microsoft's overview lists ingestion from 90+ data sources
- Billing: the Synapse pricing page text shows "$-" for pipeline, serverless and dedicated pool rates (checked Oct 2026)

Microsoft's compare page names Azure Data Factory and Azure Synapse pipelines together when it describes what Fabric changes.

Where it fits

- Microsoft's Synapse overview describes one workspace that combines SQL, Spark, Data Explorer and pipelines, with both serverless and dedicated SQL resource models.
- The same page advises creating dedicated SQL pools "for predictable performance and cost" and using the serverless SQL endpoint for unplanned or bursty workloads.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 Azure ETL tools > Microsoft services (part 6)
text:
- Microsoft says new Fabric Data Factory features "aren't backported to Azure Data Factory or Azure Synapse pipelines," and that Fabric replaces Azure Synapse Link with mirroring (checked Oct 2026).
- We couldn't read a dollar rate for pipelines from that pricing page.
- Microsoft hasn't published a retirement notice on the pages we read, so we don't call Synapse retired. The overview page itself shows "Last updated on 2024-07-12".
- The overview names Delta Lake support for Spark, but it does not state Iceberg output or change data capture for pipelines.

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 Azure ETL tools > Databricks on Azure
text:
**5. Azure Databricks Lakeflow Connect: databases into Databricks**

At a glance

- Kind: managed connectors inside Azure Databricks
- Databases with CDC: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, and Oracle (through LogMiner), per the Azure Databricks database connectors page (checked Oct 2026)
- Billing: Databricks Units (DBUs) per second, per the Databricks pricing page (checked Oct 2026). Azure rates were not captured for this post

Microsoft's Azure Databricks docs (last updated 2026-09-11) describe connectors that track changes and apply them to Delta tables. Other connector types cover SaaS apps, files, message buses and plain queries, per the ingestion overview.

Where it fits

- One connector family lists change data capture for four popular databases. Microsoft's MySQL connector page says the MySQL connector is in Public Preview and access is by request through your Azure Databricks account team (checked Oct 2026).
- Governance comes from Unity Catalog, Databricks' own catalog.
- Changes land in a staging volume first, so the docs say you can run the ingestion pipeline "at whatever schedule you'd like" while the gateway keeps capturing changes, and the pipeline itself runs on serverless compute.
- Cross-cloud connectivity is supported: the database connector page gives an Azure Databricks workspace ingesting from an AWS Aurora PostgreSQL database as an example, if the network path exists.
- The MySQL connector page lists SCD type 2, API-based column selection and automated handling of new and deleted columns as supported (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- The ingestion gateway "runs continuously" on classic compute, and per the database connector page, "you provision and pay for its classic compute even when your ingestion pipeline is idle." The same page warns the initial snapshot can fail on undersized compute (checked Oct 2026).
- Destination tables are streaming tables, "which are Delta tables" with extra support for incremental processing. MongoDB is not in the database connector list (checked Oct 2026).
- On the MySQL page, a pipeline can hold at most 250 tables, and automated schema evolution of data type changes is not supported (checked Oct 2026).
- Authentication for MySQL is username and password only. OAuth U2M, OAuth M2M and OAuth with a manual refresh token are all listed as not supported on the same page (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 Azure ETL tools > Outside tools that run on Azure
text:
**6. OLake Go: best for Azure databases into Iceberg on your own storage**

At a glance

- Kind: open-source database replication, licensed Apache 2.0
- Docs: Iceberg on Azure, Postgres connector and MySQL connector
- Runs: on your own infrastructure
- Support: contact the OLake team

OLake Go captures changes from Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB, MongoDB and SQL Server (Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, SQL Server), and it writes Apache Iceberg or Parquet. You run it yourself with Docker, Helm on Kubernetes or the OLake UI.

What's good

- Our Iceberg on Azure guide shows OLake Go writing Iceberg-compatible Parquet files directly to Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) Gen2 and updating the catalog, with Lakekeeper as the open-source REST catalog.
- Lakekeeper is one of eleven catalog types on the catalog compatibility page, so the Azure route is not tied to one catalog.
- Our Postgres connector docs cover change capture with the native `pgoutput` plugin, a replication slot and a publication, and list a guide for Azure Database for PostgreSQL.
- Our MySQL connector docs cover the binary log settings (ROW format) that change capture needs, and list a guide for Azure Database for MySQL.

**7. Fivetran: many connectors with no servers**

At a glance

- Kind: managed ELT service
- Free plan: up to 500,000 monthly active rows (MAR) for connections, per Fivetran's pricing page (checked Oct 2026)
- Pay as you go: $5 base charge per connection using 1 to 1M MAR, per Fivetran's pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Fivetran's docs describe a Managed Data Lake Service that writes to Azure Data Lake Storage. Its database docs name SQL Server CDC and Change Tracking, MySQL binary logs and Azure Cosmos DB change feed as capture methods.

Where it fits

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 Azure ETL tools > Outside tools that run on Azure (part 2)
text:
- Fivetran says it runs the pipelines for you (we did not test that), and its free plan covers up to the row limit (checked Oct 2026).
- Per its Managed Data Lake Service docs, the service supports Azure Data Lake Storage, writes Parquet files to your own storage and always creates Iceberg table metadata for them.
- Its database connector docs say database connectors sync new and modified data every 15 minutes by default, applied to the destination in batches with a merge operation. They list PostgreSQL logical replication and MongoDB change streams as further capture methods (checked Oct 2026).
- Its catalog docs say Fivetran Catalog is built on Apache Polaris and implements the Iceberg OpenAPI specification, so a compatible Iceberg REST client can connect. With Delta Lake metadata turned on, Fivetran publishes the Delta metadata to OneLake.
- Its usage docs say a row is counted once a month however many times it syncs, and some re-syncs, such as historical data after you add a column, are free (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- Per its data lake docs, there is no support for Iceberg position deletes, and decimal values beyond precision 38 or scale 10 are converted to DECIMAL(38,10) (checked Oct 2026).
- The OneLake catalog route applies only to tables with Delta Lake metadata, which Fivetran creates only if you turn it on, per its catalog docs (checked Oct 2026).
- The pricing page prints no per-row rate, but Fivetran's Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026) does. Standard starts at $495 per million MAR plus a $5 base per connection, list price before discounts (version 10, effective February 1, 2026). Deletes count as paid rows, per the usage docs.

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > FAQs
text:
Q1. What is the best ETL tool for Azure?

It depends on where your data lands. Fabric mirroring and Copy jobs suit Fabric, Azure Data Factory suits hybrid and SSIS work, and Lakeflow Connect suits Azure Databricks. Fivetran, Airbyte and Hevo add connectors for outside sources, and OLake Go suits Azure databases going into Iceberg on your own storage.

Q2. Is Azure Data Factory being replaced by Fabric Data Factory?

Microsoft calls Fabric Data Factory the next generation of Azure Data Factory and says new Fabric features are not backported to ADF. We found no retirement notice for ADF on the pages we read. Microsoft's ETL guide still keeps ADF for hybrid and non-Fabric scenarios.

Q3. Does Fabric mirroring cost anything?

Sort of. Microsoft says replication compute is free and storage is free up to 1 TB per capacity unit you buy. But you need a running Fabric capacity, and you pay for querying and for storage over the limit (checked Oct 2026).

Q4. Can Azure ETL tools write Apache Iceberg tables?

Yes, some can. Azure Data Factory lists an Iceberg sink to Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2. Fabric writes Delta tables and exposes Iceberg metadata for readers. Fivetran's data lake service always creates Iceberg metadata on that storage, while Airbyte's Azure Blob destination lists CSV and JSON Lines. OLake Go's Azure guide writes Iceberg to Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) Gen2 through the Lakekeeper catalog.

Q5. How is Azure Data Factory priced?

You pay per meter, so there's no single price. In East US, Microsoft's price feed shows $1 per 1,000 activity runs and $0.25 per data integration unit (DIU) hour for copying. Data flows are $0.274 per vCore-hour on Microsoft's pricing page ($0.27325 in the feed). Rates vary by region (checked Oct 2026).

Q6. Which Azure options read database change logs?

Fabric mirroring does for its listed sources, and Fabric Copy job offers CDC in preview for a short list. ADF has native CDC for a few connectors, and Databricks Lakeflow Connect lists MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle. Fivetran and Hevo also document log-based capture, and OLake Go documents it for Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL Flexible Server.

Q7. Should I use ETL or ELT on Azure?

title: Compare: Best Azure ETL Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > FAQs (part 2)
text:
Use Microsoft's own rule of thumb. Its ETL guide says to choose ETL for heavy transformation away from a constrained target, complex business rules or staging audits before loading. It says to choose ELT when the target is a modern warehouse or lakehouse with elastic compute, or when you need to keep raw data.

Q8. Is Azure Synapse retired?

Not that we can see. We found no retirement notice on the Microsoft pages we read. Microsoft does say Fabric replaces Azure Synapse Link with mirroring and that new Fabric features are not backported to Synapse pipelines.

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

Short version: there is no single best change data capture (CDC) tool, because these tools do different jobs. Debezium and Flink CDC suit teams that already run their own streaming systems.

Fivetran, Estuary, Airbyte and Artie suit teams that would rather have a vendor run the pipeline. Striim, Qlik Replicate and GoldenGate fit big Oracle estates, and AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) and Datastream fit teams that live on one cloud. Where your data has to land, say Apache Iceberg tables, cuts the list down fast.

- CDC is not one thing. Log-based tools read the database's change log. Query-based tools just ask, on a schedule, what changed, and that matters most for deletes and source load.
- Where the data lands decides your shortlist. Only some tools write Apache Iceberg, and the AWS DMS target list (checked Oct 2026) does not include it.

Prices and limits below link to the vendor page and end with a "(checked Oct 2026)" note.

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Log-based or query-based? Start here
text:
Change data capture sends only a database's inserts, updates and deletes to another system, instead of copying everything again.

Confluent describes log-based CDC as reading the database's transaction log, the file where the database writes down every change in order. Query-based CDC, also called timestamp-based, works differently. It runs a query on a schedule, and it needs a column that records when each row changed.

Timestamp-based CDC has limits. Confluent says it can only handle soft deletes (rows marked as deleted, not removed), and it adds load because rows must be scanned. Log-based CDC isn't free either, since the Debezium FAQ says running a connector can add load to the source database (checked Oct 2026).

Confluent also lists trigger-based CDC, where a database trigger (a stored procedure that runs on every insert, update or delete) copies each change into a shadow table. It catches deletes, but Confluent says it hurts source performance and changes the source schema.

| Method | Sees deletes | Source load | Needs |
| Log-based | Yes | Low, though not zero | Access to the transaction log |
| Query-based (timestamp) | Soft deletes only | Rows are scanned on each run | A reliable changed-at column |
| Trigger-based | Yes | Extra writes on every change | Triggers and a shadow table in the source |

Method facts: Confluent's change data capture guide and the Debezium FAQ, October 2026.

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 best change data capture tools, one by one > Run it yourself
text:
**1. Debezium: best for teams that already run Kafka**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based
- Databases: MongoDB, MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2, Cassandra, CockroachDB (connector list)
- Price: Free licence, you pay for infrastructure and staff

Debezium's docs (checked Oct 2026) describe an open-source tool for log-based CDC. It runs inside Kafka Connect, or as Debezium Server, which the docs say needs no Apache Kafka.

What's good

- Nine database connectors aren't marked incubating (checked Oct 2026), and Oracle is one of them.
- Its docs describe Debezium Server as a ready-to-use application that streams change events to messaging and storage systems without requiring Apache Kafka. The sink list includes Kinesis, Pub/Sub, Pulsar, Redis, RabbitMQ and Event Hubs besides Iceberg.
- Per the same docs, the Iceberg sink supports upsert and append modes, creates the destination tables on first startup when event and key schema information is enabled, and adds new columns when `allow-field-addition` is on (the default is true).
- The Debezium FAQ says all events within a topic are totally ordered, and that even if events are duplicated during failures, the end result after applying all of them stays the same.
- The PostgreSQL docs say that if the connector stops for any reason, it continues reading the WAL where it last left off after a restart.

Where it falls short

- You run it, all of it. The Apache Iceberg sink lives in a separate community repository (checked Oct 2026), and each Debezium Server instance runs one connector.
- In the Iceberg sink, upsert is off by default, so the default is append-only. With upsert on, `upsert-keep-deletes` defaults to true, so deleted rows are kept and marked `__deleted=true` (Debezium Server docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- Upsert keeps the record with the highest value in a dedup column (`__source_ts_ns` by default). The Debezium Server docs (checked Oct 2026) do not say what happens when two records share the same value.
- The PostgreSQL `pgoutput` plug-in does not capture values for generated columns, so those columns are missing from the connector's output (PostgreSQL docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- Delivery is at least once: in abnormal situations, such as recovering from a fault, the PostgreSQL connector might emit duplicate change events (PostgreSQL docs (checked Oct 2026)).

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 best change data capture tools, one by one > Run it yourself (part 2)
text:
**2. Apache Flink CDC: best for teams that already run Flink**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based, with Debezium as the engine for some sources
- Price: Free licence, you pay for the Flink cluster

With Flink CDC you write a pipeline in YAML, and it generates and submits the Flink job for you. In the v3.7.0 docs the YAML sources are MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server (checked Oct 2026). MongoDB and Db2 are listed only under its separate Flink sources.

What's good

- The Iceberg pipeline sink creates tables and syncs schema changes such as new columns, with catalogs of type hadoop, hive, glue or a custom class.
- Its connector overview (checked Oct 2026) lists ten pipeline sinks for version 3.6.x: StarRocks, Doris, Paimon, Kafka, Elasticsearch, OceanBase, MaxCompute, Iceberg, Fluss and Hudi. The same YAML pipeline format covers all of them.
- The overview (checked Oct 2026) lists Iceberg versions 1.6, 1.7, 1.8, 1.9 and 1.10 for the Iceberg sink.
- The sink's `partition.key` option takes partition transforms per table: truncate, hour, day, month, year and bucket (Iceberg sink docs).
- Per the same page, the sink supports both batch and streaming data synchronization.

Where it falls short

- The Iceberg sink (checked Oct 2026) needs a primary key (a column that uniquely identifies each row) on every source table, and its docs say exactly-once is not supported. It uses at-least-once writes plus the key.
- Depending on the catalog type, the sink docs (checked Oct 2026) say you may need to add extra JARs by hand and pass them with the `--jar` argument of the Flink CDC command line.
- Each Flink CDC release pairs with specific Flink versions. Version 3.6.x supports Flink 1.20.* and 2.2., and 3.5.x supports 1.19. and 1.20.* (overview (checked Oct 2026)).
- The version table (checked Oct 2026) shows YAML sources arriving over time: PostgreSQL first appears in the 3.5.x row and Oracle in the 3.6.x row, and the Iceberg sink first appears in the 3.4.x row. The v3.7.0 docs also list SQL Server as a YAML source, but the table has no 3.7 row.

**3. OLake Go: best for database changes into Iceberg on your own storage**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based CDC for four databases
- Price: Free licence (Apache 2.0), you pay for infrastructure

You run it with Docker Compose (OLake UI install), the Docker command line (Docker CLI) or Helm on Kubernetes (Kubernetes install).

text:
It reads PostgreSQL logical replication, the MySQL binlog, MongoDB change streams and SQL Server's native CDC, and writes Apache Iceberg tables. Deleted rows are marked with equality deletes (a delete by key value) or positional deletes (a delete by file position), both Iceberg version 2 delete formats. Since v0.11.0 it can also use deletion vectors, an Iceberg version 3 delete format (see the terminology page).

Docs: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, SQL Server.

What's good

- It is open source under Apache 2.0 (GitHub), and one tool does the first snapshot and then the change capture, with no per-row fee.
- It supports eleven Iceberg catalog types (compatibility page), including Glue, Hive, Unity and Representational State Transfer (REST) catalogs (REST catalog page).
- Kafka and S3 work as sources too (docs), and OLake Fusion, a companion product, handles Iceberg compaction and table maintenance (Fusion docs).
- Full Refresh + CDC, Full Refresh + Incremental and strict CDC syncs are stateful and resumable: after a crash, a network failure or a manual pause, a sync resumes from its last checkpoint instead of starting over. The Iceberg writer also uses a two-phase commit that tracks per-chunk commit status, so syncs avoid inconsistencies and duplicate writes (OLake Go overview).
- Large tables are read in parallel chunks during the first snapshot, and each job sets its own maximum number of connections to the source database (OLake Go overview).
- New source columns are added to the Iceberg schema automatically, and widening type changes such as INT to LONG, FLOAT to DOUBLE and wider DECIMAL precision are handled (schema evolution docs).

Good to know

- Change capture covers PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB and SQL Server, and Oracle, Db2 and S3 sources load by full refresh or incremental.
- Output is Iceberg and Parquet on storage you choose, and Snowflake, BigQuery and Redshift can query the Iceberg tables it writes (see the compatibility page).

Bottom line: Pick OLake Go when you run PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB or SQL Server and want database changes in Iceberg tables on storage you run. For Oracle change capture, look at Debezium, Qlik Replicate or Oracle GoldenGate above.

text:
**4. Estuary: best for one managed platform for streaming and batch**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based
- Price: $0.50 per GB moved, plus $100 a month for each of the first 6 connector instances and $50 for extra ones; free tier of 10 GB a month and 2 instances (Estuary pricing page (checked Oct 2026))

Its pricing page lists PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Oracle and SQL Server among the major databases it supports.

What's good

- Its pricing page says it unifies real-time streaming and batch movement in one system.
- The pricing FAQ says Estuary offers "200+ source and destination connectors" across databases, cloud storage, APIs, SaaS apps and streaming platforms (pricing page).
- Per the same pricing FAQ, a new pipeline runs a historical backfill and then switches to real-time CDC, and the backfill can be disabled or scoped.
- Adding a new target means paying only for that target and the data sent to it, with no need to re-extract from each source (pricing FAQ).
- Its Iceberg connector docs say AWS Glue catalogs work through the Glue Iceberg REST endpoint, and that with Glue you can configure table optimizers for compaction, snapshot retention and orphan file deletion.

Where it falls short

- The Iceberg connector (checked Oct 2026) needs an Iceberg REST catalog (a catalog with a standard web API) on Amazon S3, an AWS EMR Serverless Spark application and an S3 staging bucket (a holding folder for files in transit). Catalogs on GCP or Azure are planned, not supported.
- Each source and destination is a billed instance (pricing (checked Oct 2026)), so the bill grows as your pipelines do.
- In the Iceberg connector docs (checked Oct 2026), array and object fields are written as string columns, and the docs say nested types are not currently supported.
- Compaction through the Glue optimizer settings is off by default (Enable Compaction defaults to false), and Hard Delete is disabled by default, so rows deleted in the source are soft-deleted in Iceberg (Iceberg connector docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- A "Beta" label sits in the docs section (checked Oct 2026) on REST catalogs other than AWS Glue.
- Private and bring-your-own-cloud deployments need an annual plan and add fees based on the cloud infrastructure required, and no figure is published (pricing docs (checked Oct 2026)).

**5. Airbyte: best for scheduled syncs and a long connector list**

At a glance

text:
- Method: Log-based CDC on scheduled syncs
- Price: Core free; Cloud Standard $20 a month with 5 credits, with database data at 4 credits per GB (Airbyte pricing page and credit docs (checked Oct 2026))

Airbyte's CDC docs say syncs are scheduled, and CDC sources aren't treated as infinite streaming sources. So don't expect a live stream. Cloud Standard syncs at most hourly, and Plus syncs every 15 minutes (Cloud limits (checked Oct 2026)).

What's good

- Its pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists 700+ connectors, and the S3 Iceberg destination supports REST, Glue, Nessie and Polaris catalogs.
- The S3 Iceberg destination offers Full Refresh Overwrite, Append and Overwrite + Deduped, plus Incremental Append and Append + Deduped. Its destination docs say dedup is merge-on-read: primary keys become Iceberg identifier columns, and an upsert is an equality delete on the key followed by an insert.
- The comparison matrix on the pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists a maximum sync frequency of 5 minutes on Pro and Enterprise Flex, against 15 minutes on Plus and 1 hour on Standard.
- Its licence FAQ says anyone can use Airbyte free of charge and run it at scale on their own infrastructure, under the Elastic License 2.0 (checked Oct 2026).
- On Cloud, the credit docs (checked Oct 2026) say that if you run out of credits, syncs continue and you are billed in arrears. A trial lasts 14 days or 400 trial credits, whichever comes first.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 best change data capture tools, one by one > Managed or vendor-run (part 3)
text:
- The CDC docs (checked Oct 2026) list some limits. Views aren't supported, TRUNCATE and ALTER changes aren't picked up from the logs, and new tables need a refresh.
- Per the same page (checked Oct 2026), CDC incremental is supported only for tables with primary keys for most sources, and the first CDC sync takes a snapshot with a SELECT statement, which the docs call effectively a Full Refresh.
- In the S3 Iceberg destination, objects and unions are written as string columns of serialized JSON (destination docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- Two cautions in the same docs (checked Oct 2026): if compaction runs at the same time as a truncate refresh sync, it deletes files from the current generation and causes data loss, and changes made to the main branch outside Airbyte after a sync begins are lost.
- The Cloud limits page (checked Oct 2026) caps Standard organizations at 1 workspace and a connection at 1,000 streams. Plus has SSO but no SCIM or role-based access control.
- Pro and Enterprise Flex use capacity-based pricing, and the pricing page (checked Oct 2026) publishes no price for them.

**6. Fivetran: best for hands-off, vendor-run replication**

At a glance

- Method: Native logs plus proprietary methods
- Price: Monthly Active Rows (MAR) per connection; free up to 500,000 MAR; a $5 base charge per connection on paid plans from January 2026; paid per-MAR rates in its Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026) (Standard first tier $495 per million MAR, version 10, effective February 1, 2026)

Fivetran counts Monthly Active Rows (MAR), meaning the rows changed in a month, per connection.

Its database connectors use each source's own CDC feature (MySQL and MariaDB binlog, SQL Server CDC and Change Tracking, MongoDB change streams, PostgreSQL logical replication) or a proprietary method (database connector docs). Its proprietary Teleport Sync can force a full table re-sync if large parts of a table change.

What's good

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 best change data capture tools, one by one > Managed or vendor-run (part 4)
text:
- It runs the pipeline for you, with 700+ connectors (checked Oct 2026).
- Managed Data Lake Service writes Iceberg to S3, Azure Data Lake Storage and Google Cloud Storage, and Fivetran says it handles the table maintenance (we did not test that).
- Per its database connector docs (checked Oct 2026), database connectors sync new and modified data every 15 minutes by default, apply changes to the destination in batches with a merge (upsert and insert), and most initial syncs finish within a day.
- For the Iceberg service, Fivetran says snapshots older than the retention period are deleted once a day (the last 2 snapshots are always kept), and orphan files are moved to an `orphans` folder on the second and fourth Saturdays of each month (docs (checked Oct 2026)). We did not test this.
- A row is counted once per month even if it syncs several times, and a row deleted twice in a month is counted once (pricing update).

Where it falls short

- The Iceberg service does not support position deletes (docs), and deleted rows count as paid MAR from January 2026 (pricing update (checked Oct 2026)).
- The billing docs (checked Oct 2026) set a $5 minimum charge per connection on monthly pay-as-you-go (for usage between 1 and 1 million MAR) and a $12,000 minimum on annual contracts.
- Per the same page (checked Oct 2026), Oracle, Oracle RAC, Oracle RDS, SAP ERP on HANA and Db2 for LUW (Beta) database sources can be synced only on the Enterprise or Business Critical plans.
- Expired change logs require a full source re-sync, and schema changes in the source are the most common trigger of a full table re-sync (database connector docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- On AWS, the Iceberg service does not support the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, Glacier Deep Archive and Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers, and AWS Glue Catalog supports only one table per schema and table name combination in a Region (docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- Iceberg does not allow columns named `_deleted`, `_file`, `_partition`, `_pos`, `_spec_id`, `file_path`, `pos` or `row`, so Fivetran prefixes such names with a hash symbol (#) (docs (checked Oct 2026)).

**7. Artie: best for managed CDC with a published monthly plan**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based
- Price: Free to 1M rows a month and 2 pipelines; Growth from $500 a month billed annually; Enterprise custom (Artie pricing (checked Oct 2026))

text:
**8. Striim: best for Oracle-heavy streaming**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based
- Price: Developer tier free up to 25 million events a month; Cloud and Platform say "contact us" (Striim pricing page (checked Oct 2026))

For Oracle, Striim gives you two readers, one using LogMiner and one called OJet. Both read Oracle 11g and higher, including Oracle clusters (Oracle CDC docs (checked Oct 2026)).

What's good

- Its docs describe two Oracle readers, and its Iceberg Writer has write modes of merge and append-only with schema evolution.
- The Oracle CDC docs (checked Oct 2026) position the LogMiner-based Oracle Reader for 20 GB to 80 GB of CDC data per hour and OJet for high-volume cases of 150+ GB per hour. Both are listed as supporting Oracle 26ai.
- Per the same Oracle CDC page, its GG Trail Reader can read existing Oracle GoldenGate trail files.
- The S3 Tables writer supports APPENDONLY and MERGE modes, with an Optimized Merge option for partial-image CDC, and works with either the catalog built into S3 Tables or AWS Glue.

Where it falls short

- The Iceberg Writer says the only supported data lake in this release is Google Cloud Storage. It also needs a Spark compute service and a catalog, and you must create partitioned tables by hand. That said, Striim also documents a separate S3 Tables writer (checked Oct 2026).
- The Iceberg Writer (checked Oct 2026) needs Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Dataproc) and a Lakehouse, Nessie or Polaris catalog. A Hadoop catalog on GCS is supported but recommended only for development and testing.
- The Iceberg Writer (checked Oct 2026) writes time data types as strings, and it recovers with at-least-once processing.
- The S3 Tables writer (checked Oct 2026) uses Amazon EMR as its compute engine, and S3 Tables requires lowercase table, namespace and column names, which breaks wildcard mappings against sources with uppercase identifiers.

**9. Qlik Replicate: best for older enterprise and mainframe sources**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based
- Price: Capacity bands by data volume and job runs, no list prices (Qlik pricing page (checked Oct 2026))

On Talend Cloud, log-based CDC starts at the Standard edition and the Starter edition has none. Mainframe sources appear in the Enterprise edition (Qlik pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).

What's good

- Mainframe sources, listed in its Enterprise edition on the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Qlik's pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists Open Lakehouse, with ingestion and adaptive optimization for Apache Iceberg, in its Standard edition. We did not test it.
- The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists cloud, client-managed or hybrid deployment under the Standard edition, and the Premium edition adds ELT or ETL transformations.
- For Oracle, the Replicate docs describe reading redo logs with either Oracle LogMiner or Replicate Log Reader, with a separate limitations list for each.
- Qlik says usage is measured on data volume moved, number of job executions and execution duration, and customers can watch it on a self-serve telemetry dashboard (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).

Where it falls short

- Prices aren't published on Qlik's own pricing page (checked Oct 2026): each of the four editions shows a Contact Us button and no dollar figure.
- Iceberg comes mainly from the separate Open Lakehouse feature (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).
- For Oracle 21c, the docs say LogMiner is not supported, immutable tables and blockchain tables are not supported, and CDC is not supported if a schema, table or column name is longer than 30 characters (Oracle source limits (checked Oct 2026)).
- Capturing changes from a pluggable database (PDB) with LogMiner is not supported, capturing from several PDBs through the container database is not supported, and the docs advise against LogMiner on a RAC environment because of unpredictable behavior (Oracle source limits (checked Oct 2026)).

At a glance

- Price: Per processor or Named User Plus on premises (Oracle price list); OCI GoldenGate bills per OCPU (Oracle's compute unit) per minute (OCI billing docs (checked Oct 2026))

Oracle's FAQ says the Extract process captures changes from the source redo or transaction logs and writes them to a trail file. GoldenGate 26ai supports Oracle Database 19c to 26ai and later (FAQ (checked Oct 2026)).

What's good

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 best change data capture tools, one by one > Cloud-native services
text:
**11. AWS DMS: best for AWS-only migrations and replication**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based
- Price: Replication instance hours or Serverless DCU hours (a DCU is 2 GB of memory), plus storage (AWS DMS pricing); for example, dms.t3.medium lists at $0.0745 an hour in us-east-1, on-demand, Single-AZ (AWS price list (checked Oct 2026))

DMS reads Oracle with LogMiner or the binary reader, SQL Server with Microsoft's CDC or replication features, MySQL from row-based binary logs, PostgreSQL through logical replication slots, and MongoDB from the oplog (CDC methods).

What's good

- Tasks can do a full load and then CDC.
- AWS's pricing page lists three options (on-demand, serverless and Database Savings Plans), says you pay by the hour for the capacity you use, and says all data transfer into DMS is free (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).
- Each compute-optimized or memory-optimized instance type includes 100 GB of GP2 storage, and each burstable T2 or T3 type includes 50 GB (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).
- From DMS version 3.5.1, a CDC-only Oracle task started from an SCN or timestamp can use the `openTransactionWindow` setting to pick up open transactions (CDC page (checked Oct 2026)).
- For sign-ups after 15 July 2025, the Free Tier lets you choose between a Free Plan and a Paid Plan for DMS (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 best change data capture tools, one by one > Cloud-native services (part 2)
text:
- AWS's CDC page (checked Oct 2026) says DMS CDC is not real-time replication and has no latency guarantee.
- Apache Iceberg is not on the list of DMS targets (checked Oct 2026), which does include Amazon S3, so loading Iceberg is a separate step you build.
- Per the CDC page (checked Oct 2026), views can be migrated only with full-load-only tasks, because CDC-only and full load plus CDC tasks include only tables.
- The CDC start point is marked when the task is created and cannot be changed, and a PostgreSQL source does not support a custom CDC start time because PostgreSQL has no way to map a timestamp to an LSN (CDC page (checked Oct 2026)).
- For Oracle, starting a CDC task from an SCN or timestamp misses open transactions (those started before the start position and committed after it), unless you use the setting above (CDC page (checked Oct 2026)).
- AWS says bidirectional replication runs as two tasks, is not a full multi-master solution, and does not include conflict detection or resolution (checked Oct 2026). AWS suggests data validation on both tasks to find inconsistencies.

**12. Google Cloud Datastream: best for BigQuery on Google Cloud**

At a glance

- Method: Per-source, such as the MySQL binary log
- Price: Per GiB processed; backfill free for the first 500 GiB, then $0.40 per GiB (the pricing table says per month, a footnote on the same page says one-time per billing account); a free CDC tier of 100 GiB a month applies only to AlloyDB and Spanner sources (Datastream pricing page (checked Oct 2026))

Its sources include MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server and PostgreSQL. One thing to know before you read the price: Google warns that a "processed byte" can be 2 to 5 times larger than the real data (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).

What's good

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 best change data capture tools, one by one > Cloud-native services (part 3)
text:
- Its price is per GiB processed rather than per hour, and AlloyDB and Spanner sources get a free CDC tier (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).
- Usage is billed in per-byte increments, an idle stream does not incur any cost, and events that Datastream reads but does not write to the destination are not counted (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).
- CDC pricing is tiered, so the price per GB falls as your usage rises (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).
- Beyond the databases above, its sources page lists Spanner, MongoDB, Salesforce and several other application sources, some of them in Preview.
- Iceberg tables in BigQuery keep their data in customer-owned Cloud Storage buckets, in the Iceberg table format and Parquet file format (Iceberg destination docs).

Where it falls short

- The Iceberg destination (checked Oct 2026) is BigQuery-managed Iceberg tables in Cloud Storage, and Google says streaming to them is "supported only in the append-only write mode".
- In append-only mode the change type of every event is recorded as INSERT in the `datastream_metadata` column that Datastream adds to each table (Iceberg destination docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- Setup needs a Cloud Storage bucket, a BigQuery Cloud resource connection whose service account has the `storage.admin` permission on the bucket, and the bucket, BigQuery dataset and Datastream connection must all be in the same region (Iceberg destination docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- In the pricing page's worked example, CDC is $2.00 per GiB for the first 2,500 GiB and $1.50 per GiB after that, before BigQuery's own processing costs, which are charged separately (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Where does each tool land your data?
text:
"Does it support Iceberg?" is too loose a question. Ask which catalog (the service that tracks your Iceberg tables), which cloud, which write modes, and whether updates and deletes work.

Append-only output keeps every change as its own row, so the cleanup is on you: keep the latest row per key and drop the deleted keys.

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > So which one should you pick? > Which change data capture tool fits you?
text:
Question 1 of 5

Who should run the pipeline?

A free licence still has a bill: servers and people on call.

Open source or managed: what's the real cost?
Three of the twelve tools are open source under Apache 2.0: Debezium, Flink CDC and OLake Go. Airbyte's Elastic License 2.0 (checked Oct 2026) and Estuary's Business Source License 1.1 (checked Oct 2026) are source-available licences. Airbyte's bars providing the software to others as a managed service, and Estuary's bars using it for a "Data Processing Service", and its text says it is not an Open Source license.

A free licence is not a free pipeline. Debezium's Kafka mode needs a Kafka cluster, Flink CDC needs a Flink cluster, and someone has to be on call. Managed tools swap that work for a meter: Fivetran counts rows, Estuary gigabytes and instances, Airbyte credits and Datastream processed bytes.

Here is the maths on Estuary's Cloud plan: 50 GB a month through one capture and one destination is 2 connector instances. Estuary's docs bill data "into and out of Estuary", so 50 GB is counted twice. That is 100 GB x $0.50 = $50 for data, plus $200 for instances, so $250 a month (our arithmetic from the Estuary pricing page and docs (checked Oct 2026)).

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What to check before you commit
text:
These seven checks come from failure modes the vendors' own docs describe.

1. Exact database and version support.Qlik's docs (checked Oct 2026) say Oracle 21c cannot use LogMiner, only Qlik's own log reader. Artie lists Oracle and SQL Server log replication on Enterprise only (checked Oct 2026).

2. The initial snapshot. Most setups copy the existing rows first, then switch to changes. Debezium's PostgreSQL docs say that if the connector stops during a snapshot it starts a new one on restart, and Fivetran needs a full re-sync when you change database providers.

3. Delete handling. Timestamp-based CDC sees only soft deletes. Even log-based CDC has gaps: for MySQL, the Debezium FAQ says deletes caused by cascade delete rules are not in the binlog (checked Oct 2026).

4. Schema changes. Airbyte's Iceberg connector never rewrites data files, so it handles only some changes. Striim's Iceberg Writer writes time types as strings.

5. Latency. Ask what delay you'll really see.

6. Ordering and "at least once".Debezium's docs say it delivers at least once, so duplicates can appear after a failure, though events within a topic stay in order. Flink CDC's Iceberg sink and Striim's Iceberg Writer are also at least once, so use primary keys and upserts instead of blind appends.

7. What vendors say about delay.

| Tool | What its own pages say about delay |
| Artie | "Sub-minute latency, exactly-once delivery" on its pricing page (checked Oct 2026) |
| Airbyte | Syncs are scheduled; Standard runs at most hourly and Plus every 15 minutes ( limits (checked Oct 2026)) |

These are vendor claims, not our tests. AWS says DMS CDC has no latency guarantee (checked Oct 2026).

One more for PostgreSQL. Debezium's docs (checked Oct 2026) warn that WAL (write-ahead log) disk space can spike when a quiet captured database shares a server with a busy one. The replication slot (PostgreSQL's log bookmark for the tool) can't move, and the fix is a heartbeat setting.

title: Compare: Best Change Data Capture Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What to check before you commit > How to run a two-week trial
text:
Use the same test for every finalist. It is a checklist we suggest, not a result we measured.

- Seed rows 1, 2 and 3. Insert row 4, update row 2 twice and delete row 3.
- Add a column, then widen a number column from 32 to 64 bits.
- Stop the tool mid-run, then restart it. Every key should appear once.
- Expected result: rows 1, 2 (with its second update) and 4, no row 3, no duplicates. Append-only outputs, such as Datastream's, show every change as its own record.
- Read the bill after a week of real change volume.

Q1. What is the best change data capture tool?

It depends on who runs it and where your data has to land. Debezium suits Kafka teams, Fivetran and Artie suit teams who want a vendor to run it, and Striim, Qlik Replicate and GoldenGate suit large Oracle estates.

Q2. What are the best open source CDC tools?

Three tools here use Apache 2.0, including OLake Go. Airbyte Core (Elastic License 2.0) and Estuary (Business Source License 1.1) are close, but they use source-available licences that restrict hosted-service use (checked Oct 2026).

Q3. What is the difference between log-based and query-based CDC?

Log-based CDC reads the database's transaction log. Query-based CDC just runs queries on a schedule and needs a changed-at column, and Confluent says it handles only soft deletes.

Q4. Does CDC capture deletes?

Log-based CDC usually does, but there are exceptions. For MySQL, Debezium's FAQ says cascade deletes aren't in the binlog.

Q5. Which CDC tools can write Apache Iceberg?

The vendor pages document Iceberg output for Debezium Server, Flink CDC, Estuary, Airbyte, Fivetran, Artie, Striim, Qlik, GoldenGate and Datastream (checked Oct 2026). OLake Go writes Iceberg too (our docs). The AWS DMS target list does not include Iceberg (checked Oct 2026). The limits differ, though: Debezium's sink is community-maintained, GoldenGate's is documented in a separate guide, Datastream is append-only and Striim writes to Google Cloud Storage or Amazon S3 Tables (checked Oct 2026).

Q6. Is change data capture real time?

Not always. AWS says DMS CDC isn't real-time and has no latency guarantee (checked Oct 2026), and Airbyte syncs run on a schedule.

Q7. Do I need Kafka for CDC?

Not always. Debezium Server runs without Kafka, though Debezium in Kafka Connect mode needs it, so check which mode you mean.

title: Compare: 16 Best Data Integration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What data integration means, in plain words
text:
Data integration means getting data out of the systems where it's created, such as databases, apps like Salesforce and files, and putting it in a warehouse (a database built for reports) or a data lake (cheap file storage many tools can read).

ETL (extract, transform, load) reshapes data before it lands, and ELT (extract, load, transform) lands it first. Change data capture (CDC) reads a database's log of changes and sends only what changed.

title: Compare: 16 Best Data Integration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > How to choose
text:
Four questions, asked in order. Stop as soon as you're down to two or three tools.

- Who will run it? If nobody on your team can, look at the vendor-run tools. If you have engineers who will, add Airbyte Core, Meltano, dlt and OLake Go.
- What are the sources? Mostly SaaS apps? Look at Fivetran, Hevo or Airbyte. Databases that need fresh data point to Estuary, Qlik Talend Cloud or Fivetran Enterprise.
- Where must the data land? A warehouse is easy almost everywhere. Iceberg tables on your own catalog shrink the field to the second table above, and each tool there has limits.
- Can you price it? If the meter counts rows, events or credits, price your busiest month, not your average one. If the vendor won't print a rate, ask for a written quote that states your volume.

If your sources include databases, put three more questions to each vendor and ask them to point at a docs page:

- What happens if the change log is gone before the tool reads it? Databases keep change records for a limited time. Fivetran's SQL Server page says the default window is 3 days and recommends 7 (checked Oct 2026).
- Does it run continuously or on a schedule?Airbyte's CDC docs say syncs are scheduled, and Hevo's docs say streaming must be enabled through its sales team (checked Oct 2026).
- Which Iceberg features does the writer skip? Fivetran's Managed Data Lake Service page says it does not support position deletes for Iceberg tables (checked Oct 2026). Other tools list their own limits, so read the destination page before you sign.

title: Compare: 16 Best Data Integration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 16 best data integration tools > Vendor-run tools for databases and apps
text:
**1. Fivetran: best for SaaS sources and a hands-off setup**

At a glance

- Billing: monthly active rows (MAR) per connection
- Free option: Free plan up to 500,000 MAR

Fivetran runs pre-built connectors that copy data from apps, databases and files into a warehouse or lake. We did not test any of it.

Fivetran's billing docs say pay-as-you-go adds a $5 base charge to each connection that uses 1 to 1M rows, with a $12,000 minimum for annual contracts (checked Oct 2026). Per-row list rates are in its Service Consumption Table: Standard starts at $495 per million MAR. It then falls to $170 per extra million from 1 million MAR, before discounts (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- Its pricing page claims 700+ connectors and 200+ activation destinations (reverse ETL), with 15-minute syncs on Standard and 1-minute syncs on Enterprise (checked Oct 2026). We did not count the connectors or test the sync times, so ask for a trial on your own sources.
- Per its billing docs, the Free plan has all Standard features up to 500,000 connector MAR, 3,500 activation MAR and 5,000 model runs a month, and annual contracts carry a built-in 5% discount (checked Oct 2026).
- Its Service Consumption Table puts each connection on its own volume curve. Standard list rates run from $495 per million MAR for the smallest connections to $170 per million from 1M MAR, $58 from 4M and $19.70 from 16M, before discounts (checked Oct 2026).
- Its SQL Server page lists four incremental sync methods: change tracking, change data capture, Binary Log Reader and Teleport Sync. Teleport Sync compares row hashes between syncs instead of reading the transaction log, and the page suggests it when enabling change tracking or CDC is not feasible.
- Its Managed Data Lake Service docs say your data stays in your own cloud storage account (Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage or Google Cloud Storage), and that Fivetran always creates Iceberg table metadata and manages the catalogs and maintenance, with snapshot cleanup once a day.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: 16 Best Data Integration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 16 best data integration tools > Vendor-run tools for databases and apps (part 2)
text:
- Per its billing docs, Oracle, SAP and Db2 (Beta) database sources are only on Enterprise and Business Critical, so the free plan can't use them, and its High-Volume Agent connectors for Oracle and SQL Server are listed for those two plans as well (checked Oct 2026).
- The pricing page prints no per-row rate (the list rates are in the Service Consumption Table), and since January 1, 2026 deleted rows count as paid MAR, per Fivetran's pricing update (checked Oct 2026).
- The Service Consumption Table says you cannot combine MAR across connections for a better rate, so each connection pays its own base spend, such as the $500.00 the table lists at the 1M MAR tier on Standard (checked Oct 2026).
- On SQL Server, the same page gives a default CDC retention window of 3 days (7 recommended). With CDC on, column type changes carry over, but renamed columns, new tables and new columns do not, and new ones need a new CDC instance (checked Oct 2026).
- Its Managed Data Lake Service page lists no support for position deletes on Iceberg tables, and on AWS lakes none for the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, Glacier Deep Archive and Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers (docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- The same docs say orphan files are moved to an `orphans` folder on the second and fourth Saturday of each month, and that deleting or editing that folder can permanently damage your tables (checked Oct 2026).

**2. Airbyte: best for a big connector list you can self-host or rent**

At a glance

- Billing: credits on Cloud, nothing for Core
- Free option: Core is free; Cloud has a 14-day free trial

Airbyte is one product wearing several hats: Core (self-run), Cloud (Standard, Plus and Pro) and Enterprise Flex (hybrid). On its pricing page, Cloud has a 14-day free trial, Standard starts at $20 a month with 5 credits, and Plus starts at $189 a month for 40 credits. Pro and Enterprise Flex show "Custom" (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

title: Compare: 16 Best Data Integration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 16 best data integration tools > Vendor-run tools for databases and apps (part 3)
text:
- Core has no credit meter, so you pay for servers and staff time instead. Cloud is the rented option, billed in credits.
- Per its licence FAQ, anyone can use Airbyte free of charge and run it at scale on their own infrastructure, with "no limitations exist on volume, number of users, number of connections, etc." for open source users (checked Oct 2026).
- Its pricing page lists 700+ connectors on all four plans, with a maximum sync frequency of 1 hour on Standard, 15 minutes on Plus and 5 minutes on Pro and Enterprise Flex (checked Oct 2026).
- Its CDC docs list current support for Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, MongoDB, Oracle, SAP HANA and IBM Db2.
- Its S3 Data Lake docs say the connector writes Iceberg tables to S3 or S3-compatible storage through a REST, AWS Glue, Nessie or Polaris catalog, and its Append + Deduped mode is merge-on-read on the stream's primary keys.

Where it falls short

- Airbyte's CDC docs say "We do not treat CDC sources as infinite streaming sources", so syncs run on a schedule. Its sync schedules page lists hourly as the shortest, bar 15 minutes on Cloud Plus (checked Oct 2026).
- The same CDC docs say CDC incremental needs primary keys for most sources, changes made by TRUNCATE or ALTER do not appear in the logs and so not in the destination, and a refresh is required after you add a table to a CDC connection (checked Oct 2026).
- Core uses the Elastic License 2.0, which its licence FAQ says bars selling a hosted Airbyte service (checked Oct 2026).
- Its S3 Data Lake docs say the connector never rewrites existing Iceberg data files, so it handles only adding or removing a column, widening a column and changing the primary key. Objects and unions are written as serialized JSON strings (checked Oct 2026).
- The same S3 Data Lake page does not say who handles compaction or snapshot expiry, and it cautions that compaction running during a truncate refresh sync deletes files from the current generation and causes data loss (checked Oct 2026).
- It also warns (S3 Data Lake docs) that Snowflake does not recognize native Iceberg row-level deletes for tables in external catalogs such as Glue, so queries there return all versions of a record (checked Oct 2026).

**3. Hevo: best for a low entry price and a free plan**

At a glance

title: Compare: 16 Best Data Integration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 16 best data integration tools > Vendor-run tools for databases and apps (part 4)
text:
- Billing: events (each record inserted, updated or deleted)
- Free option: Free, up to 1M events a month and 5 users

Hevo is a managed service for ETL and ELT pipelines, and it's one of the few that shows entry prices up front. On its pricing page, Starter shows $265 a month billed annually, or $299 a month billed monthly, for 5M events. Professional shows $750 a month billed annually, or $849 a month billed monthly, for 20M events (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- Its pricing page shows a free plan (labelled "free forever for limited connectors") and entry prices up front. The 24/7 support and 170+ connector figures on the Starter card are Hevo's claims, which we did not test.
- Per its docs, log-based pipelines read BinLog (MySQL), logical replication (PostgreSQL), Streams (DynamoDB), change streams or OpLog (MongoDB), Change Tracking (SQL Server) and redo logs (Oracle).
- Its pricing page shows the Free plan with up to 5 users, and Starter adding up to 10 users, a dbt integration and SSH/SSL (checked Oct 2026).
- Its Snowflake Iceberg docs say the table data and metadata files are stored in your Amazon S3 bucket, and that external engines such as Spark and Trino can read the tables through the Horizon Iceberg REST Catalog API.

Where it falls short

- Hevo's docs say streaming pipelines must be enabled through its sales team and are not available for SQL Server or DynamoDB (checked Oct 2026).
- Its pricing page shows 1-hour scheduling on the Free and Starter plans, and "limited connectors" on Free against all connectors on Starter and above (checked Oct 2026).
- Usage above your plan's event quota is billed on-demand on top of the plan, and the page shows no rate for it (pricing FAQ) (checked Oct 2026).
- Its Iceberg option is Early Access and Snowflake-managed only, per its docs. It must be enabled through a Hevo account executive or Support, and needs a Snowflake account, warehouse and database, an S3 bucket with an IAM policy, and a Snowflake external volume (checked Oct 2026).
- The log-based docs list troubleshooting pages for "Pipeline failure due to BinLog expiry" (MySQL) and "Redo Log expiry" (Oracle), so log retention on your source matters (docs) (checked Oct 2026).

**4. Skyvia: best for small teams that want a no-code tool**

At a glance

- Billing: records per month
- Free option: Free plan, 10k records a month, once a day

title: Compare: 16 Best Data Integration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 16 best data integration tools > Vendor-run tools for databases and apps (part 5)
text:
Skyvia is a no-code cloud service from Devart, so you click rather than code. Its pricing page shows Basic at $79 a month with the annual toggle and $99 monthly (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- A low entry price and a no-code builder.

Where it falls short

- We found no Iceberg destination in its connectors docs.
- Per the pricing page, the Free and Basic plans run at most once a day and list simple mapping features, with advanced mapping starting at Standard (checked Oct 2026).
- Free allows 2 scheduled integrations and Basic 5, while Standard allows 50 (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).

At a glance

- Billing: replicated rows per month
- Free option: none, 14-day trial

Its home page says Stitch is now part of Qlik and tells new users to try Qlik Talend Cloud. Its pricing page shows Standard from $100 a month for 5M rows, Advanced at $1,500 a month billed annually, and Premium at $3,000 a month billed annually (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

title: Compare: 16 Best Data Integration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 16 best data integration tools > Vendor-run tools for databases and apps (part 6)
text:
- Its log-based replication docs name MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, SQL Server, Oracle and DynamoDB.
- Its pricing FAQ says you set the replication frequency for each integration, from minutes to hours, and every user can use cron-expression scheduling.
- The Standard card on the pricing page lists 5 to 300 million rows a month, 5 users and 7-day extraction log retention, and Premium lists 1 billion rows a month and 5 destinations (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- The home page says Stitch is now part of Qlik and points new users to Qlik Talend Cloud, and it publishes no end-of-life date.
- Per its log-based docs, log-based replication on PostgreSQL works only with a master instance, some cloud versions of the supported databases may not support it, and changes made by event types the database does not write to its log are not detected (checked Oct 2026).

At a glance

- Billing: $0.50 per GB plus connector instances
- Free option: 10 GB a month and 2 connector instances

Estuary captures data into collections and sends it on to destinations, with real-time and batch modes. The fee structure has a quirk. On the Cloud plan the first six connector instances are $100 a month each, then $50 each, according to its pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

title: Compare: 16 Best Data Integration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 16 best data integration tools > Vendor-run tools for databases and apps (part 7)
text:
- Its pricing page FAQ lists Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, Oracle and SQL Server among supported databases and says change capture streams changes in real time (checked Oct 2026).
- The same FAQ says a pipeline starts with a historical backfill and then switches to real-time CDC, and that you can disable or scope the backfill.

Where it falls short

- Its Iceberg connector (docs) runs Spark jobs on a compute system you configure, and the docs list an AWS EMR Serverless Spark application (release emr-7.7.0), an S3 bucket and dedicated IAM roles as prerequisites (checked Oct 2026).
- Each connector instance adds a monthly fee on top of the per-GB charge, and those fees add up (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- The Iceberg docs label the section for REST catalogs other than AWS Glue as Beta, and say only REST catalogs that use Amazon S3 storage are supported, with GCP and Azure planned (checked Oct 2026).
- The same Iceberg docs say nested types are not currently supported, and array and object fields are written as string columns (checked Oct 2026).
- Compaction through the Glue optimizer defaults to off, and Hard Delete is off by default, so deletes in the source stay as soft deletes unless you change it (Iceberg docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The Cloud plan lists standard support through community Slack and email, and custom SLA terms appear only in the Enterprise column (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).

**7. Integrate.io: best for a flat fee and visual pipelines**

At a glance

- Billing: flat fee, "unlimited data volumes" on the pricing page
- Free option: 14-day trial

title: Compare: 16 Best Data Integration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 16 best data integration tools > Vendor-run tools for databases and apps (part 8)
text:
Per its pricing page, Integrate.io sells ETL, ELT, CDC and reverse ETL (sending warehouse data back to apps). The page lists Core at $1,999 a month with a 60-second pipeline frequency, and the card shows only "/mo" with no billing period. title: Compare: 16 Best Data Integration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > FAQs
text:
Q1. What is data integration software?

Software that collects data from many systems and puts it in one place, such as a warehouse or a data lake.

Q2. Which data integration tools have a free plan?

Several. Fivetran has a free plan up to 500,000 MAR, Hevo up to 1M events, Estuary up to 10 GB, and Skyvia up to 10k records a month. Stitch has only a 14-day trial (checked Oct 2026).

Q3. Which tools are open source?

Meltano calls itself open source, and dlt and OLake Go use Apache 2.0 (OLake on GitHub). Airbyte Core uses the Elastic License 2.0, which its licence FAQ says does not let you sell a cloud service that gives users direct access to Airbyte.

Q4. Which data integration tool is the cheapest?

There's no single winner, because rows, events, credits, gigabytes and compute hours don't convert into each other. Price one real month on each vendor's meter.

Q5. Which tools can write Apache Iceberg tables?

Fivetran, Airbyte, Estuary, Informatica, Qlik Talend Cloud, AWS Glue, dlt, Azure Data Factory and OLake Go document Iceberg output, each with limits, and Hevo has it in Early Access. See the second table above.

Q6. Is data integration the same as ETL?

Not quite. ETL and ELT are two ways of doing data integration, which is the wider job of getting data from many systems into one place.

Q7. How much does a data integration tool cost a month?

It ranges from free plans to $12,000 a month for the dltHub platform (checked Oct 2026). Hevo Starter is $299 monthly for 5M events, while Qlik Talend Cloud and Matillion print no dollar rate (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Data Lake Tools in 2026, by Layer | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

Short version: there's no single best data lake tool, because a lake is built from layers and each layer has its own tools. Most teams start with an object store from their cloud (Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage or Google Cloud Storage). Then they add an open table format, and Apache Iceberg is the one most engines below document.

Last comes one query engine, such as Trino or Athena.

Would you rather have one vendor bundle those layers and send you one bill? Then look at Databricks, Snowflake, Dremio or Microsoft Fabric.

- A data lake is files plus the tools around them: storage, a table format, a query engine and governance.
- Storage is cheap. The tools on top set your bill.
- Open formats make switching easier, not free, because engines differ in what they can write.

Most "best data lake tools" lists throw a storage service, a file format and a full platform into one ranked table. This page sorts 15 tools by the job they do, so you can see what to combine and what each choice costs.

Prices were checked on October 8, 2026 against each vendor's own page. Plans change often, so confirm on the vendor's page before you decide.

title: Compare: Best Data Lake Tools in 2026, by Layer | OLake > What data lake tools are, in plain words
text:
A data lake holds raw data in its original form, usually as files on cheap cloud storage. The tools around it fall into six layers.

Object storage keeps the files, such as Amazon S3.

A table format makes a plain folder of files behave like a database table. It's a set of rules plus small metadata files, and it adds row changes, earlier versions and tracking of which files belong to the table. Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake and Apache Hudi are the three open ones.

A query engine reads the tables and answers questions in SQL. It doesn't store your data.

A catalog and governance layer lists the tables and controls who gets in. An ingestion tool copies data from your databases into the lake. A platform bundles several of these layers and sells them as one product.

title: Compare: Best Data Lake Tools in 2026, by Layer | OLake > How we picked
text:
A tool had to be maintained and publish documentation or pricing we could open. It also had to be one teams meet when building a lake on public cloud or open source.

We read each vendor's own pricing and documentation pages on October 8, 2026, and the page is named beside each claim. We link the pricing pages and the pages behind hard limits.

Licences come from each project's own site or GitHub repository, read the same day. This is a reading of documents, not a lab test: claims about speed, scale, ease or savings are the vendors' own.

Where a vendor hides its price, the text says "not published".

Apache Spark, Starburst, Cloudera and MinIO are left out because we didn't read a primary page for them. The order inside each group is not a ranking.
