title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > Ingestion tools: get your data into one place > 1. Fivetran: best for hands-off loading from many sources
text:
At a glance

- Price: Free up to 500,000 monthly active rows (MAR, the rows that change in a month); paid rates in its Service Consumption Table, not on the pricing page. Standard starts at $495 per million MAR plus a $5 base per connection, list price before discounts (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026)

Fivetran's pricing page lists 700+ connectors, 15-minute syncs on Standard and 1-minute syncs on Enterprise (checked Oct 2026). Fivetran says it runs the pipeline for you, a claim we did not test.

One 2026 change matters. Fivetran announced that its merger with dbt Labs closed on June 1, 2026, so a managed loader and a transform tool now share an owner. If you use both, ask whether pricing or packaging will change.

What's good

- The Free plan includes Standard plan features, with up to 500,000 monthly active rows free for connections, 3,500 for activations and 5,000 monthly model runs for transformations, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Standard lists unlimited users, 15-minute syncs, 700+ fully managed connectors and a dbt Core integration. Enterprise adds 1-minute syncs, custom roles, SCIM and a Hybrid deployment option, and Business Critical adds customer-managed encryption keys and PCI DSS Level 1 certification, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- For database sources, its docs say it captures changes with the source's native change data capture mechanism or a Fivetran proprietary method, depending on the database. They also say database connectors sync new and modified data every 15 minutes by default, per the database connector docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Each connection is billed on its own volume curve, so the per-row rate falls as one connection grows. On Standard it goes from $495 per million rows at the start to $170 per million past 1M rows and $58 per million past 4M, per the Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026).
- Transformations get 5,000 model runs a month free, then $0.01 per run up to 30,000, $0.007 up to 100,000 and $0.002 beyond that, per the Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > Ingestion tools: get your data into one place > 1. Fivetran: best for hands-off loading from many sources (part 2)
text:
- Paid list rates live in a separate table, and each connection has its own curve, so you need rows per connection to predict a bill. The table also says you cannot combine rows across connections to get a better rate (checked Oct 2026).
- Our read: the $5 base per connection is the easiest line to miss, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026). By the consumption table formula, 20 connections of 2,000 rows each come to $119.80 a month (our arithmetic).
- Deleted rows also count as paid rows: the pricing page counts updates as modifications to existing rows in your destination, including deletes (checked Oct 2026).
- Teleport Sync is its option when you cannot or do not want to give Fivetran access to your database's change logs. The docs say that if you update large portions of a table between syncs it may be unable to find the changes, and the connection then re-syncs the entire table, per the database connector docs (checked Oct 2026).
- The pricing page calls Oracle and High-Volume Agent connectors "enterprise database connectors", and the Enterprise plan card lists them where Standard lists plain database connectors, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > Ingestion tools: get your data into one place > 2. Airbyte: best for a long connector list with a free self-hosted core
text:
At a glance

- Price: Core is free; Cloud Standard $20 a month with 5 credits and $5 per extra credit; Plus from $189 for 40 credits (Airbyte release notes, September 15, 2026) (checked Oct 2026)

Airbyte's docs say it has over 600 pre-built connectors, so check the current status of the connector you actually need (checked Oct 2026).

Its CDC (change data capture) docs describe log-based replication, but they also say syncs are scheduled and CDC sources aren't treated as infinite streams.

What's good

- Per its docs, you can self-host Core or pay for the cloud, and build connectors with a no-code builder or a Python kit. We did not test how well any of these work (checked Oct 2026).
- Plus runs from 40 credits for $189 ($4.75 a credit) up to 2,000 credits for $4,999, and overage credits fall from $5 to $2.50 on the top tier. All Plus plans include 15-minute syncs, two workspaces, single sign-on and premium support, per the release notes (checked Oct 2026).
- Unused Cloud credits now roll over for 3 months, up from 2, and Cloud free trials last 14 days, per the release notes (checked Oct 2026).
- Its CDC docs list Postgres, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, MongoDB, Oracle, SAP HANA and IBM Db2 under current support. They name no plan or connector support level for Oracle, SAP HANA or Db2, per Airbyte's CDC docs (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > Ingestion tools: get your data into one place > 2. Airbyte: best for a long connector list with a free self-hosted core (part 2)
text:
- It isn't a continuous streaming tool: CDC syncs are launched on a sync interval, and the CDC docs say "We do not treat CDC sources as infinite streaming sources." (checked Oct 2026)
- For most sources, CDC incremental sync works only for tables with primary keys, and a refresh is required after any new table or collection is added to a CDC connection, per the CDC docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Changes made by `TRUNCATE` or `ALTER` won't appear in the logs, so they don't reach the destination, per the CDC docs (checked Oct 2026).
- On Cloud Standard, scheduled or cron syncs can run at most every 60 minutes and an organization gets 1 workspace; Plus allows every 15 minutes, per Airbyte's Cloud limits docs (checked Oct 2026). SSO is no longer available on Standard, except for existing users who keep their plan, per Airbyte's Cloud release notes (checked Oct 2026).
- Standard got dearer in September 2026: the base price rose from $10 to $20 a month, free credits from 4 to 5 and extra credits from $2.50 to $5.00, per the release notes (checked Oct 2026).
- The core uses the Elastic License 2.0, and Airbyte's license FAQ says it stops you providing the products to others as a managed service (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > Ingestion tools: get your data into one place > 3. Hevo: best for small teams that want no-code pipelines into a warehouse
text:
At a glance

- Price: Free up to 1M events a month (each insert, update or delete in the destination is one event); Starter $265 a month on annual billing, or $299 monthly, from 5M events, per the Hevo pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Hevo's pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists 170+ connectors. Streaming pipelines show up on the custom Business Critical card, and its comparison table also lists them for Professional.

What's good

- Its free plan lets you try it with real data before you pay, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- The Free plan is $0 forever with up to 1M events a month and up to 5 users. Starter adds up to 10 users, 170+ connectors, a dbt integration and SSH/SSL, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Professional is $849 a month, or $750 on annual billing, from 20M events, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Its docs list the log read for each log-based source: BinLog for MySQL, logical replication for PostgreSQL, Streams for DynamoDB, Change Streams or OpLog for MongoDB, Change Tracking for SQL Server and Redo Logs for Oracle, per Hevo's log-based pipelines docs.

Where it falls short

- Every update is an event, so busy tables eat a quota fast. The pricing page counts each insert, update or delete in the destination as one event (checked Oct 2026).
- Usage above your plan's quota is on-demand and charged on top of the plan, and the page shows no rate for it, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Its docs say streaming pipelines cover those log-based sources except SQL Server and DynamoDB, and you must contact Hevo Sales to enable them, per Hevo's log-based pipelines docs (checked Oct 2026).
- The comparison table gives a 1-hour sync frequency on Free and Starter, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Its connector list is also smaller than Fivetran's or Airbyte's: Hevo lists 170+, Fivetran 700+ and Airbyte's docs over 600 (checked Oct 2026).
- The Free card says "Free forever for limited connectors", while all available connectors start at Starter, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > Ingestion tools: get your data into one place > 4. OLake Go: best for copying Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB or SQL Server into Iceberg
text:
At a glance

- Price: Open source under Apache 2.0; you run it on your own infrastructure with Docker, Helm on Kubernetes or the OLake UI

OLake Go copies PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, MongoDB and SQL Server with a full load plus change data capture, and writes Apache Iceberg tables or Parquet files on storage you control. Oracle, Db2, S3 and Kafka also work as sources, without database change capture.

What's good

- One tool does the first load and then the change capture, with Full Refresh, Full Refresh + Incremental, Full Refresh + CDC and CDC Only sync modes (docs).
- It writes Iceberg tables to catalogs such as AWS Glue, with eleven catalog types listed on the catalog compatibility page.
- Those catalogs include Snowflake Horizon (OLake Go v0.11.0 and later), so OLake Go can create Iceberg tables in a Snowflake database. They also include BigLake for Google Cloud and Unity Catalog for Databricks.
- Engines such as Athena, Spark, Flink and Trino can read the Iceberg tables it writes (query engine compatibility).
- Syncs are stateful and resumable: after a crash, a network failure or a pause they resume from the last checkpoint instead of starting over (docs).
- Parallel chunking splits large tables into chunks that are read in parallel, in the Full Refresh, Full Refresh + CDC and Full Refresh + Incremental modes (docs).
- Schema discovery runs at the start of every sync, and a new source column is added to the Iceberg schema automatically when Sync new columns automatically is on (schema evolution docs).
- Jobs run on a schedule, from every minute to a cron expression you write (job settings docs).
- OLake Fusion, a companion product, compacts the Iceberg tables OLake Go writes (Fusion docs).

title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > Ingestion tools: get your data into one place > 5. Debezium: best for engineers who need every database change as an event
text:
At a glance

- Price: Free; you run it yourself; you pay for servers and staff

Its FAQ says Debezium records all row-level changes committed to each database table, so applications can react to insert, update and delete events, though after a failure they can see an event more than once. The connector index lists eight main source connectors, including PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, SQL Server and Oracle.

What's good

- It's free, and its docs describe delay in the millisecond range for MySQL and PostgreSQL. That is the project's own claim, so test it on your own load, per Debezium's features page (checked Oct 2026).
- The connector index lists eight main source connectors: MongoDB, MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2 and Cassandra. Seven more are marked incubating: Vitess, Spanner, Informix, CockroachDB, YashanDB, Ingres and Milvus, per Debezium's connector index.
- Beyond Kafka Connect, the same docs list Debezium Server, a Debezium Operator, a Debezium Management Platform and guides for running on Kubernetes and OpenShift, per the connector index.
- The FAQ says all events within a topic are totally ordered, and that even if events are duplicated during failures the end result after applying them all stays the same, per the FAQ.
- The FAQ also says Debezium connectors do not store any information inside the upstream databases, per the FAQ.

Where it falls short

- It captures changes and nothing more. You still need a place to send them, a way to run it and someone to keep it healthy.
- The FAQ says consumers see every event exactly once only when systems run nominally or shut down gracefully; when things go wrong they can see events at least once, so the destination has to cope with repeats, per the FAQ (checked Oct 2026).
- Running a connector may place additional load on the source database, per the FAQ (checked Oct 2026).
- On MySQL, the FAQ says delete events can be missing when `CASCADE DELETE` statements are used, because those deletions are not part of the binlog, per the FAQ (checked Oct 2026).
- On Amazon RDS for MySQL, `log_bin` is managed by AWS and off by default, and the FAQ's fix is to turn on read replicas or automated backups, per the FAQ (checked Oct 2026).
- Incubating connectors are released for preview and are subject to changes that may not always be backward compatible, per the connector index (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > Streaming tools: react to each change as it happens > 6. Apache Kafka: best for moving event streams between many systems
text:
At a glance

- Price: Free; managed Kafka is priced by each vendor

Kafka's own introduction calls it an event streaming platform that publishes, stores and processes streams of events. Its Kafka Connect part continuously imports and exports data from systems such as relational databases.

What's good

- It's free, and its docs say it stores streams of events durably, which we did not test (checked Oct 2026).
- Events are not deleted after consumption, so a topic can be read as often as needed. How long they are kept is a per-topic setting, per the Kafka intro (checked Oct 2026).
- Any consumer of a topic-partition reads that partition's events in the order they were written, and a common production setting is a replication factor of `3`, meaning three copies of the data, per the Kafka intro (checked Oct 2026).
- It can run on bare-metal hardware, virtual machines and containers, on-premises or in the cloud, and you can self-manage it or use fully managed services from a variety of vendors, per the Kafka intro.
- Its `4.2` design docs say it supports exactly-once delivery in Kafka Streams, and in the transactional producer paired with a read-committed consumer. The producer also has an idempotent delivery option, so resending does not create duplicate log entries, per Kafka's design docs (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- It's a platform you run, and you build the pipeline on top of it. Kafka itself doesn't reshape warehouse tables, and it needs connectors at both ends.
- The intro describes capture as something a connector does, for example a PostgreSQL connector capturing every change to a set of tables. It describes no Iceberg writer (checked Oct 2026).
- The intro says the Kafka community provides hundreds of ready-to-use connectors, and the Apache project publishes no exact count, per the Kafka intro (checked Oct 2026).
- Exactly-once is not the default: the `4.2`design docs say Kafka guarantees at-least-once delivery by default (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > Streaming tools: react to each change as it happens > 7. Apache Flink: best for reshaping streams as they flow
text:
At a glance

- Price: Free; you pay for servers and staff

Flink's site describes it as "stateful computations over data streams", and it shows `2.3` as the current stable release (checked Oct 2026). The Apache Iceberg docs say the Flink sink for Iceberg guarantees exactly-once semantics.

What's good

- Its site describes stateful computations on streams and, per the Iceberg docs, it can write batch and streaming data to Iceberg tables. We did not test either.
- The Flink home page lists low latency, high throughput and in-memory computing as features.
- The Iceberg docs say it supports `UPSERT` based on the primary key when writing to a `v2` table, per the Iceberg Flink writes.
- The same docs say `IcebergSink` can run table maintenance after each commit: compacting small data files, expiring old snapshots and removing orphan files, so a separate maintenance job is not required, per the Iceberg Flink writes.

Where it falls short

- It's a framework you program and operate, and it's overkill for hourly batch jobs.
- Streaming jobs do not support `INSERT OVERWRITE`; overwrite works in batch jobs, per the Iceberg Flink writes (checked Oct 2026).
- `UPSERT` needs the `v2` table format and a primary key or identifier fields, and `OVERWRITE` and `UPSERT` cannot be enabled at the same time, per the Iceberg Flink writes (checked Oct 2026).
- The Iceberg docs call the newer `SinkV2`-based `IcebergSink` "currently an experimental feature so use it with caution", per the Iceberg Flink writes (checked Oct 2026).
- Iceberg commits happen after a successful Flink checkpoint, in the `notifyCheckpointComplete` callback, so the job needs checkpointing set up, per the Iceberg Flink writes (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > All-in-one cloud services: several jobs, one vendor > 8. Matillion: best for teams that load and transform inside a cloud warehouse
text:
At a glance

- Price: Credits used by task hours; the pricing page shows no dollar price, per the Matillion pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Matillion's pricing page lists Developer, Teams and Scale editions. Its credit terms charge 1 credit per task hour for scheduling work and transformation 3 credits per task hour (checked Oct 2026).

Matillion's own comparison blog says Maia generates native SQL that runs inside Snowflake, Databricks or AWS Redshift.

What's good

- Matillion's pages describe one product for loading, transforming and scheduling, so there are fewer parts to join. We did not test it.
- Developer lists 1 developer user, unlimited projects, pre-built connectors, a low-code canvas with SQL/Python and a built-in Git repository. title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > How to choose, in five questions
text:
Answer these in order. The first answer usually knocks out half the list.

- Which job is missing? If data isn't landing anywhere yet, start with the ingestion group. If it lands but it's messy, look at dbt. If someone runs steps by hand, look at the schedulers.
- How fast must changes show up? Hourly or slower points to a loader or a batch tool. Seconds points to Debezium, Kafka and Flink, which you run yourself.
- Who runs it? If nobody wants to touch servers, choose a managed tool or a cloud bundle. If you have engineers, free software drops the licence bill and adds the work.
- Which cloud are you on? Inside AWS or Azure, the bundles save you from joining parts.
- How does the tool count? Rows, events, credits, models and compute hours grow in different ways. Work out your own number before you sign anything.

title: Compare: Best Data Pipeline Tools in 2026, by Job | OLake > Building a pipeline from parts: a decision table > Which pipeline tool fits you?
text:
Question 1 of 5

Which job in your pipeline is missing?

A pipeline has four jobs: ingest, store, transform and orchestrate. Most tools only do one.

FAQs
Q1. What is a data pipeline tool?

Software that does one or more jobs in a pipeline: copying data in, storing it, reshaping it or running the steps in order. Most tools do just one job, so a full pipeline usually combines several.

Q2. Is Airflow a data pipeline tool?

Not really. Airflow is a scheduler. It starts and watches the steps but doesn't copy your data, so you pair it with a loader such as Airbyte or code that you write.

Q3. Do I need both Fivetran or Airbyte and dbt?

Often, yes. dbt transforms data already in your warehouse, so it needs a loader to get the data in.

Q4. Which of these tools are free?

Debezium, Kafka, Flink and Airflow are free open-source projects, the dbt Core code is free under Apache 2.0, and Airbyte Core is free under the Elastic License 2.0 (checked Oct 2026). OLake Go is open source under Apache 2.0 and you run it on your own infrastructure. Fivetran, Hevo, dbt and Prefect have free plans with limits. Running free software yourself still means paying for servers and staff.

Q5. Which tools handle streaming?

Kafka and Flink are built for streams, and Debezium sends each database change as an event. Airflow and Azure Data Factory pipelines are batch tools, and Airbyte's CDC docs say syncs are scheduled. Hevo lists streaming pipelines on its Professional and Business Critical plans, and its docs say you must contact Hevo Sales to enable them (checked Oct 2026).

Q6. What is the cheapest way to start?

Use free plans or free software and watch the ceilings: Hevo's 1M free events, dbt's 3,000 free models and Prefect's 5 free deployments. Paid starts are Airbyte Cloud at $20 a month, Dagster Solo at $10 a month and dbt Starter at $100 per user a month (checked Oct 2026).

Q7. Can one tool do everything?

Bundles come closest. Matillion, AWS Glue and Azure Data Factory each cover loading, transforming and scheduling within one vendor's cloud, at the cost of some choice.

Q8. What does it cost to run Airflow myself or on a managed host?

The software is free, but servers and staff aren't. Amazon's managed Airflow lists $0.49 an hour for a Small environment in US East (N. Virginia), about $357.70 for a 730-hour month before extra workers (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

"Data quality tool" means three different jobs.

If you want rules you write and run in a pipeline, start free with Great Expectations, Soda Core, dbt tests, Deequ or OpenMetadata (a free data catalog with quality tests). If you want something to watch production tables for surprises, look at Elementary (free if you use dbt) or quote-based platforms such as Monte Carlo and Anomalo. For profiling, cleansing and governance in an enterprise suite, look at Informatica Data Quality and Ataccama ONE (a data quality platform).

Most paid platforms don't publish a price. Ask for a written quote and a trial before you get attached.

- Free options exist. Great Expectations Core, Deequ and Elementary's open-source tool use the Apache 2.0 licence (Great Expectations, Deequ, Elementary) (checked Oct 2026). Soda Core uses the Elastic License 2.0 (checked Oct 2026), not Apache or MIT, so read it before you build on it.
- Fit beats features. dbt tests and Elementary's open-source tool only help if you already use dbt. Deequ needs Apache Spark (a big-data engine), so no Spark, no Deequ.

IBM (International Business Machines) defines data quality as how well a dataset meets criteria for accuracy, completeness, validity, consistency, uniqueness, timeliness and fitness for purpose, according to IBM's data quality topic page. A data quality tool checks those things for you, so a wrong number gets caught before it reaches a report. Last reviewed October 2026.

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What a data quality tool actually does
text:
The simplest check is a rule, such as every order having a unique ID. dbt's documentation on data tests uses that very example, where the `order_id` column in the `orders` model should be unique.

Rules catch the problems you thought of. Observability tools go after the ones you didn't. They record facts about each table, such as how many rows arrived and how fresh the data is, and flag anything that breaks the usual pattern.

The tool turns each rule into a query that hunts for bad rows, and you get pass or fail.

Original diagram based on dbt's data test documentation, October 2026.

Cleansing is the third job: finding duplicate records, fixing formats and matching names, which the big enterprise suites handle. Data catalogs (a searchable list of your data) are now adding quality checks too.

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 9 data quality tools, one by one > 1. Great Expectations: rules written in Python
text:
At a glance: A Python library for data tests. Its paid cloud service is no longer publicly available.

Great Expectations (GX) is built around the Expectation, which its docs describe as a verifiable assertion about data. You connect to data, write Expectations, group them into suites and run them. Its docs mention SQL tables and Spark dataframes (tables held in Python memory) as data to validate.

GX Core is free under the Apache 2.0 licence (checked Oct 2026). On 6 May 2026 Great Expectations posted an update saying "GX Cloud will no longer be publicly available beginning June 1."

The same post says "Fivetran will become the new steward of the Great Expectations open source community and the GX Core project." Under the planned transition, it adds, GX Core will continue as an open source, community-driven project.

Where it fits

- Rules live in code, so you can review and version them like anything else you write.
- It can validate SQL tables and Spark dataframes, so one tool can check several kinds of data.
- In production, a Checkpoint runs your validations, and Actions can send the results to email, Slack or Microsoft Teams, per the GX Core overview.
- It writes Data Docs, human-readable pages that host your Expectation Suites and Validation Results (GX Core overview).
- One Expectation Suite can be applied to different Batches, so the same checks can cover several tables or time slices (GX Core overview).

Where it falls short

- GX Cloud is no longer publicly available from 1 June 2026, per GX's own May 2026 post (checked Oct 2026), so GX Core is the way in.
- Stewardship of GX Core moves to Fivetran under the planned transition (same post).
- You write the rules yourself. It checks data against them, and that's all. It does not move, store or catalog data.
- GX Core is a Python library, so someone has to write Python to set up the connections, Expectations and runs (GX Core overview).
- The docs' scheduled-testing example has an orchestrator trigger the run, so plan to bring your own scheduler (GX Core overview).

Pick something else if you want the tool to learn normal patterns for you. Elementary or Monte Carlo is the better place to look.

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 9 data quality tools, one by one > 2. Soda: data contracts and a free hosted tier
text:
At a glance: A data quality platform whose engine, Soda Core, runs checks written in YAML (a simple text format).

On its GitHub page, Soda describes Soda Core as a data quality and data contract verification engine.

A data contract is a written agreement about what a dataset must look like, including its columns, types and value ranges. Soda's docs split the work into testing during development and observability in production.

Soda shows its prices openly. The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists a Free plan at $0 a month, a Team plan at $750 a month, and Enterprise at custom pricing. The catch: the price of one Soda Processing Unit (SPU) is not shown.

| Plan | Price | What the page lists |
| Free | $0 per month | Free SPUs, pipeline testing, metrics observability, alerting and ticketing integrations, no credit card required |
| Team | $750 per month | All Free features, unlimited users, pay as you go for additional SPUs, catalog integrations, add-ons |
| Enterprise | Custom pricing | All Team features, collaborative data contracts, no-code interface, AI-powered data quality features, audit logs, custom roles and RBAC, private deployment, SSO, premium support, annual billing and volume discounts |

Source: Soda pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

Where it fits

- A published price for the paid Team plan. Several vendors in this category show none.
- Soda Core supports many sources, including PostgreSQL, Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and DuckDB, per its GitHub page.
- The Free plan at $0 includes pipeline testing, metrics observability and alerting integrations, with no credit card required (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).
- You can run it three ways: Soda Core in your pipelines, a Soda-hosted Runner, or a Self-hosted Runner in your own Kubernetes environment, where the docs say data stays within your network (deployment options docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Its integrations docs list Slack, Microsoft Teams, Jira, ServiceNow and webhook connections for alerts and tickets (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 9 data quality tools, one by one > 2. Soda: data contracts and a free hosted tier (part 2)
text:
- Soda's deployment options docs list the Python libraries (Soda Core) with no observability features, and say a Soda Runner is required for them (checked Oct 2026).
- Its licence file is the Elastic License 2.0 (checked Oct 2026), not Apache or MIT. The deployment options docs call the Python library open source, but have a lawyer read the licence before you build a product on it.
- Features such as SSO (single sign-on), audit logs and private deployment appear under Enterprise on the live pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- The hosted and self-hosted Runners cannot scan in-memory sources such as Spark or DataFrames. Soda Core is the option for those (deployment options docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The Self-hosted Runner needs Kubernetes expertise, per the same docs page (checked Oct 2026).
- Soda Core `v4` renamed its packages (for example `soda-postgres`), and legacy `v3` packages are named `soda-core-{data source}`, so check which version a guide or install command targets (GitHub) (checked Oct 2026).

Pick something else if you only need tests and already use dbt. dbt's free open-source distribution already includes its built-in tests.

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 9 data quality tools, one by one > 3. dbt tests: data already transformed with dbt
text:
At a glance: Tests built into dbt, a tool that transforms warehouse data with SQL (Structured Query Language).

dbt's docs describe data tests as assertions you make about your models and other resources. Each test is a query that returns the bad rows, and the test passes when zero rows come back. dbt ships four generic tests: `unique`, `not_null`, `accepted_values` and `relationships`.

dbt Core is free under Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026). The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists a free Developer plan (1 seat, `3,000` successful models built a month) and a Starter plan at $100 per user a month.

Fivetran announced in a press release the completion of its merger with dbt Labs on June 1, 2026.

dbt's docs show an `orders` example: a short block of YAML covers the order ID, the status values and the link to customers, and the `dbt test` command runs it all. The docs translate that YAML into four plain-English checks and say a test passes when zero rows are returned.

Where it fits

- No new tool to learn if you already use dbt.
- Four common checks come built in, and you can write your own in SQL.
- Newer unit tests check your SQL logic on small made-up inputs before a model is built, from dbt version `1.8` (unit tests docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Singular tests are plain SQL: you write the exact query that returns the failing records (dbt data tests docs).
- Open-source packages such as `dbt-utils` and `dbt-expectations` add more generic tests (dbt data tests docs).
- The `error_if` and `warn_if` configs set custom failure thresholds for a test (dbt data tests docs).

Where it falls short

- Ordinary data tests only run after a model is built, according to dbt's own unit test docs (checked Oct 2026).
- It only tests what dbt manages. Data that never passes through dbt is invisible to it.
- Its tests return failing rows and pass on zero rows; the docs we read do not describe cleansing or learned alerts.
- Unit tests work on SQL models only, per the dbt unit test docs (checked Oct 2026).
- On paid plans, models that build successfully are counted even if the run later fails: a job of 100 models that fails after 51 counts 51 (dbt billing docs) (checked Oct 2026).

Pick something else if you don't use dbt. Great Expectations or Soda Core work without it.

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 9 data quality tools, one by one > 5. Deequ: very large data on Apache Spark
text:
At a glance: A free library from AWS (Amazon Web Services) Labs that runs "unit tests for data" on Spark.

The Deequ repository on GitHub describes a library built on Apache Spark, written in Scala, with a Python wrapper called PyDeequ. Its repository lists data profiling, anomaly detection over time and automatic constraint suggestion, and its rule language includes completeness and uniqueness checks.

Deequ uses Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026), and its latest release on GitHub, `2.1.0`, came out on 2026-09-16.

Where it fits

- Free, and built on Spark, an engine made for large datasets.
- It can suggest checks from the data, which helps when you have no idea where to start.
- A declarative rule language called DQDL is supported.
- It is designed for very large datasets: the README says "think billions of rows".
- It works on anything you can fit into a Spark dataframe, including CSV files, database tables, logs and flattened JSON (README).
- Computed metrics can be stored and queried with a `MetricsRepository`, and updated incrementally as data grows or partitions change (README).

Where it falls short

- You need a Spark setup and a matching Java version. Release `2.1.0` and later need Java `11`, and each release targets specific Spark versions, so check before you install (README) (checked Oct 2026).
- The repository says row-level checks in DQDL mode work only for certain rule types, and dataset-level rules such as `RowCount` and `Mean` are marked as skipped (checked Oct 2026).
- It's a library from AWS Labs, not an AWS managed service.
- The Deequ `2.x` table lists Spark `3.1` through `3.5`, and Spark `3.0` and earlier need a Deequ `1.x` release (README) (checked Oct 2026).
- It is a Scala library, and Python use goes through PyDeequ, a separate Python interface (README).

Pick something else if you have no Spark. Soda Core and Great Expectations are Python-based and do not need Spark.

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 9 data quality tools, one by one > 6. OpenMetadata: quality tests inside a free catalog
text:
At a glance: An open-source data catalog with data quality tests built in.

Per its docs, you can run tests at the table and column level, write no-code test cases from the screen and use a built-in profiler. Alerts fire when a test fails. Lineage (where data came from) and governance are covered too, all under the Apache 2.0 licence (checked Oct 2026).

Where it fits

- One free tool for the catalog, the tests and the alerts, with no licence fee.
- No-code tests let analysts add checks without writing any Python.
- Its GitHub README says it has 130+ connectors (checked Oct 2026).
- The docs say quality tests are supported for all of its supported database connectors, with alerts, a health dashboard and a resolution workflow for failures (docs).
- Tests can be set up in the UI or in a YAML config file, and you can write your own tests and test suites (docs).

Where it falls short

- You run and upgrade it yourself unless you use a managed offering. The docs' production options are Kubernetes, cloud-managed services or bare metal (docs).
- Collate, which sells managed OpenMetadata, posted about a free managed tier in June 2024 with a waitlist (Collate's blog post). We did not confirm it is open today (checked Oct 2026).
- It's a full catalog with lineage and governance as well as tests.
- Quality is one feature among several in its docs. A team that only wants tests may not need all of it.
- Its connectors page marks each connector `PROD` or `BETA`, and says a `BETA` connector may have limitations or missing features (checked Oct 2026).

Pick something else if you only need pipeline tests. Great Expectations or dbt tests are lighter to carry.

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 9 data quality tools, one by one > 7. Monte Carlo: broad production monitoring with a paid platform
text:
At a glance: A paid observability platform that monitors your tables and traces issues.

Monte Carlo's pricing page (checked Oct 2026) says all tiers include Agent Observability, ML Observability and Data Observability. Its platform page describes monitors, anomaly data and lineage that shows what a problem touches downstream.

The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists four tiers: Start, Scale, Enterprise and Business Critical. Start allows up to 10 users, up to `1,000` monitors and `10,000` API calls a day.

Customers "buy credits", and the cost per credit depends on the tier. No dollar figure is shown, and a free trial is not mentioned. So you're guessing until you talk to sales (checked Oct 2026).

Where it fits

- Higher tiers add unlimited users and more API calls, up to `100,000` a day.
- The Scale tier lists SSO, SCIM, self-hosted storage, PII filtering and audit logging (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).
- Integrations grow by tier: Scale adds lakes (Databricks, Hive, Glue, Azure Data Lake) and MySQL, Postgres and SQL Server, and Enterprise adds Oracle, SAP Hana, Teradata and Microsoft Fabric (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).
- Business Critical adds a Dedicated Instance and disaster recovery that rolls over to a different region (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).

Where it falls short

- Its pricing and platform pages show no open-source edition (checked Oct 2026).
- Vendor claims on its site, such as faster resolution, come without a published method, so we do not repeat them.
- Start lists Data Warehouse, BI and ETL integrations. Lake and database integrations are listed from Scale up (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).
- Support differs by tier: Start lists a 24-hour support SLA with self-guided onboarding, Scale 8+ hours and Enterprise 4+ hours (pricing page (checked Oct 2026)).

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Your first week with a free tool
text:
- Pick the five columns your reports lean on most. Think order IDs, dates and amounts.
- Add `unique` and `not_null` to every ID. One duplicated or empty ID can quietly double-count an order.
- Add `accepted_values` to status columns. A new, misspelled status then fails a test instead of silently vanishing from a chart.
- Add `relationships` between tables. It catches an order that points to a customer who doesn't exist.
- Send failures to one chat channel. A test nobody sees is just a file.

Run it for a week before you shop for anything bigger. The failing tests show which tables deserve a monitoring tool.

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Questions to ask a paid vendor
text:
Get the answers in writing.

- What is one credit, unit or table worth in dollars on my tier?

- Is there a trial or proof of concept on my own data?
- Which of my sources and warehouse are supported today, not on the roadmap?
- What happens to unused units at the end of the period?
- Can I export my rules and results if I leave?

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Where data quality fits in the pipeline
text:
Quality checks sit after data has been loaded, and sometimes after it's been transformed. The tools here don't copy data between systems; if your tables come from database replication, checks such as row counts compare a source against its copy.

Where OLake fits
OLake Go is an open-source extract-and-load tool with no transformation step. It reads Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB and SQL Server with change capture, Oracle, Db2 and S3 with full load and incremental sync, and Kafka topics. It writes Apache Iceberg tables or Parquet files, using any of the catalogs our docs list. Once the copy lands, a quality tool that can query those Iceberg tables through an engine such as Spark or Trino (see our engine list) can run checks such as a row count against the source. OLake Go writes Iceberg or Parquet, so the checks come from the tools above.

title: Compare: 9 Best Data Quality Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > FAQ
text:
Q1. What are data quality tools?

They check whether your data is accurate, complete, valid, consistent, unique and on time, per the criteria IBM lists. Some run rules you write, some watch for unusual changes, and some clean and match records.

Q2. What is the difference between data quality and data observability?

Quality tests check your data against rules a person writes. Observability tools record facts such as row counts and freshness, then alert you when a table drifts from its usual pattern.

Q3. Which data quality tools are free?

Great Expectations Core, Deequ, Elementary's open-source tool, OpenMetadata and dbt Core are free under the Apache 2.0 licence (see each tool's section for the licence link). Soda Core is free under the Elastic License 2.0 (checked Oct 2026). Soda also has a Free cloud plan at $0 (checked Oct 2026).

Q4. Do I need dbt to use a data quality tool?

No. dbt tests and Elementary's open-source tool need dbt, but Great Expectations, Soda Core, Deequ and OpenMetadata don't. Pick the dbt-based tools only if dbt already runs your transformations.

Q5. How much do data quality tools cost?

Few vendors publish prices. Soda lists $750 a month for Team (checked Oct 2026) and dbt lists $100 per user a month for Starter (checked Oct 2026). Monte Carlo, Informatica, Ataccama and Anomalo showed no dollar price on the pages we checked (Monte Carlo, Informatica, Ataccama, Anomalo) (checked Oct 2026).

Q6. Is Soda Core open source?

Soda's docs call it open source, but the LICENSE file in its repository is the Elastic License 2.0 (checked Oct 2026), not Apache 2.0 or MIT. Read its terms before you build a product on it.

Q7. Should a small team buy a paid platform?

Usually not at first. Start with a few rules on your most important columns using a free tool, and add monitoring once you have too many tables to watch by hand.

Q8. Where does OLake fit with data quality tools?

OLake Go is an extract-and-load tool that copies databases, Kafka topics and S3 files into Apache Iceberg tables or Parquet files. A quality tool that can query the Iceberg tables through an engine such as Spark or Trino can run its checks there, such as a row count against the source.

text:
Start with the job you need done. Most teams can begin today for $0 with dbt tests, Great Expectations Core, Soda Core or Elementary. Move to a paid platform only after you know which tables hurt most, and ask each vendor for a written price.

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

"Replication" means four different jobs. You might want a standby copy for failover, a copy for reports, a copy in a data lake, or a one-time move to a new database.

Start with your database's own replication for a standby or read copy.

Reports in a warehouse point to Fivetran, Estuary, Artie, Airbyte or Google Datastream.

Iceberg tables on storage you control point to Debezium Server or OLake Go.

Big Oracle estates point to Oracle GoldenGate, Qlik Replicate or Striim, and a move into AWS points to AWS Database Migration Service (DMS).

- Replication is NOT backup.PostgreSQL's docs say restoring a backup takes much longer than failing over to a standby.
- Two-way replication is hard.AWS DMS says its two-way mode has no conflict resolution, and Oracle GoldenGate's FAQ warns of update conflicts and loops.

Prices were checked in October 2026 against each vendor's own pages. Prices move, so confirm before you decide. Facts about the other vendors in this post come from their own pages and were not tested by us.

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What data replication means
text:
AWS defines data replication as copying data from one location to another to keep several synchronized copies. In this post, "source" is where the data starts and "target" is the copy.

| Job | What it does | Keeps copy in step? | Typical use |
| Replication | Copies data and keeps the copy current | Yes, continuously or on a schedule | Standby, reports, lake |
| Backup | Saves a point-in-time copy to restore from | No, only at the time of the backup | Recovery after loss or error |
| Migration | Moves data once to a new system | Only until cutover | Changing database or cloud |
| ETL (extract, transform, load) | Copies data and reshapes it on the way | Depends on the tool | Building clean reporting tables |

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What data replication means > Full copy, incremental copy and change data capture
text:
A full copy resends the whole table every run. An incremental copy asks only for rows changed since the last run, and that needs a "changed at" column that is updated on every edit.

Change data capture (CDC) reads the database's transaction log, which is the file where the database writes down every change in order. AWS says log-based detection is preferred for databases because it is efficient and captures changes with low latency.

A "changed at" column can miss rows that were deleted for good, since a deleted row leaves no timestamp behind.

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What data replication means > Synchronous vs asynchronous
text:
Synchronous means the source waits until the replicas confirm each write. AWS says this suits mission-critical data but is sensitive to network delay.

Asynchronous means the source does not wait, but PostgreSQL's docs say transactions not yet shipped are lost if the primary fails badly.

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What data replication means > One-way or two-way
text:
Most replication is one-way. The source takes the writes and the target is a read-only copy. Two-way replication lets both sides take writes, and that's where conflicts show up.

AWS DMS supports two-way replication on Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL and the two Aurora editions. Its docs are blunt about the limits. It is not a full multi-master solution, it does not include conflict detection or resolution, and it suits data that is operationally segregated between the two nodes.

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > How we picked these
text:
Tools here copy data out of a database, are maintained, and publish documentation we could open. We compared the copy method, sources, where the data lands, how it is run, and price, using each vendor's own pages in September and October 2026. We did not run the other tools, so this is a reading of documents, not a lab test.

Backup products and warehouse-only products are left out.
