title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Built into your database
text:
**1. Native database replication (PostgreSQL and MySQL): standby copies and read replicas**

At a glance

- Method: The database's own log, shipped to another server
- Price: Included in the database. You pay for the servers.

PostgreSQL's log-shipping standby is a second server that's ready to take over if the primary fails. MySQL's replication (8.4 reference manual) copies from a source to one or more replicas, and it is asynchronous by default.

Where it fits

- No extra product to buy or run. MySQL's replication manual lists scale-out reads, running backups on a replica and analytics on a replica as benefits.
- MySQL also offers semisynchronous replication, where a commit on the source blocks until at least one replica acknowledges it, and delayed replication, where a replica deliberately lags by at least a set time (MySQL 8.4 replication).
- MySQL can replicate all databases, selected databases or selected tables within a database, depending on the configuration (MySQL 8.4 replication).
- PostgreSQL supports physical replication (byte by byte) and logical replication (per object, keyed on the replication identity, usually a primary key) at the same time (PostgreSQL logical replication docs).
- A PostgreSQL standby can also answer read-only queries, in which case it is called a hot standby (warm standby docs).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Built into your database (part 2)
text:
- It copies between servers of the same database. PostgreSQL log shipping between different major release levels is in general not possible, and the hardware architecture must match, so a 32-bit to 64-bit copy will not work (warm standby docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- PostgreSQL's logical replication does not copy the database schema, DDL commands, sequence data or large objects, and it only replicates tables, so views and materialized views raise an error (PostgreSQL logical replication restrictions) (checked Oct 2026).
- An unread replication slot, the bookmark PostgreSQL keeps for a reader, keeps log files on disk and can fill storage. The docs say slots persist across crashes and know nothing about their consumers, and a slot that is no longer needed should be dropped (PostgreSQL logical decoding docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Log shipping is asynchronous: transactions not yet shipped are lost if the primary suffers a catastrophic failure (warm standby docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- MySQL replication is asynchronous by default, so a replica can trail the source, and replicas do not need to stay connected (MySQL 8.4 replication).

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Enterprise platforms
text:
**2. Oracle GoldenGate: Oracle estates and two-way setups**

At a glance

- Method: Reads redo or transaction logs, the database's record of changes
- Price: Per OCPU (Oracle's compute unit) on Oracle Cloud, metered by the minute, per the OCI billing page (checked Oct 2026). We do not quote an on-premises licence price.

Oracle's FAQ says GoldenGate captures, transforms and delivers transactional changes across systems in real time. You can run it in one-way, two-way and multi-directional setups.

Where it fits

- Oracle's FAQ lists Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Db2 (LUW, z/OS and i) among supported databases, with Amazon RDS, Aurora, Google Cloud and Azure database services, and also names Kafka, Snowflake and Apache Iceberg as targets (FAQ).
- It documents one-way, two-way and multi-directional setups, and advises conflict detection and resolution policies plus primary or unique keys on all replicated tables (FAQ).
- The FAQ says it supports change capture from MongoDB and MongoDB Atlas, and two-way replication between MongoDB databases (FAQ).
- For Oracle databases, the FAQ says GoldenGate 26ai supports 19c to 26ai and later, and GoldenGate 19c and 21c support 11.2.0.4 to 21c (FAQ) (checked Oct 2026).
- The FAQ says OCI GoldenGate is a fully managed service where Oracle handles backups, patching and upgrades, while GoldenGate on the OCI Marketplace is customer-managed. Self-managed deployments run on a VM, bare metal or Kubernetes (FAQ).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Enterprise platforms (part 2)
text:
- The FAQ lists Apache Iceberg among targets, but the write details sit in the separate GoldenGate for Distributed Applications and Analytics (DAA) docs. Oracle's Iceberg page lists Glue, Hadoop, Nessie, Polaris and REST catalogs but, in the version we read, states no write limits such as delete handling.
- It cannot capture from Salesforce, Teradata or TimesTen (FAQ) (checked Oct 2026).
- The FAQ warns that two-way setups need careful planning because they can cause update conflicts, replication loops, data divergence, latency sensitivity and operational complexity (FAQ).
- The FAQ says the Classic Architecture (administered with GGSCI) is de-supported in 26ai, and the other model is the REST-based Microservices Architecture (FAQ) (checked Oct 2026).
- On OCI, billing is per OCPU: you pick a base size of 1 to 24 OCPUs (1 to 8 with Auto-Scale, which reaches 3 times the base), and each hour is billed at the larger of the service size and the OCPUs actually consumed (FAQ) (checked Oct 2026).
- We don't quote an on-premises dollar price.

Check before you rely on it: ask Oracle for a written quote for your own core count, because we do not quote an on-premises price.

**3. Qlik Replicate: mixed legacy and mainframe sources**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based, which Qlik calls "zero footprint" (a vendor claim we did not test)
- Price: Capacity bands by data volume and job runs, no list prices, per the Qlik pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Qlik's product page lists Oracle, SQL Server, Db2, MySQL, PostgreSQL and mainframe sources.

Replicate is client-managed software, so you install it yourself on Windows Server or Linux (Qlik support matrix).

Where it fits

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Enterprise platforms (part 3)
text:
- Qlik's product page lists mainframe sources and relational, warehouse and cloud-platform categories, and says Replicate works across hundreds of sources and targets.
- Replicate May 2026 added an IBM IMS source endpoint, an IBM Db2 for LUW target endpoint and a Cloudera Iceberg target, and added MariaDB 11.8 and Kafka 4.1 and 4.2 support (Qlik May 2026 release notes).
- Qlik's release notes say Qlik Open Lakehouse, a Qlik Talend Cloud feature, writes Iceberg tables. They describe a route where Replicate lands data in S3 and an Open Lakehouse pipeline onboards it into Iceberg tables (release notes).
- On an Oracle source, Replicate can read the redo logs with either Oracle LogMiner or Qlik's own Replicate Log Reader, and the docs list separate limits for each (Qlik Oracle source limitations).

Where it falls short

- Prices are not published. The Qlik pricing page shows a Contact Us button for each of its four Talend Cloud editions and says usage is measured by data volume moved, job runs and run time (checked Oct 2026).
- On the pricing page, log-based CDC first appears in the Standard edition list, not in Starter (checked Oct 2026).
- Oracle 21c cannot use LogMiner (Oracle's log-reading tool) with Replicate, only Qlik's own log reader. Also on 21c, immutable tables and blockchain tables are not supported, and CDC is not supported when a schema, table or column name is over 30 characters (Oracle source limitations) (checked Oct 2026).
- Capturing changes from a pluggable database (PDB) with LogMiner is not supported, and Qlik does not recommend LogMiner on a RAC environment because of unpredictable behavior (Oracle source limitations) (checked Oct 2026).
- Replicate's own Iceberg target in the May 2026 release is Cloudera Iceberg. Other Iceberg routes run through Qlik Open Lakehouse in Talend Cloud (release notes).

**4. Striim: Oracle-heavy streaming**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based
- Price: Developer tier free up to 25 million events a month; Cloud and Platform say "contact us", per the Striim pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

For Oracle, Striim's docs give you two readers, Oracle Reader (LogMiner) and OJet. Both read Oracle 11g and higher.

Where it fits

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Enterprise platforms (part 4)
text:
- Striim's Oracle docs position Oracle Reader (LogMiner) for 20 to 80 GB of CDC data an hour and OJet for 150+ GB an hour. Both read Oracle 11g and higher, RAC and PDB/CDB. We have not tested either figure.
- Its GG Trail Reader can read existing Oracle GoldenGate trail files (versions 11g, 12c, 18.1 and 19.1) without extra LogMiner sessions (Oracle docs).
- Striim's docs say the Iceberg Writer has Merge mode, which mirrors source inserts, updates and deletes, and Append Only mode, which treats every operation as an insert. Its docs add schema evolution that propagates DDL changes, and at-least-once recovery.
- Its docs say the S3 Tables Writer writes change and snapshot data into Iceberg tables in Amazon S3 Tables, using Amazon EMR for compute and either the S3 Tables catalog or AWS Glue, with DDL propagation for supported source changes.
- The pricing page shows a free Developer tier with trial access to premium, standard and 200+ preview connectors, and a Striim Cloud card that says "Pay only for the data you move" (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- The Iceberg Writer docs say the only supported data lake in this release is Google Cloud Storage. It also needs a Spark compute service and a catalog, and partitioned tables must be created by hand. Separate S3 Tables and GCP Lakehouse writers exist too (checked Oct 2026).
- The same page limits the catalog to Lakehouse, Nessie or Polaris, supports GCS only as the staging area, and recommends the Hadoop catalog only for development and testing (Iceberg Writer) (checked Oct 2026).
- It also says time source data types are written as strings in Iceberg, and recovery is at-least-once (Iceberg Writer).
- The S3 Tables Writer requires lowercase table, namespace and column names, which breaks wildcard mappings against sources that use uppercase identifiers (checked Oct 2026).
- Cloud and Platform prices are not published: the pricing page shows "Contact us for pricing" for both, and Platform says "License the connectors you need" (checked Oct 2026).

**5. Fivetran High-Volume Agent (HVA): big enterprise databases, run by a vendor**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based, through Fivetran's High-Volume Agent (HVA)
- Price: no separate HVA price found; HVA connectors need an Enterprise or Business Critical plan, per Fivetran billing docs (checked Oct 2026)

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Enterprise platforms (part 5)
text:
Fivetran's page on High-Volume Agent (HVA) connectors lists Db2 for i, Oracle, SQL Server and other enterprise systems. They run in Fivetran's cloud (SaaS), or in Hybrid mode, where data is processed in your own network.

Where it fits

- The HVA page lists connectors for Db2 for i, Oracle, SQL Server, SAP ERP and three SAP ECC variants.
- Fivetran's Managed Data Lake Service writes Parquet to your own S3, Azure Data Lake Storage or Google Cloud Storage account. Its docs say Fivetran always creates Iceberg metadata and manages the catalogs and maintenance operations.
- The same page lists optional catalog integrations, including Databricks Unity Catalog and Snowflake catalog-linked databases, and Lake Compute, a hosted DuckDB-based engine for running dbt transformations on the Iceberg tables (Managed Data Lake Service).
- Per its maintenance notes, Fivetran deletes old snapshots once a day while always keeping at least the last 2, and moves orphan files to an `orphans` folder on the second and fourth Saturdays of each month (Managed Data Lake Service).
- Fivetran's usage docs say a row is counted once a month even if it syncs several times, and every new connection has 14 days of free usage (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Enterprise platforms (part 6)
text:
- The price is not published. Billing is by Monthly Active Rows (rows changed in a month), so you'll want to estimate your change volume first (checked Oct 2026).
- MAR keys are counted separately for each connection and table, so two connections that sync the same data count twice (usage docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The HVA Oracle and HVA SQL Server connectors need the Enterprise or Business Critical plan, and annual contracts have a $12,000 minimum, against a $5 minimum per connection on monthly pay-as-you-go (billing docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The Iceberg service does not support position deletes (a way to mark a row as removed by its place in a file), and its page lists only the SaaS deployment (Managed Data Lake Service) (checked Oct 2026).
- On AWS, it does not support the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, Glacier Deep Archive or Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers, and the Glue catalog allows one table per schema and table name combination in a Region (Managed Data Lake Service) (checked Oct 2026).
- Iceberg reserves some column names (`_deleted`, `_file`, `_partition`, `_pos`, `_spec_id`, `file_path`, `pos`, `row`), so Fivetran prefixes them with a hash symbol before writing (Managed Data Lake Service).

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Cloud-native services
text:
**6. OLake Go: best for database changes into Iceberg on your own storage**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based change capture (docs)
- Price: Free licence (Apache 2.0); you pay for infrastructure and staff

OLake Go is open source. It reads PostgreSQL logical replication, the MySQL and MariaDB binlog, MongoDB change streams and SQL Server's native CDC, then writes Apache Iceberg or Parquet to storage you control.

Engines such as Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Athena, Spark and Trino can read the Iceberg tables it writes, depending on the catalog and the delete format (the engine compatibility page lists the conditions for each engine).

What's good

- It does the first copy and then change capture in one tool (docs).
- It writes eleven Iceberg catalog types, and handles deletes with equality and positional deletes plus deletion vectors since v0.11.0 (v0.11.0 release note, catalogs).
- It installs with Docker Compose and a web UI, a Docker command line, or Helm on Kubernetes (Docker Compose, Docker CLI and Kubernetes install pages).
- It follows schema changes: adds, drops and renames are detected, new source columns sync automatically when Sync new columns automatically is on, and widening type changes are documented (schema evolution).
- Full loads are split into parallel chunks, and syncs are stateful and resumable: after a crash, network failure or pause, an interrupted run resumes from its last checkpoint instead of starting over (capabilities).
- It uses a two-phase commit for the Iceberg destination in full refresh, incremental and CDC runs (MongoDB, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server), tracking per-chunk commit status so syncs avoid inconsistencies and duplicate writes (capabilities).

Good to know

- Change capture covers PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, MongoDB and SQL Server. Oracle, Db2 and S3 sources load by full refresh or incremental runs, and output is Apache Iceberg or Parquet on storage you choose (docs).

Bottom line: Pick OLake Go if you run PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, MongoDB or SQL Server and want Iceberg tables on storage you control (docs).

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Managed or vendor-run
text:
**7. AWS DMS: moving databases into AWS**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based
- Price: Replication instance hours or Serverless DCU hours, plus storage. AWS's DMS pricing page lists no separate CDC fee for DMS tasks. For example, dms.t3.medium lists at $0.0745 an hour in us-east-1, on-demand, Single-AZ, per the AWS price list (checked Oct 2026)

AWS says DMS migrates databases with one-time moves or ongoing replication. A task can do a full load first and then switch to CDC. Under the hood, its CDC docs say it reads Oracle with LogMiner or a binary reader, SQL Server through Microsoft's CDC or replication, MySQL binary logs, PostgreSQL logical slots and the MongoDB oplog.

Where it fits

- AWS's docs list two-way tasks on six engines: Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL and two Aurora editions (CDC page).
- A task can be full load plus CDC, or CDC only for data already on the target (CDC page).
- Since DMS 3.5.1, a CDC-only task that starts from an SCN or timestamp can pick up open transactions through the `openTransactionWindow` endpoint setting (CDC page).
- For S3 targets, the docs say full-load and CDC files are written as CSV by default, with Apache Parquet as an option, and each CDC row starts with I, U or D to show how the row changed (AWS DMS S3 target docs).
- AWS lists pricing options for on-demand instances, Serverless and Database Savings Plans, and says on-demand is hourly with no long-term commitment (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Managed or vendor-run (part 2)
text:
- AWS's CDC page says DMS ongoing replication has no service-level agreement for latency, that it does not provide real-time replication, and that latency can rise to several minutes or longer.
- The two-way mode does not include conflict detection or resolution. Loopback prevention tracks only DML, not DDL, and tasks that use it cannot commit changes in batches, so `BatchApplyEnabled` must be false (CDC page) (checked Oct 2026).
- Views can be migrated in full-load tasks only. A CDC-only task or a full load that goes on to CDC includes tables only (CDC page) (checked Oct 2026).
- PostgreSQL as a source does not support a custom CDC start time, and the CDC start point is fixed when the task is created, so a different one needs a new task. For Oracle, starting from an SCN or timestamp misses open transactions unless you use the 3.5.1 setting above (CDC page) (checked Oct 2026).
- Apache Iceberg is not among the target endpoints AWS's docs list for DMS, so Iceberg needs a separate step after the files land on S3 (checked Oct 2026).
- On an S3 target, DMS records no ALTER statement when a column is added, dropped or renamed and does not alter earlier records, and the docs say batch apply to S3 might lose data (S3 target docs).

**8. Google Cloud Datastream: BigQuery on Google Cloud**

At a glance

- Method: Per source, such as the MySQL binary log
- Price: Per GiB processed; backfill free for 500 GiB a month, then $0.40 per GiB; a free CDC tier of 100 GiB a month applies only to AlloyDB and Spanner sources, per the Datastream pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Datastream is a CDC and replication service on Google Cloud. Its sources are MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server and PostgreSQL, plus Spanner, MongoDB and Salesforce.

Where it fits

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Managed or vendor-run (part 3)
text:
- The pricing page says there are no costs for running streams beyond data processed, an idle stream incurs no cost, and events Datastream reads but does not write to the destination are not counted (checked Oct 2026).
- CDC costs are tiered, so the price per GB falls as usage rises. The page's worked example charges $2.00 per GiB for the first 2,500 GiB and $1.50 per GiB beyond that (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- Google's docs say Iceberg tables in BigQuery keep data in customer-owned Cloud Storage buckets, in Iceberg table format with Parquet files (Iceberg destination).
- For a SQL Server source, Google documents two methods. The transaction logs method needs fewer resources and retrieves data faster, while the change tables method has lower throughput but fewer limitations and supports encrypted tables (Datastream SQL Server source docs) (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- The Iceberg destination is BigQuery-managed Iceberg tables in Cloud Storage, and Google says streaming to them is "supported only in the append-only write mode". Each table gets a `datastream_metadata` column, and in append-only mode its change type is INSERT for every row (checked Oct 2026).
- Setup needs the Cloud Storage bucket, BigQuery dataset and Datastream connection in the same region, and a BigQuery connection whose service account holds the `storage.admin` role on the bucket (Iceberg destination) (checked Oct 2026).
- Google's docs describe no self-hosted option.
- For PostgreSQL, a stopped stream can leave log files on the source until the disk fills, so Google advises alerting on disk use (Datastream PostgreSQL source docs).
- Google says a processed byte is an internal representation of the source data and for most use cases can be 2 to 5 times larger than the actual data (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- The pricing page says the first 500 GB of backfill each month is free, while a footnote calls it a one-time 500 GiB credit per billing account, so confirm which applies (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- On the SQL Server transaction logs method, Transparent Data Encryption is not supported, column-level-encrypted data is replaced with NULL, and columns added after a stream is created are not replicated. Streams are limited to 10,000 tables (SQL Server source docs) (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Managed or vendor-run (part 4)
text: Check before you rely on it: ask Google for the expected delay on your source and size.

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Run it yourself
text:
**9. Debezium: teams that already run Kafka**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based
- Price: Free licence (Apache 2.0); you pay for infrastructure and staff (checked Oct 2026)

This entry covers Debezium Server, which sends change events to the sinks listed in its docs, including Apache Iceberg.

Where it fits

- Its docs list connectors for MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, MongoDB and more.
- The Debezium Server docs list sinks including Kinesis, Pub/Sub, Pulsar, Redis, Kafka, RabbitMQ, Event Hubs, JDBC and Apache Iceberg.
- The Iceberg sink lists upsert and append modes, offset and schema history storage in Iceberg, and automatic schema evolution. New columns are added by default (`allow-field-addition` is true), and the default file format is Parquet (Debezium Server docs).
- When event and key schema information is enabled, destination Iceberg tables are created automatically at first startup (Debezium Server docs).
- Offsets can be kept in a file, memory, a JDBC database or Redis, which suits deployments without Kafka (Debezium Server docs).
- The PostgreSQL connector reads through logical decoding with the pgoutput or decoderbufs plug-in. It takes an initial consistent snapshot on first start and can run a blocking snapshot of one table on demand.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Run it yourself (part 2)
text:
- You run it. The Apache Iceberg sink is community-maintained in a separate repository, and each Debezium Server instance runs one connector (checked Oct 2026).
- The Iceberg sink's `upsert` setting is off by default, which means append-only mode. In upsert mode, deleted rows are kept and marked `__deleted=true` unless you turn `upsert-keep-deletes` off (Debezium Server docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The docs say upsert mode and automatic primary key detection depend on the flattened event structure, and without it the connector runs only in a more limited append-only mode (Debezium Server docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The Server page gives no list of supported Iceberg catalog types. It passes any `debezium.sink.iceberg.*` property to the Iceberg library (Debezium Server docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- On PostgreSQL, logical decoding does not report DDL changes, and a table without a primary key produces only create events under the default replica identity (PostgreSQL connector) (checked Oct 2026).
- Unchanged TOAST (large) column values outside the replica identity are left out of update events and replaced by a placeholder, and the pgoutput plug-in does not capture values for generated columns (PostgreSQL connector) (checked Oct 2026).

**10. Estuary: one managed platform for streaming and batch**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based
- Price: $0.50 per GB moved plus $100 a month for each of the first 6 connector instances; free tier of 10 GB a month and 2 instances, per Estuary pricing (checked Oct 2026)

Estuary's docs list capture connectors for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle and SQL Server. Each source and each destination counts as a billed instance, per its pricing page.

Where it fits

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Run it yourself (part 3)
text:
- Estuary says it does streaming and batch in one platform, in public cloud, private cloud or your own cloud. We have not tested that claim.
- The pricing page says it offers 200+ source and destination connectors, and its Cloud card lists "Millisecond latency or batch, no extra charge" (a vendor claim we did not test) (checked Oct 2026).
- Per the pricing FAQ, a new pipeline runs a historical backfill and then switches to real-time CDC, and backfilling can be disabled or scoped for large datasets (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- The free Developer plan covers 10 GB a month and 2 connector instances, and the Cloud plan starts with a 30-day free trial that needs no credit card (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- The Enterprise column lists SOC 2 and HIPAA reports, single sign-on, custom SLA terms, and private and bring-your-own-cloud deployments on annual contracts (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- Its Iceberg connector docs say it merges updates into Iceberg tables by orchestrating Spark jobs, supports AWS Glue through the Glue Iceberg REST endpoint, and can write to S3 table buckets.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Run it yourself (part 4)
text:
- Its Iceberg connector needs an Iceberg REST catalog (a catalog with a standard web interface) on Amazon S3, an AWS EMR Serverless Spark application and an S3 staging bucket. Catalogs on GCP or Azure are planned, not supported (Iceberg connector docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The connector also needs a dedicated IAM role for running jobs on EMR Serverless, and the docs mark REST catalogs other than Glue as Beta (Iceberg connector docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Hard Delete is off by default (soft-delete), so items deleted in the source are not deleted from the destination until you enable it. Array and object fields are written as Iceberg `variant` columns (Iceberg connector docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Automatic compaction through Glue table optimizers is an option that defaults to false, and querying S3 table buckets with Athena needs lowercase column names (Iceberg connector docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Every source and destination is billed, so the cost climbs with every pipeline you add. The first 6 connector instances cost $100 a month each and extra ones $50, on top of $0.50 per GB (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- Estuary's blog works an example of 800 GB moved with 2 connector instances at $1,000 a month, because data is metered at both ingestion and materialization: $0.50 per GB each way plus $100 per instance (checked Oct 2026). Ask how your own data would be metered.

**11. Airbyte: scheduled syncs and a long connector list**

At a glance

- Method: Log-based CDC on scheduled syncs
- Price: Core free; Cloud Standard starts at $20 a month with 5 credits included and extra credits at $5 each, per Airbyte pricing (checked Oct 2026)

Airbyte's CDC docs say syncs are scheduled and CDC sources are not treated as infinite streams. In plain terms, it runs in batches, not as a live stream.

Where it fits

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Run it yourself (part 5)
text:
- Airbyte's docs list a self-hosted Core edition, and Iceberg destinations for S3 and GCS that support REST, Glue, Nessie, Polaris and BigLake catalogs (checked Oct 2026).
- Its CDC page lists Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server and MongoDB among its current CDC support. The first sync takes a snapshot with a SELECT, which is effectively a full refresh, and later syncs read the logs from the previous position.
- CDC records carry metadata columns that begin with `_ab_cdc_`, and the columns vary per source (CDC page).
- Its docs say the S3 Data Lake destination writes the Iceberg table format to S3 or S3-compatible storage. Deduplication is merge-on-read: Airbyte maps the stream's primary keys to Iceberg identifier columns, and an upsert is an equality-based delete followed by an insert.
- The pricing page lists 700+ connectors on all four cloud plans, a 14-day free trial with 400 credits, and syncs as often as every 5 minutes on Pro and Enterprise Flex (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- CDC limits in the docs: views are not supported, TRUNCATE and table-structure (ALTER) changes are not picked up from the logs, and new tables need a refresh (CDC page) (checked Oct 2026).
- CDC incremental is only supported for tables with primary keys for most sources, and the docs say to run syncs often enough to consume the logs that are generated (CDC page) (checked Oct 2026).
- Cloud Standard syncs at most hourly, and Plus every 15 minutes (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- The S3 Data Lake connector never rewrites existing Iceberg data files, so it handles only a few source schema changes: adding or removing a column, widening a column and changing the primary key (S3 Data Lake docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Objects and unions are written as string columns of serialized JSON, and column names are written as they appear in the source by default, which some query engines cannot read through a Glue catalog. An option added in September 2026 lowercases them (S3 Data Lake docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The docs caution that if compaction runs at the same time as a truncate refresh sync, it deletes files from the current generation and causes data loss (S3 Data Lake docs).

**12. Artie: managed CDC with a published monthly plan**

At a glance

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 12 data replication tools > Run it yourself (part 6)
text:
- Method: Log-based
- Price: Free to 1M rows a month and 2 pipelines; Growth from $500 a month billed annually; Enterprise custom, per Artie pricing (checked Oct 2026)

Artie's architecture page says it reads the source transaction log and buffers changes in an internal Kafka. It then writes with upserts, which insert a row or update it if it exists. Its sources include PostgreSQL, MySQL and MongoDB, with Oracle and SQL Server on Enterprise (pricing).

Where it fits

- A free plan and a published Growth price.
- The Free plan is $0 a month "forever", with up to 1M billable rows and 2 active pipelines. Backfills are always free and never count toward billable rows (Artie pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Growth is usage-based, starting at $500 a month on an annual plan or $600 month to month, and counts billable rows after the initial backfill (Artie pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- The pricing page lists sub-minute latency and exactly-once delivery on the Free plan. These are vendor claims we did not test.
- The architecture page says it subscribes to the source transaction log, buffers each change in an internal Kafka queue, and writes with idempotent upserts or merges. Its Cloud option runs the control and data planes in Artie's cloud, while BYOC runs the data plane in your cloud account.

Where it falls short

- The pricing page lists Iceberg, and Oracle and SQL Server log replication, only under Enterprise (Artie pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- BYOC and an uptime SLA are also listed under Enterprise only, and PrivateLink on Growth costs $500 a month per connection (Artie pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- The Free plan caps at 1M billable rows a month and 2 active pipelines, and Growth cost follows billable rows (Artie pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Artie's pricing page and docs state no licence, so we do not call it open source (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What to check before you choose
text:
1. The job. Failover, reports, a lake and a migration all need different tools.

2. The delay you will see. Ask for the real lag. AWS's docs say DMS has no service-level agreement for CDC latency, and Airbyte runs on a schedule.

3. The first copy. Most tools copy existing rows first and then switch to changes. Test an interrupted snapshot on your biggest table.

4. Deletes and schema changes. Timestamp-based copies miss hard deletes, and the table above shows how schema changes are handled.

5. Log growth on the source. The PostgreSQL, Datastream and DMS docs all warn that a stopped slot keeps log files on the source disk. Alert on disk use before you go live.

6. How the copy is checked.AWS lists a checksum consistency check as the last stage of replication. Ask each vendor how it proves the two sides match.

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What to check before you choose > A small test for any finalist
text:
We have not run this test on the other tools.

- Create a table with three rows: (1, "a"), (2, "b") and (3, "c"). Start the copy.
- Insert (4, "d"), update row 2 to "b1" and then to "b2", and delete row 3.
- Add a column, then stop the tool mid-run and restart it.
- Expected result on a current-state target: (1, "a"), (2, "b2") and (4, "d"), with no row 3 and no duplicates. Append-only targets, such as Datastream's Iceberg tables, show each change as its own record.
- Finally, read the bill after a week of real change volume.

Q1. What are data replication tools?

They copy data from a source, usually a database, to another place and keep that copy up to date.

Q2. What is the difference between data replication and backup?

Replication keeps a live copy current, while a backup is a point-in-time copy you restore from. PostgreSQL's docs say restoring from a base backup takes considerably longer than failing over to a warm standby.

Q3. What is the difference between replication and change data capture?

CDC finds and sends only the changes, while AWS treats it as the change-detection stage inside replication.

Q4. Is data replication real time?

Not always. AWS describes strategies from real-time synchronous replication to scheduled asynchronous replication. Asynchronous copies, AWS says, run with some lag.

Q5. What are the best free or open-source data replication tools?

Debezium uses an Apache 2.0 licence, OLake Go is open source under Apache 2.0 (docs), and PostgreSQL and MySQL include replication in the database. Airbyte Core is free to self-host, so read its licence terms before you call it open source. A free licence still isn't a free ride, because you pay for servers and the people who run them.

Q6. Can I replicate in both directions?

Some can, but tread carefully. Oracle GoldenGate documents one-way, two-way and multi-directional setups, and AWS DMS supports two-way tasks, though its docs say they do not include conflict detection or resolution.

Q7. Does replication slow down my source database?

Log-based tools read the transaction log instead of querying your tables, which AWS says is efficient. The cost shows up elsewhere: PostgreSQL's docs say a replication slot keeps log files on disk even with no reader connected. Qlik calls its approach zero footprint, a vendor claim, so measure on your own source.

title: Compare: Best Data Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What to check before you choose > A small test for any finalist (part 2)
text:
Q8. What happens to my copy when I add a column?

It depends on the tool; see the schema-change table above, and test it with the small test.

Q9. Which tools write Apache Iceberg?

Per their docs: GoldenGate (its FAQ lists Iceberg; write details are in the separate Iceberg docs), Qlik, Striim (Google Cloud Storage or Amazon S3 Tables) and Fivetran. Datastream (append-only), Debezium (community sink), Estuary, Airbyte and Artie (Enterprise) also do. OLake Go writes Apache Iceberg or Parquet, with eleven catalog types. AWS DMS's target list does not include Iceberg.

Start with the job, not the tool list. If Apache Iceberg is the goal, check the catalog, the cloud and whether updates and deletes work. Then run the small test above on your own data before you commit.

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

There's no single best data streaming platform. If you already use Apache Kafka tools, pick Kafka itself, Confluent Cloud, Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK) or Redpanda, depending on who you want running the servers. If you live in one cloud and want the least work, use that cloud's own service: Amazon Kinesis, Azure Event Hubs or Google Cloud Pub/Sub.

Striim is a vendor option for teams that want change capture and streaming together (its price is not published), and Pulsar suits teams that like its multi-tenant design and will run it themselves.

- A data streaming platform stores and delivers a stream of events. An event is one small record, such as "order 1234 was paid". The platform keeps those records in order, so lots of programs can read them.
- Decide who runs the servers first. Self-run open-source projects such as Kafka and Pulsar have no licence fee, but your team runs them. Managed services take much of that work off your plate and bill on their own meters.
- Decide which API your code uses second. Kafka, Confluent, MSK, Redpanda, WarpStream and the Event Hubs Kafka endpoint say they speak the Kafka API (from each vendor's own docs). The Kinesis and Pub/Sub pages we read do not mention Kafka API support, so plan for code changes.
- Prices use different meters, so list rates don't compare directly. Price a real workload instead, like the worked example below.

We checked prices on October 8, 2026 against each vendor's own pages, and we name the region where the vendor does. Plans change often, so confirm on the vendor's page before you decide.

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > What a data streaming platform is
text:
Picture a conveyor belt that never stops, with a notebook beside it that writes down everything that passes. That's a data streaming platform: software that takes in a continuous flow of events, stores them, and lets other programs read them in order. The notebook is called a log, an ordered list of events that readers can replay from any point still kept.

Most platforms split that log into topics (named channels) and spread each topic across partitions (parallel lanes), so many machines share the work. A broker is a server that holds part of the log. Producers write events in, and consumers read them out.

It isn't a database or a batch tool.

Five questions cut the list fast; the first two do most of the cutting.

- Who will run it? Your team, a vendor, or your cloud provider.
- Which API does your code use? The Kafka API, or another interface.
- How long must events stay replayable? Pub/Sub topics stop at `31 days` and Kinesis at `365 days`.

text:
Each platform here moves events between programs, is still maintained, and publishes documentation we could open. Apache Flink and Spark process streams, and Fivetran and Airbyte copy data. All four sit on top of a platform, so they are out. For tools that move data between systems, see our best data pipeline tools comparison.

Vendor facts come from each vendor's own pages, read on October 8, 2026. We did not run the other tools, so there are no speed rankings. The "What users say" lines come from public Hacker News threads and PeerSpot reviews that we opened on October 8, 2026. Each one is a single person's view, with its date and link.

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Platforms that speak the Kafka API
text:
The Kafka API is the set of commands Kafka programs use to write and read events. The platforms in this group say they support it, and Microsoft says existing Kafka code can often use the Event Hubs endpoint after a settings change.

**1. Apache Kafka: for teams that want full control**

At a glance

- Run by: You, on servers, containers or in the cloud
- Price: No licence fee (Apache License 2.0) (checked Oct 2026); you pay for machines and staff

Kafka is the open-source project whose API most of the platforms here copy. By the project's own account (its intro page) it does three things: publish and subscribe to streams of events, store them durably, and process them. Its downloads page (checked Oct 2026) lists `4.3.1`, `4.2.2` and `4.1.2` as supported releases and says the project ships a release about every four months.

What's good

- No licence fee (Apache License 2.0) (checked Oct 2026). The Kafka intro page says you can run it on bare-metal hardware, virtual machines and containers, on premises or in the cloud, either self-managed or through fully managed services from a variety of vendors.
- Kafka Connect continuously imports and exports data as event streams to link Kafka with existing systems such as relational databases, and the same page says the community already provides hundreds of ready-to-use connectors.
- Events are not deleted after consumption, so they "can be read as often as needed", and retention is a per-topic setting. Each partition is read in the order its events were written, and a replication factor of `3` is named as a common production setting.
- The Kafka design page (checked Oct 2026) says the producer has had an idempotent delivery option since `0.11.0.0`, so resending does not create duplicate log entries, and that exactly-once delivery is supported in Kafka Streams and, with a transactional producer and a read-committed consumer, when reading, processing and writing Kafka topics.
- Consumers pull, so a slow one "simply falls behind and catches up when it can". Share groups let a group have more consumers than a topic has partitions, with records acknowledged one by one.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Platforms that speak the Kafka API (part 2)
text:
- The Kafka intro page (checked Oct 2026) describes Kafka Connect, not the brokers, as the part that imports data from systems such as relational databases, and it describes no Iceberg writer. So those jobs come from add-on connectors, vendor features or a reader such as OLake Go, which reads Kafka topics into Iceberg or Parquet (see our Kafka docs). To read database changes into Iceberg without Kafka, see our comparison of the options.
- Your team owns upgrades, sizing and failures, all of it.
- Defaults need a look. Per the Kafka broker config docs (checked Oct 2026), `default.replication.factor` is `1` for automatically created topics, `log.retention.hours` is `168` (seven days) and `message.max.bytes` is `1048588`, about 1 MB.
- Delivery is at-least-once by default, per the Kafka design page (checked Oct 2026). At-most-once means disabling producer retries and committing offsets before processing.
- Exactly-once into outside systems takes extra work: the design page (checked Oct 2026) says many output systems will not support a two-phase commit, so the consumer may have to store its offset in the same place as its output.
- Patch releases carry real fixes. The Kafka downloads page (checked Oct 2026) says `4.3.1` fixed "a critical Kafka Streams RocksDB native memory leak (KAFKA-20616)" and about 15 other issues, so running Kafka means tracking releases like this.

What users say: One Hacker News commenter on "Kafka is Fast" (October 2025) wrote "self-managing kafka is a job in of itself". Another on the Ursa thread (July 2025) called Kafka "one of the pieces of software that has been rock solid for me".

**2. Confluent Cloud: for Kafka without running servers**

At a glance

- Run by: Confluent, on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud
- Price: Basic from $0 a month, Standard about $385, Enterprise about $895, per the Confluent Cloud pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Confluent's docs overview describes Confluent Cloud as a fully managed Kafka service.

Confluent's press release of March 17, 2026 says International Business Machines (IBM) completed its acquisition of Confluent. The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists those three starting monthly figures for cluster tiers. It says the figures assume 70% utilization (clusters active about 70% of the time) and that prices vary by cloud region.

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Platforms that speak the Kafka API (part 3)
text:
Confluent also sells ready-made connectors, and says its Tableflow feature turns Kafka topics into Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake tables.

What's good

- Its Tableflow docs (checked Oct 2026) (the overview page) say Tableflow materializes Kafka topics or Flink tables as Iceberg or Delta Lake tables, publishes new data to a table approximately every `5 minutes`, and compacts and cleans up small files for you.
- The same docs list a built-in Iceberg REST catalog plus catalog integration with AWS Glue, Databricks Unity, Apache Polaris and Snowflake Open Catalog, and say you can use your own storage on Amazon S3, Azure or Google Cloud Storage.
- With Confluent Cloud for Apache Flink you can filter, deduplicate, remove personally identifiable information (PII) and join streams on topics that Tableflow then materializes.
- Its connectors page (checked Oct 2026) says Confluent offers "120+ pre-built connectors" (open source or community, commercial and premium, plus partner-verified ones). Its connector docs (checked Oct 2026) list Debezium change capture connectors for MongoDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server. The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) says connectors are billed per task-hour and per GB.
- The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) feature table lists uptime SLAs of 99.5% for Basic, 99.9% or 99.99% for Standard and Enterprise (depending on eCKU count) and 99.99% for Freight.
- The same table (checked Oct 2026) lists throughput in and out of `250` and `750` MBps for Basic and Standard, `1,920` and `5,760` MBps for Enterprise, and `9,120` and `27,360` MBps for Freight.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Platforms that speak the Kafka API (part 4)
text:
- The bill has lots of moving parts: cluster, network, storage, connectors and Flink. Confluent's billing dimensions page (checked Oct 2026) says a cluster unit (an eCKU) is billed per hour at the maximum used in that hour (usage between 2 and 3 eCKUs bills as 3), and storage is charged after replication, so billed storage is typically about 3x the volume written.
- Confluent charges for all data transfers, including requests the Cloud Console makes to show messages in the message browser, and ingress and egress charges are multiplied by a regional multiplier. A paused managed connector keeps accruing hourly task costs (billing dimensions) (checked Oct 2026).
- The Tableflow overview says Tableflow is not available for Confluent Platform (the self-managed product). Tableflow has its own meters (topic hours, data processed and storage on the billing dimensions page), and neither the Tableflow billing docs nor the pricing page we read shows a dollar rate (checked Oct 2026).
- The Tableflow overview (checked Oct 2026) lists these limits: schemaless topics are not supported (the key and the value must both have a schema), retract tables are not supported, and Confluent Cloud for Apache Flink cannot query Iceberg tables.
- The same overview (checked Oct 2026) says tables are exposed read-only and that only topics using custom storage sync to external catalogs.
- It also says Tableflow keeps between `10` and `100` snapshots, not user-configurable, and that once a topic is enabled with custom storage, changing the bucket is not supported (Tableflow overview) (checked Oct 2026).

**3. Amazon MSK: for AWS teams that already use Kafka**

At a glance

- Run by: AWS
- Price: Standard broker $0.21 an hour for a `kafka.m5.large`, plus $0.10 per GB-month of storage (US East, N. Virginia), per the MSK pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

AWS says Amazon MSK runs open-source Kafka and that your existing applications and tools work without code changes. The MSK pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists three styles: Standard brokers, Express brokers ($0.408 an hour for an `msk.m7g.large` in US East, N. Virginia, plus $0.01 per GB ingested) and Serverless ($0.75 per cluster-hour plus per-partition and per-GB charges, US East, Ohio).

What's good

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Platforms that speak the Kafka API (part 5)
text:
- AWS's MSK developer guide says MSK "runs open-source versions of Apache Kafka", and that existing applications, tooling and plugins from partners and the Apache Kafka community work without changes to application code.
- Provisioned clusters offer two broker types, Standard and Express, and in MSK Serverless AWS manages the broker nodes. KRaft controllers are included at no additional cost.
- It names MSK Connect for streaming data to and from your cluster and MSK Replicator for replicating data across MSK Provisioned clusters, in the same or different Regions. MSK Connect is billed in units of 1 vCPU and 4 GB of memory at one-second resolution, $0.11 per hour per unit in AWS's US East (N. Virginia) example (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) says you are not charged for data transfer used for replication between brokers or between metadata nodes and brokers.
- Per the MSK quotas page (checked Oct 2026), Express brokers have unlimited maximum storage and up to `15 MB/s` per partition, and MSK Serverless retention is unlimited.
- Its streaming tables docs (checked Oct 2026) say Kafka topics are continuously materialized as Apache Iceberg tables on Amazon S3 Tables, with freshness set between `5` and `15` minutes, at $10.00 per TB delivered and no extra charge for inline compaction.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Platforms that speak the Kafka API (part 6)
text:
- In Provisioned mode you still pick broker types and counts, with a minimum of one broker per Availability Zone (MSK developer guide) (checked Oct 2026).
- Amazon MSK is an AWS service (the MSK developer guide calls it a fully managed service from AWS) (checked Oct 2026), so teams on other clouds need a different option.
- MSK Serverless has per-cluster caps of `200 MBps` in and `400 MBps` out, per-partition caps of `5 MBps` in and `10 MBps` out, a maximum message size of `8 MiB` and `2,400` partitions for non-compacted topics (MSK quotas) (checked Oct 2026).
- Standard brokers top out at `60` brokers per KRaft-based cluster and `16,384 GiB` of storage per broker (MSK quotas) (checked Oct 2026).
- The MSK streaming tables docs (checked Oct 2026) say they need Express brokers (Standard brokers and MSK Serverless are not supported). They deliver to S3 Tables in the same Region, cross-account delivery is not supported, and they need a dead-letter queue bucket and JSON data with an AWS Glue Schema Registry schema.
- The same docs (checked Oct 2026) say a streaming tables channel does not backfill earlier data, and that it creates a new Iceberg table for each configuration because delivery to existing Iceberg tables is not supported.

**4. Redpanda: for the Kafka API in a single program**

At a glance

- Run by: You, or Redpanda (Serverless or bring your own cloud)
- Price: Serverless is pay as you go or annual commit, with a "Start for free" sign-up; BYOC needs an annual commitment, per the Redpanda pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Redpanda says producers and consumers use the Apache Kafka API, and that it comes packaged as a single binary with no outside systems to wire up.

The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists three plans. Serverless allows up to `100 MB/s` of writes with a 99.9% service level agreement (SLA), which is the uptime promise in the contract. Bring your own cloud (BYOC) allows `2 GB/s` with 99.99%, and a self-managed Enterprise Edition has a 30-day trial.

What's good

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Platforms that speak the Kafka API (part 7)
text:
- Serverless is multi-tenant on AWS and GCP, with pay as you go or an annual commit plan. The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists `100 MB/s` write, `300 MB/s` read and `5,000` partitions.
- BYOC runs fully managed Redpanda clusters in your own VPC on AWS, GCP or Azure, and the page (checked Oct 2026) lists `2 GB/s` write, `4 GB/s` read and `112,500` partitions. The Enterprise Edition is the run-it-yourself option, with a 30-day trial.
- Per Redpanda's licensing docs (checked Oct 2026), every new cluster gets a 30-day trial license, and after a trial or license expires the cluster keeps operating without data loss while enterprise features are restricted.
- Its Iceberg topics docs say brokers store topic data as Parquet files in an Iceberg-compatible format in object storage, with the catalog in the same bucket or an Iceberg REST catalog endpoint, and that the feature requires an enterprise license (checked Oct 2026).
- The same docs describe per-topic Iceberg modes: `key_value` (a key column and a binary value column), `value_schema_id_prefix` (matches the topic's Redpanda schema) and `value_schema_latest` (matches the latest schema in the Schema Registry). The default is `disabled`.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Platforms that speak the Kafka API (part 8)
text:
- Dollar rates weren't in the text we read on the pricing page (checked Oct 2026), so we can't quote them, and the SLA figures are Redpanda's own promises (ask for the contract terms).
- Iceberg topics need an enterprise license and Tiered Storage (Iceberg topics docs) on the topics that generate tables. The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists them under BYOC and Enterprise Edition, not in the Serverless feature list, and shows no Iceberg-specific rate, so ask Redpanda which plan includes them.
- Enabling Iceberg on an existing topic does not backfill the table, and topic data cannot be appended to an existing Iceberg table that Redpanda did not create (Iceberg topics docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The Iceberg topics page we read (checked Oct 2026) does not describe compaction, upsert or delete handling.
- BYOC needs an annual commitment, with a 14-day trial available by contacting Redpanda (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- JSON schemas for Iceberg topics are supported starting with Redpanda version `25.2` (Iceberg topics docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The free Community Edition uses the Business Source License, which is source-available and not Apache 2.0. You can't offer Redpanda as a commercial streaming service to others, and the code converts to Apache 2.0 four years after each merge (licensing docs) (checked Oct 2026).

**5. WarpStream: for Kafka that stores data in your own bucket**

At a glance

- Run by: Your cloud account for data, WarpStream's cloud for control
- Price: Billed by cluster tier and by Tableflow usage, per the WarpStream pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

WarpStream's Tableflow launch blog post calls it a drop-in replacement for Apache Kafka, built on object storage. Confluent's press release of September 9, 2024 says Confluent acquired WarpStream.

WarpStream says its Tableflow product turns Kafka topics into Iceberg tables too. The Tableflow docs (checked Oct 2026) say it currently supports append-only tables, and that you cannot use another system to write or maintain those tables.

What's good

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Platforms that speak the Kafka API (part 9)
text:
- The Tableflow docs say compaction and table maintenance are "included out-of-the-box with no tuning required".
- Its Tableflow product page says Tableflow works with any Kafka-compatible source (open-source Kafka, MSK, Confluent Cloud, WarpStream) and can ingest from several Kafka clusters at once. It says raw data is processed on your VMs and stored in your object storage buckets.
- On the pricing page (checked Oct 2026), BYOC keeps the data plane in your cloud account and the control plane in WarpStream's, and new users get "$400 in non-expiring credits" with no credit card.
- The same page (checked Oct 2026) publishes usage rates: Kafka write throughput from $0.01 per GiB and Tableflow write throughput from $0.04 per GiB for the first 50 TiB a month (uncompressed).
- The docs say schema migrations follow Iceberg schema evolution rules, covering added columns, required fields made optional, and widened integer and floating point types. Inline schema mode supports JSON, Avro and Protobuf.
- By default data is ingested from the start of the topic, and a `start_ingestion_at: latest` setting skips what is already there.

Where it falls short

- Rows from a compacted source topic are not deduplicated and tombstones may not comply with the schema. Compacted topic support is "coming soon" in the docs (checked Oct 2026).
- A Tableflow cluster is separate from a WarpStream Kafka cluster, because Tableflow agents "only perform Tableflow operations and do not expose the Apache Kafka protocol" (Tableflow docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Reordering, renaming and removing a column are not supported as in-place migrations (Tableflow docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- A table can have at most `5` sort fields ("Contact support if you need a higher limit", per the Tableflow docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Neither the Tableflow docs page (checked Oct 2026) nor the product page states a delivery guarantee such as exactly-once.
- Billing has several meters (from the pricing page) (checked Oct 2026): Tableflow cluster minutes are billed in 15-minute increments for any interval in which the cluster receives requests, and the 99.999% uptime tier needs Multi-Region Clusters. We didn't compare cluster rates, because its units differ from Confluent's.

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Cloud services with no stated Kafka API
text:
**6. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams: for AWS-only teams**

At a glance

- Run by: AWS
- Price: On-demand $0.08 per GB in and $0.04 per GB out, plus $0.04 per stream-hour (US East, Ohio), per the Kinesis pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

AWS says Kinesis Data Streams collects and processes large streams of records in real time. Its pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists On-demand Standard at $0.08 per GB in, $0.040 per GB out and $0.040 per stream-hour (US East, Ohio). AWS says it may suit you if you prefer not to manage capacity. Provisioned mode bills $0.015 per shard-hour, where one shard carries `1 MB/s` in and `2 MB/s` out.

Per the Kinesis quotas page (checked Oct 2026), records can be up to `10 MiB` and are kept from `24 hours` to `365 days`.

What's good

- The Kinesis introduction page says the put-to-get delay is "typically less than 1 second".
- Producers push data directly into a stream. AWS gives the example of two applications reading the same stream, one updating an Amazon DynamoDB table and the other archiving to a store such as Amazon S3.
- A record payload can be up to `10 MiB` before base64 encoding, and retention runs from `24 hours` to `365 days` (quotas page) (checked Oct 2026).
- New on-demand streams start at `4 MB/s` write and `8 MB/s` read. In US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon) and Europe (Ireland) they scale up to `10 GB/s` write and `20 GB/s` read, and elsewhere to `200 MB/s` and `400 MB/s` (quotas page) (checked Oct 2026).
- AWS's pricing page (checked Oct 2026) describes it as a fully managed, serverless streaming data service. On-demand Advantage uses lower per-GB rates in its US East example ($0.032 ingested, $0.016 retrieved) with no fixed stream-hour charge, and AWS says it might suit you with at least `10 MB/s` of ingest in aggregate.
- Its data delivery docs (checked Oct 2026) describe streaming tables on Apache Iceberg with freshness configurable from `5` to `15` minutes, and say records from a shard are delivered exactly once, with no duplicates or omissions within the shard.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Cloud services with no stated Kafka API (part 2)
text:
- AWS's pricing page (checked Oct 2026) says Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is "NOT currently available in AWS Free Tier".
- The Kinesis pages we read do not mention Kafka API support, and the quotas page (checked Oct 2026) lets each stream register up to `20` enhanced fan-out readers in most modes (`50` in On-demand Advantage).
- In provisioned mode each shard supports up to `1 MB/sec` or `1,000 records/sec` of writes and `2 MB/sec` or `2,000 records/sec` of reads. By default you can create up to `50` on-demand streams (quotas page) (checked Oct 2026).
- Provisioned mode charges extra for retention: $0.020 per shard-hour for extended retention and $0.023 per GB-month beyond seven days, and enhanced fan-out retrieval is $0.013 per GB (pricing page examples) (checked Oct 2026).
- On-demand Advantage has (per the pricing page) (checked Oct 2026) a minimum charge of `25 MB/s` ingested and `25 MB/s` retrieved at account level across all on-demand streams.
- Streaming tables and Amazon S3 delivery are not supported in provisioned mode (data delivery docs) (checked Oct 2026). They need a dead-letter queue in Amazon S3, and the stream, the S3 table bucket and the AWS Glue Schema Registry must be in the same account and Region.

What users say: One PeerSpot reviewer (October 2025) gave stability a 10, saying "We have never had any stability issues", but the same review said "We are contemplating moving away from Amazon Kinesis primarily because of the cost."

**7. Azure Event Hubs: for Azure teams, including Kafka clients**

At a glance

- Run by: Microsoft
- Price: Throughput units (Basic, Standard), processing units (Premium), capacity units (Dedicated); we could not read dollar rates on the Event Hubs pricing page (checked Oct 2026), so check the live page

Microsoft calls Event Hubs a fully managed, real-time data streaming platform that supports the Kafka, HTTPS and Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP) `1.0` protocols. Its Capture feature writes events to Azure Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage.

What's good

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Cloud services with no stated Kafka API (part 3)
text:
- Microsoft's Event Hubs overview (checked Oct 2026) states an SLA of up to 99.99%, and retention of up to `90 days` on Premium and Dedicated.
- The Event Hubs overview lists native integration with Stream Analytics, Azure Functions and Data Explorer, and says the ecosystem also supports Azure Spring Apps, Kafka Connectors, Apache Spark and Apache Flink.
- Microsoft's Event Hubs for Apache Kafka overview (checked Oct 2026) says you can often use the Kafka endpoint without code changes, modifying only the configuration, and that Apache Kafka version `1.0` and later is supported.
- Events up to `20 MB` are supported with dedicated clusters, listed as large message support (preview) (Event Hubs overview) (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- The Kafka endpoint needs Standard or higher, and Kafka Streams and transactions are public previews on Premium and Dedicated (Kafka overview) (checked Oct 2026).
- Kafka compression is supported only in Premium and Dedicated, and the `compression.type` setting accepts `none` or `gzip` (Kafka overview) (checked Oct 2026).
- Delivery is at least once, so a consumer can see the same event twice. Your code has to cope with that, and Microsoft's docs (checked Oct 2026) call for the idempotent consumer pattern.
- On Standard, retention tops out at `7 days`, so replay beyond a week means Premium or Dedicated (Event Hubs overview) (checked Oct 2026).
- Capture writes to Azure Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage, and the pages we read (checked Oct 2026) do not describe an Iceberg writer.

**8. Google Cloud Pub/Sub: for Google Cloud apps that need messaging**

At a glance

- Run by: Google
- Price: First 10 GiB a month free, then $40 per TiB, in all regions, per the Pub/Sub pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Google describes Pub/Sub as an asynchronous and scalable messaging service that decouples the programs that produce messages from the ones that process them. A GiB (gibibyte) is about 1.07 billion bytes, and a TiB is 1,024 GiB. The throughput rate is on the Pub/Sub pricing page, and import topics and export subscriptions are priced separately (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Cloud services with no stated Kafka API (part 4)
text:
- A free monthly allowance, and per-use billing with no servers or capacity to set. The first 10 GiB each month is free and the price after that is $40 per TiB in all Google Cloud regions (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- Google's Pub/Sub overview says latencies are "typically on the order of 100 milliseconds".
- It offers push-based delivery of messages as HTTP POST requests to webhooks.
- Google describes using a stream processing tool such as Dataflow to deliver events to BigQuery, Bigtable and Cloud Storage.
- BigQuery and Cloud Storage subscriptions read from a subscription and write straight to those stores, at $50 per TiB in all Google Cloud regions (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- Per the quotas page (checked Oct 2026), a topic can keep messages for at most `31 days` when retention is turned on, a subscription keeps unacknowledged messages for `7 days` by default, and a message can be up to `10 MB`.
- Publisher throughput defaults to `4 GB/s` per region in the seven regions the page calls large (`europe-west1`, `europe-west4`, `us-central1`, `us-east1`, `us-east4`, `us-west1` and `us-west2`) (quotas page) (checked Oct 2026).
- When a topic is set to retain messages, the Pub/Sub pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists storage at $0.27 per GiB-month.
- A minimum of `1 KB` is billed for each request whatever the message size, so batching small messages is cheaper (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- The first 10 GiB of BigQuery and Cloud Storage subscription throughput is not free, and import topics and export subscriptions are priced separately (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- Google defines throughput as bytes written to a topic plus bytes read from a subscription, so one message read by one subscription is billed twice (pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).
- We found no Kafka protocol statement on the pages we read (checked Oct 2026), so assume your Kafka code needs changes. They also describe no self-hosted option and no Iceberg writer.

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Other platforms
text:
**9. Apache Pulsar: for multi-tenant use with geo-replication**

At a glance

- Run by: You
- Price: No licence fee (Apache License 2.0) (checked Oct 2026)

The Pulsar docs describe it as a multi-tenant, high-performance solution for server-to-server messaging. It also supports geo-replication across clusters, tiered storage that moves old data to cold storage such as S3 and GCS, and several subscription types.

What's good

- Its concepts overview docs list multi-tenancy and geo-replication as built-in features: native support for multiple clusters in an instance, with geo-replication of messages across clusters.
- Subscription types are `exclusive`, `shared`, `failover` and `key_shared`, and the docs list native transactions for atomic operations across topics and partitions.
- Tiered storage offloads older data from hot or warm storage to cold storage such as S3 and GCS (concepts overview).
- The client API has bindings for Java, Go, Python, C++, C#/.NET, Node.js and WebSocket (concepts overview).
- Pulsar Functions is described as a serverless lightweight framework for stream-native processing, and Pulsar IO as a serverless connector framework built on it (concepts overview).
- The Pulsar IO connector docs list source connectors including Debezium MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Oracle and SQL Server, DynamoDB, Kafka, Kinesis and RabbitMQ.

Where it falls short

- The Pulsar download page (checked Oct 2026) lists `5.0` (LTS) as the latest version, released October 5, 2026, with active support until October 5, 2028. The `4.0` LTS line's active support ended on October 21, 2026, and its security support runs until October 21, 2027.
- You run it, and we didn't cover managed versions from vendors. The Pulsar architecture docs (checked Oct 2026) describe brokers, a BookKeeper cluster of bookies for persistent storage, and a metadata store cluster ("Oxia, ZooKeeper, or other supported backend").
- Kafka protocol compatibility is not stated on the architecture page (checked Oct 2026).
- Connectors live in a separate repository with their own release cycle, and the server distribution and Docker image do not bundle them (IO connectors page) (checked Oct 2026).
- The IO connectors page (checked Oct 2026) does not name an Iceberg source or sink connector.

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Other platforms (part 2)
text:
What users say: A Hacker News commenter on "Kafka is Fast - I'll use Postgres" (October 2025) liked that standalone Pulsar is "easy to setup and requires almost no maintenance". Another in the same thread said running it "on your own is a bit of a beast though".

**10. Striim: for database change capture plus streaming from one vendor**

At a glance

- Run by: Striim Cloud (managed), or you with Striim Platform
- Price: Contact sales, with a free developer tier, per the Striim pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Striim calls itself a real-time data integration and streaming platform. Its Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQL Server docs describe change capture readers for those databases.

What's good

- Its Oracle CDC docs (checked Oct 2026) describe two change capture readers: Oracle Reader, which uses LogMiner and is positioned for 20 GB to 80 GB of CDC data per hour, and OJet, positioned for 150+ GB per hour. Both read Oracle `11g` and higher, RAC and PDB / CDB.
- A GG Trail Reader can read existing Oracle GoldenGate trail files (the page names versions `11g`, `12c`, `18.1` and `19.1`) (checked Oct 2026), and Oracle Database `26ai` is marked as supported by both readers.
- On Striim's pricing page (checked Oct 2026), the Striim Developer tier is free for up to 25 million events a month.
- The Striim Cloud card on the pricing page lists dedicated compute and networking, SOC-2 Type II, HIPAA, PCI DSS and customer managed encryption keys. The Platform card lists your own compute, clustered deployments with HA and self-managed monitoring.
- Its Iceberg Writer docs list two write modes, `Merge` (inserts, updates and deletes at the source are mirrored in Iceberg) and `Append Only` (all operations are treated as inserts), and say it supports schema evolution for DDL changes from supported sources.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 10 best data streaming platforms > Other platforms (part 3)
text:
- Its Iceberg Writer docs say "In this release, the only supported data lake is Google Cloud Storage (GCS)" (checked Oct 2026), with Google's managed Spark service and a catalog. Separate S3 Tables and GCP Lakehouse writers are documented too.
- The same docs (checked Oct 2026) say the Iceberg Writer recovers with at-least-once processing, partitioned tables need manual table creation, time source data types are written as strings, and the Hadoop catalog is recommended only for development and testing.
- The Striim writers overview (checked Oct 2026) marks the Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and Redshift writers as `A1P` (at-least-once), which it says can mean duplicate events after recovery. The Kafka Writer shows `E1P` (exactly once).
- Striim publishes no open-source licence, and the price isn't published for Cloud or Platform: Striim's pricing page (checked Oct 2026) shows "Contact us for pricing".
- The Platform card on the pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists "License the connectors you need" among its features, so ask Striim for the connector licence terms.

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > Which data streaming platform should you pick? > A worked cost example
text:
Take one steady workload: 1,000 GB written in a month, read once by one application, in records of 1 KB each. We use a 730-hour month and the rates quoted above, so treat the results as a sketch (and we ignore the roughly 7% gap between GB and GiB).

| Service | Arithmetic from the published rates | Monthly total |
| Kinesis on-demand (US East, Ohio) | $80 in + $40 out + $29.20 stream-hours (730 x $0.04) | $149.20 |
| Kinesis provisioned, 1 shard | $10.95 shard-hours (730 x $0.015) + $14 for 1 billion records at $0.014 per million | $24.95 |
| Pub/Sub | 1,000 GiB in + 1,000 GiB read = 2,000 GiB, less 10 free, at $40 per TiB | $77.73 |

Sources, each the vendor's own page (checked Oct 2026): Amazon Kinesis Data Streams pricing and Google Cloud Pub/Sub pricing.

Provisioned Kinesis is the cheapest of the three, but you size the shards, and one shard takes `1 MB/s` in at most. On-demand adds per-GB and per-stream-hour charges. Pub/Sub has nothing to size, and a second subscription would add another 1,000 GiB of reads to the bill.

Kafka, MSK, Confluent and Redpanda are left out because their bills depend on broker or cluster choices that one example can't pin down.
