title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > Getting streams into Apache Iceberg tables
text: Several platforms above say they can write Iceberg tables, but the fine print differs. Confluent and WarpStream say Tableflow handles compaction. Amazon MSK and Kinesis have streaming tables with their own limits, Redpanda needs an enterprise licence, and Striim's Iceberg Writer names Google Cloud Storage as its only data lake (checked Oct 2026). OLake Go, our open-source tool, also reads Kafka topics into Iceberg or Parquet (see where OLake Go fits).

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > Where OLake Go fits
text:
OLake Go, our open-source tool, reads Kafka topics and writes them to Apache Iceberg or Parquet (see our Kafka docs). It needs Kafka `2.4.0` or later and reads JSON or Avro messages (Avro needs a Confluent Schema Registry). It was tested with Amazon MSK and uses standard Kafka protocols, so other Kafka distributions should work. Each topic can run in Append or Upsert mode. Upsert mode as a whole needs OLake Go `0.12.1` and OLake UI `0.7.1` or later. With `_kafka_key` as the only deduplication key, a message with a null value deletes the row for that key. A topic pattern, which is a regular expression, limits which topics are discovered.

OLake Go cannot sync messages Kafka has already deleted, so run syncs more often than your topic's retention period. It adds `_kafka_key`, `_kafka_offset`, `_kafka_partition` and `_kafka_timestamp` columns to each row, and it works with eleven Iceberg catalog types. You run it yourself, from the OLake UI, the Docker CLI or Kubernetes with Helm (see the quickstart). Each job runs on a schedule you set in the UI, from every minute to a cron expression (job settings).

If your events start in a database instead of a topic, OLake Go also reads Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB, MongoDB and SQL Server with change capture (CDC). It writes straight to Iceberg or Parquet, with no Kafka in between. See our comparison of the options.

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > FAQs
text:
Q1. What is a data streaming platform?

It's software that takes in a continuous flow of events, stores them in order and lets other programs read them. Think Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis or Google Cloud Pub/Sub.

Q2. What is the difference between a streaming platform and a message queue?

A queue usually hands each message to one worker and then throws it away. A streaming platform keeps events as a log, so many readers can read and replay them. Microsoft's Event Hubs docs say Apache Kafka does not implement the competing-consumer queue pattern or dead-letter queues, which its Service Bus and Event Grid products cover.

Q3. Which data streaming platform is cheapest?

It depends on your workload, because the meters differ: per GB, per hour, per unit or per tier. Kafka and Pulsar have no licence fee, but they need staff and servers. Pub/Sub gives the first 10 GiB each month free, then charges $40 per TiB (Google's pricing page) (checked Oct 2026).

Q4. Is Apache Kafka a data streaming platform?

Yes. The Apache project describes Kafka as an event streaming platform that publishes, stores and processes streams of events. Kafka's own intro page describes Kafka Connect, not the brokers, as the part that imports data from databases, and it describes no Iceberg writer, so you'll need connectors, vendor features or a reader such as OLake Go for those.

Q5. Can I move from Kafka to a cloud service later?

It's much easier if both speak the Kafka API. Microsoft says Kafka applications can often use an Event Hubs endpoint by changing only their configuration, and AWS says MSK runs open-source Kafka. The Kinesis and Pub/Sub pages we read do not mention Kafka API support, so plan on code changes.

Q6. How long can each platform keep events?

Kinesis keeps records from `24 hours` to `365 days` (quotas) (checked Oct 2026), and Pub/Sub keeps topic messages up to `31 days` (quotas) (checked Oct 2026). With Kafka, retention is a per-topic setting and the broker default is `168` hours (seven days). Pulsar sets storage quotas and message time to live (TTL) per namespace (multi-tenancy docs).

Q7. Do these platforms write Apache Iceberg tables?

title: Compare: Best Data Streaming Platforms in 2026, Compared | OLake > FAQs (part 2)
text:
Some say they do, through add-on features: Confluent Tableflow, WarpStream Tableflow, Redpanda Iceberg topics (enterprise licence), Amazon MSK streaming tables (Express brokers), Kinesis streaming tables (on-demand mode) and Striim (Google Cloud Storage or Amazon S3 Tables). Kafka's intro page, the Event Hubs overview and the Pub/Sub overview describe no Iceberg writer. OLake Go reads a Kafka topic into Iceberg or Parquet, as our Kafka docs describe.

Q8. Who owns Confluent now?

IBM. Confluent's own press release says IBM completed its acquisition of Confluent on March 17, 2026. Kafka itself is an Apache Software Foundation project, as the Kafka downloads page shows.

Q9. Does Pub/Sub charge for both writing and reading?

Yes, both. Google's pricing page (checked Oct 2026) counts bytes written to a topic and bytes read from a subscription as throughput.

Q10. Is Redpanda open source?

Not fully, no. Redpanda's licensing docs (checked Oct 2026) say the Community Edition uses the Business Source License, which is source-available, and the code converts to Apache 2.0 four years after each merge. Enterprise features need a separate licence.

text:
Two questions settle most of it. Who runs the servers, and does your code speak the Kafka API? Those cut the list to two or three names. Then price a real workload on each, since the meters differ.

title: Compare: Best Reverse ETL Tools, Compared and Sourced (2026) | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

Reverse ETL, short for reverse extract, transform, load, copies cleaned data from your data warehouse into the tools your team lives in, like a customer relationship management (CRM) system or an ad platform. So who should pick what? Go with Hightouch if marketing will own the syncs, and Fivetran Activations or Segment if you already pay that vendor.

Want a printed starting price? Look at RudderStack or Polytomic. Multiwoven is the open-source one you run yourself, and Hevo Activate is still in early access.

Before you sign anything, check how each tool bills and where it keeps its sync state. And if you only feed one or two destinations, a short script may be all you need.

- Reverse ETL moves data out of the warehouse. It sends your modeled tables to the CRMs, ad tools and support desks where teams work, usually on a schedule and not in real time.
- The bill follows a meter, and the meters differ. Hightouch counts active syncs, Fivetran Activations counts changed rows, Segment counts records sent to each destination, and RudderStack counts events.
- Several tools write to your warehouse. Segment, RudderStack and the Fivetran Advanced engine keep sync state in your warehouse, so they need write access and may use your compute.
- Some prices are not published. Hightouch self-serve, Segment and Hevo Activate show no dollar figure on the pages we read.
- You may not need one. Got one or two destinations? A short script is often cheaper.

We checked prices and limits in October 2026 against each vendor's own pages. Plans change often, so confirm on the vendor's page before you decide.

title: Compare: Best Reverse ETL Tools, Compared and Sourced (2026) | OLake > What reverse ETL is, in plain words
text:
Let's start with the boring bit. ETL stands for extract, transform, load: you pull data from apps and databases, reshape it, and drop it into a warehouse where analysts work. Reverse ETL just runs the other way.

In Fivetran's words, reverse ETL pushes enriched, modeled data back into CRMs, marketing platforms, support desks and ad networks. dbt Labs paints the same picture: transformed data goes out to end platforms to build ad audiences, personalize email or add fields to sales records.

Per Fivetran, a typical setup has four parts.

A source holds the data, usually a warehouse. A model says what to sync, as a SQL query, a dbt model or a visual picker.

A sync maps fields and sets a schedule. A destination is the tool that receives the rows.

Most syncs run on a batch schedule, such as every hour or every day. dbt Labs adds a caution: weigh how often you hit your warehouse against what you gain, and move with care on real time. So find out what the business really needs before you chase real time.

title: Compare: Best Reverse ETL Tools, Compared and Sourced (2026) | OLake > Do you need a reverse ETL tool at all?
text:
Honest question, and worth asking before you open a pricing page. Fivetran's own guide names three other ways to get warehouse data into business tools, and each fits a different case.

| Option | Where it fits | Where it hurts (Fivetran's view) |
| Custom API code | One or two destinations and an engineer to own it | Every API change, schema change and new destination means more work |
| iPaaS tools (Zapier, Workato, Tray) | Simple app-to-app automations | Not designed to use a warehouse as the source |
| Customer data platform (CDP) | Event-based use cases | Creates a second copy of your data outside the warehouse |

One catch: Fivetran sells a reverse ETL product, so read its list with that in mind.

dbt Labs adds a caution from the modeling side: the models you sync out should not do the heavy lifting that fact and dimensional models already do, so keep them thin.

text:
You may still spot Grouparoo in some lists.

Its GitHub repository was archived by its owner on April 12, 2022, and Grouparoo's own site says it has been acquired by Airbyte. So we did not list it as an option.

Hidden costs and limits to check before you buy
The sticker price is only half the story. Three checks save the most pain.

Where does sync state live? Tools that track what changed need somewhere to keep the record. Segment and RudderStack create tables in your warehouse. Fivetran's Advanced engine keeps state in your warehouse too, and its Basic engine keeps it on Fivetran's side.

In-warehouse state means write access and your own compute, so ask your security team first. (They'll thank you for asking early.)

What is counted? Active syncs, changed rows, records per destination and events are four different meters.

The worked example below shows how one job reads on each meter. Do the sums for your own numbers before you commit.

How fast is fast enough? Published floors range from hourly (Hightouch Free and Self-serve) to 15 minutes (Segment) (checked Oct 2026). Hevo Activate says 5 minutes, but it is in early access. dbt Labs says to weigh how often you hit your warehouse against the benefit and to move with caution on real time, so ask what the business needs before you pay for speed.

title: Compare: Best Reverse ETL Tools, Compared and Sourced (2026) | OLake > FAQ
text:
Q1. What is reverse ETL in simple terms?

It's copying cleaned data from your data warehouse into the business tools your team uses, such as a CRM, an ad platform or a support desk. Regular ETL loads data into the warehouse, and reverse ETL sends the results back out. Fivetran describes it as pushing enriched, modeled warehouse data into the systems where teams work.

Q2. What is the difference between ETL and reverse ETL?

The direction, that's all. ETL pulls data from apps and databases into a warehouse, and reverse ETL pushes warehouse data into apps. Fivetran calls them different halves of the same data lifecycle, not competitors.

Q3. Is reverse ETL real time?

Usually not. Fivetran says syncs often run every hour or every day, and published limits back that up: Hightouch Free and Self-serve are hourly, and Segment's shortest gap is 15 minutes (checked Oct 2026). dbt Labs advises moving with caution on real time, and says there is a cost-benefit question in how often you hit your warehouse.

Q4. How much do reverse ETL tools cost?

It depends on the meter. RudderStack's Growth plan is $265 a month at 1 million events, Polytomic says pricing begins at $500 a month, and Hightouch has a free plan with 2 active syncs. Fivetran Activations bills by Monthly Active Rows with a free cap of 3,500 a month. Fivetran's Standard rates are in its Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026). Segment, Hevo Activate and Hightouch self-serve show no dollar price on the pages we read.

Q5. Do reverse ETL tools need write access to my warehouse?

Some do, so check. Segment keeps its sync state in a schema in your warehouse, RudderStack uses a schema you create, and Fivetran's Advanced engine needs read and write access. Fivetran's Basic engine needs read-only access and keeps state on its own side, but it is slower.

Q6. Is there an open-source reverse ETL tool?

Yes. Multiwoven is open source under AGPL-3.0, and GitHub lists regular releases through October 2026. Airbyte also describes its platform as covering reverse ETL, and its pricing page says Airbyte Core is free to self-host, under the Elastic License 2.0 (ELv2). Grouparoo's repository was archived in April 2022, so skip that one.

Q7. Do I need a reverse ETL tool?

title: Compare: Best Reverse ETL Tools, Compared and Sourced (2026) | OLake > FAQ (part 2)
text:
Not always. For one or two destinations, a script or a general automation tool can be enough. Fivetran lists custom code, iPaaS tools and customer data platforms as the main alternatives, each with tradeoffs. A dedicated tool starts to pay off once your destinations, mappings and audiences multiply.

Q8. Is OLake Go a reverse ETL tool?

No. It runs the other direction: OLake Go copies Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB, MongoDB and SQL Server data into Apache Iceberg or Parquet, so it can fill the lake that engines read from. For sending warehouse data to CRMs and ad tools, use one of the tools above.

title: Compare: Best Reverse ETL Tools, Compared and Sourced (2026) | OLake > Conclusion
text:
Reverse ETL is a simple idea: take the tables your team already trusts and put them where people work. Picking a tool is the hard part. The meters, the sync floors and the access each one needs all differ, and several prices aren't public.

So start from your own situation.

Already on Fivetran or Segment? Test their own product first. Want a free start?

Try Hightouch or RudderStack, and if you'd rather host the software yourself, look at Multiwoven. Whatever you pick, ask where sync state is kept before anyone signs.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

There is no single best big data tool. Big data work has four jobs, and most tools only do one of them. Hadoop (HDFS), Amazon S3, Cassandra and MongoDB store data, Kafka moves streams, Spark and Flink process data, and Trino, BigQuery, Snowflake and Databricks answer queries.

Pick one tool per job, or one cloud platform that bundles several. Then check how each one bills before you commit.

A small team that only needs reports can start with S3 files and one managed warehouse. Jump to which tool for which situation for a quick pick.

- Big data tools aren't rivals. A storage tool, a streaming tool and a query tool sit side by side in one stack, so one ranked list of all three misleads you.
- The open-source projects here are still shipping. Hadoop `3.5.0` came out April 2, 2026, Kafka `4.3.1` on June 25, Flink `2.3.0` on June 25, Spark `4.2.0` on July 14 and Trino `483` on July 17. Yes, Hadoop is still maintained.
- Kafka no longer needs ZooKeeper.Kafka `4.0` removed it, so any list that names ZooKeeper as a requirement is out of date.
- Cloud bills follow different meters. BigQuery bills by data scanned, Snowflake by credits and Databricks by DBUs. So you can't line the dollar figures up side by side.
- Free software still costs money to run. Hadoop, Spark, Flink, Kafka, Cassandra and Trino cost nothing to download. Self-hosting moves the bill to servers and the person who gets paged at 2 a.m.

We checked prices and release dates on October 8, 2026 against each vendor's or project's own pages. Plans change often, so double-check the vendor's page before you decide.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > So what does "big data" mean?
text:
AWS's "What is big data?" page describes big data as data management problems, caused by growing volume, velocity and variety of data, that traditional databases cannot solve. Volume means terabytes to petabytes, velocity means how fast data arrives and answers are needed, and variety means many sources and formats.

A "big data tool" is any software that helps with one of those problems. That's a very wide net, so one ranked list would mix wildly different products. Here, we sort them by the job each one does.

The four jobs, in plain words:

- Store: keep the data, either in files or in a database built to spread across many machines.
- Move: carry data between systems, often as a stream of events (see what a data pipeline is).
- Process: clean, join and calculate over the data, in batches or as it arrives.
- Query: let people ask questions in SQL (the standard database query language) and get answers fast.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > How we picked the 11
text:
Each of the 11 tools has a current primary page we could open: the project's own site, docs or pricing page, checked on October 8, 2026. Each claim names its source, so you can check us.

Vendor facts come from each vendor's own pages, read on October 8, 2026. We did not run the other tools.

User opinions come from named public sources only (Hacker News, PeerSpot, GitHub and BARC (an analyst firm)), opened and checked on October 8, 2026. Where a page shows a date, the quote shows its month and year. These are individual opinions and prices; one person's view, with its date and link.

Dashboard tools such as Tableau and Microsoft Power BI (business intelligence software) are out of scope. They chart data that already sits somewhere.

Same for any tool whose current status we couldn't confirm from a primary page.

The order inside each group is not a ranking.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Storage tools: where your data lives > 1. Apache Hadoop: best for storing and batch processing huge files on your own servers
text:
At a glance

- Price: Free under Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026); you pay for servers and staff
- Latest: Hadoop `3.5.0`, April 2, 2026, the first stable release of the Hadoop `3.5` line (Hadoop site)

Hadoop is really four parts in a trench coat. The first, Hadoop Common, holds shared utilities, and HDFS (the Hadoop Distributed File System) stores files across many machines. YARN (the job scheduler) shares cluster resources, and MapReduce is a system for parallel processing.

If a list calls Hadoop outdated, check its date. We found no primary source that says so, and the project shipped `3.4.3` on February 24, 2026 and `3.5.0` on April 2, 2026 (Hadoop releases).

What's good

- It's free, and you control the machines and the data.
- The Hadoop site says the library is designed to scale from single servers to thousands of machines, each offering local computation and storage.
- The same site says it handles failures at the application layer instead of relying on hardware for high availability, so a cluster of machines that may fail can still serve data.
- Per the HDFS design page (checked Oct 2026), the blocks of a file are replicated for fault tolerance, and block size and replication factor can be set per file. A typical block is `128 MB`.
- It keeps shipping. The Hadoop site (checked Oct 2026) says release `3.5.0` (April 2, 2026) holds 485 bug fixes, improvements and enhancements since `3.4`.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Storage tools: where your data lives > 1. Apache Hadoop: best for storing and batch processing huge files on your own servers (part 2)
text:
- The HDFS design page (checked Oct 2026) says a typical file is gigabytes to terabytes and that the emphasis is on high throughput of data access rather than low latency of data access. It adds that HDFS is designed more for batch processing than for interactive use.
- The same HDFS design page (checked Oct 2026) says files are write-once (appends and truncates aside) and have strictly one writer at any time, so it is not a place for many writers to edit one file.
- The HDFS design page (checked Oct 2026) says a cluster has a single NameNode that manages the file system namespace. Uber's engineering blog on its big data platform says HDFS is bottlenecked by NameNode capacity, a limit that usually occurs when data grows beyond ten petabytes and becomes a real issue beyond 50 to 100 petabytes.
- The `3.4.3` release does not include the `bundle.jar` with the AWS SDK that the `s3a` connector (the part that reads S3) needs. The Hadoop site (checked Oct 2026) tells you to download it from Maven Central yourself.

What users say:PeerSpot reviewers say, in a March 2025 review, "It scaled well" and, in a December 2023 review, "You have to create and maintain servers on your own, which can be hectic."

Better choice if you run your own cluster and your jobs are large batch jobs. If people want quick, interactive answers, look elsewhere.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Storage tools: where your data lives > 2. Amazon S3: best for file storage with no cluster to run
text:
At a glance

- Price: in US East (N. Virginia), S3 Standard storage is $0.023 per GB a month for the first 50 TB, $0.022 for the next 450 TB and $0.021 over 500 TB, per the AWS S3 price list for US East (checked Oct 2026)

S3 is AWS object storage, so you pay for the objects you store, at a rate that depends on object size, time stored and storage class.

The same price list has lower rates for other storage classes, for example $0.0125 per GB for S3 Standard Infrequent Access (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- You pay for what you store, and AWS runs the machines. No cluster to babysit.
- AWS's storage classes page (checked Oct 2026) says S3 is designed to exceed 99.999999999% (11 nines) data durability. That is a design target, not a guarantee.
- The S3 user guide says S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for `PUT` and `DELETE` requests in all AWS Regions, and that updates to a single key are atomic.
- The S3 user guide's upload page (checked Oct 2026) says one object can be up to `50 TB` when you upload it in parts with the multipart upload API.
- For Iceberg tables, AWS's S3 pricing page says S3 Tables bills on storage, requests and a monitoring fee per object stored in table buckets. That page's worked example is a daily ETL job updating an Apache Iceberg table in a table bucket (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- It stores objects and does not process or query them.
- Requests are billed by type and quantity. S3 Standard `PUT`, `COPY`, `POST` and `LIST` requests are $0.005 per 1,000 and `GET` requests are $0.0004 per 1,000 on the US East price list (checked Oct 2026).
- AWS's S3 pricing page says you pay for all bandwidth into and out of S3, except data coming in from the internet and the first 100 GB a month going out to the internet (counted across AWS services and Regions, China and GovCloud excluded) (checked Oct 2026).
- The same user guide (checked Oct 2026) says there is no way to make atomic updates across keys, so a change that touches several objects is not all-or-nothing.
- The upload page (checked Oct 2026) says a single `PUT` uploads up to `5 GB`, and the S3 console tops out at `160 GB` per file.
- Rates depend on region and storage class, and the pricing page examples each name a Region (checked Oct 2026). Check the Region before you budget.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Storage tools: where your data lives > 2. Amazon S3: best for file storage with no cluster to run (part 2)
text:
What users say: In an April 2026 Hacker News thread on S3 versus Cloudflare R2, one commenter put it this way: "S3 if you're already in the AWS ecosystem. R2 if egress costs are killing you." (Egress just means data transfer out.)

Better choice if you want storage you don't operate yourself. HDFS is better if you must keep everything on your own hardware.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Storage tools: where your data lives > 3. Apache Cassandra: best as an always-on database for application data
text:
At a glance

- Price: Free under Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026); you pay for servers and staff
- Latest: Cassandra `5.0.9`, August 7, 2026; the `4.1` line is maintained until the `7.0` release (Cassandra downloads page)

Cassandra is an open-source NoSQL distributed database. NoSQL loosely means a database outside the classic relational model.

What's good

- The project describes itself as built for scalability and high availability, with data spread across many machines. That is the project's own claim.
- Its architecture docs describe multi-master replication with tunable consistency. Consistency levels run from `ONE` (a single replica must respond) through `QUORUM` (a majority) to `ALL`.
- You choose how many copies to keep. With a replication factor (RF) of `3`, the architecture docs (checked Oct 2026) say data is written to three distinct replicas.
- The download page (checked Oct 2026) lists `5.0` as the latest GA line (`5.0.9`, August 7, 2026), maintained until the `8.0` release. The `4.1` line (`4.1.12`) is maintained until `7.0`.

Where it falls short

- Its change data capture (CDC) feature, which copies changes out, rejects writes to a flagged table (checked Oct 2026) once the CDC log reaches its configured size. So whatever reads that log has to keep draining it, or writes stop. The docs say not to enable CDC without a consumption process in place.
- The Cassandra data modeling docs (checked Oct 2026) say joins are not supported, so all required fields must sit in a single table. Because each query is backed by a table, data is duplicated across tables (denormalization).
- The same page (checked Oct 2026) gives a general guideline of under `100,000` values and under `100MB` of disk space per partition, though it says requirements vary by application.
- Concurrent updates to a key are settled by last-write-wins. The architecture docs (checked Oct 2026) say every mutation is timestamped, deletes included, and the latest version is the winning value.

What users say: In an August 2026 Hacker News thread about ACID (safe, all-or-nothing updates) in Cassandra 6, one commenter said it has "demonstrably better cost and availability" than anything else they tried. Their condition: "as long as you have a competent team".

Better choice if you need a database that keeps taking writes across many machines. It is not a reporting tool.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Storage tools: where your data lives > 4. MongoDB: best for JSON-shaped application data
text:
At a glance

- Price: Not covered here. The licence file for the server code in MongoDB's GitHub repository is the Server Side Public License (SSPL), which is not an Apache licence: MongoDB licence file (checked Oct 2026)

MongoDB stores data as flexible, JSON-like documents. Think of a document as one record, like a row, except it can hold nested fields.

What's good

- Its change streams let applications follow data changes in real time without tailing the oplog, the database's own change log, by hand.
- Applications can subscribe to all data changes on a single collection, a database or an entire deployment.
- Change streams are resumable. You pass a resume token to `resumeAfter` or `startAfter` when you open the cursor, and the `_id` field of each change event acts as that token.
- Change streams only notify on changes that have persisted to a majority of the data-bearing members in the replica set.
- By default an update event carries only the changed fields (the delta). A stream can be configured to return the most current majority-committed version of the updated document.

Where it falls short

- The change streams docs (checked Oct 2026) say change streams are restricted to database events. The same page says Atlas Stream Processing has extended functionality.
- The same change streams page (checked Oct 2026) lists replica sets and sharded clusters, and says they must use the WiredTiger storage engine and replica set protocol version `1`.
- Per the change streams docs (checked Oct 2026), time series collections do not support change streams, because they use an optimized storage format instead of tracking changes at the document level.
- Per the change streams docs (checked Oct 2026), resuming needs enough oplog history to find the token. Also, `resumeAfter` cannot resume after an `invalidate` event such as a collection drop or rename, although `startAfter` can start a new stream.
- By default MongoDB sets no minimum oplog retention period and truncates the oldest entries to hold the configured size. The MongoDB oplog docs (checked Oct 2026) put the WiredTiger default at 5% of free disk space, with a `990 MB` minimum and a `50 GB` maximum.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Storage tools: where your data lives > 4. MongoDB: best for JSON-shaped application data (part 2)
text:
What users say:PeerSpot reviews cover MongoDB Atlas, the managed service. One says "MongoDB Atlas is our primary database, and we prefer this because of the reliability of MongoDB Atlas". Another (November 2025) says "I would say pricing is an area where MongoDB Atlas could improve".

Better choice if your data is naturally nested, such as product catalogs or user profiles. For reports across many tables, a warehouse is the better home.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Moving and processing: Kafka, Spark and Flink > 5. Apache Kafka: best for sharing one stream of events between many systems
text:
At a glance

- Price: Free under Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026); the Kafka intro says fully managed services are offered by a variety of vendors
- Latest: Kafka `4.3.1`, June 25, 2026 (Kafka downloads page)

Kafka is an event streaming platform. Programs publish events to it, it stores them durably, and other programs read them back. It's a broker, which means a middle layer between the programs that write events and the ones that read them.

One stale claim is worth fixing. Kafka's upgrade notes say "Apache Kafka 4.0 only supports KRaft mode - ZooKeeper mode has been removed", so lists that name ZooKeeper as a Kafka requirement are out of date.

What's good

- Many programs can read the same stream without ever knowing about each other.
- The Kafka intro says events in a topic can be read as often as needed, because they are not deleted after consumption. Retention is a per-topic setting, and a consumer reads a partition's events in the order they were written.
- Copies are built in. The intro (checked Oct 2026) calls a replication factor of `3` a common production setting, and says a topic can be replicated even across geo-regions or datacenters.
- Kafka Connect imports and exports data as event streams, and the intro says the community already provides hundreds of ready-to-use connectors.
- Per Kafka's design docs, Kafka supports exactly-once delivery in Kafka Streams. The transactional producer plus a read-committed consumer can provide it when you read, process and write data on Kafka topics.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Moving and processing: Kafka, Spark and Flink > 5. Apache Kafka: best for sharing one stream of events between many systems (part 2)
text:
- The Kafka intro (checked Oct 2026) describes Kafka Connect, not the brokers, as the part that imports data from existing systems such as relational databases. For tools that capture database changes, see our change data capture comparison.
- The design docs (checked Oct 2026) say Kafka guarantees at-least-once delivery by default. At-most-once means disabling producer retries and committing offsets before processing.
- For exactly-once into outside systems, the same design page (checked Oct 2026) notes that many output systems will not support a two-phase commit. The workaround is to store the consumer's offset in the same place as its output.
- Check Kafka's broker defaults (checked Oct 2026): automatically created topics get a replication factor of `1`, and the largest record batch allowed is `1048588` bytes (`message.max.bytes`), about `1 MB`.
- The Kafka downloads page (checked Oct 2026) says Kafka `4.3.1` fixed a critical Kafka Streams RocksDB native memory leak along with about 15 other issues. The project aims for 3 releases a year, one every 4 months.

What users say: A July 2025 Hacker News thread about Ursa, a Kafka alternative, has a commenter calling Kafka "one of the pieces of software that has been rock solid for me". In the October 2025 Hacker News thread "Kafka is Fast", another says "Managed hosting is expensive to operate and self-managing kafka is a job in of itself."

Better choice if several systems must publish and read the same events. If hourly data is fine, a scheduled copy job is simpler.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Moving and processing: Kafka, Spark and Flink > 6. Apache Spark: best for large batch jobs and mixed workloads on one engine
text:
At a glance

- Price: Free under Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026); you pay for servers and staff
- Latest: Spark `4.2.0`, July 14, 2026; also `4.1.3` and `4.0.4` on July 15 and `3.5.9` on July 16 (Spark news page)

Spark is a distributed engine for data engineering, data science and machine learning. It runs on one machine or on a cluster.

What's good

- Spark's docs list batch work, SQL and machine learning on one engine, so there may be fewer tools to learn.
- Spark's streaming docs say micro-batch processing, the default for Structured Streaming, achieves end-to-end latencies as low as 100 milliseconds with exactly-once fault-tolerance guarantees.
- The Structured Streaming guide (checked Oct 2026) lists three types of time windows: tumbling (fixed), sliding and session. Since Spark `4.0` it encourages the `transformWithState` operator for complex stateful applications.
- Feature releases arrive steadily: `4.0.0` on May 23, 2025, `4.1.0` on December 16, 2025 and `4.2.0` on July 14, 2026, per the Spark news page (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- The Spark news page (checked Oct 2026) lists releases in July 2026 for four lines (`4.2`, `4.1`, `4.0` and `3.5`). Check which line your connectors and cloud service support before you upgrade.
- The Spark downloads page (checked Oct 2026) says Spark `4` is pre-built with Scala `2.13` and support for Scala `2.12` has been officially dropped. Check your Scala version before moving to Spark `4`.
- The Structured Streaming guide (checked Oct 2026) says streaming Datasets do not support `limit` or taking the first N rows, or `distinct` operations. Sorting works only after an aggregation in `Complete` output mode.
- Late data needs care. In the guide's (checked Oct 2026) 2-hour watermark example, the guarantee is strict in only one direction: data delayed by more than 2 hours is not guaranteed to be dropped, and may or may not get aggregated.
- For stream-stream joins, the guide (checked Oct 2026) says you have to define extra join conditions so that indefinitely old inputs cannot match future inputs. Without them the state grows without bound.

What users say:PeerSpot reviewers say "As it uses in-memory data processing, Spark is very fast" and also "Apache Spark is very difficult to use. It would require a data engineer."

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Moving and processing: Kafka, Spark and Flink > 6. Apache Spark: best for large batch jobs and mixed workloads on one engine (part 2)
text: Better choice if you have large batch jobs, or you want SQL and machine learning in one place. For stateful streams that need low delay, look at Flink.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Moving and processing: Kafka, Spark and Flink > 7. Apache Flink: best for stateful, low-delay stream processing
text:
At a glance

- Price: Free under Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026); you pay for servers and staff
- Latest: Flink `2.3.0`, June 25, 2026; `1.20.5` is the long-term support line, dated June 3, 2026 (Flink downloads page)

Flink describes itself as a distributed engine for stateful computations over unbounded and bounded data streams. "Stateful" means it remembers earlier events, such as a running total, while new ones arrive.

What's good

- The project's own site lists low latency and high throughput among its features.
- Flink's Kafka connector docs say Flink reads from and writes to Kafka topics with exactly-once guarantees.
- Big state is allowed. The Flink state backends docs say that with `EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend` the state you can keep is limited only by disk space, and that it is currently the only backend with incremental checkpoints.
- There is a long-term support line. The Flink site labels the `1.20` line as LTS, and the downloads page (checked Oct 2026) dates `1.20.5` as June 3, 2026, while `2.3.0` (June 25, 2026) is the latest stable release and `2.2.1` came out May 15, 2026.

Where it falls short

- The downloads page (checked Oct 2026) says the community supports the current and previous minor release with bugfixes, so you upgrade on the project's schedule.
- The Kafka connector docs (checked Oct 2026) say there is no connector (yet) available for Flink version `2.3`, and that Flink's streaming connectors are not part of the binary distribution.
- The default in-memory option has a ceiling. The state backends docs (checked Oct 2026) say `HashMapStateBackend` is very fast, but its state size is limited by the available memory within the cluster.
- The disk-based option is slower. The same page (checked Oct 2026) says RocksDB access leads to average performance about an order of magnitude slower than the memory state backends.
- The newer `ForStStateBackend` is, per the docs (checked Oct 2026), still experimental and not fully available for production.

What users say:PeerSpot reviews of Apache Flink include "Apache Flink makes it easy to write on-the-fly transformations on streaming data". Another reviewer says "We also need to simplify operational procedures, such as developing tools and tuning Flink clusters, as these processes can be quite complex."

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Moving and processing: Kafka, Spark and Flink > 7. Apache Flink: best for stateful, low-delay stream processing (part 2)
text: Better choice if results must update within moments of an event. If batches every few minutes are enough, Spark is simpler.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Query tools and cloud platforms: answers, on demand > 8. Trino: best for asking SQL questions across data that lives in many places
text:
At a glance

- Price: Free under Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026); you pay for servers and staff
- Latest: Trino `483`, July 17, 2026 (Trino release index)

Trino is a distributed SQL query engine. It reads data where it already sits, in files or other databases, and doesn't keep the data itself.

What's good

- Per its docs, one SQL query can reach several systems. The use cases page says Trino can be, and has been, extended to traditional relational databases and sources such as Cassandra.
- The same use cases page says it was designed as an alternative to tools that query HDFS with pipelines of MapReduce jobs, such as Hive or Pig, though it is not limited to HDFS.
- It was designed for data warehousing and analytics, meaning aggregating large amounts of data and producing reports.
- Its Iceberg connector (checked Oct 2026) supports Iceberg table spec versions `1` and `2` and data files in Parquet, ORC or Avro. Catalogs can be a Hive metastore, AWS Glue, JDBC, REST, Nessie or Snowflake.
- The same connector supports `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE` and `MERGE` statements on Iceberg tables.

Where it falls short

- The use cases page (checked Oct 2026) says Trino "is not a general-purpose relational database" and "was not designed to handle Online Transaction Processing (OLTP)", meaning many small app-style reads and writes.
- Per the Iceberg connector docs (checked Oct 2026), support for Iceberg format version `3` is experimental, and row-level updates, deletes and `OPTIMIZE` are not supported on version `3` tables.
- Writing to encrypted Iceberg tables is not supported, per the Iceberg connector docs (checked Oct 2026).
- The `table_changes` function, which reads row-level changes between two versions of an Iceberg table, does not support tables with delete files, per the Iceberg connector docs (checked Oct 2026).

What users say: A Hacker News commenter in the May 2025 thread "Databricks acquires Neon", who used Trino through AWS Athena, wrote "I really can't speak highly enough of Trino". A September 2025 GitHub issue on the Trino project reports that queries on Iceberg tables were "taking more than 1 minutes and up to 10 minutes to complete the planning stage".

Better choice if your data is already in files and you want SQL over it without loading it elsewhere. A managed warehouse is better if you'd rather not run servers.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Query tools and cloud platforms: answers, on demand > 9. Google BigQuery: best for a serverless warehouse on Google Cloud
text:
At a glance

- Price: On-demand queries bill per TiB scanned, and "the first 1 TiB of query data processed per month is free", per BigQuery pricing (checked Oct 2026)

BigQuery is a managed, serverless data warehouse. Serverless means Google runs the machines, so there is no cluster to run.

It also sells reserved capacity under three editions: Standard, Enterprise and Enterprise Plus. The pricing page says on-demand queries generally get up to `2,000` concurrent slots, shared among all queries in a project. It also says the older flat-rate model is no longer offered as of July 5, 2023, so older cost guides may be out of date (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- Google runs the servers, and the free monthly tier covers the first 1 TiB of queries.
- Standard edition slots need no commitment. The pricing page default column lists $0.04 per slot-hour (Enterprise is $0.06), billed per second with a 1-minute minimum. The rendered table does not state its region (checked Oct 2026).
- You can check cost before you pay. Google's cost best practices docs say a dry run estimates the bytes a query will read, and with a `maximum bytes billed` setting a query over the limit fails without a charge.
- Storage gets cheaper on its own. A table or partition not modified for 90 consecutive days drops to long-term storage, which cuts its price by approximately 50%, and the first 10 GiB of storage each month is free, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Enterprise and Enterprise Plus can take a 1-year commitment at a 20% discount or a 3-year commitment at 40%, per Google's editions page (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Query tools and cloud platforms: answers, on demand > 9. Google BigQuery: best for a serverless warehouse on Google Cloud (part 2)
text:
- The on-demand bill follows how much data each query scans, so a query that reads a huge table in full costs real money. We found no self-hosted option in Google's docs (checked Oct 2026).
- A `LIMIT` clause does not cut the bill. The pricing page says you are charged for the data processed in the columns you select even with an explicit `LIMIT`, and the cost best practices add that on non-clustered tables a `LIMIT` won't reduce compute costs (checked Oct 2026).
- On-demand charges are rounded up to the nearest MB, with a minimum of `10 MB` processed per table a query references and per query, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- The editions page shows the Standard edition has no access to capacity commitments, fine-grained security controls (column-level access, row-level security, data masking), BigQuery ML or VPC Service Controls (checked Oct 2026).
- Capacity (slot) pricing does not apply to streaming inserts or to using the BigQuery Storage API, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

The pricing page's table lists $6.25 per TiB on demand and states no region (checked Oct 2026). At that rate, scanning 10 TiB in a month bills 9 TiB after the free first TiB, so 9 x $6.25 = $56.25. Scanning 100 TiB bills 99 x $6.25 = $618.75.

The bill follows what queries read, not how long anything runs, and the pricing page's own advice is to use partitioning and clustering to read less.

What users say: A respondent to the BARC panel survey (April 2025) wrote "I love using it as a product, but it can get pricey if you handle large datasets."

Better choice if you already live in Google Cloud and want no cluster to manage.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Query tools and cloud platforms: answers, on demand > 10. Snowflake: best for a managed warehouse with published per-credit prices
text:
At a glance

- Price: $2.00 per credit on Standard, $3.00 on Enterprise and $4.00 on Business Critical, on demand, AWS US East, per the Snowflake Service Consumption Table, effective October 15, 2026 (checked Oct 2026)

In Snowflake, a warehouse is a block of compute, and it uses credits at an hourly rate. For Standard warehouses: Extra Small uses 1, Small 2, Medium 4 and Large 8, according to the Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026). On-demand storage on AWS US East is $23.00 per terabyte per month, per the same table (checked Oct 2026).

From those published rates: a Medium warehouse (4 credits an hour) running 2 hours a day for 30 days uses 240 credits, or $480 on Standard at $2.00 a credit.

That is compute only. Storage and other charges are extra.

What's good

- Prices per credit, by edition and region, are published in one table (checked Oct 2026). So you can work out compute cost in advance.
- Per Snowflake's compute cost docs, credits are billed per second with a 60-second minimum, and a suspended warehouse does not use any credits.
- Sizes double in cost at each step. The same table lists Standard warehouses at 1 credit an hour for Extra Small, then 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 and 512 for the 6XL size (checked Oct 2026).
- Ingestion has published rates too. The table lists Snowpipe at 0.0037 credits per GB, and Snowpipe Streaming (high-performance architecture) at 0.0037 credits per uncompressed GB (checked Oct 2026).
- Snowflake's Time Travel docs (checked Oct 2026) say a 1-day (24-hour) retention period is automatic for all accounts. On Enterprise Edition and higher, permanent tables can be set from 0 up to 90 days.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Query tools and cloud platforms: answers, on demand > 10. Snowflake: best for a managed warehouse with published per-credit prices (part 2)
text:
- Credit prices vary by region. For example, AWS EU Frankfurt is $2.60 on Standard and $3.90 on Enterprise on the same table (checked Oct 2026).
- A Time Travel period longer than 1 day requires Enterprise Edition or higher, and the docs (checked Oct 2026) say extended retention needs extra storage that shows up in your monthly storage charges.
- Cloud services usage is charged only when daily cloud services consumption exceeds 10% of the daily usage of virtual warehouses, per the compute cost docs (checked Oct 2026). So an account that leans on cloud services can see a charge beyond warehouse hours.
- Gen 2 warehouses list more credits per hour than the standard-warehouse table. It shows Extra Small at 1.35 on AWS and 1.25 on Azure, against 1 for a standard Extra Small (checked Oct 2026).
- Ingestion charges depend on file type. A footnote on the table says text files such as CSV, XML and JSON are charged at uncompressed size, while binary files such as Parquet, Avro and ORC are charged at their observed size regardless of compression (checked Oct 2026).

Better choice if you want one managed warehouse and can estimate your hours of compute. If you're fully on Google Cloud, BigQuery is simpler.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Query tools and cloud platforms: answers, on demand > 11. Databricks: best for teams that want managed Spark-style jobs and SQL in one paid platform
text:
At a glance

- Price: On AWS, US East, Premium plan: SQL Serverless $0.70, SQL Pro $0.55 and SQL Classic $0.22 per Databricks Unit (DBU), per Databricks SQL pricing (checked Oct 2026)

Databricks meters compute in DBUs, its own unit. The warehouse types doc says Classic and Pro warehouses keep their compute layer in your own cloud account. On the pricing page, the SQL Serverless price includes cloud instance cost (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- SQL warehouses and jobs are both priced in DBUs on Databricks' pricing pages, so one unit covers both (checked Oct 2026).
- Serverless SQL warehouses start quickly. The SQL warehouse types doc puts startup typically between 2 and 6 seconds.
- Its Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026) say Databricks supports Iceberg tables that use Parquet and versions `1`, `2` and `3` of the Iceberg specification. They can be managed by Unity Catalog or by foreign catalogs such as AWS Glue, Hive metastore or Snowflake Horizon Catalog.
- The same page says managed Iceberg tables can also be created from outside engines that support the Iceberg REST Catalog API, such as Apache Spark, Flink, Trino or Kafka.

Where it falls short

- You can't total a monthly bill from the page alone. DBUs per hour for each warehouse size weren't on the pricing pages we read (checked Oct 2026), so use the vendor's calculator.
- Pro and Classic warehouses are slower to start. The warehouse types doc (checked Oct 2026) says each takes several minutes, typically about 4, and a Classic warehouse's compute layer lives in your own AWS account.
- Plan names shift by cloud. The SQL pricing page notes that the Premium tier on Azure Databricks corresponds to the Enterprise tier on AWS and GCP, so check the tier before comparing numbers (checked Oct 2026).
- Iceberg has conditions. The Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026) say foreign Iceberg tables are read-only in Databricks, branching and tagging are not supported, and the external access page says external Iceberg engines can't read views.
- Managed Iceberg tables can only be created if predictive optimization is enabled for table maintenance, and the docs (checked Oct 2026) ask for Databricks Runtime `16.4` LTS or above.

Better choice if you want managed jobs and SQL together. If SQL reports are most of your work, compare it with Snowflake, whose pricing table lists credit rates by warehouse size.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Other names you'll meet
text:
You'll bump into a few more names. Apache HBase and Apache Storm are open-source projects for random-access storage and real-time streams. ClickHouse is a column database for analytics, and Apache Airflow schedules the steps of a pipeline.

Open table formats such as Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake and Apache Hudi sit between files and query engines. Several engines can read the same tables. For those lake layers in more depth, see our best data lake tools comparison.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > How to choose: four questions
text:
- Is the work batch or real time? Big batch jobs point to Spark or Hadoop. If results must update within moments of an event, think Kafka with Flink.
- Do you want to run servers? Hadoop, Cassandra, Kafka, Spark, Flink and Trino are free to download but need staff to run. S3, BigQuery, Snowflake and Databricks are run for you, and you pay by meter.
- Which cloud are you on? BigQuery runs on Google Cloud and S3 on AWS. Snowflake and Databricks publish prices by cloud and region, so the same workload can cost different amounts in different places.
- Can you estimate the meter? If you know your hours of compute, credits and DBUs are predictable. If you know the bytes your queries read, the per-TiB model is easier to forecast.

If you can't answer question 4 yet, start on a free tier or a small open-source setup, and don't sign a commitment on a rate you can't turn into a monthly figure.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Which tool for which situation?
text:
| If you need to... | Start with | Why | Watch out for |
| Keep files on your own hardware | Hadoop (HDFS) | You control the machines | Built for large batch files, not quick answers |
| Store files without running servers | Amazon S3 | AWS runs it | Requests and transfer bill separately |
| Run an always-on app database | Cassandra or MongoDB | Built for application data | CDC log limit (Cassandra); change streams limits (MongoDB) |
| Share one event stream | Kafka | Many readers, one stream | Database import goes through Kafka Connect |
| Crunch large batches | Spark | One engine for SQL and machine learning | Releases on four lines in July 2026 |
| React to events in moments | Flink | Stateful stream processing | Upgrade on its support schedule |
| Query files in place | Trino | No loading step | Not for app-style reads and writes |
| Run a managed warehouse | BigQuery, Snowflake or Databricks | No cluster to run | Three different bill meters |
| Copy database tables into Iceberg or Parquet | OLake Go | Open source loader you run yourself | Pair it with a catalog and a query engine |

Most real stacks mix three or four of these. Think files in S3 or HDFS, a stream in Kafka, processing in Spark or Flink, and a query tool on top.

For a quicker pick, answer the five short questions below.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Which tool for which situation? > Which big data tool fits you?
text:
Question 1 of 5

What is the main job you need done?

Big data has four jobs: store, move, process and query. Pick the one that hurts most.

Where OLake Go fits
The tools above store, process and query data that already sits somewhere. Getting database data into a lake in the first place is a separate job, and it is the one OLake Go handles. It is our open-source tool, licensed Apache 2.0 (OLake on GitHub).

It runs a full load of your tables, and change data capture is available for PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, MongoDB and SQL Server. It also reads Oracle and Db2 tables, Kafka topics and S3 files. It writes Apache Iceberg tables or Parquet files to storage you control, with many Iceberg catalogs to choose from, including AWS Glue, Unity Catalog (Databricks), BigLake (Google) and S3 Tables.

Our compatibility page lists Spark, Flink and Trino among the engines that read those Iceberg tables. For Snowflake, OLake Go can write Iceberg tables into a Snowflake database through the Snowflake Horizon Catalog from v0.11.0, and Snowflake reads tables in other catalogs as read-only. You run OLake Go yourself with Docker or Helm; the quickstart walks through it, and the sources and sync modes are in the OLake docs.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > FAQs
text:
Q1. What are big data tools?

They're software for storing, moving, processing and querying data that is too large or fast for a traditional database. AWS ties big data to growing volume, velocity and variety. Most tools do one job, so a stack usually combines several.

Q2. Is Hadoop still maintained?

Yes. The Hadoop releases page lists `3.5.0`, released April 2, 2026, and `3.4.3`, released February 24, 2026. HDFS is built for large files and batch work, so it suits some jobs better than others.

Q3. Should I pick Spark or Flink?

Depends on the job. Spark is the broader engine for large batch jobs, SQL and machine learning. Flink describes itself as an engine for stateful computations over streams, so it fits results that must update within moments, and many teams use both.

Q4. Does Kafka still need ZooKeeper?

No. Kafka's upgrade notes say Kafka `4.0` only supports KRaft mode and that ZooKeeper mode has been removed. If a list calls ZooKeeper a requirement, it's out of date.

Q5. How do BigQuery, Snowflake and Databricks bill?

BigQuery's on-demand model bills per TiB scanned, with the first 1 TiB each month free (BigQuery pricing) (checked Oct 2026). Snowflake bills credits, at $2.00 each on Standard in AWS US East (Service Consumption Table) (checked Oct 2026). Databricks bills DBUs, for example $0.70 each for SQL Serverless on AWS US East Premium (Databricks SQL pricing) (checked Oct 2026). Compare real workloads.

Q6. Which big data tools are free?

Hadoop, Spark, Flink, Kafka, Cassandra and Trino are open-source projects you can download at no charge. You still pay for servers and the people who run them, which is the catch. BigQuery has a free tier of 1 TiB of queries a month (BigQuery pricing) (checked Oct 2026). We didn't check trials for Snowflake or Databricks, so read their pages.

Q7. Is Spark a replacement for Hadoop?

Not exactly. Hadoop bundles storage (HDFS), a scheduler (YARN) and MapReduce. Spark is a processing engine, and Spark's cluster overview lists Hadoop YARN as one of several cluster managers it supports. Many teams keep HDFS or S3 for files and use Spark for the work.

Q8. Do I need all of these tools?

No. Start from the job you must do. A small team may need only S3 files and a managed warehouse.

Q9. How do I get database data into a lake for Spark, Flink or Trino to read?

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > FAQs (part 2)
text: You need a loading tool. OLake Go is our open-source option: it loads database tables into Apache Iceberg or Parquet on storage you control. Our docs list Spark, Flink and Trino among the engines that read those Iceberg tables, and from v0.11.0 it can write Iceberg tables into Snowflake through the Snowflake Horizon Catalog.

title: Compare: Best Big Data Tools in 2026, Sorted by Job | OLake > Conclusion
text:
Big data tools work as a kit. Figure out whether your problem is storing, moving, processing or querying, then pick one tool for that job, or one platform that bundles several. Read the bill meter as closely as the feature list.

title: Compare: Best Data Migration Tools in 2026, Picked by Job | OLake
text:
There is no single best pick among data migration tools, because "migration" covers four different jobs. This post sorts twelve tools by job, with dated prices and what each one cannot do.

Key takeaways

- Pick by job first. For a database, start with your target cloud's own service (AWS Database Migration Service (DMS), Azure Database Migration Service or Google Database Migration Service); for Oracle or mixed estates, look at Oracle GoldenGate or Qlik Replicate.
- For files, split the job. Copying files between storage systems is AWS DataSync. Loading CSV, JSON or Parquet files from S3 into Iceberg tables is OLake Go (S3 source docs). Warehouse tables and business apps go to Fivetran, Airbyte, Hevo or Skyvia.
- Some cloud moves list no charge.Google says native moves to Cloud SQL or AlloyDB for PostgreSQL carry no additional charge (checked Oct 2026).
- Check for retirements first. Microsoft's retirement notice (checked Oct 2026) says Azure Database Migration Service (classic) for SQL Server scenarios is not supported after 15 March 2026.
- Few tools write Apache Iceberg. The AWS DMS targets page, the Azure DMS overview and the Google DMS overview do not name Iceberg as a destination.

title: Compare: Best Data Migration Tools in 2026, Picked by Job | OLake > What data migration means
text:
AWS defines data migration as moving data from one computing environment or storage system to another, and lists storage, database and application migration among the types. In this post, "source" is where data starts and "target" is where it ends up.

Migration is a one-time move with an end date. Replication keeps a copy current for as long as you need it, which is a different job.

| Job | What it does | Ends when | Example tools in this post |
| Database migration | Moves a database to a new server, cloud or engine | You switch the app to the new database | AWS DMS, Azure DMS, Google DMS |
| Storage migration | Moves files and objects between storage systems | The files are copied and checked | AWS DataSync |
| Loading for analysis | Copies data into a warehouse or lake, often on a schedule | You stop the pipeline (it often runs for years) | OLake Go, Datastream, Fivetran, Airbyte, Hevo, Skyvia |
| Schema migration | Versions changes to a database's tables with scripts | Never; it is part of normal development | Not covered here |

The last row is a different tool family. Flyway's docs describe its migrations as SQL scripts that capture incremental schema and data changes, so it's version control for your tables, not a way to move data between systems.

title: Compare: Best Data Migration Tools in 2026, Picked by Job | OLake > What data migration means > Homogeneous or heterogeneous
text:
Google's docs say a homogeneous migration moves between the same database technology, for example MySQL to Cloud SQL for MySQL. A heterogeneous one changes the technology, such as Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL.

Heterogeneous moves are harder, because table definitions, data types and code all have to be converted. AWS lists Database Migration Service (DMS) Schema Conversion for that job.

title: Compare: Best Data Migration Tools in 2026, Picked by Job | OLake > What data migration means > Offline or online
text:
Offline copies a point-in-time snapshot, so changes made after it starts are not carried over, and you normally stop writes during the copy. The online (continuous) kind follows a full load with a flow of changes until you switch, as Google's docs describe.

Online usually reads the database's transaction log, where every change is recorded in order. That's change data capture (CDC).

title: Compare: Best Data Migration Tools in 2026, Picked by Job | OLake > How we picked
text:
Each tool had to move data out of a database or storage system, still be maintained, and publish documentation we could open. We compared job, sources and targets, ongoing changes and price from each vendor's own pages, checked in October 2026. This is a reading of vendor documents, not a lab test, and what vendors say about themselves is reported as their claim.

Schema-migration tools and backup products are left out.

title: Compare: Best Data Migration Tools in 2026, Picked by Job | OLake > The 12 best data migration tools > Database to database
text:
**1. AWS Database Migration Service: best for moving databases into AWS**

At a glance

- Job: One-time moves or ongoing replication between databases
- Price: Replication instance hours or Serverless DCU hours (a DCU is 2 GB of memory), plus storage, with no separate CDC fee; dms.t3.medium lists at $0.0745 an hour in us-east-1, on demand, Single-AZ (AWS DMS pricing (checked Oct 2026); price file published September 11, 2026)

AWS says a DMS task can run a full load first and then capture changes. The docs list sources such as Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, MongoDB and Db2.

What's good

- AWS's targets list includes S3, Redshift, DynamoDB, Kafka and many database engines.

Where it falls short

- AWS's best practices page (checked Oct 2026) says DMS ongoing replication does not provide real-time replication and that AWS offers no SLA (service level agreement) for CDC latency. It adds that latency can spike to several minutes or longer when the source is busy.
- The target list (checked Oct 2026) names S3, Kinesis, Kafka and others, and not Apache Iceberg. An AWS blog has DMS write S3 files and Glue jobs load them into Iceberg.

Ask AWS: its product page (checked Oct 2026) says "Zero data loss and data accuracy are maintained" through data validation. That is AWS's claim, and the validation limits further down show what it cannot check.

**2. Azure Database Migration Service: best for SQL Server into Azure**

At a glance

- Job: Moves SQL Server databases to Azure SQL targets
- Price: Not established for the current service. The only pricing page we found is for Azure DMS (classic): a free Standard tier for offline moves and Premium 4-vCore at $0.37 an hour, free for the first 6 months (Central US, Microsoft's pricing page (checked Oct 2026))

Microsoft's overview lists three targets: Azure SQL Database (offline), Azure SQL Managed Instance and SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines (both online and offline). It also lists schema migration, Azure CLI and PowerShell automation, and private endpoints. The pricing page says "classic" and does not say whether the portal service has the same rates, so treat those figures as history.

What's good

- Microsoft's overview lists online moves for two of its three targets.
- Schema migration and command-line automation are listed as supported in the overview.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Migration Tools in 2026, Picked by Job | OLake > The 12 best data migration tools > Database to database (part 2)
text:
- Microsoft's overview table (checked Oct 2026) does not list assessment, login migration or databases encrypted with Transparent Data Encryption for the portal version.
- Microsoft's retirement notice (checked Oct 2026) says DMS (classic) for SQL Server scenarios was not supported after 15 March 2026.
- That notice (checked Oct 2026) points users to the portal service and puts MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB scenarios out of scope.

Check before you rely on it: Microsoft's product page says the service supports SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB migrations (checked Oct 2026). The Learn overview names Azure SQL targets only, so confirm your exact source and target pair on Microsoft's supported-scenarios page.

**3. Google Database Migration Service: best for moving into Cloud SQL or AlloyDB**

At a glance

- Job: One-time or continuous moves into Google Cloud databases
- Price: No additional charge for native same-engine moves to Cloud SQL or AlloyDB for PostgreSQL; per GiB processed for different-engine moves (Google's pricing page (checked Oct 2026))

Google's overview lists same-engine moves to Cloud SQL for MySQL, Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, AlloyDB and Cloud SQL for SQL Server. It also lists different-engine moves from Oracle or SQL Server to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL or AlloyDB.

What's good

- Native same-engine moves to Cloud SQL or AlloyDB for PostgreSQL carry no additional charge, and the pricing page (checked Oct 2026) says per-GiB billing counts raw, uncompressed bytes.
- A continuous mode that follows the first copy with changes.

Where it falls short

- Destinations are Google Cloud databases only, and no lake or warehouse is listed there.
- The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) gives the free backfill allowance two ways, 500 GiB in the summary and 50 GiB in the details, so we quote neither.

Ask Google: its product page (checked Oct 2026) says the service gives "highly accurate, high-fidelity migrations" and that you can run a validation first. Ask what the validation compares.

**4. Oracle GoldenGate: best for Oracle estates and long-running or two-way copies**

At a glance

title: Compare: Best Data Migration Tools in 2026, Picked by Job | OLake > The 12 best data migration tools > Database to database (part 3)
text:
- Job: Real-time copies between many systems, including one-way, two-way and multi-way setups
- Price: Oracle's Technology Global Price List (checked Oct 2026) (edition dated September 15, 2026) lists GoldenGate at $17,500 per Processor or $350 per Named User Plus, and counts the processors or users at both the capture and the apply database. This is list price, and we do not know what any buyer pays.

Oracle's FAQ says GoldenGate captures, transforms and delivers changes across systems in real time, and lists zero-downtime migrations among its uses. Its supported list includes Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Db2, MongoDB, Kafka, Snowflake and Apache Iceberg.

What's good

- Oracle's FAQ lists Oracle among its supported sources and documents two-way setups, with advice to define conflict rules.
- GoldenGate Free (checked Oct 2026) is limited to Oracle databases of 20 GB or smaller. Oracle says it can be used in production but is not supported by Oracle Support (community forums only), and it cannot be used with fully licensed GoldenGate products.

Where it falls short

- Iceberg writing sits in a separate product, GoldenGate for Distributed Applications and Analytics, per Oracle's FAQ and Iceberg docs.
- Oracle's FAQ (checked Oct 2026) says it cannot capture from Salesforce, Teradata or TimesTen.

title: Compare: Best Data Migration Tools in 2026, Picked by Job | OLake > Which data migration tool should you pick? > Which data migration tool fits you?
text:
Question 1 of 5

What are you moving?

The post says migration is really four different jobs, so start here.

How an online database cutover runs
Google's architecture guide splits an online database migration into six phases and uses the term "near-zero downtime" for the goal.

Phase 6, fallback, is a contingency for a switchover that goes wrong. Google says clients of the old source databases "need to be kept available and operational so that they can be turned on in a fallback".

| Phase | What happens | What Google's guide says to check |
| 1. Initial load | The existing data is copied | Note the source system time right before the migration starts |
| 2. Continuing migration | Changes keep flowing to the target | Avoid changing schema, data values or migration processes |
| 3. Draining | You quiesce the source and apply the last changes | No data changes at the source; wait for all changes to reach the target |
| 4. Switchover | Clients are pointed at the target | Test basic client functions before opening production access |
| 5. Source deletion | The old database is removed after a successful switchover | Take a final backup of each source database first |
| 6. Fallback (contingency) | Changes on the target are applied back to the source | Treated as a full migration, with testing |

Quiesce means pause writes. Google says a fallback might be required days or weeks after the switchover, so keep the source until you are sure you will not need to go back.

AWS's best practices page adds two tool-level points. AWS DMS does not automatically create secondary indexes, foreign keys or user accounts on the target, so those are on you. AWS also recommends running a small test migration first.

title: Compare: Best Data Migration Tools in 2026, Picked by Job | OLake > How an online database cutover runs > Prove the copy matches
text:
AWS DMS has a data validation feature that compares each source row with its target row and reports mismatches. Ask every vendor for something like it.

AWS lists these limits on its data validation page (checked Oct 2026):

- Tables need a primary key or unique index, so a table without one cannot be checked.
- Validation adds queries on both databases and takes extra time beyond the migration itself.
- Rows that change constantly cannot be compared, and views are not supported.
- AWS says validation stops if it finds more than 10,000 failed or suspended records.
- A validation-only task checks rows without migrating data, for a check just before a cutover.

title: Compare: Best Data Migration Tools in 2026, Picked by Job | OLake > How an online database cutover runs > A small check you can try (an illustration, not a result)
text:
This is a made-up example. We have not run it on the other tools.

- Make a test table with three rows: (1, "a"), (2, "b") and (3, "c"). Start the migration.
- While it runs, insert (4, "d"), update row 2 to "b2" and delete row 3.
- Switch over, then count rows and compare a checksum on both sides. Expect (1, "a"), (2, "b2") and (4, "d"), with no row 3 and no duplicates.
- For a lake target, check whether deletes arrive as removed rows or as extra change records.

What are data migration tools?

Tools that move data from one system or storage location to another.

What is the difference between data migration and data replication?

Migration is a one-time move. Replication keeps copies in step for as long as you need them.

What is the difference between online and offline migration?

Offline copies a point-in-time snapshot and you normally stop writes during the copy. Online follows a first full copy with a flow of changes, so your app keeps running until a short switch.

Are there free data migration tools?

Some moves list no charge. Google says native same-engine moves to Cloud SQL or AlloyDB for PostgreSQL carry no additional charge (checked Oct 2026). Fivetran, Hevo and Skyvia have capped free plans (checked Oct 2026), and Airbyte Core is free to self-host under the Elastic License 2.0, though you pay for your own servers.

What is the best tool to migrate a database to the cloud?

Start with the service from the cloud you're moving to: AWS DMS, Azure Database Migration Service or Google Database Migration Service. For Oracle-heavy or mixed estates, look at Oracle GoldenGate or Qlik Replicate.

Can data migration tools write Apache Iceberg?

A few can, with limits. The AWS DMS target list, the Azure DMS overview and the Google DMS overview do not name it. Datastream writes Iceberg in BigQuery in append-only mode. Fivetran's Managed Data Lake Service does not support position deletes. Airbyte has Iceberg destinations for S3 and GCS. OLake Go (ours) writes Iceberg and Parquet (checked Oct 2026).

How do I check that migrated data is correct?

Check both sides before you switch. AWS DMS can compare source and target rows, but it needs a primary key or unique index. For other tools, count rows and compare a checksum, as in the small check above.

What is a cutover in a database migration?

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

An orchestrator is the thing that runs your data jobs in the right order, on time, and yells when one fails. It doesn't copy or reshape the data itself. If your team writes Python, start with Prefect or Dagster.

Apache Airflow is free and open source, and you can host it yourself or rent it from Astronomer, Amazon or Google. Already living inside one cloud? Its own service (Step Functions, Data Factory or Databricks Lakeflow Jobs) is often the shortest path.

- The billing meters differ more than the prices. One tool charges per hour of a running server. Another charges per step, another per credit and another per seat. The same daily job can cost $0 on one meter and more than $250 a month on another (worked example below).
- Free software still has a cost. Airflow, Dagster, Prefect and Kestra all have a free open-source version, but you run the servers and carry the pager.
- Some prices are not published.Kestra Cloud and Enterprise, and Astronomer's Business plan, show no price (checked Oct 2026).

We checked prices on October 1, 2026 against each vendor's own pages.

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What is data orchestration?
text:
IBM (the computer company), in its explainer on this topic, defines the idea as the management and coordination of data flows across different systems, processes and tools.

IBM adds that tasks often start on a clock (every night at 2 a.m.), a dependency (when the earlier task finishes) or an event (a real-world signal, such as an API call). It also says this isn't the same as data integration. Integration, such as extract, transform, load (ETL, which copies data and reshapes it on the way), is one of the jobs an orchestrator coordinates.

Most tools here describe a workflow as a DAG, short for directed acyclic graph. It's a set of steps with arrows showing which step must finish before another starts, and no loops back.

Airflow won't copy your database, and an ingestion tool won't decide that the report job must wait for the load job. If you are choosing the copying tool, see our best data pipeline tools comparison.

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > How we picked (and what we didn't do)
text:
A tool had to be actively maintained, publish its own documentation, and be built to run data workflows on a schedule or an event. Vendor facts come from each vendor's own pages, read on October 1, 2026. We did not run the other tools.

Some tools get a "What users say" line. It is a real public comment or review that we re-opened on October 1, 2026, with its site and month. The sites include Hacker News (HN, a tech discussion site), PeerSpot (a software review site) and DEV (a blog site for developers). We kept opinions and first-hand cost experience only, and a tool gets a quote line only when we found both a positive and a critical comment for it. These are individual opinions and prices; one person's view, with its date and link.

One bit of news matters here. In July 2026, Prefect announced that it is acquiring Dagster Labs. Prefect's announcement page says Dagster and Dagster+ stay, and nothing changes for current users (checked Oct 2026).

We left out Matillion and Informatica because they're bundled data platforms. The order below is by group, not a ranking.
