title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The open-source orchestrators > 1. Apache Airflow: best for Python teams that want free software and many hosting choices
text:
At a glance

- Price: free software under Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026); managed hosting is sold separately (see the three hosted options below)

Airflow is the name you'll hear first. According to the Airflow documentation, it's an open-source platform for developing, scheduling and monitoring workflows, such as batch data pipelines.

The docs showed version `3.3.2` (checked Oct 2026). You write each workflow as Python code. Its docs say workflows with a clear start and end that run on a schedule are the best fit.

What's good

- It's a free, open-source project. The apache/airflow GitHub page shows the Apache-2.0 licence (checked Oct 2026), so there's no licence fee and you can move between hosts.
- The docs say you can run it from a single process on a laptop up to a distributed system, so the same code can start small and grow.
- The docs say you can backfill Dag runs to process historical data, or rerun only failed tasks to minimize cost and time.
- Retries are configurable in the task docs: `retry_delay`, `retry_exponential_backoff` and `max_retry_delay`, plus an `execution_timeout` that caps how long a task may run.
- The docs describe time-based or event-triggered batch pipelines, machine learning, model training and agentic or LLM-based workloads as the use cases.
- Astronomer, Amazon and Google each sell a hosted version, so you can start self-run and hand off the servers later.

Where it falls short

- The docs (checked Oct 2026) say plainly that "if you prefer clicking over coding, Airflow might not be the best fit," because workflows are code.
- It's built for batch work. The docs (checked Oct 2026) call it "a platform for orchestrating batch workflows."
- A minimal install has several parts to run. The core concepts page (checked Oct 2026) lists a scheduler, a metadata database (usually PostgreSQL or MySQL) and an API server, with workers and a triggerer as optional extras.
- Tasks must be safe to repeat. The best practices page (checked Oct 2026) says "Do not use INSERT during a task re-run" because it can duplicate rows, so use `UPSERT` instead, and never read the latest available data inside a task.
- The task docs say the SLA feature from Airflow `2` was removed in `3.0` and replaced in `3.1` with Deadline Alerts (checked Oct 2026), so teams moving between major versions have a feature to rework.

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The open-source orchestrators > 2. Dagster: best for teams that think in tables and datasets
text:
At a glance

- Price: free open-source project; Dagster+ Solo $10 a month, Starter $100 a month, Pro by quote, from the Dagster pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Its pricing page (checked Oct 2026) shows Solo at $10 a month (one user, one code location). Starter costs $100 a month (up to three users, five code locations). Credits cost $0.040 on Solo and $0.035 on Starter.

The page defines a credit as "the sum of asset materializations and ops executed." An asset is a table or file that a job produces. So Dagster counts the things your jobs build and run.

What's good

- Its docs describe Dagster as built around assets, with "integrated lineage, observability, a declarative programming model, and best-in-class testability." That is Dagster's own claim, and we did not test it.
- Asset checks are tests on a data asset, such as a column that must have no nulls, and the docs say they do not count toward Dagster+ credit usage.
- Sensors react to events such as a file appearing in an S3 bucket or a run failing. A run key makes Dagster skip a request it has already seen, so duplicate runs are not created.
- The concurrency guide lists run queue limits, concurrency pools (to protect a shared database or API), run executor limits and run tag limits.
- Dagster+ Hybrid has no compute charge because you run the compute, and the pricing page offers a 30-day free trial of everything in Dagster+ (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The open-source orchestrators > 2. Dagster: best for teams that think in tables and datasets (part 2)
text:
- Every asset materialized and every op executed is 1 credit, at $0.040 on Solo and $0.035 on Starter (Dagster pricing) (checked Oct 2026). We did not find how many credits each plan includes, so ask Dagster what a typical month costs for jobs like yours.
- If you use Dagster+ Serverless, compute is billed on top of the credits at $0.010 a minute (Dagster pricing) (checked Oct 2026). The entry plan is $10 a month before any credits.
- Plan ceilings are small. Solo has 1 user, 1 code location and 1 deployment, and Starter has up to 3 users, 5 code locations and 1 deployment. Unlimited code locations and deployments are listed under Pro, which is contact-sales (Dagster pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Cards are accepted on Solo and Starter, while custom invoicing and ACH are for Pro customers. The page says there is no self-enrollment discount for not-for-profits (checked Oct 2026).
- Sensors poll. The sensor docs (checked Oct 2026) say the sensor interval is a minimum between evaluations and not the exact frequency, so a slow check delays the next one.
- Dagster is an orchestrator (docs), so other tools it runs do the copying.

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The open-source orchestrators > 3. Prefect: best for Python teams that want a free plan to start on
text:
At a glance

- Price: free Hobby plan; Starter $100 a month; Team $100 per user a month; Enterprise custom, from the Prefect pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Prefect's own docs describe it as an open-source engine for running workflows that turns Python functions into production pipelines. A workflow is a Python function marked with `@flow` or `@task`, and it can run in containers, on Kubernetes or in a single process. The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists the free Hobby plan with 2 users and up to 5 deployments. Starter has 3 users and up to 20 deployments.

What's good

- Prefect's docs say plain Python control flow (`if`, loops) works inside a workflow and tasks can be created while it runs, which we did not test. They also list type hints, `async`/`await` and your existing IDE, debugger and testing tools.
- On failure, the docs say you can resume interrupted runs from the last successful point and cache expensive computations. The retries guide covers a `retries` count, `retry_delay_seconds`, an `exponential_backoff` helper and a `retry_jitter_factor`.
- Flows can be triggered on schedules, external events or via API, and paused for human intervention or approval. The docs (checked Oct 2026) add that Prefect `3.0` open-sourced its events and automations backend.
- The docs say workflows run from a single process to containers, Kubernetes or cloud services.
- The free plan has a stated ceiling. The pricing page lists 500 minutes of Prefect Serverless on Hobby, 75 hours on Starter and 225 hours on Team (checked Oct 2026).
- Eligible startups get credits toward the Team plan through the Prefect Startup Program, the pricing page says (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The open-source orchestrators > 3. Prefect: best for Python teams that want a free plan to start on (part 2)
text:
- The free Hobby plan keeps run history for only 7 days, and the plan comparison shows 7 days on Starter and 14 days on Team (Prefect pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Team costs $100 per user a month for 4 to 8 users (Prefect pricing) (checked Oct 2026), so by our arithmetic four people pay $400 a month.
- Uptime SLA is None on Hobby, Starter and Team, and 99.9% on Enterprise. Support is Community on Hobby and Starter and Email on Team (Prefect pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Audit log retention is None on Hobby and Starter and 24 hrs on Team. API rate limits are `625` a minute on Hobby, `1,250` on Starter and `2,500` on Team (Prefect pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- SSO (SAML/OIDC) and RBAC with ACLs are listed under Enterprise, which is custom-priced. Automations are capped at `5` on Hobby, `10` on Starter and `50` on Team (Prefect pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Prefect is a scheduling engine (docs), so other tools do the copying, as with Dagster.

What users say: A July 2026 PeerSpot review on the AWS Marketplace page for Prefect Cloud covers cost. It says "Pricing is based on how much computing you use" and that once set up, "It doesn't cost a lot." The same review says "There's a lot of mental and engineering cost involved to set it up."

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The open-source orchestrators > 4. Kestra: best for teams that prefer YAML files to Python
text:
At a glance

- Price: Open Source edition under Apache-2.0 (checked Oct 2026); Kestra Cloud and Enterprise Edition not published on the Kestra pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Its pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists an Open Source edition with declarative workflows, "2,100+ Plugins" and "Unlimited Flows & Executions". Its GitHub page shows an Apache-2.0 licence. YAML is a plain text format for settings, so you describe a workflow in a text file instead of writing code.

Kestra Cloud is pay-as-you-go. The Enterprise Edition is an annual per-instance subscription. Neither shows a dollar price on the pricing page (checked Oct 2026). The page calls the open-source edition production-ready by default. That is Kestra's own claim, and we did not test it.

What's good

- Workflows live in plain files. The pricing page lists a code editor and a guided form editor, and says "both stay in sync".
- Both editions include scheduling and event triggers, Git integration and versioning, and air-gapped deployment, the pricing page says.
- The pricing page says most of the 2,100+ plugins are in both editions, and one workflow can orchestrate SQL, Python, shell, APIs, Terraform, dbt, Spark or custom tools.
- The open-source edition has no flow or execution cap, and it runs its queue and repository on PostgreSQL or MySQL, "with nothing else to operate" (Kestra pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Upgrading from Open Source to Enterprise means adding the licence key to the configuration file and restarting the server, according to the pricing FAQ (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The open-source orchestrators > 4. Kestra: best for teams that prefer YAML files to Python (part 2)
text:
- Single sign-on (SSO), LDAP, SCIM, role-based access control and audit logs are listed under the Enterprise Edition (Kestra pricing) (checked Oct 2026). If your team needs them, you'll be asking for a quote.
- Cloud and Enterprise prices are not published. Enterprise shows Contact Sales and is an annual subscription per instance, and Cloud shows Request Access (Kestra pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Human-in-the-loop approvals (pausing an execution until someone approves it) sit under the Enterprise Platform part of the feature table (Kestra pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- So do queues on Kafka, Redis or AMQP and worker groups. The open-source queue runs on PostgreSQL or MySQL (Kestra pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Plugins differ by edition: the pricing page says most of the 2,100+ are in both, and it lists Enterprise Plugins separately (checked Oct 2026).
- Support terms are an Enterprise item. The `P0` response target is 24 hours on Standard, 6 hours on Premium and 1 hour on Platinum, with 24x7 coverage on Platinum only (Kestra pricing) (checked Oct 2026).

What users say: A DEV post about Kestra said Kestra "fills a gap that I didn't realize existed" (July 2025). A Procycons guide to Kestra, Temporal and Prefect warns "it's still YAML" and that "you're fundamentally limited by what you can express declaratively" (2025, month not shown).

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Hosted Airflow: let someone else babysit the servers
text: Three vendors in this list sell open-source Airflow with the servers handled for you, and they differ in what they bill. The Airflow docs cited above cover the shared software, so each block below is about the host.

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Hosted Airflow: let someone else babysit the servers > 5. Astronomer (Astro): best for teams that want Airflow help, on any cloud
text:
At a glance

- Price: Developer from $0.35 an hour, Team from $0.42 an hour, Business and above by quote, from the Astronomer pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Astronomer's pricing page (checked Oct 2026) shows five plans. The two lower ones, Developer and Team, show hourly "deployments starting at" prices and a "Try for Free" button. Business, Enterprise and Enterprise Business Critical say "Contact us for pricing" with annual agreements, and workers start at $0.13 an hour and dedicated clusters at $2.40 an hour on Team and above.

What's good

- Developer and Team prices are on the pricing page, and support tiers are listed (24x5 on Team, 24x7 with a 1-hour response on Business) (checked Oct 2026). The support claims are Astronomer's own.
- Workers are billed only while tasks run and scale to zero when idle. There are 7 worker sizes (`A5` to `A160`) starting at $0.13 an hour (Astronomer pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Each deployment includes the scheduler, webserver and triggerer, and the Team plan adds network isolation with dedicated clusters and high availability deployments (Astronomer pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Worker queues let a few heavy tasks use a bigger worker, and the pricing page says you are charged for the larger size only when a task that needs it runs (checked Oct 2026).
- You can buy Astro through the AWS, Azure or Google Cloud marketplaces, and the pricing page says existing marketplace commitments apply.
- Astro Private Cloud runs Airflow in your own environment, and its listing on the pricing page includes air-gapped deployment support.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Hosted Airflow: let someone else babysit the servers > 5. Astronomer (Astro): best for teams that want Airflow help, on any cloud (part 2)
text:
- "Starting at" prices are a floor. The pricing page lists workers and dedicated clusters as separate charges (checked Oct 2026), so ask Astronomer for a full-bill example.
- Deployments run continuously at a fixed hourly price per size, so the deployment charge does not fall when no tasks are running (Astronomer pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Other meters are on top: dedicated clusters from $2.40 an hour, Astro Observe priced as a percentage of compute, AI token usage and extra worker storage at $0.0002 per GiB per hour. Networking costs are passed through from the cloud provider (Astronomer pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- The top three plans are quote-only, so no price tag there (Astronomer pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Controls arrive by tier. SSO enforcement, 90-day audit logs and the 1-hour SLA start at Business, custom RBAC and SCIM at Enterprise, and Team has 7-day audit logs (Astronomer pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) text we read does not say how long the "Try for Free" trial lasts or what credit it includes.

What users say: The Hacker News comments are older and split. One, in Lessons learned from running Apache Airflow at scale, said "it's dirt cheap considering what you get" (May 2022). Another, in Ask HN: Companies of one, what is your tech stack?, said "Astronomer is too expensive for this project" (September 2022).

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Hosted Airflow: let someone else babysit the servers > 6. Amazon MWAA: best for teams already on AWS
text:
At a glance

- Price: environment per hour in US East: Small $0.49, Large $0.99, plus extra workers, from the Amazon MWAA pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (MWAA) bills each environment by the hour, at one-second resolution. AWS says there are no minimum fees or upfront commitments (checked Oct 2026).

The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists these hourly rates for one environment (the table we read was for US East (Ohio)):

| Size | Recommended workflow capacity | Price per hour |
| Micro | Up to 25 DAGs | $0.29 |
| Small | Up to 50 DAGs | $0.49 |
| Medium | Up to 250 DAGs | $0.74 |
| Large | Up to 1000 DAGs | $0.99 |
| XL | Up to 2000 DAGs | $1.98 |
| 2XL | Up to 4000 DAGs | $3.96 |

Extra workers cost $0.055 an hour on Small, and metadata storage is $0.10 per GB-month (Amazon MWAA pricing) (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- A full public rate table by size, with the DAG capacity AWS recommends for each. The environment class page (checked Oct 2026) gives the default concurrent tasks too: `5` on `mw1.small` and `20` on `mw1.large`.
- AWS says MWAA scales workers between a minimum and maximum you set, and that the MWAA team updates and patches the images for new Airflow versions (see the MWAA docs).
- Access to the Airflow webserver is controlled with IAM policies (MWAA docs), data is encrypted with AWS Key Management Service, and the webserver can use a public or a private access mode.
- Airflow logs and metrics go to Amazon CloudWatch, so task delays and workflow errors can be found without third-party tools (MWAA docs).
- The docs list integrations with Athena, Glue, EMR, Redshift, Lambda and more, plus hundreds of built-in and community operators and sensors. We did not test them.
- AWS says there are no minimum fees or upfront commitments, with billing at one-second resolution. The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) also lists MWAA Serverless, which charges per task for its duration, with a 1-minute minimum.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Hosted Airflow: let someone else babysit the servers > 6. Amazon MWAA: best for teams already on AWS (part 2)
text:
- AWS bills an environment by the hour, so a Small one costs $0.49 an hour however many jobs run on it, even zero (Amazon MWAA pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Extra workers, additional schedulers, additional web servers and metadata storage ($0.10 per GB-month) are separate meters. AWS's own example for a Small environment with a one-hour spike of 50 workers a day totals $449.11 a month, against $364.56 for the environment alone. Its Large example, with scaled workers, schedulers and web servers plus 40 GB of storage, totals $1047.46 (Amazon MWAA pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Size sets the ceiling: `mw1.micro` does not support auto-scaling, and `mw1.small` is rated for up to `50` DAGs and `5` concurrent tasks by default (environment class docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- CloudWatch, S3, SQS and KMS are separate services that must be reachable from the schedulers and workers, per the MWAA docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Free tier terms were not shown on the pricing page (checked Oct 2026) we read.
- It's Airflow, so the same code-first limits apply.

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Hosted Airflow: let someone else babysit the servers > 7. Google Managed Airflow (Cloud Composer): best for teams already on Google Cloud
text:
At a glance

- Price: Gen 3 standard rate $0.06 per DCU-hour, plus database storage, from the Google Cloud pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Google's pricing page (checked Oct 2026) is now titled "Managed Service for Apache Airflow," although the price lines still say Cloud Composer. It bills in Data Compute Units (DCU), which Google calls "an abstract metering unit" for the vCPU, memory and storage an environment has set aside. The Gen 3 table shows $0.06 per 1,000 milli-DCU hours, which is $0.06 per DCU-hour, and $0.000232877 per GiB hour of database storage.

Committed-use discounts apply to Gen 3. They are $0.054 for one year and $0.048 for three years per 1,000 milli-DCU hours (Google Cloud pricing) (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- Billing follows the actual time an environment ran, and committed-use discounts apply to Gen 3 (rates above). The pricing page's example: an environment that runs 6 hours 30 minutes is billed for 6.5 hours (checked Oct 2026).
- Google's overview calls it a fully managed orchestration service for pipelines that span clouds and on-premises data centers.
- Besides schedules, DAGs can be triggered manually or in response to events such as changes in a Cloud Storage bucket, the overview says.
- Environments can be created (overview) through the Google Cloud console, the `gcloud` CLI, the API or Terraform, and you can install custom Airflow plugins such as in-house operators, hooks and sensors.
- Worker costs follow the number of autoscaled workers, so the bill moves with load. The pricing page says resources used by your own workloads in the cluster (for example with `KubernetesPodOperator`) also count as DCU-hours.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Hosted Airflow: let someone else babysit the servers > 7. Google Managed Airflow (Cloud Composer): best for teams already on Google Cloud (part 2)
text:
- The price depends on how many DCUs your environment uses, so the pricing page can't give you one monthly figure. Region changes the rate too (checked Oct 2026).
- Google says highly resilient mode roughly doubles the database storage cost (Google Cloud pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- The database disk grows with demand and, per the pricing page, does not shrink if the Airflow database gets smaller later (checked Oct 2026).
- Network data transfer is its own SKU group, and the pricing page says an environment has additional costs that are not part of the Airflow pricing (checked Oct 2026).
- The overview (checked Oct 2026) says some Airflow configuration options are blocked and you cannot change their values.
- Gen 3 has committed-use discounts, but the pricing page says none apply to Gen 2 (checked Oct 2026), so check which generation you are on.

What users say:Tasrie IT Services sells its own managed Airflow and wrote "Best-in-class BigQuery integration. The operators just work" (June 2026, "Managed Airflow Services Compared"). A DEV case study says Composer 3 "bills for compute units every hour the environment is alive" (September 2026, "Moving Your Local Airflow to GCP for under $150 a month").

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Cloud-Built Workflow Services > 8. AWS Step Functions: best for step-by-step workflows inside AWS
text:
At a glance

- Price: Standard $0.000025 per state transition; 4,000 free a month; Express $1.00 per million requests plus duration, from the AWS pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Step Functions is the odd one out here, because it isn't only for data. AWS's documentation says it lets you build workflows, also called state machines, for applications, microservices and data pipelines. It can control AWS Glue to create extract, transform, load workflows.

The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists $0.000025 per state transition (one step moving to the next) on Standard workflows in US East. A free tier of 4,000 transitions a month doesn't expire, and each retry is charged as one more state transition.

What's good

- AWS bills per step, so a workflow that rarely runs costs little, and the first 4,000 transitions a month are free and do not expire. Retries count as steps, so a flaky job costs more (AWS pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- Standard workflows can run up to a year, which suits long jobs with human approvals (AWS docs). AWS says the free tier is available to new and existing accounts indefinitely (AWS pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- The workflow type guide (checked Oct 2026) says Standard workflows are exactly-once, which suits non-idempotent actions such as starting an Amazon EMR cluster, and the full execution history can be retrieved through the API for up to 90 days after a run ends.
- The docs list AWS SDK integrations with "over two hundred services," and optimized integrations that include Athena, AWS Batch, AWS Glue and EMR.
- Express workflows can start from events such as API Gateway requests, IoT rules and over 140 other EventBridge event sources, and are billed by executions, duration and memory (AWS docs).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Cloud-Built Workflow Services > 8. AWS Step Functions: best for step-by-step workflows inside AWS (part 2)
text:
- It's built around AWS services. The docs describe AWS SDK integrations, so check the fit before you connect systems outside AWS.
- AWS describes it for applications and microservices as well as data pipelines, so it's a general workflow tool.
- Express workflows run for up to five minutes, use an at-least-once model, and do not support the Job-run (`.sync`) or Callback (`.waitForTaskToken`) patterns. The workflow type cannot be changed after you create a state machine (AWS docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The quotas page (checked Oct 2026) says new AWS accounts have reduced state transition quotas, which AWS raises based on usage.
- A state machine definition is capped at `1 MB`, a hard quota (AWS quotas page) (checked Oct 2026).
- Services the workflow calls bill separately, the pricing page says (checked Oct 2026), so the per-step price is not the whole bill.

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Cloud-Built Workflow Services > 9. Azure Data Factory: best for Microsoft shops with copy-heavy pipelines
text:
At a glance

- Price: per activity run plus integration runtime hours; most rates on Microsoft's pricing page load dynamically (checked Oct 2026)

Microsoft's introduction calls Azure Data Factory a managed cloud service for hybrid ETL, extract, load, transform (ELT, load first and reshape after) and data integration projects. A pipeline is a group of activities, and triggers decide when it starts. The same page carries a note that Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric is "the next generation". It says new users should start with Fabric Data Factory (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- Microsoft describes it as doing the copying and the scheduling in one product, with triggers for events such as files landing in storage. We did not test it.
- The triggers page lists three trigger types: schedule, tumbling window (which fires at a set interval while retaining state) and event-based.
- A storage event trigger can run a pipeline when a file arrives in Azure Blob Storage (triggers page), and a tumbling window trigger run waits for the pipeline run to finish and takes on its state.
- The integration runtime that does the work is, per Microsoft's pricing page, "serverless in Azure and self-hosted in hybrid scenarios".
- The pricing page's data flow table lists General Purpose at $0.274 per vCore-hour pay as you go, with about 25% savings on a 1-year reservation and about 35% on a 3-year one (checked Oct 2026). Most other rates on that page load dynamically.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Cloud-Built Workflow Services > 9. Azure Data Factory: best for Microsoft shops with copy-heavy pipelines (part 2)
text:
- Microsoft points new users to Fabric Data Factory, so check which one your plan targets before you commit. Microsoft's Fabric comparison page says new Fabric features "aren't backported to Azure Data Factory or Azure Synapse pipelines" and the two keep separate roadmaps (checked Oct 2026).
- Microsoft's CDC page says "Pipelines in ADF are batch only, but the CDC resource can run continuously," and its native-CDC connector list names SAP CDC, Azure SQL Database, SQL Server, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Azure Cosmos DB and Snowflake (checked Oct 2026).
- The self-hosted integration runtime is, in Microsoft's integration runtime docs (checked Oct 2026), "only supported on a Windows operating system."
- Stopping and restarting an event-based trigger resumes the old trigger pattern, which Microsoft says may start the pipeline unexpectedly. The fix it gives is to delete the trigger and create a new one (triggers page) (checked Oct 2026).
- The bill has several meters: orchestration (activity runs, trigger executions and debug runs), integration runtime hours, and data flow vCore hours. An inactive pipeline, one with no trigger and zero runs in a month, is charged after that month (Azure pricing) (checked Oct 2026).
- The pricing page still says CDC artifacts are billed at General Purpose rates for 4-vCore clusters "during public preview of CDC" (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Cloud-Built Workflow Services > 10. Databricks Lakeflow Jobs: best for teams that already run on Databricks
text:
At a glance

- Price: serverless or classic compute billed per DBU, with a 14-day free trial; on AWS in US East, Jobs Classic is $0.15 and Jobs Serverless $0.35 per DBU on Premium, and $0.20 and $0.45 on Enterprise (Databricks pricing page) (checked Oct 2026)

Databricks' documentation describes Lakeflow Jobs as workflow automation for Databricks that coordinates and runs multiple tasks. Tasks include notebooks, pipelines and Python scripts, and triggers are time-based or event-based, such as new files arriving in cloud storage.

The docs list limits of `1000` tasks per job, `12,000` saved jobs and `2000` concurrent task runs per workspace (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- Databricks documents it as workflow automation for Databricks, so it runs inside the platform if your data work is already there.
- The limits are written down in the docs, which makes planning easier.
- A repair run re-runs only the unsuccessful tasks and their dependents, and you can change job or task settings first. Tasks that succeeded are not re-run.
- File arrival triggers, per the Databricks file arrival docs, have a "Minimum time between triggers" setting (a cooldown of at most one run per interval) and a "Wait after last change" setting (a debounce for files that land in batches).
- The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) says pay as you go with a 14-day free trial, or contact Databricks for committed-use discounts or custom requirements.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Cloud-Built Workflow Services > 10. Databricks Lakeflow Jobs: best for teams that already run on Databricks (part 2)
text:
- It runs work inside Databricks (docs) (checked Oct 2026), so check the task-type list before you count on it for tools outside.
- The rate depends on plan, cloud and region, and the pricing page has a selector for each. For AWS in US East it shows Jobs Classic at $0.15 and Serverless at $0.35 per DBU on Premium, and $0.20 and $0.45 on Enterprise (Databricks pricing) (checked Oct 2026). Check the rate for your own plan, cloud and region.
- On that page, the Classic rates are "plus underlying compute costs billed by cloud provider," so the DBU price is only part of the Classic bill. Serverless rates say they include underlying compute (checked Oct 2026).
- A repair re-runs each unsuccessful task from the beginning. The docs (checked Oct 2026) say Lakeflow Jobs "doesn't make tasks idempotent," so a task that wrote part of its output before failing can duplicate data.
- Repair is supported only for jobs with two or more tasks. A failed single-task job is triggered again with Run now (Databricks docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- File arrival triggers require a workspace with Unity Catalog enabled, plus a volume or external location in Unity Catalog (Databricks docs) (checked Oct 2026).

What users say: Independent talk about Lakeflow Jobs alone is thin. Most public comments are about the whole Databricks platform. For the platform, PeerSpot reviewers wrote "Databricks tech support has been great every time I've dealt with them" and "It is an expensive tool" (page read October 2026, quotes undated).

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Cloud-Built Workflow Services > Others Worth Knowing
text:
A quick nod to one more. Argo Workflows is the Kubernetes-native choice. Its docs call it "an open source container-native workflow engine for orchestrating parallel jobs on Kubernetes," where each step is a container.

Argo fits teams that already run Kubernetes and want every step in a container. If nobody on your team runs Kubernetes, it's a poor fit. We did not review Luigi, Flyte or Mage.

What's good

- The docs say Argo is a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) graduated project, that about 200+ organizations officially use it, and that it can run on any Kubernetes cluster.
- A workflow can be a sequence of tasks or a directed acyclic graph (DAG), and each step is a container (docs).
- Its feature list includes scheduled workflows using cron, retries at step and workflow level, suspend and resume, and artifact support for S3, GCS, Azure Blob Storage and others.
- It lists single sign-on (OAuth2/OIDC) and SDKs for Java, Golang, Python (Hera) and Typescript (Juno) (docs).

Where it falls short

- It is implemented as a Kubernetes custom resource (CRD), so you need a Kubernetes cluster to run it (Argo docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The cron workflows page (checked Oct 2026) lists `startingDeadlineSeconds` with a default of `0`. It also says that when you set it to recover missed schedules, only a single instance is run.
- With a timezone set, daylight saving means a schedule may run once, twice or not at all when the clock changes, the same page (checked Oct 2026) says.
- Argo is open source under Apache-2.0 (checked Oct 2026), so hosting and staff costs are yours.

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > How the bills differ: a worked example
text:
Each tool counts something different, so the same small setup costs very different amounts. This example uses our own simple assumptions: one daily job of 5 steps, 730 hours in a month, and no extra workers or storage.

| Meter | Tool | Arithmetic | Monthly result |
| Per hour the server exists | Amazon MWAA Small | $0.49 x 730 hours | $357.70 |
| Per hour the server exists | Astro Developer (starting rate) | $0.35 x 730 hours | $255.50 |
| Per step | Step Functions Standard | 5 steps x 30 days = 150 transitions (assuming one transition per step), well under the 4,000 free | $0 |
| Per plan, plus credits | Dagster Solo | $10 plan + 150 credits (5 steps x 30 days, assuming each step counts as one op) x $0.040 | $16 at most (the page shows no included credits) |
| Flat plan | Prefect Starter | $100 a month flat, 3 users | $100 |

Sources: Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow pricing, Astronomer pricing, AWS Step Functions pricing, Dagster pricing and Prefect pricing (checked Oct 2026)

A free row doesn't make Step Functions the best pick. Always-on hosts like MWAA and Astro charge for being ready, which makes sense when you have many jobs. Per-step billing is cheap for rare jobs but grows with every step and retry, so redo the arithmetic at your real volume.

title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > How to choose in 5 minutes
text:
| Your situation | Start with | Why |
| Team writes Python, wants a free plan to try | Prefect | Python functions are workflows; free Hobby plan ( Prefect pricing ) (checked Oct 2026) |
| Want lineage between tables and jobs | Dagster | Assets are the main concept |
| Already know Airflow, want no servers | Astro, Amazon MWAA or Google Managed Airflow | Hosted Airflow; pick the host that matches your cloud |
| Want workflows as YAML files | Kestra | Declarative files, open-source edition |

Where does your data work mostly live?

Cloud services often win inside their own cloud.

Where OLake Go fits
An orchestrator decides when and in what order jobs run, and something else does the copying. OLake Go can be the copying step. It replicates Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB, MongoDB, SQL Server, Oracle and Db2, plus S3 and Kafka, into Apache Iceberg or Parquet (the driver list is on our Docker CLI page). The Docker CLI runs a sync as a command, so an orchestrator can start it, and our team has written guides for doing that from Airflow on Kubernetes and on EC2. title: Compare: Best Data Orchestration Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > FAQ
text:
Q1. What is data orchestration in simple terms?

It's the part of your data setup that runs jobs in the right order, on time, and alerts you when one fails. It coordinates the other tools but doesn't copy or reshape data itself.

Q2. Is Airflow the best data orchestration tool?

Not for everyone. Airflow is free and open source and fits scheduled workflows with a clear start and end, but its docs say it may not suit people who prefer clicking over coding. Prefect, Dagster or a cloud service can fit you better.

Q3. What is the difference between orchestration and ETL?

ETL copies data and reshapes it on the way. The orchestrator decides when each ETL job runs, and what happens when one fails. IBM treats integration such as ETL as one process that orchestration coordinates.

Q4. Are there free data orchestration tools?

Yes. Airflow, Dagster, Prefect and Kestra all have free open-source versions, and Prefect has a free Hobby plan. The free Prefect plan keeps run history for only 7 days (Prefect pricing) (checked Oct 2026).

Q5. Which orchestration tool is cheapest?

It depends on the meter. Step Functions Standard gives you 4,000 free state transitions a month (AWS pricing) (checked Oct 2026), so a few small jobs can cost nothing. Always-on hosts such as Amazon MWAA Small at $0.49 an hour (MWAA pricing) (checked Oct 2026) keep charging even when nothing is running.

Q6. Do I need an orchestrator if I use a managed ingestion tool?

Not always. A managed ingestion tool can run its own schedule for the copying step, and OLake Go's UI takes a frequency or a cron expression for its jobs (job settings). You'll want an orchestrator once several steps must run in order, such as load, then transform, then report.

Q7. What should I check before choosing an orchestrator?

Check how it re-runs only failed steps, whether it can backfill past dates, what can trigger a job (clock or event), who can write workflows (Python or YAML), and what the billing meter counts.

Q8. Where does OLake Go fit next to an orchestrator?

OLake Go does the copying: it replicates databases, S3 and Kafka into Apache Iceberg or Parquet and runs from the Docker CLI, the OLake UI or Kubernetes with Helm. The OLake UI has its own schedule (frequency or cron).

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

Short answer: yes, database to Iceberg without Kafka works. It relies on change data capture (CDC), which reads a database's own change log, and seven tools document a path for it: Debezium Server, Flink CDC, RisingWave, Estuary, Fivetran, dlt and OLake Go.

Amazon Data Firehose is not on that list, because AWS says its database preview ended on September 30, 2025 (checked Oct 2026). Before you pick a tool, ask whether you need a streaming platform at all.

- Kafka isn't required to write Iceberg. Debezium's own maintainers wrote on May 22, 2026 that Kafka Connect is "one deployment model, not a requirement."
- "No Kafka" isn't the same as "no moving parts". Flink CDC needs a Flink cluster, RisingWave is a streaming system in its own right, and Estuary's Iceberg connector needs a Spark job on Amazon EMR Serverless.
- Table upkeep (compaction, which merges many small files into fewer big ones) is usually your job. Check who does it before you pick, not after.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > Do you need a streaming platform at all?
text:
Apache Kafka calls itself an open-source distributed event streaming platform: changes sit in named topics on machines called brokers until something reads them. Debezium's maintainers give three reasons teams keep it, in their May 2026 post. Kafka Connect has a large library of sink connectors, it handles worker failures with built-in high availability, and it spreads work across a cluster.

The same post gives a test: ask "do I need the capabilities that Kafka provides?" If you don't, you're paying to run brokers for a pipeline with one reader. Also ask whether you need to hold changes while the lake is down, or replay them later, and check how each tool's docs handle restarts.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > How we picked
text:
An option made this list if its own documents say it can read database changes and write Apache Iceberg tables, it can run without Kafka today, and its public pages say enough for us to check catalogs, deletes and table upkeep. We added one baseline, Debezium on Kafka Connect, so you can see what you'd be skipping.

We read each vendor's documentation in September and October 2026 and link every claim. We did not run the other tools, so for them this is a reading of documents, not a lab test.

Where a page says nothing, the table says "not stated". We left out speed claims, because no vendor publishes a comparable test.

Two tools were left out on those rules. We explain why below.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > Updates, deletes and delivery: what each tool's docs say
text:
This is where the options differ most. A primary key is the column that identifies each row. An upsert updates the row if its key already exists and inserts it if not, while an append adds every change as a new row, so the table holds both versions of a changed row.

Iceberg can handle a delete in two ways. Copy-on-write rewrites the affected data files, and merge-on-read writes the delete as a small separate file that is applied when someone reads the table.

Equality deletes match rows by key values, and positional deletes point at a file and a row position. Delivery guarantee means whether a change can land twice (at-least-once) or exactly once.

| Option | Update to a row | Delete of a row | Delivery guarantee (per docs) |
| Iceberg Kafka Connect sink | Not described on the page we read | Not described on the page we read | Exactly-once listed; needs Kafka 2.5 or later |
| Debezium Server sink | Append-only by default; upsert mode is off by default and keeps the record with the highest value in a dedup column | In upsert mode, kept and marked __deleted=true by default | Not stated for the Iceberg sink; the Server page's JDBC sink section warns exactly-once features may differ from Kafka Connect |
| Flink CDC (Iceberg pipeline connector) | Primary key keeps repeated writes safe | Not described on the pipeline page | At-least-once; the pipeline page says exactly-once is not supported |
| RisingWave | Append-only or upsert sink | Upsert sink is for updates and deletes; with force_append_only, deletes are ignored | Exactly-once setting, on by default |
| OLake Go | Upsert by default, append per table | Equality deletes, positional deletes or deletion vectors | Two-phase commit for Iceberg writes, which avoids duplicate writes ( v0.5.0 notes ) |
| Estuary | Merge job on Spark | Soft delete by default, hard delete optional | Not stated on the page we read |
| Fivetran | Not described on the destination page | Not described; position deletes aren't supported | Not stated on the page we read |
| dlt | Merge supports upsert and insert-only | Not described on the Iceberg page | Not stated on the page we read |

Each cell links to the page it comes from (checked Oct 2026). "Not described" and "not stated" mean we couldn't find the answer on the pages we read. If your tool lands there, test one update and one delete yourself.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > Baseline: Debezium on Kafka Connect with the Iceberg sink
text:
At a glance: Software you run under Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026), plus a Kafka cluster. It's the route most tutorials teach.

Debezium reads the database log and puts each change into a Kafka topic, and the Apache Iceberg docs describe a Kafka Connect sink that reads those topics and writes Iceberg tables. Debezium's own sink list for Kafka Connect shows only JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) and MongoDB, so the Iceberg sink comes from the Iceberg project, not from Debezium.

What it writes: Iceberg tables through catalogs such as REST, Glue, Hive and Nessie. The sink docs list exactly-once delivery, which relies on Kafka 2.5 or later. Automatic table creation and schema evolution are listed too, but both default to off (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- Debezium's post says Kafka Connect's distributed mode spreads work across workers and handles worker failures. We did not test that. If many systems already read the same topics, the Iceberg sink is just one more reader.

Where it falls short

- You run Kafka brokers and Kafka Connect workers, plus the Debezium and Iceberg connectors that run inside them. The sink page's install steps also have you build the connector zip from the Iceberg source code.
- The page we read doesn't explain how updates and deletes are applied, even though it mentions a "CDC feature". The Debezium transform that feeds it is marked experimental.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > 1. Debezium Server with the community Iceberg sink: the same Debezium connectors with no Kafka
text:
At a glance:Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026), you run it. Debezium Server is, in its docs' words, a ready-to-use application that streams change events "without requiring Apache Kafka."

The Debezium Server docs list an Apache Iceberg sink. It is "a community-maintained, open-source project" in a separate repository, memiiso/debezium-server-iceberg, not part of Debezium itself.

What it writes: Parquet files by default, with Avro and ORC (two other file formats) selectable. It has upsert and append modes, but upsert is off by default. Even in upsert mode, deleted rows are kept and marked `__deleted=true` unless you change a setting (Debezium Server docs (checked Oct 2026)).

What's good

- You keep Debezium's connector list: its index shows MongoDB, MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2 and Cassandra as main connectors.
- The sink's README claims it replicates "from any database to Iceberg tables" without Spark, Kafka or a streaming platform, which we did not test. The latest release is 1.2.0.Final from October 4, 2026.

Where it falls short

- The sink is community maintained, and the Debezium Server docs (checked Oct 2026) name no catalog types. Upsert depends on a Debezium transformation called event flattening, so tables with no primary key stay append-only.
- Each Debezium Server instance runs exactly one connector. A July 2026 Debezium post about its JDBC sink says Kafka Connect's multi-task setting is "not yet available in DS." (checked Oct 2026)
- The sink's FAQ (checked Oct 2026) says to run periodic maintenance on delete files, so that chore is yours. Full schema evolution isn't supported, though adding fields and promoting types is, and a column dropped at the source stays in the table with nulls.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > 2. Flink CDC: when you already run Apache Flink
text:
At a glance:Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026), you run it, and it needs a Flink cluster. Flink CDC calls itself "a distributed data integration tool for real-time data and batch data, built on top of Apache Flink". Its docs also say some sources use Debezium as the engine inside.

What it writes: The Iceberg pipeline connector creates tables and syncs added columns. The catalog type can be Hadoop, Hive or Glue, or a custom class. It first appears in the Flink CDC 3.4 line.

What's good

- Its docs describe reshaping data in the same job. Iceberg's own Flink docs describe upserts on version 2 tables with a primary key.
- Its docs list Standalone, YARN or Kubernetes deployment, with no Kafka listed as a requirement.

Where it falls short

- The pipeline page says "The source table must have a primary key." It also says exactly-once isn't supported, and offers at-least-once writes made safe by the primary key (checked Oct 2026).
- Schema change inference for the Postgres pipeline source is off by default (`schema-change.enabled`) (checked Oct 2026). MongoDB CDC is a Flink SQL source, not a YAML pipeline source, so you write more code for it. SQL Server joined the YAML pipeline sources in 3.7, per the pipeline connector overview (checked Oct 2026).
- Someone has to run Flink, which is cluster work like Kafka.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > 3. RisingWave: for a SQL-first team that wants processing and Iceberg together
text:
At a glance: Apache 2.0 core, self-hosted or hosted, with premium features behind a licence. RisingWave describes itself as an "event streaming platform" (checked Oct 2026), so you're skipping Kafka, but not streaming.

What it writes: The Iceberg docs show append-only and upsert sinks, merge-on-read writes by default, and an `is_exactly_once` setting that defaults to true. Exactly-once needs sink decoupling, a RisingWave setting that is on by default, and turning it off disables exactly-once. Catalogs include Glue, S3 Tables, JDBC, REST, Lakekeeper, Hive, Snowflake and Unity.

What's good

- Its ingestion overview lists CDC for PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server, labels MongoDB "CDC via Kafka", and offers SQL for shaping data.
- Its docs say Iceberg maintenance, including compaction and snapshot cleanup, is automatic. We did not test how that behaves on your table sizes, so ask what it costs to run.

Where it falls short

- Some features need a licence key, and RisingWave's pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists direct SQL Server CDC as premium. So "open source" applies to the core only.
- Schema evolution on the Iceberg sink covers adding columns only, and works only while exactly-once is on, per its docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Its Postgres source needs primary keys that match upstream tables (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > 4. OLake Go: for scheduled copies from Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB or SQL Server
text:
At a glance:Apache 2.0 open source (checked Oct 2026) that runs on your own infrastructure. OLake Go does a full load and then change capture straight from the database, and writes Apache Iceberg or Parquet on storage you control, with no Debezium or Kafka to run. Install with Docker, Helm or the UI (see the Docker install page).

What it writes: Iceberg tables. For updates, OLake Go has an Upsert mode with three delete formats: equality deletes and positional deletes (both Iceberg v2), and deletion vectors (Iceberg v3). The default (see the terminology page) is the first format your selected query engine supports, checking equality deletes, then positional deletes, then deletion vectors.

Different streams in one job can use different formats.

Deletion vectors were added in release 0.11.0. That release note lists them as a delete mode and says nothing wider about Iceberg v3 tables. The engine compatibility page lists Amazon Athena as not supporting deletion vectors, so check your engine first.

What's good

- CDC covers PostgreSQL, MySQL and its MariaDB flavor, MongoDB and SQL Server. The setup pages are Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB and SQL Server.
- In the Streams panel, every table starts as Upsert (Kafka sources default to Append) and you can switch a table to Append. Full refresh is always append, and a table found later defaults to Upsert unless every table is set to Append; see the terminology page above.
- The v0.5.0 release notes describe a two-phase commit for Iceberg writes from MongoDB, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server, which avoids duplicate writes. The v0.7.0 notes name the Iceberg table property that records it, `olake_2pc`.
- The catalogs compatibility page lists a wide set of Iceberg catalogs, including AWS Glue, JDBC, Hive Metastore, S3 Tables, Nessie, Polaris, Unity and Lakekeeper.
- The schema page documents schema evolution for widening type changes.
- OLake Fusion, a separate OLake product, handles compaction and Iceberg table maintenance.

Good to know

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > 4. OLake Go: for scheduled copies from Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB or SQL Server (part 2)
text:
- Oracle, Db2 and S3 sources load by full refresh or incremental sync.
- Jobs run on a schedule you set: every minute, hourly, daily, weekly or a cron expression (see the job settings page). By default CDC captures recent changes, replicates them, then stops (see the terminology page), and an orchestrator such as Airflow can run jobs at frequent intervals for near real-time replication. Freshness follows the schedule you choose, so set it to match your target.

Bottom line: Pick OLake Go for scheduled copies from PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB or SQL Server into Iceberg or Parquet on storage you run, with one tool to install, Apache 2.0 licensing and 11 catalog options to choose from.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > 5. Estuary: a hosted pipeline where you don't run the capture side
text:
At a glance: Hosted, with private and bring-your-own-cloud options. The platform code is under the Business Source License 1.1, which its own text says "is not an Open Source license" (checked Oct 2026).

What it writes: Estuary's Iceberg connector writes to catalogs that implement the Iceberg REST API (a standard web interface for catalogs). The docs walk through AWS Glue, Snowflake Open Catalog and Dremio Cloud. A second connector appends Parquet files to Iceberg tables on an interval.

What's good

- Its docs list log-based capture connectors for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle and MongoDB (see the capture links in the table above).
- Its docs list optional Glue table optimizers for compaction, snapshot retention and orphan file deletion.

Where it falls short

- The REST connector needs an Amazon EMR Serverless application running Spark, an S3 staging bucket and IAM roles in your AWS account (checked Oct 2026).
- The docs say only REST catalogs on Amazon S3 are supported, and label the connector Beta for catalogs other than Glue (checked Oct 2026). Nested types aren't supported on the Parquet-append connector, so arrays and objects arrive as strings (checked Oct 2026).
- The optimizers are off by default, and without them the docs say to run regular maintenance yourself.
- Estuary's pricing page lists $0.50 per GB moved plus $100 a month per connector (checked Oct 2026), so the bill grows with your data volume. Ask for an estimate on your own change volume before you commit.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > 6. Fivetran Managed Data Lake Service: if Fivetran already moves your data
text:
At a glance: Hosted by Fivetran, and the destination page lists the SaaS deployment model only. Fivetran's docs say it "always creates Apache Iceberg metadata" for these tables, and Delta Lake metadata is optional.

What it writes: Iceberg tables on S3, Azure Data Lake Storage or Google Cloud Storage. The default catalog is the Fivetran Catalog, an Iceberg REST catalog built on Apache Polaris, with Glue and BigLake as options.

What's good

- Fivetran hosts the service, and the destination page asks you for no brokers, cluster or sink.
- Fivetran also sells connectors for databases and SaaS apps, so one vendor could cover both if your sources are on its list.

Where it falls short

- Fivetran bills by monthly active rows per connection, and its pricing updates page says deletes count as paid rows from January 1, 2026 on pay-as-you-go plans, and at renewal on annual contracts signed after March 1, 2025 (checked Oct 2026). Ask for an estimate on your own row counts before you commit.
- The destination docs say there's no support for Iceberg position deletes (checked Oct 2026). Fivetran's catalog docs warn that editing Fivetran-managed tables from outside can corrupt them.
- Maintenance lists snapshot and unreferenced-file cleanup, but compaction isn't listed. A troubleshooting page says Glue compaction on these tables is reverted at the next sync.
- The destination page says Fivetran ingests data from "supported sources" and names no database connectors. Fivetran's PostgreSQL connector page documents capturing deletes through logical replication, but the MongoDB connector page doesn't mention this destination, so confirm your own source by name with Fivetran.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > 7. dlt: for Python teams who want pipelines as code
text:
At a glance: dlt is an open-source Python library, and dltHub is the paid platform on top of it. The Iceberg docs say dlt writes Iceberg tables through its filesystem destination, using the PyIceberg library.

What it writes: Parquet only, to whatever catalog PyIceberg can load, "including REST and SQL catalogs" (Iceberg docs). Merge supports upsert and insert-only. You bring your own catalog, since the docs describe no managed one.

What's good

- Pipelines live in your code and your repo, so you can review them like any other code.
- Its Postgres source reads a replication slot with the built-in pgoutput plugin, as the pg_replication docs explain.

Where it falls short

- Log-based CDC in the open-source library is PostgreSQL only. The SQL database source docs describe no log-based CDC for MySQL or Oracle, and SQL Server uses Change Tracking under the commercial dltHub licence (checked Oct 2026).
- The Iceberg docs list limits: no partition evolution (changing how an existing table is split into folders), Parquet only, and schema evolution isn't supported with upsert on PyIceberg 0.10.0 (checked Oct 2026).
- You write, schedule and watch the code.
- dltHub's pricing FAQ says paid subscriptions include a licence for CDC and Iceberg support (checked Oct 2026). The open-source Iceberg docs show no licence notice, so check which features need one before you rely on them.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > Left out of the list, and why
text:
Two tools did not meet the three rules in How we picked. The first is Amazon Data Firehose, which is not a current Kafka-free option.

In November 2024 AWS announced that Firehose could read PostgreSQL and MySQL and replicate changes to Iceberg tables, as a preview. AWS then added an update to that announcement post: "The preview period has ended on 09/30/2025 and its not possible to try this capability." We found no AWS page that offers database-to-Iceberg replication today (checked Oct 2026).

Firehose still writes Iceberg from other sources. Its prerequisites page says it supports Iceberg version 2 only and writes Parquet, and its destination docs say that for self-managed tables "you manage all the table optimizations such as compaction, and snapshot expiration" (checked Oct 2026).

The second is Supermetal. Its announcement of April 1, 2026 describes a single Rust program that reads the database log and writes Iceberg with no Kafka, Spark or Flink. We read only that post, not documentation on catalogs, deletes and upkeep, so it didn't get a full entry.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > Postgres without Debezium or Spark
text:
Of the options above, only Estuary's REST connector lists a Spark application as a prerequisite. Flink CDC's docs say some of its sources use Debezium inside, so ask each vendor if that matters to you.

All of them still read the same thing: Postgres's write-ahead log (WAL), through a replication slot, which is a bookmark that Postgres keeps for the reader. Several also need a publication, which is a list of tables whose changes Postgres will stream.

Estuary's docs (checked Oct 2026) warn that if a slot stops advancing, Postgres keeps WAL without limit by default. That risk follows you into every route.

| Option | What the docs say Postgres needs |
| Estuary ( Postgres capture docs ) | wal_level=logical , a user with the REPLICATION attribute, a slot and a publication, PostgreSQL 10 or later |
| RisingWave ( Postgres CDC source docs ) | wal_level = logical , PostgreSQL 10 through 18, one slot per source |
| dlt ( pg_replication docs ) | A replication slot with the pgoutput plugin |
| Flink CDC ( Postgres pipeline source docs ) | A required slot.name , with decoderbufs or pgoutput |
| OLake Go ( Postgres connector page ) | pgoutput plugin, PostgreSQL 10 or later, a replication slot and a publication in the same database, not shared between jobs |

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > Which one should you pick?
text:
| Your situation | Option to check | What you run or watch |
| Kafka runs and others read the topics | Kafka Connect with the Iceberg sink | You run Kafka brokers, Connect workers and two connectors |
| No Kafka, need Oracle CDC | Debezium Server sink or Estuary | Community sink with no stated catalogs, or hosted with AWS setup |
| You join or reshape data in flight | Flink CDC or RisingWave | A Flink cluster , or a streaming system and some licensed features |
| You want it hosted | Fivetran, or Estuary if your lake is on S3 | No position deletes on Fivetran , and Estuary needs EMR Serverless |
| Python team, Postgres source | dlt | Log-based CDC for Postgres only |
| Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB or SQL Server only, with scheduled copies | OLake Go | One process from Docker , Helm or the UI , on a schedule you set |

Each vendor link in this table goes to the page the claim comes from (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > Which one should you pick? > Which route to Iceberg fits you?
text:
Question 1 of 5

Is Kafka already running in your company?

Think about whether other teams or tools read the same change feed.

FAQs
Can I write Iceberg from a database without Kafka?

Yes. Each of the seven options on this page documents a path that doesn't need a Kafka cluster.

Does Debezium need Kafka?

No, it doesn't. Debezium Server is described in its docs as a ready-to-use application that streams changes without requiring Apache Kafka. Its Iceberg sink is community maintained and lives in a separate repository.

Does Flink CDC to Iceberg work without Kafka?

Yes, but you'll need a Flink cluster. The Iceberg pipeline connector requires a primary key on the source table and doesn't support exactly-once (checked Oct 2026).

Can Amazon Data Firehose replicate a database into Iceberg?

Not through the database preview. AWS announced it in November 2024 and added an update to that post saying the preview ended on September 30, 2025 and can't be tried. That update covers the database replication preview only, and Firehose's docs still describe Iceberg as a destination for other sources (checked Oct 2026).

Do I need Spark to get Postgres changes into Iceberg?

Not for most options. Among the tools here, only Estuary's REST connector lists a Spark application (Amazon EMR Serverless) as a prerequisite (checked Oct 2026), and the other pages we read list none.

Who compacts the Iceberg tables?

Usually you do. RisingWave lists automatic maintenance, and Estuary offers optional Glue optimizers (checked Oct 2026).

Which options document exactly-once delivery?

Two of the options in this post do: the Iceberg Kafka Connect sink (Kafka 2.5 or later) and RisingWave (an on-by-default setting). OLake Go uses a two-phase commit that avoids duplicate writes, and Flink CDC says exactly-once isn't supported (checked Oct 2026). For Debezium Server, Estuary, Fivetran and dlt, the pages we read don't state a guarantee.

When should I keep Kafka?

Keep it when several systems read the same changes, or when you need Kafka Connect's built-in fault tolerance and large sink library, per Debezium's own post. If the Iceberg table is your only reader, a direct writer is lighter to run.

title: Compare: Database to Iceberg Without Kafka: 7 Options | OLake > Conclusion
text:
Ask whether you need what Kafka provides, then test one update and one delete before you commit.

Last reviewed October 2026. If a vendor spots a statement here that's out of date, tell us and we'll correct it.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

No single alternative fits every app. The right one depends on how much of your app you're willing to change. Want to keep your MongoDB code?

Look at Amazon DocumentDB, Azure DocumentDB or FerretDB, and read each one's list of missing features first. Want JSON documents with a new query language? That's Couchbase.

Ready for a new data model? PostgreSQL with JSONB (JSON stored in a binary column type) suits joins and reports.

Amazon DynamoDB suits known key lookups on AWS. Apache Cassandra suits write-heavy work you run yourself.

- "MongoDB-compatible" does not mean MongoDB. Amazon DocumentDB emulates MongoDB APIs on its own engine. Azure DocumentDB's 99.03% figure counts operators only, and FerretDB lists commands it hasn't built yet (checked Oct 2026).
- Every option has a named limit. DynamoDB items stop at `400 KB`. Couchbase Community Edition stops at five nodes. FerretDB has no transaction commit command yet (checked Oct 2026).

We checked prices in October 2026 against each vendor's own page. Plans change often, so confirm on the vendor's page before you decide. Last reviewed October 2026.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > Why teams look for a MongoDB alternative
text:
MongoDB's release notes page lists the `9.0` series as the current stable release (checked Oct 2026). Three reasons usually start the search.

- The licence. The MongoDB server's licence file is the Server Side Public License (SSPL), Version 1, dated October 16, 2018, with copyright held by MongoDB, Inc. You can read it yourself in the `LICENSE-Community.txt` file in MongoDB's GitHub repository (checked Oct 2026). Microsoft's Azure DocumentDB overview says the SSPL doesn't apply to DocumentDB or Azure DocumentDB, because they don't run the MongoDB server.
- The bill. MongoDB's managed service, Atlas, lists a Free tier at $0, a Flex tier that "can cost between $8 and $30 for a month's usage", and Dedicated clusters from $0.08 an hour, with a headline that reads "Starts at $56.94/month". See the Atlas pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Joins. MongoDB can join collections with `$lookup`, a left outer join to another collection in the same database. Its own `$lookup` docs page warns that unindexed or correlated-subquery lookups on large collections can slow queries. They suggest an embedded data model instead.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > How we picked
text:
Vendor facts come from each vendor's own docs and pricing pages, read in October 2026. We did not run the other tools. User opinions come only from named public sources, with a month and year where the page shows one. These are individual opinions and prices; one person's view, with its date and link.

CouchDB, Redis, Firestore, Elasticsearch, RethinkDB, OrientDB and others are left out. We didn't check their current docs for this page.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > First, pick a route
text:
Route 1 keeps your MongoDB code. An API (application programming interface) is the set of commands your app sends. These engines accept MongoDB's commands but aren't MongoDB: Amazon DocumentDB, Azure DocumentDB and FerretDB. You'll still need to test for missing features.

Route 2 keeps the documents. Couchbase also stores JSON documents, but you use its own driver and query language, SQL++. Your data shape carries over, and you rewrite the data access code.

Route 3 changes the data model. PostgreSQL stores rows and tables, DynamoDB stores items found by key, and Cassandra stores rows grouped by a partition key. This is the most work. It's also the route where joins, for example in PostgreSQL, become possible.
