title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 1. PostgreSQL with JSONB
text:
At a glance: PostgreSQL License · you run it or rent it from a host · route 3 · software is free

`JSONB` is a PostgreSQL column type that stores JSON documents in a binary format. Its documentation says most applications should prefer `jsonb`, and that it supports several index types.

What its docs list

- `jsonb` is stored in a decomposed binary format, which the docs say makes input slightly slower but processing significantly faster than plain `json`. It also supports indexing, and GIN indexes can search for keys or key/value pairs across a large number of `jsonb` documents.
- It speaks SQL, so joins, reports and the tools your analysts already know work as they do on any relational database. Its docs say it supports most of the major features of `SQL:2023` and conforms to at least 170 of the 177 mandatory Core features, per its SQL conformance appendix (checked Oct 2026).
- Under its multiversion concurrency control (MVCC) model, the concurrency docs say reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading.
- Its change feed, called logical replication, can publish inserts, updates, deletes and truncates, according to its publication docs, so downstream systems can follow it.

Where it falls short

- Any update takes a row-level lock on the whole row, so the JSON docs (checked Oct 2026) say to keep JSON documents a manageable size. Large documents that change a lot are a poor fit.
- `jsonb` does not keep white space, the order of object keys or duplicate keys, and if a key appears twice only the last value is kept, per the same page (checked Oct 2026). The docs also recommend a somewhat fixed document structure, which is typically not enforced by the database.
- The built-in partitioning described in its partitioning docs (checked Oct 2026) splits a table by range, list or hash, and the page doesn't mention sharding across servers. Ask any host how it scales writes.
- Your MongoDB queries become SQL, so your data access code has to change.
- A logical replication slot that nobody reads keeps write-ahead log (WAL) files on disk, and in extreme cases could shut the database down to prevent transaction ID wraparound, according to its logical decoding docs (checked Oct 2026).

Fits: reports and joins matter more than a drop-in swap. Less suited if your existing MongoDB code has to keep working.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 2. Amazon DocumentDB
text:
At a glance: proprietary · AWS managed service · route 1 · `db.r5.large` at $0.277 an hour standard

Amazon DocumentDB "emulates the MongoDB 3.6, 4.0, 5.0, and 8.0 APIs on a purpose-built database engine", according to AWS's functional differences page. It isn't MongoDB code. AWS says query plans and `explain()` output may differ.

What its docs list

- AWS describes it as fully managed. Its developer guide says storage keeps six copies of your data across three Availability Zones (separate data centers in one region), and grows in `10 GB` steps up to `256 TiB` for engine version `8.0` and later (`128 TiB` for earlier versions) (checked Oct 2026). You don't provision extra storage for growth.
- A cluster holds `0` to `16` instances and all writes go through the primary. AWS says that on an instance failure it fails over automatically (checked Oct 2026) to one of up to `15` replicas that you create in other Availability Zones.
- Point-in-time recovery restores a cluster to any second in the retention period, up to the last `5 minutes`, and automatic backup retention can be set up to `35 days`, per the same guide (checked Oct 2026).
- Elastic clusters, the horizontally scaled type, are described as supporting workloads with millions of reads and writes per second and petabytes of storage.
- Change streams are supported on instance-based clusters for all four API versions, per the supported-commands table in AWS's MongoDB APIs page. Explicit multi-statement ACID transactions are supported from DocumentDB `4.0`, according to the functional differences page (checked Oct 2026).
- AWS offers a one-month free trial of 750 hours on `db.t3.medium`, with 30 million I/Os and 5 GB of storage, per its pricing page (checked Oct 2026). It is not available in the AWS GovCloud (US) regions or the China (Ningxia) region.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 2. Amazon DocumentDB (part 2)
text:
- AWS's supported-index table (checked Oct 2026) marks wildcard and hashed indexes as not supported, and capped collections, `cloneCollectionAsCapped` and `convertToCapped` are marked No for every engine version.
- Change streams are not supported on elastic clusters, the horizontally scaled type, per the MongoDB APIs page (checked Oct 2026).
- Retryable writes arrive in engine version `8.0.2`. Earlier versions return an error unless the driver turns them off, per the functional differences page (checked Oct 2026).
- Only one index build can run on a collection at a time, per the functional differences page (checked Oct 2026).
- It does not support the `admin` or `local` database, or MongoDB `system.*` collections, and it does not guarantee result ordering unless you sort explicitly, per the functional differences page (checked Oct 2026).
- Do the sums: one `db.r5.large` instance running 30 days is 720 hours, or about $199 at $0.277 an hour (our own sum, not a price on the page: 0.277 x 720 = 199.44), before storage and I/O. Billing has more moving parts than a flat tier: instance hours, I/O, storage, backup and data transfer. The pricing page example (checked Oct 2026) lists $0.10 per GB-month and $0.20 per million I/O requests on standard, or an I/O-Optimized option at $0.3047 an hour and $0.30 per GB-month.

Fits: an app already on AWS that sticks to the supported features. Test the exact features you use; AWS publishes the list of what is and isn't supported.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 3. Azure DocumentDB
text:
At a glance: open source engine, proprietary Azure service · route 1 · free tier, other rates not shown in the page text we read

Azure DocumentDB is described by Microsoft as "a fully managed, open-source, 99.03% MongoDB-compatible database". It is built on the open source DocumentDB engine, which is governed by the Linux Foundation and, according to the DocumentDB project's GitHub page, built on PostgreSQL. The engine uses the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) licence, a permissive open source licence (checked Oct 2026), and the service does not run the MongoDB server.

The overview page was last updated on June 12, 2026.

What its docs list

- Microsoft says the open source engine can run on-premises or in any cloud, and that a Kubernetes operator is provided to get started, per the overview.
- Microsoft says the service supports high-capacity vertical and horizontal scaling, with no shard key required until the database surpasses terabytes, per the overview. That is Microsoft's description, and we didn't test it.
- Its compatibility page (checked Oct 2026) lists all 181 aggregation operators and all 22 update operators as supported.
- The same page lists wildcard, hashed, text, multikey, compound, geospatial and vector indexes. The vector index is marked as available only in DocumentDB.
- The `$changeStream` stage is marked supported for versions `5.0` to `8.0`, per the compatibility page (checked Oct 2026).
- Microsoft's pricing page lists a free tier cluster, and a savings plan at 20% off per node on one and three year terms (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 3. Azure DocumentDB (part 2)
text:
- The 99.03% is Microsoft's own measure. It counts operators: 58 of 60 aggregation stages, 181 of 181 aggregation operators, 44 of 45 query and projection operators, and 22 of 22 update operators. Commands and admin operations are excluded, per Microsoft's compatibility page (checked Oct 2026). That does not mean 99% of your app will run.
- Commands marked not supported on the compatibility page (checked Oct 2026) include `bulkWrite`, `serverStatus`, `top`, `dataSize`, `compact` and `setDefaultRWConcern`.
- Creating a unique index takes an exclusive lock on the collection for the whole build, which blocks reads and writes, per the compatibility page (checked Oct 2026).
- `$changeStreamSplitLargeEvent` is marked not supported on the compatibility page (checked Oct 2026), even though `$changeStream` itself is.
- Compute and storage rates are not shown in the text of the pricing page that we could read without picking a region (checked Oct 2026), so we can't price a cluster from it.
- The savings plan needs a one or three year term, so the 20% discount requires that commitment, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

Fits: Azure, or an engine whose licence you can read in full. Less suited if your app depends on the unsupported commands.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 4. FerretDB
text:
At a glance: Apache 2.0 · you run it · route 1 · software free, hosted price not published

FerretDB's documentation home page describes it as an open-source alternative to MongoDB. In plain terms, it's a proxy that converts MongoDB `5.0+` wire protocol queries to SQL, and it uses PostgreSQL with the DocumentDB extension as its database engine. The wire protocol is how a driver talks to the server.

What its docs list

- The licence is Apache 2.0, shown on its GitHub page (checked Oct 2026).
- The project README (its front page on GitHub) says it is compatible with MongoDB drivers and popular MongoDB tools, and works as a drop-in replacement for MongoDB `5.0+` in many cases. The "in many cases" is the project's own wording.
- Your data sits in PostgreSQL, which many teams already run.
- The README lists managed FerretDB at FerretDB Cloud, Civo, Tembo, Elestio and Cozystack, and a Go library package that embeds FerretDB into your application.
- The project states its own policy on gaps in its compatibility docs: "We consider all other differences in behavior to be problems" and want to address them. That is the project's stated intent. It also says it uses the same error names and codes as MongoDB.

Where it falls short

- On the `v2.7` compatibility page, `abortTransaction` and `commitTransaction` are "Not implemented yet". The newer `v2.8` docs (checked Oct 2026) are labelled unreleased and show the same two gaps.
- The role management commands, such as `createRole`, `dropRole` and `rolesInfo`, are not implemented, per the compatibility page (checked Oct 2026).
- `bulkWrite`, `cloneCollectionAsCapped` and `convertToCapped` are not supported, per the compatibility page (checked Oct 2026).
- Change streams are not documented as supported on the compatibility page (checked Oct 2026) we read.
- Exact error messages may sometimes differ from MongoDB's, and collection names must be valid UTF-8, which MongoDB does not require, per the compatibility page (checked Oct 2026).
- The README (checked Oct 2026) says the quickstart Docker command is unsuitable for production use because it keeps all data inside and loses it on shutdown. It also advises users not to build FerretDB themselves, and to use the binaries, Docker images or packages it provides.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 4. FerretDB (part 2)
text: Fits: self-hosted and permissively licensed, if you can live without those commands. Less suited if you need multi-statement transactions or change streams today.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 5. Couchbase
text:
At a glance: editions: Community and Enterprise · you run it, or use Capella · route 2 · Capella Basic from $0.15 an hour per node

Couchbase Server stores items with a key and a value, inside buckets, scopes and collections. A value can be binary or a JSON document, and its query language is SQL++, which looks like SQL but works on JSON. The data docs say the maximum size of a value is `20 MiB` (checked Oct 2026).

What its docs list

- Data is saved as items, each with a unique key and a value that can be binary or JSON. The data docs put the maximum size of a value at `20 MiB` (checked Oct 2026).
- A bucket can have up to `3` replicas, and XDCR (cross data center replication) copies data between clusters that may sit in different data centers, per its replication docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Capella, the managed service, lists a Free plan with 1 node and 8 GB, per its pricing page. Basic starts at $0.15 an hour per node, Developer Pro at $0.35 and Enterprise at $0.49 (checked Oct 2026).
- The transactions docs describe atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability (ACID) guarantees, meaning all-or-nothing changes. Changes are not visible until commit, which the docs call Read Committed isolation, and transactional reads are stricter (Monotonic Atomic View).
- Transactions offer three durability levels, from `majority` (the default) to `persistToMajority`, which the docs call the strongest protection and the least performant.
- Couchbase's docs describe a Kafka connector that streams changes using its Database Change Protocol (DCP). We didn't test it, so check it yourself if you feed analytics.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 5. Couchbase (part 2)
text:
- Community Edition is free for clusters of up to five nodes and supports a maximum of `4` cores per node, with limited concurrency and parallelism, per the editions page (checked Oct 2026).
- Its licence was updated to disallow XDCR, now an Enterprise-only feature, and Community Edition does not include the latest bug fixes, per the editions page (checked Oct 2026).
- The transactions docs say to use transactions only on documents under `10 MB`, inside one data center, and not with active-active two-way XDCR (checked Oct 2026).
- The default transaction expiry is `15 seconds`, and transactions need Network Time Protocol (NTP) to keep time in sync across all cluster nodes, per the same page (checked Oct 2026).
- The Capella Free plan lists forum support only, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- You'll change drivers and rewrite queries.

Fits: the document model with a different query language. Less suited if you need to keep MongoDB commands.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 6. Amazon DynamoDB
text:
At a glance: proprietary · AWS service · route 3 · $0.625 per million write request units

AWS's DynamoDB introduction page describes it as a serverless, fully managed, distributed NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond performance at any scale. That is AWS's own claim, and we didn't test it.

What its docs list

- On-demand mode is pay per request. The worked examples on the on-demand pricing page, use $0.625 per million write request units and $0.125 per million read request units, and standard storage at $0.25 per GB (checked Oct 2026).
- A write request unit covers an item up to `1 KB`, and a read request unit covers `4 KB`, per the same page. An eventually consistent read costs half a read request unit per `4 KB` (checked Oct 2026).
- The free tier lists 25 GB of storage, 25 write and 25 read capacity units, 2.5 million stream read requests and 1 GB of data transfer out, per the on-demand pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Transactions can group up to `100` write actions on up to `100` items, with a `4 MB` total. The transactions docs say each item costs two underlying reads or writes, one to prepare and one to commit (checked Oct 2026).
- Global tables replicate item changes to other Regions typically within a second by default, and multi-Region strong consistency is available as an option, per the read consistency docs.
- Strongly consistent reads are available on tables and local secondary indexes, so you can choose per read between cost and freshness, per the read consistency docs.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 6. Amazon DynamoDB (part 2)
text:
- The maximum item size is `400 KB`, which includes attribute names, per the quotas docs (checked Oct 2026). AWS's best-practices page suggests storing a large item as an object in Amazon S3 and keeping the object identifier in the DynamoDB item.
- There is no `JOIN` operator, according to the AWS introduction page (checked Oct 2026). AWS recommends denormalizing, which means copying data into the shape each query needs.
- A `Scan` reads the whole table or index before filtering and returns up to `1 MB` per call, per the query and scan guide (checked Oct 2026).
- Reads are eventually consistent by default, and reads from global secondary indexes and streams always are. Strongly consistent reads work only on tables and local secondary indexes, per the read consistency docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Change history in DynamoDB Streams is removed after `24 hours`, according to AWS's Streams docs (checked Oct 2026).
- It's an AWS service. AWS also offers a downloadable DynamoDB Local for developing and testing applications, and transactions give ACID guarantees only in the Region where the write API was called, per the transactions docs (checked Oct 2026).

Fits: known questions on AWS. Less suited if your documents are large or your questions keep changing.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 7. Apache Cassandra
text:
At a glance: Apache 2.0 · you run it · route 3 · software free, project publishes no price

Cassandra is an open source distributed database. It keeps several copies of each partition, and any copy can take a write (multi-master replication).

You pick a consistency level per operation, such as one replica or a majority (called quorum). The latest stable version is `5.0`, with `5.0.9` released on August 7, 2026, per the download page.

What its docs list

- The storage engine docs say it is optimized for write-oriented workloads, using log structured merge (LSM) trees with an append-only approach, so the write path has no read lookups. We didn't benchmark it.
- Its architecture docs describe multi-master replication, so there is no single primary to fail over. With a replication factor of `3`, data is written to three distinct replicas.
- Consistency levels include `ONE`, `TWO`, `THREE`, `QUORUM` (a majority of replicas) and `ALL`, so you tune the trade-off per operation.
- Version `5.0`adds (checked Oct 2026) Storage Attached Indexes, a vector data type, trie memtables and trie SSTables, the Unified Compaction Strategy and Dynamic Data Masking.
- CQL `INSERT` and `UPDATE` accept a time to live (TTL) in seconds, and the values are removed automatically after that time. Updates within one partition key are applied atomically and in isolation, per the CQL docs.
- The project publishes no price list, and the software itself is free, per the project site (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > The 7 MongoDB alternatives > 7. Apache Cassandra (part 2)
text:
- Its query language, Cassandra Query Language (CQL), runs no joins or sub-queries, and a `SELECT` reads one table, per the CQL docs. The data modeling guide (checked Oct 2026) says to group all required columns in one table, which duplicates data.
- The guarantees page says Cassandra picks availability and partition tolerance and compromises on consistency to some extent. Single-table writes are eventually consistent, and its architecture docs (checked Oct 2026) say concurrent updates are settled by last-write-wins.
- Conditional writes such as `IF NOT EXISTS` use a protocol called Paxos, which needs the replicas to agree. The CQL docs (checked Oct 2026) say this carries a non-negligible performance cost and should be used sparingly.
- Its guideline is under `100,000` values and `100 MB` of disk per partition, though the docs say requirements vary by application (checked Oct 2026).
- The storage engine docs (checked Oct 2026) list trade-offs in read performance and write amplification for the append-only design.
- A CQL query that needs a full scan of all partitions has to add `ALLOW FILTERING`, which the docs (checked Oct 2026) say runs the full scan and makes performance unpredictable.

Fits: write volume as the problem and people to run clusters. Less suited if you need ad hoc queries or joins.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > Other options worth knowing
text:
MySQL also stores JSON, and its docs say JSON columns validate the documents stored in them. We didn't compare it in full, because we found fewer MongoDB-specific facts than for the seven above.

What happens to your change feed
If other systems read your MongoDB change streams today, that feed doesn't come along. Each option has its own change data capture (CDC) feed: PostgreSQL has logical replication, DynamoDB has Streams, and Cassandra has a per-table change data capture log, switched on with a table property. Our CDC tools comparison covers tools that read these feeds.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > Which MongoDB alternative should you pick?
text:
- You want to keep your MongoDB code: Amazon DocumentDB on AWS, Azure DocumentDB on Azure, FerretDB if you self-host. Test first, always.
- You want documents but are fine with a new language: Couchbase.
- You need joins, reports and SQL: PostgreSQL with JSONB.
- You know your key lookups and you're on AWS: DynamoDB.
- You have heavy writes and a team to run a cluster: Cassandra.
- You want to keep MongoDB and add analytics: copy its changes into Iceberg or Parquet (see Where OLake Go fits). Our OLTP vs OLAP explainer covers why teams split the two.

If you can't say which route you're on yet, stay on MongoDB until you can. Or try this short quiz.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > Which MongoDB alternative should you pick? > Which MongoDB alternative fits you?
text:
Question 1 of 5

How much of your app can you change?

This one answer removes most of the list.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > Where MongoDB fits
text:
Choose MongoDB if your app uses features the alternatives list as missing or limited.

What its docs list

- ACID transactions across documents. They need `featureCompatibilityVersion``4.0` on a replica set (a group of servers holding copies of the same data) or `4.2` on a sharded cluster, per the transactions docs (checked Oct 2026), and MongoDB says a distributed transaction usually costs more than single-document writes.
- An operation on a single document is atomic. MongoDB says that because embedded documents and arrays can hold related data in one document, many practical use cases don't need multi-document transactions.
- Sharding with hashed and ranged keys, and a changeable shard key (the field that decides which server holds a document).
- Change streams with pre- and post-images, which you can switch on per collection (checked Oct 2026) from MongoDB `6.0`. There is no pre-image for an inserted document and no post-image for a deleted one.
- Change streams work on replica sets and sharded clusters, and a stream can resume from a resume token as long as the oplog still holds enough history.

Where it falls short

- A document can't exceed `16 MiB`, nesting stops at `100` levels, and a collection can have at most `64` indexes, per MongoDB's limits page (checked Oct 2026).
- By default a transaction must run for less than one minute, and it waits up to `5 milliseconds` for the locks it needs before it aborts, per MongoDB's transactions production considerations page (checked Oct 2026).
- With a hashed shard key, range queries on that key are less likely to hit one shard and cause more cluster-wide broadcast operations, per the sharding docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Change streams are restricted to database events, time series collections do not support them, and they only report changes persisted to a majority of data-bearing replica set members, per the change streams docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Pre- and post-images use storage space and add processing time, and a change stream event must stay within the `16 MB` document limit, per the change streams docs (checked Oct 2026).
- On Atlas, the Free tier includes 512 MB of storage and Flex includes 5 GB, and Dedicated clusters start at $0.08 an hour, with a headline that reads "Starts at $56.94/month", per the Atlas pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > Where MongoDB fits (part 2)
text: On a Hacker News thread about MongoDB costs (November 2025), one commenter wrote "MongoDB Atlas was around 500% more expensive than in-house every time I evaluated it". A PeerSpot reviewer in April 2026 wrote "we prefer this because of the reliability of MongoDB Atlas", per PeerSpot's Atlas reviews.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > Worked example: one app, five answers
text:
Take an app that sends `bulkWrite` calls, uses a wildcard index, and stores some `5 MB` documents. It's a made-up app, but each cell below comes from the vendor pages cited in the sections above. "Unknown" means we didn't read a page that answers it.

| Need | Amazon DocumentDB | Azure DocumentDB | FerretDB | Couchbase | DynamoDB |
| Wildcard index | Marked "No" | Listed as supported | Unknown | Not MongoDB code, so rewrite | Not MongoDB code, so rewrite |
| bulkWrite | Unknown | Not supported | Not supported | Not MongoDB code, so rewrite | Not MongoDB code, so rewrite |
| 5 MB document | Unknown | Unknown | Unknown | Fits ( 20 MiB value limit) | Fails ( 400 KB item limit) |

The result: no compatible engine passes without a change. Two fail on a named item, and the rest need a test. Write your own feature list before you pick.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > What to test before you switch
text:
- Your feature list. Write down every command and operator your app uses, then check each against the vendor's compatibility page. If you're on Route 1, do this before anything else.
- Your biggest document. Compare it with the item limit: `400 KB` on DynamoDB, `20 MiB` on Couchbase, `16 MiB` on MongoDB, `1 GB` per field in PostgreSQL (checked Oct 2026).
- Your consistency assumptions. MongoDB's default write concern is `majority`, except on some replica sets with arbiters, where it is `{ w: 1 }`. DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default, and Cassandra single-table writes are eventually consistent.
- Your change feed. List who reads change streams today and how long history must be kept.
- Your real bill. List prices use different meters (monthly tier, hourly instance, request), so price your own traffic in the vendor calculator.
- What to ask each vendor. For any compatibility, speed or scale claim (Azure's 99.03%, DynamoDB's single-digit milliseconds, DocumentDB's "fast, reliable" wording), ask what was measured, on which versions, and whether your commands were in the test. We tested none of them.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > A safe order for moving
text:
This order is our own suggestion and does not come from a vendor.

- Audit. List every command, operator and index your app uses, and the biggest document it stores.
- Test in parallel. Run the same queries against the new engine with copied data, then compare answers.
- Move reads first. Send read traffic to the new system while MongoDB stays the source of truth.
- Move writes last. Switch writes only after you've tested a rollback.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > Where OLake Go fits
text: OLake Go is not a MongoDB alternative. It is for the team that keeps MongoDB for the app and wants analytics somewhere else. It is open source. It reads MongoDB `4.0` or higher with full refresh, incremental sync or change capture (CDC), which needs a replica set, and writes Apache Iceberg tables or Parquet files that analysts can query outside MongoDB. Our docs cover self-hosted MongoDB and Atlas, and a data filter can limit which rows a stream replicates. Setup steps are on our MongoDB connector page. You run it yourself, with Docker, Helm on Kubernetes or the OLake UI; the quickstart walks through it.

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > FAQs
text:
Q1. What is the best MongoDB alternative?

It depends on how much you can change. Same MongoDB code: test Amazon DocumentDB, Azure DocumentDB or FerretDB. Joins and SQL: PostgreSQL with JSONB. Known key lookups on AWS: DynamoDB.

Q2. Is there a free MongoDB alternative?

Sort of. PostgreSQL, FerretDB and Cassandra are free software, but you still pay to run them. Atlas also has a free tier at $0 with 512 MB, Azure DocumentDB offers a free tier cluster, and Couchbase Community Edition is free for up to five nodes (checked Oct 2026).

Q3. Is Amazon DocumentDB the same as MongoDB?

No. AWS says it emulates the MongoDB `3.6`, `4.0`, `5.0` and `8.0` APIs on its own engine, and that query plans may differ. Its docs list what's missing, such as wildcard and hashed indexes (checked Oct 2026).

Q4. Is FerretDB a drop-in replacement for MongoDB?

Not fully. Its `v2.7` compatibility page lists transaction commit and abort, role commands and `bulkWrite` as unimplemented or unsupported (checked Oct 2026). It fits only if your app avoids those.

Q5. Can PostgreSQL replace MongoDB?

For many apps, yes. `JSONB` stores documents inside a table and supports indexes. You'll have to rewrite queries as SQL, and the docs say any update locks the whole row, so keep documents a manageable size (checked Oct 2026).

Q6. Why do teams leave MongoDB?

The usual reasons are the SSPL licence on the server, Atlas cost, and joins. Some teams stay and fix their data model instead.

Q7. Should I move to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB?

Microsoft's Cosmos DB for MongoDB overview page now tells people migrating a MongoDB app to consider Azure DocumentDB, so check the current docs before starting a new project on Cosmos DB.

Q8. Do I have to leave MongoDB at all?

No. If the app works and you only need reports or search, keep MongoDB and copy its changes elsewhere. OLake Go does this for MongoDB, with change capture, into Iceberg or Parquet. Other options are in our data replication tools comparison.

Q9. Do I lose change streams if I switch?

Yes, you move to the new system's equivalent. Amazon DocumentDB supports change streams on instance-based clusters, Azure DocumentDB marks `$changeStream` supported, FerretDB does not document them, and DynamoDB Streams keep records for `24 hours` (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: MongoDB Alternatives: 7 Options and Their Limits | OLake > Conclusion
text:
Start with your own feature list, pick your route, and test before you trust any "compatible" label. If you only need reports or search, keep MongoDB and copy its changes into a second system.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

Almost every MongoDB change data capture (CDC) tool does the same trick under the hood: it reads MongoDB's change streams. So the choice comes down to who runs the reader and where the changes land.

If you already run Kafka, Debezium and the MongoDB Kafka connector fit, and if you want someone else to run it, look at Airbyte, Fivetran, Estuary, Artie and AWS Database Migration Service (DMS). To land the changes in Apache Iceberg tables you run yourself, without Kafka, see OLake Go. Either way, MongoDB must run as a replica set or sharded cluster, and three limits bite hardest: the oplog window, the `16 MB` limit and deletes.

- Change streams are the main method. They let apps read changes without manually tailing the oplog (the log MongoDB keeps of recent writes).
- You need a replica set or sharded cluster.MongoDB's manual says change streams are available only on those, and each tool below reads them or the oplog.
- The oplog window is a documented failure mode. A tool that stays offline longer than the oplog holds can lose its place, and then it has to copy the data all over again.
- Deletes carry only the document key by default. To see what was deleted you need pre-images, which need MongoDB `6.0` or later and extra storage.

Vendor facts come from each vendor's own pages, read in September and October 2026. We did not run the other tools. Quotes from users carry their source and date. These are individual opinions and prices; one person's view, with its date and link. We quote no dollar figures here.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > How MongoDB CDC actually works
text:
Change data capture means spotting the inserts, updates and deletes in a database and sending only those to another system. MongoDB's own tool for it is the change stream, an API that gives your app a live feed of changes. The MongoDB manual says it works without "the prior complexity and risk of manually tailing the oplog".

Change streams run on replica sets and sharded clusters, not on a standalone server. The manual also lists WiredTiger storage and replica set protocol version `1`. On a sharded cluster you open the stream from the `mongos` router, which makes one stream per shard and merges the results.

Each event carries a resume token in its `_id` field, which works like a bookmark. A tool saves the latest token, and after a restart it asks MongoDB to pick up from there. The manual adds a condition: the oplog "must have enough history to locate the operation associated with the token".

Tools read changes in one of three ways. The table sticks to what MongoDB and the vendors document.

| Way to read changes | What the docs say | Deletes |
| Change streams | MongoDB's supported API. Debezium , Airbyte , Fivetran , Estuary and Artie all use it | Yes, key only unless pre-images are on |
| Reading the oplog directly | Striim does this before MongoDB 4.2 . AWS DMS has an endpoint setting, useOplog , which is off by default ( AWS docs ) | Yes |
| Scheduled full or batch copies | Airbyte's Full Refresh mode and Estuary's Batch Snapshot and Batch Incremental modes | Estuary says only its change stream mode captures deletes ( Estuary docs ) |

That bookmark rule is behind a documented failure mode. Airbyte's troubleshooting page says a first import longer than the oplog retention can leave an invalid resume token that needs a re-import.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > Size the oplog first
text:
Check your oplog size before you pick a tool. Airbyte, Fivetran, Estuary and AWS DMS all say in their own docs to keep at least 24 hours of changes in the oplog: Airbyte, Fivetran, Estuary and AWS DMS (checked Oct 2026). Airbyte and Fivetran add that a week is better.

MongoDB's change oplog size tutorial shows how to check and change the size, on self-managed replica sets.

javascript

```
use local
db.oplog.rs.stats().maxSize
rs.printReplicationInfo()
db.adminCommand({replSetResizeOplog: 1, size: Double(16000)})
```

Line one shows the oplog size in bytes. MongoDB's reference page says `rs.printReplicationInfo()` prints the configured size and the "log length start to end", which is your window in hours. Resizing (checked Oct 2026) takes a size above `990 MB`, and the example sets `16 GB`.

Here is our own arithmetic. MongoDB's sample output shows a window of 18.17 hours.

If your tool could be down over a 60 hour weekend, that oplog is about 3.3 times too small (60 divided by 18.17). You'd need roughly 3.3 times the size, plus room to catch up. Read your own window first.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > Three limits that decide whether a tool works
text:
The `16 MB` limit applies to change events as well as documents. MongoDB's production recommendations say change stream responses must stay within the `16 MB` limit for a BSON (binary JSON) document (checked Oct 2026). An update that returns the full document, or a large insert, can push an event over the line, and then the notification fails.

MongoDB's limits page sets the maximum BSON document size at 16 mebibytes and limits nesting to 100 levels (checked Oct 2026).

Updates show only the changed fields by default. If a tool wants the whole document, it either asks MongoDB to look it up later (`updateLookup`) or uses post-images. The manual warns that `updateLookup` with a filter can cause "Resume Token Not Found" errors during rapid deletions, and suggests pre- and post-images instead.

Deletes are thin. MongoDB's delete event leaves out the full document because it no longer exists. Pre-images fix that (more below).

Pre-images arrived in MongoDB `6.0`. You switch them on per collection with `changeStreamPreAndPostImages`, and MongoDB's `collMod` page says they use storage and processing time.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > A worked example: two quick updates, then a delete
text:
Take order number 7. In one minute it's inserted as "new", updated to "packed", updated to "shipped", then deleted.

The table shows what each documented setting records, reasoned from the vendors' docs.

| Setting | Insert | The two updates | The delete |
| Default change stream | Full document | Changed fields only | Key only |
| Lookup ( updateLookup , Airbyte's default) | Full document | The latest version at processing time, which MongoDB says is null if the document is gone | Key only |
| Post-images (MongoDB 6.0 +) | Full document | The document right after each update | Key only |
| Post- and pre-images | Full document | After each update | The document as it was before the delete |

Per Airbyte's docs, with Lookup the "packed" state may be lost, while post-images can keep it if they were on before the update.

A Kafka topic holds all four events. A tool that mirrors the latest state, such as Fivetran, ends with one row for order 7, flagged as deleted.

An audit trail needs every state. A daily report on current orders doesn't.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > How we picked
text:
We included maintained tools whose own documentation shows they read MongoDB changes. Tools with no MongoDB CDC page we could read didn't make the cut.

For the same question on other databases, see our SQL Server CDC tools comparison and the wider best change data capture tools list.

The tools are grouped by how you run them, and the numbers are not a ranking. Kafka Connect is the framework that runs connectors against Apache Kafka, a system that stores event streams as topics.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > MongoDB CDC tools at a glance
text:
Apache Iceberg is an open table format for data lakes. "Supports Iceberg" can mean a direct writer or a separate route, so the last column says which.

| Tool | Runs as | Kafka needed? | Iceberg route, from each tool's own docs |
| Native change streams | Your own app | No | You write it |
| Debezium | Kafka Connect, or Debezium Server | Kafka Connect mode, yes; Debezium Server, no | Community-maintained Debezium Server sink, in a separate repository |
| MongoDB Kafka connector | Kafka Connect | Yes | No Iceberg writer found in its docs |
| Airbyte | Core self-hosted, or Cloud | No | S3 Data Lake and GCS Data Lake destinations; objects and unions become JSON strings |
| Fivetran | Vendor-run, or Hybrid on Enterprise and Business Critical plans ( Fivetran docs ) (checked Oct 2026) | No | Managed Data Lake Service, which creates Iceberg metadata by default |
| OLake Go | You run it yourself ( install ) | No | Writes Iceberg or Parquet directly ( our docs ) |
| Estuary | Vendor-run; private and bring-your-own-cloud on Enterprise | No | Two Iceberg destinations: one merges with serverless Spark jobs on AWS Elastic MapReduce, the other appends delta updates through AWS Glue or a REST catalog |
| Artie | Vendor-run; bring-your-own-cloud on Enterprise | No | Iceberg destination through Iceberg REST catalogs (services that track tables over an open API) and S3 Tables, per its changelog ; its pricing page lists Iceberg only under Enterprise (checked Oct 2026) |

| Striim | Self-managed or cloud | Reader docs do not mention it | Iceberg Writer (Google Cloud Storage) or S3 Tables Writer (Amazon S3 Tables), with a compute engine and catalog |

Sources for the Iceberg column: AWS DMS's Targets page, Estuary's Iceberg and delta updates connector pages, and Striim's Iceberg Writer page. Also the S3 Data Lake and GCS Data Lake pages at Airbyte, the Managed Data Lake Service page at Fivetran, and the changelog at Artie (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Build it yourself
text:
**1. Native change streams: best for small apps that react to changes**

At a glance

- Method: MongoDB's own change stream API
- Price: Included with MongoDB; you write and run the reader

This is the API most other tools here wrap. Your app opens a stream on a collection, a database or the whole deployment.

What's good

- No extra software to install, and you can filter events with an aggregation pipeline.
- A stream can cover a single collection, a database or an entire deployment, per the manual.
- Streams are resumable: you pass the saved resume token to `resumeAfter` or `startAfter` when you open the cursor, and `startAfter` can open a new stream after an invalidate event such as a collection drop or rename.
- Change streams only notify on changes that have persisted to a majority of the data-bearing members of the replica set.
- On a sharded cluster, `mongos` opens a change stream on each shard and then sorts and filters the results.
- From MongoDB `6.0` a stream can output a document before and after a change, switched on per collection with `changeStreamPreAndPostImages`.

Where it falls short

- You're on the hook for storing resume tokens, handling retries and coping with schema changes yourself.
- The manual (checked Oct 2026) says time series collections do not support change streams.
- Pre- and post-images are not available for an event if they were not enabled on the collection when the update or delete happened, or if they were removed after the `expireAfterSeconds` retention time (`collMod` page) (checked Oct 2026). An inserted document has no pre-image and a deleted one has no post-image.
- Pre-images are written to the `config.system.preimages` collection, which the docs (checked Oct 2026) say "may become large", and they add processing time.
- If you drop or rename a collection or database with a stream open against it, the stream cursors close when they reach that point in the oplog (MongoDB's production recommendations page) (checked Oct 2026).
- By default MongoDB sets no minimum oplog retention period and truncates the oldest entries to hold the configured maximum size (oplog page) (checked Oct 2026). The default size on WiredTiger is 5% of free disk space, with a `990 MB` floor and a `50 GB` cap.

What users say: This is MongoDB's own API and has no product reviews, so we found no review-site or forum thread to quote.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Run it with Kafka
text:
**2. Debezium: best for teams that already run Kafka**

At a glance

- Method: Change streams, wrapped by a Debezium connector
- Price: Free licence, you pay for infrastructure and staff

Debezium has a MongoDB connector in its current stable `3.7` release series. Its MongoDB docs say the connector tracks a replica set or a sharded cluster and "does not read the oplog directly". Change streams do that job instead.

What's good

- On MongoDB `6.0` or later you can fill the `before` field by turning on pre-images and setting `capture.mode` to a `*_with_pre_image` option.
- Version `3.7` lists MongoDB `6.0`, `7.0` and `8.0` as tested, per its `3.7` release page (checked Oct 2026). That page dates `3.7.0.Final` to 29 September 2026, with a new dedicated transform (SMT) that converts MongoDB events into relational-style structs.
- Its docs (checked Oct 2026) say a snapshot copies collections in parallel, using as many threads as possible up to `snapshot.max.threads`. Incremental snapshots default to chunks of `1024` rows and track progress with watermarks.
- By default it streams from the replica set's primary, and you can stream from a secondary by setting the read preference in the connection string. For a sharded cluster you set `mongodb.connection.string` to the sharded cluster connection string.
- Its `snapshot.mode` option `when_needed` takes a new snapshot only if it finds no topic offsets or a recorded offset points to a log position the server no longer has.
- Its exactly-once page lists the MongoDB connector among the source connectors that can take part in Kafka Connect's exactly-once delivery.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Run it with Kafka (part 2)
text:
- An update event carries an `after` value (connector docs) (checked Oct 2026) only if `capture.mode` is `change_streams_update_full` or its pre-image variant. The `after` value is always a string holding a JSON representation of the document.
- You run it yourself, and the Apache Iceberg sink for Debezium Server (checked Oct 2026) is community-maintained in a separate repository.
- The pages of that community sink that we read describe replication from "any database" and do not name MongoDB (project docs). The Debezium Server page (checked Oct 2026) shows no MongoDB example.
- The connector cannot monitor a standalone MongoDB server, because standalone servers have no oplog. The docs (checked Oct 2026) say it works if you convert the server to a replica set with one member.
- A MongoDB change stream event is limited to `16 megabytes`, and the docs (checked Oct 2026) say pre-images raise the chance of exceeding it, "which can lead to failures".
- If the last stream position was removed from the oplog, the connector might fail to start with an invalid resume token error, depending on `snapshot.mode`. The docs (checked Oct 2026) say you then must create a new connector to continue.

What users say: Debezium's own April 2026 survey says "65.2% of respondents gave Debezium a 5 out of 5" on how likely they are to recommend it, though the project ran it itself and the page gives no count of responses. On Hacker News in November 2025, one commenter wrote "Even with Debezium I have run into myriad issues" while still recommending it. Neither is about MongoDB.

**3. MongoDB Kafka connector: best for MongoDB shops that want the official connector**

At a glance

- Method: One change stream per source connector
- Price: Not published on the docs pages we read

MongoDB's Kafka connector docs call it a Confluent-verified connector. Per its change streams page, the source connector opens one change stream and stores the resume token as its offset in a Kafka topic.

What's good

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Run it with Kafka (part 3)
text:
- It's MongoDB's own connector, and the compatibility page (checked Oct 2026) says the source needs MongoDB `3.6` or later (`4.0` or later to watch a whole database or deployment).
- MongoDB's integration page says it is "developed and supported by MongoDB and verified by Confluent", and that the connector is open source.
- The compatibility page says it works with any Apache Kafka platform that supports Kafka Connect. The overview lists Confluent Cloud, Amazon MSK and Redpanda Cloud as partner hosting offerings.
- The change stream settings let you pick how updates look: `updateLookup`, or `whenAvailable` / `required` for the full document and for the pre-image.
- Its troubleshooting page documents two ways to recover from an invalid resume token and says to turn on heartbeats with `heartbeat.interval.ms` to help prevent one.
- A setting can send tombstone events for deletes, holding the key of the deleted document with a null value.

Where it falls short

- It needs a Kafka Connect cluster (compatibility page) (checked Oct 2026), and we found no Iceberg writer in its docs.
- Pre-images aren't available for rows copied during the initial copy (change stream settings). The `copy_existing` start mode can create duplicate events (all properties) (checked Oct 2026), so delivery is "at-least-once" (you may see the same change twice).
- It requires Confluent Kafka Connect `v2.1.0` or later and is tested against Apache Kafka `v2.3` and later (compatibility page) (checked Oct 2026).
- The resume token is stored as an offset in a Kafka topic (troubleshooting page) (checked Oct 2026). If the oplog entry for it is deleted while the connector is paused, or the source namespace sees no update before MongoDB rotates that event out of the oplog, the token becomes invalid.
- Recovery (checked Oct 2026) is manual: set `errors.tolerance=all` and make a change so the token updates, or change `offset.partition.name` to reset the offset data.
- The tombstone setting applies only when `publish.full.document.only` is `true` (all properties) (checked Oct 2026).

What users say: We found no substantive 2025 or 2026 thread from users.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Packaged or vendor-run
text:
**4. Airbyte: best for scheduled syncs with a self-hosted option**

At a glance

- Method: Change streams, run as scheduled syncs
- Price: Core is free to self-manage; Cloud is billed in credits, per Airbyte's pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

Airbyte's MongoDB source is listed as a certified connector in its docs, with CDC through change streams and a full refresh mode too.

What's good

- A setting called `Invalid CDC position behavior` lets you choose: fail the sync, or re-sync automatically when the saved position is stale.
- Its docs say the certified connector offers CDC through change streams, checkpointing and chunking of data reads, and full refresh syncing of collections.
- Schema enforcement is optional. When it is off, each document becomes a record with an `_id` and a `data` field holding a JSON of all the fields in the document.
- The connector changelog (checked Oct 2026) lists version `2.1.0` (2 September 2026) as adding support for sharded clusters and object-type `_id` fields.

Where it falls short

- The default update mode, Lookup, fetches the latest document (Airbyte docs) (checked Oct 2026), so several quick updates can show the same final version and the steps in between vanish.
- The Post Image mode needs MongoDB `6.0` or later with images turned on, and Airbyte's page (checked Oct 2026) says failing to set that up "may lead to data loss".
- Syncs run on a schedule, not all the time.
- If you pick Re-sync data for a stale position, Airbyte triggers a full refresh. Its docs (checked Oct 2026) say this increases cloud costs and may miss incremental changes made while the cursor was invalid, and the default is Fail sync.
- During CDC syncs, change events can exceed the `16 MB` BSON limit and raise a `BSONObjectTooLarge` error (Airbyte's troubleshooting page) (checked Oct 2026). The suggested fix is to switch that stream to Full Refresh, which does not use change streams.
- The docs disagree on sharded clusters: the changelog says `2.1.0` supports them, while the troubleshooting page (checked Oct 2026) still says "Only supports replica set cluster type".

**5. Fivetran: best for vendor-run loading into a warehouse**

At a glance

- Method: Change streams, after a first copy with `find()`
- Price: Billed per monthly active row, per Fivetran's pricing page (checked Oct 2026)

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Packaged or vendor-run (part 2)
text:
Fivetran's MongoDB page says it supports replica sets and sharded clusters, versions `4.0` and above, but not MongoDB Serverless. It copies existing data with a `find()` call, then switches to change streams, opening one against each selected collection.

What's good

- Fivetran uses `_id` as the key, and when you delete a document, it stays in the destination with `_fivetran_deleted` set to `true`.
- For large collections, its docs say the first copy takes a limited amount of data at a time, so a lost connection does not restart the sync from the beginning.
- When a change stream cursor expires, its docs say Fivetran reschedules the sync, triggers an automatic re-sync and shows a warning in the dashboard.
- It maps all first-level fields of your documents to columns, and recommends packed mode (no unpacking) because syncs are faster.
- Its docs (checked Oct 2026) say it supports the SaaS and Hybrid deployment models for all MongoDB implementations, and replica sets and sharded clusters on MongoDB `4.0` and above with WiredTiger and protocol version `1`.

Where it falls short

- Your queries have to filter on the deleted flag, because rows are never removed (Fivetran docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Nested objects and arrays stay as JSON (Fivetran docs) (checked Oct 2026), and Fivetran does not unpack them into separate tables beyond one layer in unpacked mode. Further layers need a transformation in your destination, and unpacked syncs tend to be slower than packed ones.
- Self-run is limited to its Hybrid deployment, which needs an Enterprise or Business Critical plan, and its docs (checked Oct 2026) list a limit of `3` connections per database.
- Its docs (checked Oct 2026) say it does not support MongoDB Serverless databases.
- Cursors expire when syncs are too infrequent or the oplog is too small to hold the changes (Fivetran docs) (checked Oct 2026), and the automatic re-sync that follows means copying the data again.
- Its setup guide (checked Oct 2026) asks for an oplog that keeps at least 24 hours of changes and recommends seven days.

**6. OLake Go: best for MongoDB into Apache Iceberg on your own storage**

At a glance

- Method: Change streams with the oplog on; replica set or sharded cluster
- Price: Free licence (Apache 2.0), you pay for infrastructure and staff

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Packaged or vendor-run (part 3)
text:
OLake Go is open source under Apache 2.0. Its MongoDB connector has four sync modes: Full Refresh, Full Refresh plus Incremental, Full Refresh plus CDC, and CDC only. CDC needs MongoDB `4.0` or higher running as a replica set with the oplog on. The connector docs include a CDC setup guide for self-hosted MongoDB and Atlas. Its connection test checks that change streams are available and warns if the oplog window is too short for expected pauses.

OLake Go's MongoDB connector docs, October 2026.

What's good

- It writes Iceberg or Parquet with no Kafka in the path, using equality deletes, positional deletes or deletion vectors (see our docs; deletion vectors need OLake Go `0.11.0` or later, per the release notes).
- Without access to a replica set, Incremental sync still works (MongoDB connector docs).
- On deletes, the `v0.7.4` release (pull request 964) returns the full document by using pre-images on MongoDB `6.0` or later with pre-images on.
- It works with eleven catalog types, including AWS Glue, REST, Nessie, Polaris, Unity, Lakekeeper, S3 Tables, JDBC, Hive Metastore, BigLake and Horizon (see the catalog compatibility page).
- Large collections are read in parallel chunks. You choose the chunking strategy, `splitVector` (the default) or `timestamp`, and the `Max Threads` setting caps the parallel threads. Our MongoDB connector docs describe checkpointing and automatic resume for failed full loads.
- Sharded clusters are covered: the v0.2.5 release notes describe resume-token handling for each shard's stream after a failover or shard migration.
- A data filter can limit which rows a stream replicates, including in CDC and incremental syncs (see our docs and the v0.6.0 release notes). New source columns are added to the Iceberg schema automatically (schema evolution).
- The connector takes a read preference such as `secondaryPreferred`, DNS SRV connection strings, SSL modes (`require`, `verify-ca`, `verify-full` or `disable`), an SSH tunnel, IAM authentication, and a retry count with exponential backoff.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Packaged or vendor-run (part 4)
text:
Scope: output goes to Iceberg or Parquet on storage you choose, and CDC runs when your orchestrator starts a job. Our engine compatibility page lists Athena, BigQuery (BigLake) and Snowflake among the engines that query the Iceberg tables it writes. With the Horizon catalog (OLake Go `0.11.0` or later), OLake Go can also create those Iceberg tables inside a Snowflake database (Horizon setup).

Bottom line: Pick it for MongoDB changes in Iceberg tables you control, without Kafka.

**7. Estuary: best for continuous capture with batch fallbacks**

At a glance

- Method: Change streams, with two batch modes
- Price: Not covered here; see Estuary's pricing page

Estuary's MongoDB connector uses change streams when available. Each collection runs in one of three modes: Change Stream Incremental, Batch Snapshot or Batch Incremental.

What's good

- Only the change stream mode captures deletes (Estuary docs). The batch modes cover views and time series collections that change streams can't.
- Its docs say that during the first snapshot the connector keeps reading change streams while it scans collections to backfill existing documents.
- Captured update events always include a full post-image (Estuary docs), because the change stream is set up with `fullDocument: updateLookup`.
- Pre-images for update, replace and delete operations are captured if they are available (Estuary docs), and an advanced setting called `Disable Pre-Images` turns the request off.
- Batch modes also work on deployments that do not support change streams at all (Estuary docs).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Packaged or vendor-run (part 5)
text:
- If a pause outlasts the oplog, you may have to redo the backfill, which is why Estuary's MongoDB capture page (checked Oct 2026) recommends at least 24 hours of retention.
- Batch Snapshot rescans the entire collection on a set schedule (Estuary docs) (checked Oct 2026), and Batch Incremental captures only documents with a higher cursor field value than previously observed.
- Pre-images are captured only when the source collection has `changeStreamPreAndPostImages` enabled (Estuary docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- For Apache Iceberg, the merging connector needs an AWS EMR Serverless application with the Spark runtime, an S3 staging bucket and an Iceberg REST catalog (Iceberg connector page) (checked Oct 2026). The page shows a Beta label, and says only REST catalogs that use Amazon S3 are supported for now.

What users say: A G2 review on AWS Marketplace (December 2025) said the reviewer could "connect my MongoDB to Snowflake for analytics purposes within just a few hours". The same reviewer wrote "Setting up the tool does demand a certain amount of data engineering work."

**8. Artie: best for a vendor-run MongoDB pipeline with typed columns**

At a glance

- Method: Change streams
- Price: Not covered here; see Artie's pricing page

Artie's MongoDB page says it reads change streams for inserts, updates and deletes. The server must be a replica set, and its docs say a standalone server can be turned into one with a single member.

What's good

- Its docs describe how it handles schema-less data: it types each column from the first non-null value, unions the fields it sees, and writes missing fields as `NULL`.
- Full document before change works with MongoDB `6.0` or later (Artie docs) (checked Oct 2026), and Artie says it helps deletes when the destination table is partitioned.
- Its changelog (checked Oct 2026) says that in July 2026 MongoDB pipelines gained an opt-in `collectionScopedMode` for tighter isolation between collections.
- The same changelog entry says database-wide change streams now apply your database and collection filters before Artie decodes events.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Packaged or vendor-run (part 6)
text:
- A field with mixed types (a number in one document, text in another) lands as a string (Artie docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Nested documents and arrays are kept as JSON objects. Artie's docs (checked Oct 2026) say it does not flatten or unfurl nested structures into separate columns.
- Each column's type comes from the BSON type of the first non-null value Artie sees for that field (Artie docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Fields missing from a document are written as `NULL` in the destination (Artie docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Artie's pricing page lists the Iceberg destination only under Enterprise, and Enterprise pricing is custom (checked Oct 2026).

What users say: We found no substantive 2025 or 2026 thread from users, only the vendor's own customer stories, which we don't treat as peer opinion.

**9. AWS Database Migration Service: best for moves inside AWS**

At a glance

- Method: Reads the oplog or change streams, depending on an endpoint setting
- Price: Not covered here; see AWS's pricing page

AWS DMS's MongoDB source page says CDC needs access to the oplog, so a replica set is required, and you can read from the primary or a secondary. DMS `3.5.4` and later support MongoDB `7.0` and `8.0`.

What's good

- There are two modes: document mode keeps each document in one `_doc` column, and table mode makes a column for each top-level field.
- In table mode, deleting a document is "fully supported" (AWS docs), and the docs describe parallel full load for large collections.
- CDC can use either the primary or a secondary node of the replica set as the source endpoint (AWS docs).
- In table mode, nested values are flattened into columns with dot-separated names (AWS docs) (checked Oct 2026). To build the target columns DMS scans a number of documents you can set, `1000` by default.
- The self-managed source list (checked Oct 2026) names MongoDB `3.x`, `4.0`, `4.2`, `4.4`, `5.0`, `6.0`, `7.0` and `8.0`.
- An endpoint setting, `useOplog`, makes the task read the oplog directly instead of using the change stream. It is off by default.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Packaged or vendor-run (part 7)
text:
- If MongoDB flushes oplog records before DMS reads them, the task fails (AWS docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Table mode needs the same data type for the same field in every document, and it doesn't support time series collection migration or live resharding (AWS docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Apache Iceberg is not in DMS's list of target endpoints, per its Targets page (checked Oct 2026).
- In table mode, when you add a document to an existing collection, fields that do not exist in the target are not replicated (AWS docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- Source filters are not supported for MongoDB, documents nested deeper than `97` levels are not supported, and UTF-8 encoded source data is required for non-DocumentDB targets (AWS docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- MongoDB is among the endpoints that do not support the CDC native start point feature (CDC task page). Client-side field level encryption is also unsupported (AWS docs) (checked Oct 2026).

What users say: On Hacker News in January 2024, one commenter in a thread about a PostgreSQL migration with 11 seconds of downtime wrote "it's always been more than up to the task". On PeerSpot, a reviewer in September 2024 wrote "the error messages from DMS are very ambiguous and sometimes misleading." Neither is about MongoDB.

**10. Striim: best for large enterprise estates**

At a glance

- Method: Change streams on MongoDB `4.2` and later, oplog before that
- Price: Not covered here; see Striim's pricing page

Striim's MongoDB Reader guide says Incremental mode reads change streams on `4.2` or later and the oplog on earlier versions.

What's good

- It covers MongoDB before `4.2` through the oplog path.
- When it reads change streams (MongoDB `4.2` or later), its CDC guide (checked Oct 2026) says the reader can read from multiple shards and supports transactions, providing transaction metadata. With `4.1` or earlier, a separate reader is needed for each shard.
- Its recovery page says the MongoDB Reader is recoverable when reading from change streams or when not using transactions.
- Its BigQuery Writer docs name MongoDB among the NoSQL databases it can write from (BigQuery Writer).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > The ten tools, one by one > Packaged or vendor-run (part 8)
text:
- The default mode only loads existing data and stops, so you must set Incremental to get CDC (easy to miss; reader guide) (checked Oct 2026).
- If it gets no messages for a whole oplog retention period, it halts on restart with a `ChangeStreamHistoryLost` error (per its operational considerations page) (checked Oct 2026).
- Its Iceberg Writer (checked Oct 2026) is Google Cloud Storage only; S3 Tables has its own writer.
- The reader reads only collections that exist when the application starts (reader guide) (checked Oct 2026). Collections added later are ignored until you restart the application.
- When it uses transactions and reads the oplog, the MongoDB Reader is not recoverable (recovery page) (checked Oct 2026).

What users say: On PeerSpot in August 2026, a reviewer describing use from 2019 to 2022 wrote "I did interact with support, and it was very positive". The same reviewer wrote "Striim would not intuitively tell me the culprit table or database behind the lag". This is older experience and not about MongoDB.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > What happens to deletes, and to schema-less documents
text:
MongoDB collections have no fixed schema, so two documents in one collection can hold the same field with different types. A table needs a fixed type per column, and each tool answers that clash differently.

| Tool | Deletes | Nested objects and arrays | Mixed types |
| Fivetran | Row kept, _fivetran_deleted set | Kept as JSON | Not documented on the page we read |
| Airbyte | Captured by CDC | Iceberg writer stores objects and unions as JSON strings | Not documented on the page we read |
| OLake Go | Full document with pre-images on 6.0 +, else _id only ( PR 964 ) | Written as a string | Type mapping lists the destination type for each BSON type ( type mapping ) |
| Estuary | Captured in change stream mode only | Not documented on the page we read | Not documented on the page we read |
| Artie | Captured, pre-image for partitioned tables | Kept as JSON, not flattened | Lands as a string |
| AWS DMS | Table mode: "fully supported" | Table mode flattens nested values into dot-named columns; arrays map to CLOB | Table mode needs one type per field |

Sources: Fivetran, Airbyte and its S3 Data Lake page, Estuary, Artie, AWS DMS and, for OLake Go, our MongoDB docs (checked Oct 2026).

Where a cell says "not documented", the vendor's page was silent, and we don't guess. Run a test with a sample collection that mixes types.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > Which MongoDB CDC tool should you pick? > Which MongoDB CDC tool fits you?
text:
Question 1 of 5

Who should run the change reader?

Almost every tool here reads MongoDB's change streams, so the choice is who runs the reader.

Check this before you choose
- Replica set or sharded cluster.`rs.status()` shows a replica set's state. A standalone server can't give you change stream CDC, and the fallbacks are weaker: Estuary's batch modes can't capture deletes (checked Oct 2026).
- Oplog window. Compare the hours it holds with your longest outage and your first-copy time.
- Large documents. Find your biggest documents. Anything near `16 MB` can break change events.
- Delete needs. Decide whether you need the deleted document's contents. If yes, you need MongoDB `6.0` or later and pre-images, and the tool must use them.
- Landing format. Check whether nested data stays as JSON or strings, and whether you can query it where it lands.
- Recovery test. Stop the tool, restart it inside the oplog window, and confirm it resumes. Then test an expired position: Airbyte can fail or re-sync by setting, Fivetran re-syncs automatically, and Estuary may redo the backfill (checked Oct 2026).
- Delete test. Delete a document in MongoDB, then go look at the destination. Is the row gone, flagged, or still there as a history row?

Then ask each vendor in writing what happens when the oplog window is missed, and what a full re-copy costs on your plan.

title: Compare: Best MongoDB Change Data Capture Tools in 2026 | OLake > FAQs
text:
Q1. What is MongoDB change data capture?

Spotting the inserts, updates and deletes in MongoDB and sending only those changes to another system. MongoDB's feature for this is change streams.

Q2. Does MongoDB change data capture need a replica set?

Yes. MongoDB's manual says change streams are available for replica sets and sharded clusters, so a standalone server doesn't qualify. Artie's docs say a standalone server can be turned into a replica set with one member.

Q3. Is oplog tailing still used for MongoDB CDC?

Sometimes, but it's the older route. MongoDB's manual describes change streams as the way to avoid manually tailing the oplog. Debezium says its MongoDB connector does not read the oplog directly, while Striim reads the oplog only on MongoDB versions before `4.2` (checked Oct 2026).

Q4. Can MongoDB CDC capture the deleted document?

Not by default. A delete event leaves out the full document. With MongoDB `6.0` or later and pre-images switched on for the collection, Debezium, Estuary and Artie document use of the before image (checked Oct 2026).

Q5. What is a resume token?

A marker in each change event that lets a tool continue from that point after a restart. It only works while the oplog still holds the matching entry, so a long outage can make it invalid.

Q6. Can I run MongoDB CDC without Kafka?

Yes. Debezium's docs describe a Server mode that runs without Kafka, and OLake Go reads MongoDB without it. Debezium in Kafka Connect mode and the MongoDB Kafka connector do need Kafka.

Q7. How big should the MongoDB oplog be for CDC?

Read your window with `rs.printReplicationInfo()`, then size it for your longest expected outage. Airbyte, Fivetran, Estuary and AWS DMS advise at least 24 hours (checked Oct 2026).

Q8. Does the 16 MB limit affect change streams?

Yes. MongoDB says change stream responses must stay within the `16 MB` BSON limit, so notifications can fail for documents at or near it. Airbyte documents a `BSONObjectTooLarge` error and suggests Full Refresh (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

Short version: none of these MySQL to Iceberg tools is best for everyone. They copy MySQL changes into Apache Iceberg using a technique called change data capture (CDC), and your pick depends on who will run it and what you already own.

- Already on Kafka? Look at Kafka Connect.
- On Flink? Try Flink CDC.
- Want a vendor to run it for you? Fivetran, Airbyte and Estuary are the ones to check.

Before you commit, ask three things. Which MySQL settings does the tool need, how does it write deletes, and who compacts the small files?

- Most tools here read MySQL through its binary log (the binlog), in ROW format with a full row image.
- The tools don't agree on the settings. Some tools, such as Supermetal, list `binlog_row_metadata=FULL` in their prerequisites, while the Debezium, Airbyte and Fivetran pages don't (checked Oct 2026).
- MySQL deletes old binlog files after a set time. Keep your tool down longer than that and you're taking a new snapshot.
- Fivetran's lake destination doesn't support Iceberg position deletes (checked Oct 2026), and Flink CDC's Iceberg sink needs a primary key (checked Oct 2026). Good to know before you pick.

Every fact about a tool comes from its own documentation or pricing page, linked next to the claim. Prices and limits end with "(checked Oct 2026)" right after the link. When a page says nothing, we write "not stated" instead of guessing.

We did not run the other tools, so any "easy", "fast" or "reliable" claim below about them is the vendor's, not ours. There are no user quotes either, because the public threads we found were about Postgres, SaaS sources or came from vendors, and we would rather print none.

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > What "MySQL to Iceberg" involves
text:
Picture it: your MySQL database is busy all day, and you want its changes sitting in cheap storage where query tools can read them as tables. That's the whole job. Two parts matter, how you read MySQL and how you write Iceberg.

Reading MySQL. MySQL writes down every change in its binary log, like a diary that never skips an entry. Debezium's MySQL docs call it a record of all operations in commit order, including schema changes. A CDC tool reads each entry and turns it into an insert, update or delete event.

Three settings decide what your tool can actually see.

First, `binlog_format` must be `ROW`, so the log holds the changed rows and not just the SQL text. Second, `binlog_row_image` set to `FULL` makes MySQL write every column of the row. Supermetal's docs say it's needed "to capture complete before and after row images".

Third, `binlog_row_metadata` set to `FULL` adds column details to each event. Only some tools ask for this one, which is where the confusion starts.

The tool joins as a replica.Fivetran's docs say "we connect to your database as a replica", and Flink CDC's docs say its reader joins the cluster as another server. That means most binlog readers here need their own unique server id and a user with replication privileges, as their docs describe. Fivetran calls it a replica ID, and Estuary has an advanced Node ID setting that it picks for you if you leave it unset.

GTID is optional in most docs. A global transaction identifier (GTID) is just a label MySQL sticks on each transaction. Debezium says you don't need it, Supermetal recommends it for failover, and Flink CDC needs it for high availability.

Snapshot, then changes. First the tool copies the rows that already exist. That's the initial snapshot. Then it reads the binlog from where the snapshot began, and Debezium's docs explain why that matters: MySQL purges binlogs after a set time.

Retention is the clock. MySQL throws old logs away, and it won't wait for your tool. Debezium's docs say that if the saved position is gone, the connector fails and asks for a new snapshot, unless you set `snapshot.mode` to `when_needed`. See the Debezium MySQL docs (checked Oct 2026).

Advice on how long to keep logs runs from 3 days at Supermetal to 10 days at Airbyte (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > What "MySQL to Iceberg" involves (part 2)
text:
Writing Iceberg. Apache Iceberg is a table format: Parquet data files plus metadata that lets engines such as Spark, Trino and Athena treat them as one table. A catalog keeps track of where each table's metadata lives, and many offer a REST (web API) interface. Every commit makes a new snapshot, which is just a saved version of the table.

Updates and deletes get into Iceberg one of two ways. Either you rewrite data files, or you write delete files that mark old rows as removed.

A tool that applies each change this way is said to upsert, meaning update or insert. Equality deletes match rows by key value, and positional deletes point at a file path and row position. The kind you pick decides which query engines can read the result.

Frequent commits leave lots of small files. Compaction rewrites them into fewer big ones, and old snapshots need expiring too.

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > How we picked
