title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > The 8 tools, one at a time > 1. Debezium Server with the community Iceberg sink: best for Kafka-free Debezium
text:
At a glance:Apache 2.0 · self-hosted · Java 21 (sink repo) · free licence (checked Oct 2026)

Debezium is an open-source change reader. Debezium Server's docs describe an Iceberg sink that consumes events from a source Debezium connector and calls it "a community-maintained, open-source project" kept in a separate repository.

Its MySQL connector docs list `server-id`, `log_bin`, `binlog_format=ROW` and `binlog_row_image=FULL` as the settings to enable (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- Its docs describe running Debezium's own MySQL reader without Kafka, which is the main reason to pick it.
- The MySQL docs spell out the user privileges and cover Amazon RDS and Aurora, where the snapshot needs `LOCK TABLES`.

Where it falls short

- It's community maintained, not part of Debezium's core, and the Iceberg sink's docs page doesn't list supported catalogs. Its own FAQ says upsert tables need periodic jobs to compact data and rewrite delete files (checked Oct 2026).
- Upsert is off by default, so a fresh setup just appends every event (the sink's configuration page lists the settings (checked Oct 2026)). Even once upsert is on, deleted rows are kept and marked unless you change a second setting.
- On RDS the binlog stays off unless automated backups are on, and `binlog_row_value_options` must not be `PARTIAL_JSON`. Both come from the MySQL docs (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > The 8 tools, one at a time > 2. OLake Go: best for a self-hosted MySQL to Iceberg job run from a UI
text:
At a glance:Apache 2.0 · self-hosted · UI or CLI · Iceberg or Parquet only

OLake Go is open source under Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026) and copies databases into Iceberg tables on storage you control. It reads the binlog on MySQL 5.7 or newer and supports the MariaDB flavour as a CDC source (see the MySQL connector page).

It has four sync modes:

- Full Refresh (`full_refresh`) copies every row.
- Full Refresh + Incremental (`incremental`) copies rows past a cursor column, such as an updated-at timestamp.
- Full Refresh + CDC (`cdc`) takes a snapshot, then reads the binlog.
- CDC Only (`strict_cdc`) reads the binlog with no initial snapshot.

What's good

- Catalogs include Glue, JDBC, Hive and REST catalogs such as Lakekeeper and S3 Tables, on S3, MinIO, GCS or Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2.
- You choose between equality deletes, positional deletes and deletion vectors, which lets you match your query engine, subject to the reader limits below.
- Full loads use parallel chunking and automatic resume for failed runs, with setup guides for Aurora, RDS, Azure and Cloud SQL.
- Compaction is covered too, as OLake Fusion, with Lite, Medium and Full types.

Good to know

- You run it on your own infrastructure, through the UI or the command line (see the UI install guide).
- Deletion vectors are an Iceberg v3 feature that the v0.11.0 release notes add as a delete mode. Pick the delete mode that matches your query engine, and use the engine compatibility page to see which engines read each one.
- The catalogs compatibility page lists Nessie and Polaris as REST catalogs with setup links.
- The prerequisites list `binlog_row_metadata=FULL`, and the v0.10.0 release notes say MySQL CDC also works without it.

Bottom line: Pick OLake Go if you want a UI, a documented catalog list and no licence fee. Fivetran, Airbyte Cloud and Estuary suit teams that want a vendor to run the pipeline, and Kafka Connect suits several systems reading one change stream.

The OLake Go MySQL connector page, October 2026.

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > The 8 tools, one at a time > 3. Kafka Connect with a Debezium source and the Iceberg sink: best for teams already on Kafka
text:
At a glance: you run Kafka and Kafka Connect · Iceberg sink from the Iceberg project · no licence fee (Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026))

The Iceberg docs describe a Kafka Connect sink that writes Kafka data into Iceberg tables, and name Debezium source connectors as the way to bring database changes into Kafka. Debezium reads MySQL into Kafka topics, and the sink moves them on from there. Exactly-once delivery is a listed feature, and it relies on Kafka 2.5 or later (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- Many consumers can read the same Kafka topics, so the lake is just one of several readers.
- Catalog examples include REST, Glue, Nessie and Hive, and one sink can write several tables.

Where it falls short

- The Debezium transform that prepares change events is marked experimental in the Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Table creation and schema evolution are off by default, and the page doesn't cover compaction (checked Oct 2026).
- You end up running three systems, not one.

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > The 8 tools, one at a time > 4. Flink CDC: best for teams that already run Flink
text:
At a glance:Apache 2.0 · runs on Apache Flink · Java 11 or later (docs (checked Oct 2026)) · pipeline YAML

Flink CDC has a MySQL pipeline source and an Iceberg pipeline sink, so both halves live in one project. The MySQL source docs describe a snapshot followed by the changes. The Iceberg sink docs list automatic table creation, schema synchronisation, and batch or streaming writes.

What's good

- One tool covers both the snapshot and the change stream, and the snapshot is split into chunks of 8,096 rows by default (checked Oct 2026).
- Per the pipeline docs, unlike the Postgres source, the MySQL source sends schema change events by default, so the sink can follow table changes (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

- The MySQL JDBC driver isn't bundled, because its GPLv2 licence doesn't fit the project. You download `mysql-connector-java` 8.0.27 yourself and pass it with `--jar` (docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- The source table must have a primary key, and the Iceberg sink doesn't offer exactly-once semantics. It's at-least-once, so the docs lean on the primary key to make a repeated write give the same result (checked Oct 2026).
- Catalog types are Hadoop, Hive, Glue or a custom class. REST isn't stated (Iceberg sink docs (checked Oct 2026)), and each parallel reader needs its own server id (MySQL source docs).

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > The 8 tools, one at a time > 5. Airbyte: best for teams that want one tool for databases and SaaS apps
text:
At a glance: Core self-managed, free to self-host under the Elastic License 2.0 (licence FAQ (checked Oct 2026)) · Cloud · Enterprise Flex hybrid · S3 Data Lake destination

Airbyte's MySQL source reads the binlog and recommends CDC over its cursor-based method. Its S3 Data Lake destination calls itself "official support for the Iceberg protocol on S3" and supports REST, Glue, Nessie and Polaris catalogs. The two live on separate docs pages.

What's good

- Airbyte's connectors page counts its connectors in the hundreds, so MySQL is one of many sources you can wire up.
- The MySQL page lists the exact settings and suggests 10 days of retention (checked Oct 2026).
- Deduplication is documented as merge-on-read (docs), meaning updates are written as delete files and applied when you query. Each update is an equality delete plus an insert. Core is free to self-host under the Elastic License 2.0 (ELv2), and Cloud is credit based (pricing (checked Oct 2026)).

Where it falls short

- On Amazon RDS, the binlog retention parameter defaults to 0 hours. The docs say that means logs are removed at once, so you must raise it (checked Oct 2026).
- The destination never rewrites existing Iceberg data files, so only some schema changes work, and objects are written as JSON strings. The page doesn't describe compaction (checked Oct 2026).
- Core uses the Elastic License 2.0, which is NOT an open-source licence (checked Oct 2026). Syncs run on a schedule, not as a continuous stream (CDC docs).

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > The 8 tools, one at a time > 6. Fivetran Managed Data Lake Service: best for hands-off, vendor-run pipelines
text:
At a glance: SaaS · writes Parquet to your S3, Azure or GCS bucket · Iceberg metadata always created · monthly active rows pricing

Fivetran's MySQL setup guide offers the binary log or Teleport Sync, and wants `binlog_format=ROW`. Its Managed Data Lake Service docs say your data stays in your cloud storage while Fivetran keeps the Iceberg metadata. We found no page that pairs the two, so treat Fivetran as a conditional candidate and ask it to confirm the combination.

What's good

- Fivetran's docs say it runs the pipeline and the table upkeep, including snapshot cleanup every day. We have not tested that.
- Per its docs, your data stays in your own bucket, with a Fivetran Catalog built on Apache Polaris by default, or another supported catalog.

Where it falls short

- The lake docs say there's no support for Iceberg position deletes, and they don't say which delete method is used (checked Oct 2026).
- Teleport Sync, the alternative to the binary log, "disables large, rapidly changing tables if they fail to sync" (setup guide (checked Oct 2026)). Compaction isn't in the lake page's list of maintenance operations.
- The destination runs as SaaS only. Fivetran's connector pricing counts monthly active rows, and we found no separate lake rate (checked Oct 2026).

Ask Fivetran before you rely on it: does the MySQL connector write to the Managed Data Lake Service? Which delete method does it use? What does the lake destination add to the monthly active rows bill?

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > The 8 tools, one at a time > 7. Estuary: best for AWS teams that want a vendor to run it
text:
At a glance: Cloud, private or Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) · Business Source License (checked Oct 2026) · MySQL capture plus Iceberg materialization

Estuary's MySQL capture docs need `binlog_format=ROW` and a binlog expiry of at least 7 days (checked Oct 2026). Its Iceberg connector works differently: it "orchestrates Spark jobs running on your configured compute system to merge updates into materialized tables".

What's good

- One product documents both MySQL capture and Iceberg materialization, plus a hosted option, with MySQL setup steps for self-hosted, RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL and Azure.
- The Iceberg docs describe catalog setups for Glue, Snowflake Open Catalog and Dremio Cloud.

Where it falls short

- The Iceberg connector needs an AWS EMR Serverless application you configure, an S3 staging bucket and IAM roles (checked Oct 2026). That is three AWS pieces to set up before a first sync.
- Today it supports only REST catalogs on Amazon S3 storage. GCP and Azure are planned (same docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- Billing has two meters. Estuary's pricing page lists $0.50 per GB moved, plus connector instances: $100 a month each for the first six, $50 each after that. It also lists a free tier of 10 GB a month with 2 connector instances (checked Oct 2026).

Ask Estuary before you rely on it: how GB moved is counted for a busy MySQL table, since the bill has two meters.

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > The 8 tools, one at a time > 8. Supermetal: best for a single self-hosted agent priced on compute
text:
At a glance: Self-hosted, described by Supermetal as a single binary · Iceberg V3 or V2 · compute-based price · licence not stated

Supermetal's Iceberg target docs say it writes Parquet to Iceberg through REST, Glue or S3 Tables catalogs on S3 or GCS. New tables default to Iceberg V3, and V2 is selectable for engines that lack V3 support. Its MySQL source docs say it reads the binlog, takes snapshots in parallel, and lists `binlog_format=ROW`, `binlog_row_image=FULL` and `binlog_row_metadata=FULL` as required settings (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- You get merge-on-read by default (updates are written as delete files and applied at query time), or positional deletes only, per its docs (checked Oct 2026).
- The MySQL source works without GTID, so that's one less thing to turn on.
- Pricing is compute based, and there's a free trial of 1,000 sync hours on that page. Its pricing page shows Enterprise Self-Hosted starting at $10K a year (pricing (checked Oct 2026)).

Where it falls short

- Data type promotion isn't supported yet, and changing partitioning needs a new table (Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026)).
- Compaction is on you, using Spark, Trino or a table service.
- It asks for `binlog_row_metadata=FULL`, it's paid after the trial and the free pilot on its pricing page (checked Oct 2026), and the pages we read don't state a licence.

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > Also considered
text:
Three more names keep coming up in searches. They don't get a full entry.

RisingWave is a streaming engine. Its MySQL CDC docs list MySQL 5.7, 8.0 and 8.4, plus MariaDB and TiDB, and ask for a unique server id. Its Iceberg docs describe automatic maintenance and a manual `VACUUM FULL` that compacts data files (checked Oct 2026).

Some compaction behaviour needs a licence, per its release notes (checked Oct 2026). It fits if you also want to run SQL on the stream.

AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) reads MySQL's row-based binary logs. Apache Iceberg isn't in its list of target endpoints, though Amazon S3 and Kafka are (checked Oct 2026). So you'd have to build an extra step to reach Iceberg.

Upsolver now sits inside Qlik as Qlik Open Lakehouse, which Qlik says "writes data as fully spec-compliant Apache Iceberg tables". The pages we read don't say which databases it reads by log.

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > Which Route for Which Team
text:
Short answer: pick by what you already run, then read the "watch for" column before you get excited.

| Your situation | Look first at | Watch for |
| You already run Kafka and several teams read changes | Kafka Connect with Debezium | Experimental transform; you run three systems |
| You already run Flink | Flink CDC | Primary key needed; MySQL JDBC driver added by you |
| You want a vendor to run it | Fivetran, Airbyte Cloud or Estuary | Position deletes, EMR Serverless, credits |
| You want few moving parts | OLake Go or Debezium Server | Both run on your own servers |
| You want one self-hosted agent and have a budget | Supermetal | Paid tier; no type promotion |

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > Which Route for Which Team > Which MySQL to Iceberg tool fits you?
text:
Question 1 of 5

Who should run the pipeline?

Free software still has a bill: servers and people.

MariaDB notes
MariaDB has a binlog like MySQL's, but tools treat it differently. Debezium and Estuary each have a separate MariaDB connector, and Flink CDC lists MariaDB 10.x with MySQL versions (checked Oct 2026).

Fivetran's connector list names MariaDB for the binary log method. The Airbyte and Supermetal pages we read don't (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > How to test before you commit
text:
This is a test plan, not results. Take each finalist for a spin on one table with real deletes, updates and a large text column.

- Run `DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 1;`, then read the table from your engine. Pass: the row is gone.
- Update another column on a row with a large text value. Pass: the large value is intact, and `SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_row_image';` returns FULL.
- Run `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note VARCHAR(50);`. Pass: the tool carries it over, or fails loudly.
- In a test system, stop the tool for longer than your binlog retention, then run `SHOW BINARY LOGS;`. Make a few inserts, updates and deletes while the tool is stopped, then compare the source and Iceberg rows after it comes back. Pass: the tool says plainly that it needs a new snapshot, or the two sides match exactly. A silent gap in the data is a fail, full stop.
- After a day, query the Iceberg `files` metadata table, for example `SELECT file_path, file_size_in_bytes FROM my_catalog.my_db.orders.files;` in Spark. Lots of tiny files mean you need a compaction plan.

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > FAQs
text:
Q1. What is the easiest way to replicate MySQL to Iceberg?

A vendor-run service means less to operate yourself, such as Fivetran, Airbyte Cloud or Estuary, but each has limits in its docs, listed in the entries above, and we have not tested any of them. Self-run tools put the operating work on your team. So ask yourself who'll carry the pager.

Q2. Do I need Kafka to move MySQL changes into Iceberg?

No. The Debezium Server Iceberg sink runs Debezium without Kafka, and Flink CDC, Airbyte, Fivetran, Estuary and Supermetal also read MySQL directly (their docs are linked in the table above). Only the Kafka Connect route needs Kafka.

Q3. Which MySQL settings do I need for CDC?

Every set of MySQL source docs we read lists three things: binary logging on, the row-based format (`binlog_format`) and a user with replication privileges. All of them list a unique server id (a replica ID at Fivetran, an optional Node ID at Estuary). Most also want the full row image (`binlog_row_image`). Supermetal also lists `binlog_row_metadata` in its prerequisites, and Estuary lists it only in its Aurora steps (checked Oct 2026).

Q4. What happens if my tool is down longer than the binlog retention?

That's the awkward one. MySQL purges old binlog files by age. Debezium's docs say that if the saved position is gone, the connector fails and needs a new snapshot, unless snapshot.mode is when_needed (checked Oct 2026). Rule of thumb: keep retention longer than your worst outage.

Q5. How are deletes handled in MySQL CDC to Iceberg?

It depends on the tool. Either it writes delete files (equality or positional) or it merges changes into rewritten data files, as Estuary does with Spark jobs. Debezium's Iceberg sink appends by default, Fivetran's lake destination doesn't support position deletes, and Flink CDC needs a primary key (checked Oct 2026).

Q6. Do I need to compact Iceberg tables?

Yes, if you write often, because CDC leaves a trail of small files. Fivetran lists cleanup tasks, and Supermetal leaves it to you. The Debezium sink's FAQ also advises periodic maintenance jobs (checked Oct 2026).

Q7. Which of these tools have no licence fee?

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > FAQs (part 2)
text: A few. Debezium Server and its sink, Kafka Connect with the Iceberg sink and Flink CDC carry no licence fee, and Airbyte Core is free under the Elastic License 2.0. You still pay for servers and people's time, though. Fivetran, Estuary and Supermetal charge for use, beyond any free tier, trial or pilot (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: MySQL to Iceberg Tools: 8 Compared (2026) | OLake > Conclusion
text:
MySQL to Iceberg is really two jobs: reading a binlog safely and writing tables that stay fast. The tools differ most in the settings they demand, how they handle deletes, and who compacts the files, so test those on your own data first.

One last tip: from day one, watch the tool's lag against your remaining retention. If the lag grows toward the retention window, the oldest logs MySQL keeps are closing in on the tool's saved position, so step in before they pass it.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

There's no single best Oracle replication tool, because the tools answer different questions. Oracle Active Data Guard copies a whole Oracle database to another Oracle database, and Oracle GoldenGate moves changes to other systems for a licence fee.

Qlik Replicate, Striim, Quest SharePlex, Fivetran, AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) and Google Datastream read Oracle for you, and Debezium is the open-source log reader. OLake Go copies Oracle tables into Iceberg or Parquet on a schedule. Before you shortlist anything, check how the tool reads Oracle's logs, whether that route needs a GoldenGate licence, and where your data has to land.

- How a tool reads Oracle's logs, and one logging setting, decide licence and risk. LogMiner needs no extra licence unless GoldenGate Supplemental Logging is on, XStream generally needs a GoldenGate licence, and a tool that parses log files itself is called unsupported by Oracle (checked Oct 2026).
- Log retention and large objects bite first. Archived logs must be kept long enough, and several tools handle large-object columns badly.

We checked prices and facts in October 2026 against each vendor's own pages.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > How we picked
text:
We included tools that copy data out of Oracle, by reading its logs or by scheduled table reads, are still sold or maintained, and publish documentation we could open. We compared how each tool reads Oracle, the licence rule that follows, the price basis, where data lands, and the documented limits.

Vendor facts come from each vendor's own pages and docs, read in October 2026. We did not run the other tools. Entries are grouped by maker and carry no ranking. This page covers Oracle only; for tools across many databases, see our best change data capture tools and best data replication tools comparisons.

One term you'll see a lot: change data capture (CDC) means finding the inserts, updates and deletes in a database and sending only those on.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > First, pick how the tool reads Oracle
text:
Oracle writes every change to redo logs, which are files where the database records each change in order. When a log fills up, Oracle copies it to an archived redo log.

Log-based tools read these files. How they read them sets the licence rule and the risks.

| Method | How it reads Oracle | Oracle licence | Limits that Oracle or vendors document |
| LogMiner | Oracle's built-in utility reads redo and archived logs through SQL | Oracle's GoldenGate Advantages paper says it is accessible without additional licensing. Oracle's licensing guide adds one condition, covered below (checked Oct 2026) | Needs at least minimal supplemental logging; table and column names over 30 characters are not supported; Oracle's paper says it was designed for diagnostics, not high-volume continuous replication, and is single-threaded |
| XStream | An Oracle programming interface that streams changes out of the redo log | Oracle's paper says use generally needs GoldenGate for Oracle licences on each database where it is used (checked Oct 2026) | The tool must track how far it has read (checkpoints) and handle large objects itself |
| GoldenGate Extract | Oracle's own capture process, which writes GoldenGate's own change record, a trail file | A GoldenGate licence | Cost and setup effort |
| Direct log reading | The tool parses redo and archive files itself | Oracle's paper says it does not support this approach, and that its Master Agreement addresses reverse engineering (checked Oct 2026) | Oracle's log format is undocumented, per the OpenLogReplicator project |

Sources: Oracle's GoldenGate Advantages paper (undated, with references accessed in June 2026), Oracle's Licensing Information guide and the LogMiner documentation for Oracle `26ai` (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > First, pick how the tool reads Oracle > One setting can turn a free reader into a licensed one
text:
Oracle's Licensing Information guide (checked Oct 2026) for Oracle `26ai` says LogMiner is available in all offerings. Then it adds that when LogMiner is used with GoldenGate Supplemental Logging turned on, a GoldenGate licence is required.

That logging is on when the database parameter `ENABLE_GOLDENGATE_REPLICATION` is `TRUE`.

For on-premises databases, the same guide (checked Oct 2026) says a GoldenGate licence is required "regardless of which APIs are used for log consumption (e.g., LogMiner, XStream or 3rd party tools)". The setting decides the licence, whatever the tool is called.

We found no vendor page that says whether its setup turns the parameter on, so ask each vendor.

Original diagram, drawn from Oracle's Licensing Information guide for Oracle `26ai`, accessed October 2026.

Caveat: Oracle sells GoldenGate, so its papers are a vendor view. It names no tool, though.

Quick definition: supplemental logging is an Oracle setting that adds extra detail to the redo log so tools can rebuild a full row. LogMiner needs at least the minimal level (LogMiner docs), and Debezium's Oracle setup guide also asks for all-column logging on captured tables.

Oracle's LogMiner documentation says the `continuous_mine` option was desupported in Oracle `19c`, and it still documents LogMiner for `26ai`.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Oracle replication tools at a glance
text:
| Tool | Maker type | Reads Oracle with | Lands data in | Price basis |
| Oracle GoldenGate | Oracle | Extract on the redo log | Many targets; Iceberg in a separate product | Per processor or user; cloud per OCPU per minute |
| Oracle Active Data Guard | Oracle | Redo shipped to a standby | Another Oracle database | Extra-cost option on Enterprise Edition |
| Qlik Replicate | Commercial | LogMiner or Replicate Log Reader | Many targets; Iceberg through Qlik Open Lakehouse | Not published |
| Striim | Commercial | Oracle Reader (LogMiner) or OJet | Many targets; Iceberg on Google Cloud Storage or Amazon S3 Tables | Free Developer tier; others "contact us" |
| Quest SharePlex | Commercial | Redo log, method not stated | Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Kafka, Parquet files | Not published |
| Fivetran | Managed service | Binary Log Reader, XStream Out, Teleport, HVA | Warehouses and lakes | Monthly Active Rows |
| Debezium | Open source | LogMiner, XStream or OpenLogReplicator | Kafka; community Iceberg sink | Free licence, you pay for servers |
| OLake Go | Open source | Table reads: Full Refresh or Full Refresh + Incremental | Apache Iceberg, Parquet | Free licence, you pay for servers |
| AWS DMS | AWS service | LogMiner or Binary Reader | AWS targets, S3 files; Iceberg not on its target list | Instance or serverless hours |
| Google Datastream | Google service | Binary reader (Preview) or LogMiner | BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Iceberg (append-only) | Per GiB processed |
| Confluent Oracle XStream connector | Managed Kafka | XStream Out | Kafka topics | Not published |

OCPU is Oracle's unit of compute. Append-only means each change is a new row. Each price and limit in this table is sourced, with a link and a date, in the tool's own section below.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools
text: Grouped by who makes them. The order carries no ranking.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Made by Oracle
text:
**1. Oracle GoldenGate: for Oracle estates with a licence budget**

At a glance

- Price, on premises: licensed per processor or Named User Plus, at both the capture and apply ends. Oracle's price list of 15 September 2026 shows GoldenGate at $17,500 per processor ($350 per Named User Plus) with $3,850 of support for the first year (checked Oct 2026)
- Price, Iceberg product: GoldenGate for Distributed Applications and Analytics is $20,000 per processor ($400 per Named User Plus), counted on the source side only, per the same price list (checked Oct 2026)
- Price, cloud and free: Oracle Cloud bills per OCPU per minute (checked Oct 2026). GoldenGate Free is a starter version, usable in production for Oracle databases up to 20 GB with community support instead of Oracle Support (checked Oct 2026)

Oracle's GoldenGate FAQ says Extract captures changes from the source database's redo or transaction logs and writes them to a trail file. GoldenGate `26ai` supports Oracle Database `19c` to `26ai` and later, and the `19c` and `21c` releases cover Oracle `11.2.0.4` to `21c`.

The FAQ lists plenty of targets, including MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Kafka and Apache Iceberg.

What's good

- The FAQ (checked Oct 2026) also names Db2, Hadoop, Snowflake, Parquet, Avro, MongoDB and Cassandra among its supported databases and targets, and Oracle says GoldenGate supports hundreds of sources and targets.
- Per Oracle high availability guide, it fits a read/write replica, multimaster and bidirectional replication, subset and many-to-one replication, data transformations, and replication between endian formats or across database major versions.
- The FAQ lists unidirectional, bidirectional and multi-directional setups. For bidirectional ones it recommends conflict detection and resolution policies and primary or unique keys on every replicated table.
- It runs as Microservices Architecture, managed through Service Manager, on a VM, bare metal or Kubernetes. OCI GoldenGate is a fully managed service where Oracle handles backups, patching and upgrades.
- Oracle's Apache Iceberg connection docs (checked Oct 2026) list Glue, Hadoop, Nessie, Polaris and REST catalogs, with dependency downloaders for Google Cloud Storage, Amazon S3 and Azure Data Lake Storage.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Made by Oracle (part 2)
text:
- Iceberg writing lives in a separate product, GoldenGate for Distributed Applications and Analytics, and its docs sit in Oracle's big-data documentation set, not in the core GoldenGate docs. It has its own line on the price list (checked Oct 2026).
- The older Classic Architecture is de-supported in `26ai` (FAQ) (checked Oct 2026), so check which one you run.
- The FAQ (checked Oct 2026) says bidirectional setups are more complex than one-way setups and can cause update conflicts, replication loops, data divergence, latency sensitivity and operational complexity.
- The FAQ (checked Oct 2026) says GoldenGate cannot capture from Salesforce, Teradata or TimesTen.

**2. Oracle Active Data Guard: for a standby copy of a whole Oracle database**

At a glance

- Price: An extra-cost option on Enterprise Edition, per Oracle's Licensing Information guide. Oracle's price list of 15 September 2026 shows $11,500 per processor, with $2,530 of support for the first year (checked Oct 2026).

Oracle's best-practice page says to use Active Data Guard when the focus is simplicity, data protection and availability. It calls it the simplest and fastest one-way replication of a complete Oracle database, with all data types and automatic replication of data definition language (DDL) changes, the statements that change table structure.

What's good

- Oracle's page says a synchronized standby can be opened read-only, so your reports can run there and leave the main database alone.
- It says Active Data Guard detects silent corruptions that can occur on the source or target and automatically repairs corrupt blocks.
- It lists zero data loss protection at any distance without impacting database performance. That is Oracle's own claim, and we did not test it.
- It says a Data Guard primary and standby are physically exact copies, so RMAN backups are interchangeable.
- It lists standby-first patching, database rolling upgrades and select platform migrations as ways to cut planned downtime.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Made by Oracle (part 3)
text:
- It's all or nothing: a whole Oracle database goes to another Oracle database. Oracle's page (checked Oct 2026) points to GoldenGate for subset replication and for a replica that must be open read/write.
- The same page (checked Oct 2026) sends multimaster and bidirectional replication, many-to-one replication and data transformations to GoldenGate.
- It also sends replication between endian-format platforms, or across database major versions, to GoldenGate (Oracle's page) (checked Oct 2026).
- The licensing guide (checked Oct 2026) lists it as an extra-cost option on Enterprise Edition and shows it as not available in the Free edition.
- Oracle's page (checked Oct 2026) describes a copy of a whole Oracle database to another Oracle database, and names no lake or other database engine as a target.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Commercial and managed tools
text:
**3. Qlik Replicate: for mixed legacy sources**

At a glance

- Price: Not published. Qlik Talend Cloud uses capacity bands based on data volume, job runs and run time. For client-managed Replicate, Qlik tells customers to contact sales (see the Qlik pricing page and Qlik Community) (checked Oct 2026)

Qlik's Oracle source limits list separate rules for each reader, so read them before you plan. For Oracle `21c`, LogMiner access is not supported, and only the Replicate Log Reader works (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- Qlik's product page describes Replicate as log-based with a zero-footprint design. For Oracle, Qlik's docs say it reads redo logs with either LogMiner or its own Replicate Log Reader.
- The same page (checked Oct 2026) lists IMS/DB, Db2 for z/OS, RMS and VSAM as mainframe sources, and Apache Kafka, Confluent, Azure Event Hubs and AWS Kinesis as streaming platforms.
- On Iceberg, Qlik's launch release of September 2025 says Qlik Open Lakehouse combines CDC ingestion with automatic Iceberg optimization, runs in the customer's own cloud account with bring-your-own compute, and can be read by Amazon Athena, Snowflake, Spark, Trino and Amazon SageMaker. Replicate's May 2026 release notes (checked Oct 2026) added a Cloudera Iceberg target.
- Replicate is client managed. Qlik's page says it can be installed on premises or as a virtual machine image in any location you choose.
- Under Qlik's product descriptions, the initial full load of a table is not counted in Data Moved, and Qlik waives overage charges incurred in the first six months of an initial subscription.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Commercial and managed tools (part 2)
text:
- Qlik's pricing page shows a "Contact Us" button for each of the four Talend Cloud editions (Starter, Standard, Premium and Enterprise) and no dollar figure, so you can't budget without a sales call (checked Oct 2026).
- Log-based CDC first appears in the Standard edition list on that page. It is not in the Starter list (checked Oct 2026).
- On Oracle `21c`, CDC is not supported if a schema, table or column name is longer than `30` characters (Qlik's Oracle source limits) (checked Oct 2026).
- Capturing from a pluggable database with LogMiner is not supported, and neither is capturing several pluggable databases through the container database. Qlik's docs (checked Oct 2026) also advise against LogMiner on RAC because of unpredictable behavior.
- Open Lakehouse is part of Qlik Talend Cloud, not Replicate alone. The release notes (checked Oct 2026) describe Replicate landing data on S3 for an Open Lakehouse pipeline to turn into Iceberg tables, plus a Cloudera Iceberg target.
- Data Volume is counted where data lands, so the same data replicated to two targets is counted twice (Qlik's product descriptions) (checked Oct 2026).

**4. Striim: for high-volume Oracle streaming**

At a glance

- Price: Developer tier free up to 25 million events a month. Striim Cloud and Striim Platform say "contact us" (see the Striim pricing page) (checked Oct 2026)

Striim gives you two readers. Its Oracle CDC documentation describes Oracle Reader, which uses LogMiner, and OJet, a high-performance log mining interface. Both read Oracle `11g` and higher, Oracle clusters (RAC, several servers sharing one database) and pluggable databases.

Striim's own sizing guidance puts Oracle Reader at 20 GB to 80 GB of change data an hour and OJet at 150 GB or more (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Commercial and managed tools (part 3)
text:
- Striim's feature table (checked Oct 2026) marks Oracle Database `26ai` as supported by both Oracle Reader and OJet.
- Per Striim's docs (checked Oct 2026), a GG Trail Reader can read existing GoldenGate trail files (the page names GoldenGate versions `11g`, `12c`, `18.1` and `19.1`), which matters if you're moving off GoldenGate. We did not test it.
- On Iceberg, Striim's docs describe an Iceberg Writer with Merge and Append Only modes that propagates DDL changes, and an S3 Tables Writer (checked Oct 2026) with `MERGE` and `APPENDONLY` modes that runs on Amazon EMR with either the S3 Tables catalog or AWS Glue.
- The Striim Cloud SLA sets monthly availability at 99.5% for Striim Cloud Enterprise and 99.9% for Mission Critical (checked Oct 2026). It applies only to customers whose order forms reference it.
- Under the consumption terms (checked Oct 2026) updated on 17 September 2026, Monthly Plan customers pay monthly in arrears for credits used, with no long-term commitment.

Where it falls short

- Striim's Iceberg Writer has one documented limit. Striim's Iceberg Writer docs (checked Oct 2026) say that in this release Google Cloud Storage is the only supported data lake (S3 Tables has its own writer), and that it needs Google's managed Spark service plus a Lakehouse, Nessie or Polaris catalog. A Hadoop catalog is for development and testing only.
- Iceberg Writer partitioned tables need manual creation, time source types are written as strings, and recovery uses at-least-once processing (Iceberg Writer docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The S3 Tables Writer (checked Oct 2026) needs lowercase table, namespace and column names, which breaks wildcard mappings against sources with uppercase identifiers.
- Oracle Reader and GG Trail Reader are premium adapters. At the entry tier, premium adapters use 200 credits per million events against 100 for standard ones, and events are counted when they are read and when they are written (consumption terms (checked Oct 2026), checked Oct 2026).
- Unused credits are forfeited at the end of a Capacity Purchase term (consumption terms (checked Oct 2026), checked Oct 2026).
- The SLA (checked Oct 2026) credit is the sole remedy for a missed service level, and scheduled upgrade or maintenance downtime of up to 24 hours a month is excluded.

**5. Quest SharePlex: for Oracle-to-Oracle and Oracle-to-PostgreSQL replication**

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Commercial and managed tools (part 4)
text:
At a glance

- Price: Not published. Quest's SharePlex page offers "Request Pricing" (checked Oct 2026)

Quest says SharePlex operates outside the Oracle database instance and reads from redo logs. Its targets include Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Kafka, and Parquet files in cloud storage such as Amazon S3 and Azure Blob. It supports two-way replication with conflict handling.

What's good

- Quest lists Oracle-to-Oracle and Oracle-to-PostgreSQL replication, including active-active with conflict resolution, and says the same works between Oracle and Google Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, AlloyDB and AlloyDB Omni.
- Beyond the targets above, Quest's page lists MySQL (including AWS RDS, Aurora and Azure Database for MySQL), MariaDB, Azure SQL Database, Azure Event Hubs, JMS queues and Snowflake.
- Quest says SharePlex can replicate to an unlimited number of targets. That is a vendor claim, and we did not test it.
- File output can be Parquet, JSON, XML or SQL.
- The page offers a free trial ("Request Free Trial").

Where it falls short

- Quest's page (checked Oct 2026) describes replication from Oracle and PostgreSQL databases; it lists no other source.
- Quest doesn't say on its page (checked Oct 2026) whether it uses LogMiner, XStream or its own parser.
- The pages we read (checked Oct 2026) don't list Apache Iceberg as a target. The lake output is Parquet files in object storage.
- Quest's marketing (checked Oct 2026) says SharePlex costs a fraction of native tools, but it publishes no figures or method.
- Per-datatype and per-version limits are not on the pages we read (checked Oct 2026).

**6. Fivetran: for hands-off pipelines into a warehouse**

At a glance

- Price: Monthly Active Rows (MAR) per connection, meaning the rows changed in a month

- Free up to 500,000 MAR, per the billing docs (checked Oct 2026)
- A $5 base charge per connection with 1 to 1 million MAR, per the same billing docs (checked Oct 2026)
- Paid per-MAR rates are in its Service Consumption Table. The first tier, per million MAR, is Standard $495, Enterprise $661.67 and Business Critical $1,061.67, each plus a $5 monthly base (checked Oct 2026)

Fivetran bills by Monthly Active Rows (MAR). Its Oracle docs list two connectors. The Oracle connector offers Binary Log Reader, Teleport and XStream Out, and the High-Volume Agent (HVA) connector offers Direct Capture and Archive Log Only.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Commercial and managed tools (part 5)
text:
Per the docs, Teleport works differently: it reads tables, doesn't support large objects and is limited to tables under `100 GB` (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- Per Fivetran's setup docs, Binary Log Reader reads Oracle redo log files directly, with no agent on the source database host. It reads both online and archived redo logs, and access to archived logs is required.
- The Oracle connector docs (checked Oct 2026) list database versions `11g R2` to `21c`.
- Fivetran's Hybrid Deployment docs say the pipeline runs in your own environment and only metadata, including MAR information, and logs are sent to Fivetran. It needs the Enterprise or Business Critical plan (checked Oct 2026).
- Fivetran's docs (checked Oct 2026) say its Managed Data Lake Service writes Parquet files to your own Amazon S3, ADLS or GCS bucket and always creates Iceberg metadata, with a default Fivetran Catalog built on Apache Polaris.

Where it falls short

- The LogMiner method is sunset. Fivetran ended support for LogMiner connections on April 15, 2026, and said those still on it would stop syncing at the end of May 15, 2026 (LogMiner migration FAQ, checked Oct 2026). Its Oracle docs (checked Oct 2026) also say the LogMiner method "is sunset and is no longer available for new Oracle connections".
- Oracle sources, including Oracle RAC and Oracle RDS, and the High-Volume Agent Oracle connector are on the Enterprise and Business Critical plans only, per Fivetran's billing docs. Annual contracts have a $12,000 minimum (checked Oct 2026).
- The Oracle docs list a `5 TB` limit on the sum of replicated tables and a `200 GB` limit on redo per hour, for both Binary Log Reader and the HVA connector (checked Oct 2026).
- The Oracle docs' (checked Oct 2026) instance table lists a physical standby instance as unsupported for every method, and Binary Log Reader support for an Active Data Guard standby is in Private Preview.
- The Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026) defines MAR as distinct primary keys reflecting inserts, updates and deletes, and says MAR cannot be combined across connections to get a better rate.
- Fivetran says (checked Oct 2026) the Managed Data Lake Service does not support position deletes for Iceberg tables. On AWS it does not support the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, Glacier Deep Archive or Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Open source
text:
**7. Debezium: for teams that already run Kafka**

At a glance

- Price: Free Apache 2.0 licence, per Debezium's licence page (checked Oct 2026). You pay for servers and staff.

Debezium's Oracle docs say it can read Oracle through LogMiner, XStream or OpenLogReplicator, and you choose with the `database.connection.adapter` setting (`logminer`, `logminer_unbuffered`, `olr` or `xstream`). The docs call XStream "a commercial component of Oracle GoldenGate". Debezium `3.7` lists tested Oracle versions `19c`, `21c`, `23ai` and `26ai` (release overview).

Then there's OpenLogReplicator, a separate open-source C++ project that parses Oracle's redo files and sends changes to Kafka, files or a network stream. GitHub lists it under the Affero General Public License (AGPL) version 3 (checked Oct 2026). Its stable line is `1.9`, and the `2.0.0` release (shown as 19 Jul on the releases page, with no year) is still called under development on the project page.

What's good

- Debezium's Oracle docs let you pick the reader, so you pick the licence route too: LogMiner, or XStream if you own GoldenGate. Check the logging setting described earlier either way.
- Debezium's exactly-once page (checked Oct 2026) lists Oracle among the connectors that can take part in Kafka Connect's exactly-once delivery. It needs Kafka Connect `3.3.0` or higher in distributed mode, with `exactly.once.source.support=enabled` on every worker.
- The Debezium Server docs say it streams change events from a source database directly to messaging and storage systems without requiring Apache Kafka. Its sink list includes Kinesis, Pub/Sub, Pulsar, Redis, Kafka, RabbitMQ, Event Hubs and Iceberg.
- The docs say the Iceberg sink consumes change events from a source Debezium connector and writes Apache Iceberg tables, with upsert and append modes, automatic table creation when event and key schema information is enabled, and automatic schema evolution.
- The OpenLogReplicator README (checked Oct 2026) says it can be used with Debezium as a replacement for the LogMiner reader. For Debezium `2.x` and `3.x` its table gives `1.3.0` as the minimum version and `1.9.0` as the recommended one.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Open source (part 2)
text:
- Watch the first snapshot. The docs (checked Oct 2026) say an `ORA-01555` error can occur if the first snapshot outlasts the database's `UNDO_RETENTION` time, `15 minutes` by default.
- Before deploying, the docs say to run the database in archive log mode and enable supplemental logging. For Debezium Server (checked Oct 2026) you also copy the Oracle JDBC driver into its `lib` directory yourself, and each Server instance runs exactly one connector.
- LogMiner has a memory trade-off (checked Oct 2026). In the default mode the connector buffers events until a commit or rollback. The `logminer_unbuffered` mode needs much less connector memory but shifts a much greater burden to the source database, and for large transactions it can exceed the database's PGA memory.
- OpenLogReplicator's README (checked Oct 2026) says it is primarily developed and maintained by its author, and that issue reports are handled on a best-effort basis.
- The Iceberg sink is community-maintained in a separate repository. Upsert is off by default, and the Server docs say upsert and automatic primary key detection depend on the flattened event structure. The sink's own FAQ (checked Oct 2026) says to run periodic table maintenance jobs to compact data and rewrite delete files, especially in upsert mode.
- The exactly-once page (checked Oct 2026) says Debezium does not implement an internal deduplication layer, and that it is unclear whether Kafka's exactly-once implementation is fully correct or has edge cases.

**8. OLake Go: for scheduled copies of Oracle tables into Iceberg or Parquet**

At a glance

- Method: Oracle source with Full Refresh and Full Refresh + Incremental sync modes (Oracle connector docs)
- Price: Free licence (Apache 2.0, GitHub), you pay for infrastructure

OLake Go reads Oracle tables and writes Apache Iceberg tables or Parquet files to storage you control. You run it from the OLake UI (install, or start with the quickstart), with the Docker command line (Docker CLI) or with Helm on Kubernetes (Kubernetes install).

What's good

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Open source (part 3)
text:
- The Oracle source offers parallel chunking, checkpointing and automatic resume for failed full loads (Oracle connector docs).
- It supports Oracle Database `11g` or above, tested with `19c` and `23ai`, and the docs list the privileges the database user needs (Oracle connector docs).
- Iceberg output works with eleven catalog types, including Glue, Hive Metastore, JDBC and REST catalogs such as Nessie, Polaris and Unity (compatibility page). Parquet goes to Amazon S3, MinIO or Google Cloud Storage (OLake Go overview).
- The connector page documents the Oracle-to-Iceberg data type mapping and how date and time values are handled (Oracle connector docs).

Scope: OLake Go reads Oracle tables with Full Refresh or Full Refresh + Incremental syncs and has no database CDC for Oracle (Oracle connector docs).

Bottom line: Pick OLake Go for scheduled copies of Oracle tables into Iceberg or Parquet on storage you run.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Cloud services
text:
**9. AWS DMS: for moving Oracle into AWS**

At a glance

- Price: Replication instance hours or Serverless capacity hours, plus any extra log storage. The AWS DMS pricing page says you pay by the hour for the capacity you use, and it lists a per-GB CDC charge only for its zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift (checked Oct 2026)

AWS's Oracle source documentation says DMS uses LogMiner by default and offers Binary Reader, which parses the raw redo files. For a full-load-only task, no extra setup is needed. A CDC task is different: you choose one reader and prepare the source.

What's good

- Per AWS, Binary Reader has a lower impact on source CPU and I/O and better CDC performance on high change volumes. Its feature table lists LogMiner as the easier of the two to configure.
- AWS lists (checked Oct 2026) self-managed Oracle sources from `10.2` and higher, `11g` up to `12.2`, `18c` and `19c`.
- A CDC task can start from an `SCN` or a timestamp (AWS docs) (checked Oct 2026). From DMS version `3.5.1` the `openTransactionWindow` endpoint setting covers open transactions on a CDC-only task that starts that way.
- Per the same page, bidirectional replication is supported on Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL and the Aurora editions, as two tasks, one in each direction.
- AWS's DMS pricing page says that Free Tier sign-ups after 15 July 2025 can choose a Free Plan or a Paid Plan with $100 in credits, plus up to $100 more, valid for up to twelve months (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Cloud services (part 2)
text:
- LogMiner doesn't give large-object support on Oracle `12c`, and it doesn't handle updates that touch only large-object columns (AWS docs) (checked Oct 2026). Binary Reader does, but it doesn't support table clusters, compression or most encryption options.
- DMS's CDC setup steps (checked Oct 2026) say it does not support an Oracle Standby as a source. Per the Binary Reader section, a self-managed standby works only if it is an Active Data Guard standby.
- Apache Iceberg is not on AWS's list of DMS target endpoints (checked Oct 2026). In an AWS blog example, DMS writes files to S3 and a Glue job loads Iceberg tables, and the blog says the job does not process a file when no primary key is set.
- During CDC, DMS skips events for objects whose identifiers are longer than `30` bytes without stopping the task, which can leave data missing on the target (AWS docs) (checked Oct 2026).
- The CDC page says there are no SLAs for CDC latency, and that latency can rise to several minutes or longer. AWS's best practices page (checked Oct 2026) advises against DMS CDC for sub-second or guaranteed low-latency replication.
- Starting a CDC task from an `SCN` or timestamp misses open transactions (AWS docs) (checked Oct 2026), those that started before the start position and committed after it, unless you use the setting above.

AWS's Oracle source documentation compares the two readers in a table. Some of its rows (checked Oct 2026):

| Feature | LogMiner | Binary Reader |
| Easy to configure | Yes | No |
| Lower impact on source I/O and CPU | No | Yes |
| Better CDC performance | No | Yes |
| Oracle table clusters | Yes | No |
| LOB columns on Oracle 12c | No | Yes |
| UPDATE statements that touch only LOB columns | No | Yes |
| All Oracle compression methods | Yes | No |
| XA transactions | No | Yes |
| RAC | Yes, not recommended for performance reasons | Yes, highly recommended |

**10. Google Datastream: for Oracle into BigQuery**

At a glance

- Price: Per GiB processed, and a processed byte is an internal representation that for most use cases can be 2 to 5 times larger than the data itself. Backfill is free for the first 500 GiB a month, then $0.40 per GiB. The free CDC tier covers only AlloyDB and Spanner sources (Datastream pricing page) (checked Oct 2026)

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Cloud services (part 3)
text:
Google's Oracle source page lists Oracle `11.2.0.4` (LogMiner only), `12c`, `18c`, `19c` and `21c`. It supports RAC, Exadata, Amazon's managed Oracle service and an Active Data Guard standby. Oracle Autonomous Database is not supported, though.

What's good

- One difference to know, per Google's docs: the binary reader sends only committed changes, while LogMiner can also read uncommitted ones and emits the opposite operation after a rollback.
- The binary reader (Preview) falls back to archived log files (Google's docs) (checked Oct 2026) if there is a read lag on the online logs, and it supports Oracle `VARCHAR2` columns longer than `4000` characters.
- The pricing page says an idle stream does not incur any cost, there are no costs for running streams other than data processed, and events read but not written to the destination are not counted. CDC costs are tiered, so the price per GB falls as usage rises.
- Per the Iceberg destination docs, Iceberg tables in BigQuery store data in customer-owned Cloud Storage buckets in the Iceberg table format and Parquet file format.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Cloud services (part 4)
text:
- Large-object columns arrive as `NULL` unless you set the `streamLargeObjects` flag (Google's Oracle source page) (checked Oct 2026). Even then Datastream looks values up in the source, so fast back-to-back changes can be missed.
- Per Google's docs (checked Oct 2026), columns of types such as `LONG`, `LONG RAW`, `BFILE`, `UROWID`, user-defined types, `VARRAY` and `SDO_GEOMETRY` arrive as `NULL`. Index-organized tables and temporary tables are not supported.
- For a table without a primary key, Datastream merges on the row's `ROWID` (checked Oct 2026), which might not be unique and can change after an export and import.
- Google says (checked Oct 2026) not all source schema changes are detected automatically. Dropping a column, adding one in the middle of a table, changing a data type or truncating a table can cause data corruption or failures downstream.
- The binary reader is in Preview (checked Oct 2026) and does not support Transparent Database Encryption, Hybrid Columnar Compression or Secure files. If a column name is longer than `30` characters, an `UPDATE` makes Oracle silently abort supplemental logging for the row, and unchanged columns arrive as `NULL`.
- With an Active Data Guard standby as the source (Google's docs) (checked Oct 2026), Datastream waits for the standby to apply each log before it reads it, so a paused standby apply delays your data.

**11. Confluent Oracle XStream connector: for Oracle into Kafka without a GoldenGate purchase**

At a glance

- Price: Task price not published; Confluent lists its Oracle XStream connector as "Contact us" and data transfer at $0.025 per GB (Confluent connector pricing) (checked Oct 2026)

Confluent's connector documentation says the fully managed connector reads the redo log through XStream Out and captures both data and DDL changes. Confluent says it has an agreement with Oracle, so users don't need to buy extra Oracle licences for XStream with this connector (checked Oct 2026). That's Confluent's claim, so confirm it in writing.

What's good

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > The 11 best Oracle replication tools > Cloud services (part 5)
text:
- It's the one XStream route here where the vendor says the licence is covered (checked Oct 2026).
- For updates it emits the state of the row before and after the update (Confluent's docs), and it receives changes in transaction commit order.
- Confluent's docs say it fully supports Oracle RAC. They also describe downstream capture, where the capture process runs on a separate Oracle database so production isn't hit by capture overhead, and cascading downstream capture through an Active Data Guard standby.
- An ad hoc blocking snapshot signal can backfill specific tables after the connector has started streaming, and automated retries try up to three times before the connector stops in a failed state.

Where it falls short

- The connector writes changes to Kafka topics (Confluent's docs) (checked Oct 2026), so you still need a second step to reach a lake.
- The managed connector needs Confluent Cloud. A self-managed version for Confluent Platform exists as a Premium connector under the Confluent Enterprise licence (checked Oct 2026).
- Delivery is at-least-once (Confluent's docs) (checked Oct 2026). If the connector is interrupted during a snapshot it restarts all snapshots from the beginning, and a long snapshot can hit `ORA-01555` unless you raise `UNDO_RETENTION`.
- Per Confluent's docs (checked Oct 2026), each connector instance captures from one pluggable database, and an XStream outbound server supports only one active client session, so every connector needs its own outbound server.
- An unmodified large-object column (Confluent's docs) (checked Oct 2026) is left out of the change event and replaced by a placeholder. Large-object events can also exceed Kafka's maximum message size, in which case Kafka rejects the message.
- Low database activity can add about 3 seconds of latency because of XStream batching (Confluent's docs) (checked Oct 2026), and heartbeats are off by default, so the connector can't advance its position on a quiet database.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Where Oracle changes can land in Iceberg
text:
Ask which catalog (the service that tracks your Iceberg tables), which cloud, which write mode, and whether the route is one step or two.

| Route | What the docs show | Limit to know |
| GoldenGate for Distributed Applications and Analytics | An Iceberg connection used by Replicat processes that write to Iceberg tables, with Glue, Hadoop, Nessie, Polaris and REST catalogs | A separate product from core GoldenGate |
| Qlik Open Lakehouse | Qlik says it writes spec-compliant Iceberg tables in your own cloud account | Part of Qlik Talend Cloud, not Replicate alone |
| Google Datastream | Iceberg tables managed by BigQuery, stored in your Cloud Storage | Append-only write mode |
| AWS DMS | An AWS blog shows DMS writing S3 files, then Glue jobs loading Iceberg tables | Two steps; Iceberg is not on DMS's target list |
| Debezium Server | An Iceberg sink that consumes events from a Debezium connector | Community-maintained, and we found no Oracle-specific guide |
| Fivetran Managed Data Lake Service | Parquet files in your own S3, ADLS or GCS bucket with Iceberg metadata and a default Fivetran Catalog built on Apache Polaris | Fivetran says position deletes are not supported for Iceberg tables, and we did not check the Oracle connector against it |
| Striim | Iceberg Writer with merge and append-only modes | Iceberg Writer: Google Cloud Storage only; a separate S3 Tables Writer targets Amazon S3 Tables |
| Oracle connector to Kafka, then Tableflow | Each step is documented separately: Confluent's XStream connector, then Tableflow turning topics into Iceberg | We found no single Oracle-to-Iceberg guide for this route |

Sources: GoldenGate Iceberg docs, Qlik Open Lakehouse, Google Datastream, AWS blog, Debezium Server, Fivetran, Striim and Confluent (checked Oct 2026).

One more trick for append-only output. To get current state, take the latest record per key by the tool's ordering field, then drop keys whose latest record is a delete.

text:

Prefer a quick answer? Try the quiz.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > Which Oracle replication tool for which job > Which Oracle replication tool fits you?
text:
Question 1 of 5

What job do you need done?

The post says there is no single best Oracle replication tool, because the tools answer different questions.

What to check before you commit
1. The licence route. Ask which reader the tool uses and whether its setup turns on GoldenGate Supplemental Logging (see the licence section above). Oracle's paper says XStream generally needs GoldenGate licences, Confluent says its connector comes with its own agreement with Oracle, and Oracle's paper calls a direct reader unsupported (checked Oct 2026).

2. Log retention. Archived redo logs must stay on disk through an outage plus the catch-up time, so don't let a cleanup job eat them. Fivetran says Binary Log Reader requires archived redo access (Fivetran docs), and Datastream's setup includes a retention policy (Datastream docs).

3. The first snapshot. Tools copy your existing rows before they follow changes. A snapshot that outlasts undo retention can raise `ORA-01555` in Debezium (checked Oct 2026).

4. Large objects. A large object (LOB) is a text or binary column that can be huge. Datastream writes them as `NULL` by default (Datastream docs), and DMS LogMiner has gaps on Oracle `12c` (AWS docs).

5. Names. LogMiner needs names of `30` characters or less (LogMiner docs), Datastream's LogMiner mode has the same limit (Datastream docs), and Qlik's `21c` notes say longer names are not replicated (Qlik docs).

6. Standby and pluggable databases. Datastream reads one pluggable database per stream (Datastream docs). DMS's Binary Reader section says it currently supports only an Active Data Guard Standby, and Fivetran lists no Oracle method on a physical standby (Fivetran docs).

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > What to check before you commit > A two-week trial
text:
Run the same test on every finalist and compare each tool's own records with the final table.

| Step | Operation | Append-only records | Current-state rows |
| 1 | Snapshot of existing keys 1, 2, 3 | Three snapshot records | 1, 2, 3 |
| 2 | Insert key 4 | Insert 4 | 1, 2, 3, 4 |
| 3 | Update key 2 to a , then to b | Two update records | 1, 2 ( b ), 3, 4 |
| 4 | Delete key 3 | A delete record for 3 | 1, 2 ( b ), 4 |
| 5 | Kill the tool mid-batch, restart, insert key 5 with a large object | Insert 5 | 1, 2 ( b ), 4, 5 |

A missing event is a failure, full stop. Accept a duplicate only if the tool documents at-least-once delivery and your load collapses it by key. Last, stop the tool for your longest expected outage and check that the archived logs it needs are still there.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > A worked example: one Oracle setup, six configurations
text:
Take Oracle `12c`, an Active Data Guard standby as the source, large-object columns, and Iceberg as the goal. The cells repeat facts that are linked in the tool sections above.

| Candidate | Reads a standby | Large objects on 12c | Iceberg | Verdict |
| AWS DMS with LogMiner | No | No | Iceberg not on DMS's target list | Eliminated |
| AWS DMS with Binary Reader | Yes | Yes | S3 files, then Glue jobs | Passes, in two steps |
| Fivetran Binary Log Reader | Yes (marked Private Preview on the docs page) | Supported | Managed Data Lake Service, not checked with Oracle | Needs a check on Iceberg |
| Fivetran HVA | Yes, with Direct Capture or Archive Log Only | Supported | Managed Data Lake Service, not checked with Oracle | Needs a check on Iceberg |
| Datastream | Yes | NULL unless the flag is set | Append-only | Passes only if append-only is acceptable |
| GoldenGate with DAA | Not checked | Not checked | Documented | Needs a check on standby and large objects |

Sources: AWS DMS, Fivetran Oracle docs, Google Datastream and GoldenGate Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026).

If you need current-state Iceberg tables, Datastream drops out. That leaves DMS with Binary Reader plus a Glue step, and three candidates to check.

title: Compare: Best Oracle Replication Tools in 2026, Compared | OLake > FAQs
text:
Q1. What is the best Oracle replication tool?

It depends on the job. Active Data Guard suits an Oracle-to-Oracle standby, and GoldenGate suits two-way replication and other target systems.

Q2. Is Oracle LogMiner free?

Mostly, with a catch. Oracle's paper says LogMiner is accessible without additional licensing, but its licensing guide says a GoldenGate licence is required when GoldenGate Supplemental Logging is on (checked Oct 2026). The paper also calls LogMiner single-threaded and not the recommended route for high-volume continuous replication (checked Oct 2026).

Q3. Do I need a GoldenGate licence to use XStream?

Usually, yes. Oracle's paper says XStream generally requires a GoldenGate licence on any database where it is used (checked Oct 2026). Confluent says its agreement with Oracle covers its own connector (checked Oct 2026).

Q4. What is the difference between Data Guard and GoldenGate?

Oracle's page says Active Data Guard is the simplest one-way copy of a whole Oracle database. GoldenGate fits read/write replicas, multimaster or two-way replication, and subset replication.

Q5. Can I replicate Oracle to Apache Iceberg?

Yes, with limits, and it's rarely one step. GoldenGate for Distributed Applications and Analytics and Qlik document Iceberg writing, and Datastream is append-only (checked Oct 2026). OLake Go copies Oracle tables into Iceberg with full refresh or incremental syncs.

Q6. Are third-party Oracle log readers allowed?

Oracle's paper says it does not support readers that parse redo files without an Oracle interface, notes that the Oracle Master Agreement addresses reverse engineering, and advises independent legal review. It names no tool, so ask each vendor (checked Oct 2026).
