title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

Both are free, mature relational databases, and either one can run most web apps. Pick PostgreSQL if you want schema changes you can roll back, a full outer join, materialized views or the six index types its manual lists. Pick MySQL if your team, tools or hosting already run on it, because switching costs more than it looks.

Which one is faster? We found no neutral, linked benchmark, so test your own queries.

- Money first: PostgreSQL is free under a BSD or MIT style licence. MySQL Community Edition is free under the GPL version 2, and Oracle sells commercial editions (checked Oct 2026).
- In MySQL `8.4`, the default storage engine is InnoDB, which gives transactions that follow ACID (atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, explained below). The old line that MySQL isn't fully ACID only applies if you pick another engine.
- PostgreSQL can undo a schema change inside a transaction. MySQL `8.4` makes each schema change atomic, but it's not transactional, and it ends any open transaction first.
- MySQL's join syntax lists no full outer join. PostgreSQL's does.
- MySQL's own manual says it has no materialized views. PostgreSQL has them.
- For JSON, PostgreSQL has a binary `jsonb` type that can be indexed directly. MySQL indexes JSON through a generated column.
- We found no neutral, linked benchmark that says one is faster. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey shows more respondents reporting extensive development work with PostgreSQL, but it measures popularity.

Every fact below comes from the PostgreSQL and MySQL manuals, project pages or a named survey, read on October 8, 2026, with the page linked beside the claim. We did not run either database.

Last reviewed October 2026.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Postgres vs MySQL at a glance
text:
Each cell links to its source.

|  | PostgreSQL | MySQL |
| Who runs it | Community project, copyright held by the PostgreSQL Global Development Group ( licence page ) | Developed by Oracle ( MySQL LICENSE file (checked Oct 2026)) |
| Licence | PostgreSQL License (checked Oct 2026), similar to BSD or MIT | Community: GPL version 2 (checked Oct 2026). Enterprise: commercial (checked Oct 2026) |
| Versions we found (Oct 2026) | 14 to 18 supported; 19 is a release candidate (RC 1, October 15, 2026) (checked Oct 2026) | Download page lists a 26.x release, 9.7 LTS, 8.4 LTS and 8.0.46 (checked Oct 2026); 8.0 is in Sustaining Support (checked Oct 2026) |
| Default table engine | Not applicable | InnoDB , with other engines available |
| Concurrency model | MVCC: readers do not block writers | InnoDB: row-level locks, consistent reads and MVCC |
| Schema changes (DDL) | Can run inside a transaction | Atomic, but ends the open transaction |
| Full outer join | Supported | Join syntax lists none |
| Materialized views (saved query results) | Supported, refreshed with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW | Manual FAQ answer: "No." |
| JSON | json and jsonb types, jsonb can be indexed | JSON type, indexed through a generated column |
| Index types | Six types, B-tree by default, plus the bloom extension | B-tree and hash described |
| Replication | Streaming, cascading and synchronous options documented | Asynchronous by default, with semisynchronous and Group Replication |
| Reported extensive development work with ( Stack Overflow 2025 ) | 55.6% of all respondents | 40.5% of all respondents |

On price, there's nothing to split here. Both Community editions are free (see the licence row above), so what you pay for is hosting, staff time and, for MySQL, optional Enterprise features.

On Oracle's store page (checked Oct 2026), a MySQL Enterprise Edition subscription is listed from US$5,350 for a 1 to 4 socket server. It doesn't say what that price range covers, so ask Oracle for a quote.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > So, what is each one?
text:
PostgreSQL is, in the project's own words, an open-source database that uses and extends SQL. Its history goes back to 1986, and the project calls its licence (checked Oct 2026) "liberal", similar to the BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution) or MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) licenses.

Both are short, permissive open-source licences. Read the real text before you rely on our summary.

The project's versioning page (checked Oct 2026) lists versions `14` to `18` as supported, with `18` the current one, first released on September 25, 2025. PostgreSQL `14` gets its final release on November 12, 2026. PostgreSQL `19` is at release-candidate stage, since the page's banner announces RC 1 on October 15, 2026, so it's not a final release yet.

MySQL is developed by Oracle. The Community release comes under version 2 of the GNU (GNU's Not Unix) General Public License (GPL, a licence that requires derived software to stay open), with extra permissions (checked Oct 2026). Oracle also sells commercial editions.

Two release tracks exist, says MySQL's manual: LTS (long-term support) and Innovation.

The download page lists a `26.x` release, `9.7` LTS, `8.4` LTS and `8.0.46` (checked Oct 2026).

Oracle's notice (checked Oct 2026) says that as of April 21, 2026, MySQL `8.0` is under Sustaining Support, and it encourages a move to `8.4` LTS or `9.7` LTS. So if an older comparison treats `8.0` as the version to pick, that page is out of date.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Transactions and ACID: does the old advice still hold?
text:
ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. You've probably heard that MySQL isn't "really" ACID. In plain terms, ACID means a group of changes either all happen or none do, and a committed change survives a crash.

Older comparison pages say MySQL is ACID only with some engines.

That's still true for engines that aren't transactional. MySQL's manual lists InnoDB and NDB (the engine behind MySQL's clustered edition) as the transactional engines among its built-in ones, and MyISAM, MEMORY (a RAM-based engine) and Archive as not transactional. An engine is the part of MySQL that stores and reads table data.

What changed is the default. In MySQL `8.4`, InnoDB is the default engine, so a `CREATE TABLE` without an `ENGINE` clause gives you an InnoDB table. Its manual says InnoDB operations follow the ACID model, with commit, rollback and crash recovery.

You'd only lose that by choosing another engine on purpose.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Concurrency: how each handles many users
text:
When a hundred people hit your app at once, both databases rely on MVCC, short for multi-version concurrency control. It keeps more than one version of a row so that readers and writers can work at the same time.

PostgreSQL's manual says each statement sees a snapshot of the data. So a reader doesn't wait for a writer, and a writer doesn't wait for a reader (the vacuum section below explains why old row versions are kept). MySQL's InnoDB manual says it uses row-level locking and consistent reads, and lists MVCC as supported.

Some pages boil this down to a rule of thumb that MySQL is better for reads and Postgres for writes. Neither manual makes that claim as a measured result, so test your own workload.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Schema changes: the difference that bites in production
text:
Picture a migration that dies halfway through. DDL means data definition language, the commands that change structure, such as adding a column.

The PostgreSQL project's wiki says PostgreSQL can perform transactional DDL. That means you can start a transaction, change a table, spot your mistake and roll everything back. One caveat: the wiki page was last edited in June 2012, so treat it as a description of a long-standing feature and test your own version.

MySQL `8.4` supports atomic DDL (checked Oct 2026), so a single statement either fully succeeds or fully rolls back, even if the server stops partway. Its manual says atomic DDL is not transactional DDL. A DDL statement implicitly commits any open transaction first, so it can't sit inside one.

If your team ships lots of database migrations (scripted schema changes), this matters. In PostgreSQL, a failed migration can be wrapped so nothing is half applied. In MySQL, you plan around it, with smaller steps and backups.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > SQL features and standards
text:
PostgreSQL's SQL Conformance appendix says it supports most major features of SQL:2023 and conforms to at least 170 of the 177 mandatory Core features. It also notes that no current database claims full Core conformance.

The clearest gap we could confirm is joins.

The join syntax in MySQL's manual lists `INNER`, `CROSS`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `NATURAL` and `STRAIGHT_JOIN` joins, and no full outer join. PostgreSQL's select command reference lists a full outer join.

We didn't compare every other SQL feature.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Data types, JSON and indexes
text:
Odds are your app stores some JSON (JavaScript Object Notation, a text format for nested data) next to normal columns. Both databases can handle it, but they index it differently.

PostgreSQL offers two JSON types. Its manual says `json` keeps an exact copy of the input text, while `jsonb` is stored in a binary format that's faster to process. And `jsonb` also supports indexing.

MySQL has one `JSON` type that validates documents and stores them in an internal binary format. Its `8.4` manual says JSON columns aren't indexed directly. Instead, you index a generated column that pulls out one value.

InnoDB also supports multi-valued indexes on JSON arrays.

Indexes are the other place the manuals part ways. PostgreSQL lists six types, and B-tree is the default.

The others are Hash, GiST (Generalized Search Tree) and Space-Partitioned GiST. Then come GIN (Generalized Inverted Index, for values with many parts such as arrays) and BRIN (Block Range INdex, which summarizes ranges of table blocks).

A bloom extension is also named for PostgreSQL. MySQL's index page describes B-tree and hash indexes, and says hash indexes serve only equality tests.

A longer list doesn't make a database faster for you, and the pages we read don't compare the two on index choice. You only gain if your queries actually need one of these types, such as for arrays or very large tables.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Views, extensions and replication
text:
A materialized view stores the result of a query so that a report does not rerun it each time. PostgreSQL supports them and refreshes them with `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`. The MySQL `8.4` manual's views FAQ asks whether MySQL has materialized views and answers "No."

PostgreSQL also packages add-on features as extensions. Its manual says a package of related SQL objects is called an extension, and one `CREATE EXTENSION` command loads it. We didn't check MySQL's plugin system line by line, so we make no claim about it.

For copies of the database used for failover or reads, MySQL's manual says replication is asynchronous by default, and it also documents semisynchronous replication, delayed replication and Group Replication.

PostgreSQL's high availability chapter describes synchronous and asynchronous options and lists streaming, cascading and synchronous replication. Both have built-in replication, so on its own it's not the deciding factor.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Housekeeping and limits of each
text:
Each database has chores.

PostgreSQL's chore is `VACUUM`. An update or delete does not remove the old row version at once, because other transactions may still need it. `VACUUM` reclaims that space, updates planner statistics and guards against transaction ID wraparound.

Autovacuum, a background helper that runs `VACUUM` for you, is on in the default configuration. For many installs, that's enough.

MySQL's trade-offs are different. Its join syntax lists no full outer join, its views FAQ says no materialized views, and its schema changes commit the open transaction.

The pages we read don't describe a matching routine chore, so check its manual for your engine. Oracle also sells paid editions with extra features, priced above.

Neither list rules one out; use them as a checklist against your team's habits.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Where each fits
text:
- Choose PostgreSQL if you need schema changes that roll back, a full outer join, materialized views or its six documented index types, per the sources in the table below.
- Choose MySQL if your team, tools and hosting already run on it, you rely on Oracle support, or a vendor product you depend on is built for it.

| Your situation | Lean toward | Why, with the source |
| New project, no existing database | PostgreSQL, unless a tool you need targets MySQL | Rollback of schema changes and full outer join |
| Already run MySQL well | MySQL | Switching cost is real, and Oracle's download page lists 8.4 LTS (checked Oct 2026) |
| Heavy use of migration scripts | PostgreSQL | DDL can sit inside a transaction |
| Reports that reuse slow queries | PostgreSQL | Materialized views exist , and MySQL's manual says it has none |
| Lots of JSON you want to search | Test both | jsonb is indexable directly , and MySQL can index through generated columns |
| Need Oracle vendor support | MySQL | Oracle sells commercial MySQL editions |
| Worried about "not ACID" | Either | InnoDB is the default in 8.4 |
| Running version 8.0 or PostgreSQL 14 | Plan an upgrade | MySQL 8.0 is in Sustaining Support , PostgreSQL 14 ends November 12, 2026 (checked Oct 2026) |

Answer five quick questions to narrow it down.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Where each fits > Which database fits you?
text:
Question 1 of 5

Where are you starting from?

Moving a working system has real costs, so your current setup counts.

Performance: what we can (and can't) say
Pages that rank for this topic often say MySQL is faster for simple reads and PostgreSQL is faster for complex queries. The top-ranking pages we read in October 2026 had no linked benchmark behind those claims.

We won't repeat a speed figure, and we won't offer our own number either, because we ran no tests.

A test on your own data is cheap and more reliable. Take your ten slowest real queries and your busiest write path. Run them on both databases on the same hardware with your real data size, then compare.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Common myths, checked against the manuals
text:
Repeated claims we could check against the manuals.

- Myth: MySQL is not ACID. Wrong for the default engine in `8.4`, where InnoDB follows the ACID model (checked Oct 2026). Right only for non-transactional engines such as MyISAM.
- Myth: PostgreSQL follows the SQL standard fully. Close, but no. Its own manual says at least 170 of 177 mandatory Core features, and that no current database claims full Core conformance.
- Myth: MySQL `8.0` is the version to pick. Not anymore. As of April 21, 2026 it is in Sustaining Support (checked Oct 2026).
- Myth: one of them is clearly faster. Nobody showed us a linked benchmark that says so.
- Myth: PostgreSQL has no cost. The software is free. Hosting, backups, upgrades and staff time are not.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > What we couldn't source
text:
On the pages we could read, we didn't find what Oracle's store price range for MySQL Enterprise Edition covers, a neutral benchmark, or a side-by-side of every SQL feature.

We also left out data types, extensions, full-text search and JSON handling. Both databases cover these in their manuals, and the details change from version to version. If one of them could decide your choice, read that chapter for the exact version you plan to run.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > How to test both on your own data
text:
Most teams can do this in a day or two.

- Load a copy of your real data, at your real size, into both databases on the same hardware.
- Pick your ten slowest queries and your busiest write path, and run them on each one.
- Run your real schema changes, then try to roll back a failed one in each database.
- Write down the version numbers you tested, and check them against the support dates above.
- Ask who on your team can fix each one at 3 a.m. (count that as a result too).

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Popularity and ecosystem
text:
On adoption, the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey shows 55.6% of all respondents reporting extensive development work with PostgreSQL and 40.5% with MySQL.

It's a survey of developers who chose to answer it. So it shows what people work with and says nothing about speed or safety.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Copying data out for analytics
text:
Sooner or later, someone asks you to copy the database into a data warehouse or lakehouse. Both databases can feed that, using the change log each one already keeps.

For PostgreSQL, change capture uses logical decoding and replication slots. MySQL tools read its binary log. Either way, this is change data capture (CDC), which means copying only the changes.

OLake Go is an open-source tool that runs a full load and then change capture for Postgres and MySQL. For Postgres (version 10 or above) it uses the `pgoutput` plugin with a replication slot and a publication. For MySQL (version 5.7 or above) it reads the binary log in row format, and MariaDB works as a CDC source too. Both connectors also offer incremental sync. OLake Go writes Apache Iceberg tables or Parquet files to object storage such as S3, MinIO or GCS. See the OLake documentation for connector details and limits.

Q1. Is Postgres better than MySQL?

Not in every case, no. PostgreSQL has transactional schema changes and a full outer join. MySQL fits when your team and tools already use it. We found no neutral linked benchmark that settles speed.

Q2. Is Postgres faster than MySQL?

We can't say from public sources. The top-ranking pages we read state speed claims without a linked benchmark. So test your own slowest queries and write path on both, with your real data size.

Q3. Is MySQL ACID compliant?

Yes, with InnoDB, which is the default engine in MySQL `8.4`. MySQL's manual lists InnoDB and NDB as transactional, and engines such as MyISAM and MEMORY as not transactional. Just don't pick another engine by accident.

Q4. Is PostgreSQL free for commercial use?

Yes. The project describes its licence as a liberal open-source licence, similar to BSD or MIT (checked Oct 2026). MySQL Community Edition is free too, under the GPL version 2 (checked Oct 2026), and Oracle sells commercial editions with extra features.

Q5. Which is easier to learn?

We found no study showing either one is easier to learn. Both use standard SQL for everyday work. Pick the one your hosting and teammates already know.

Q6. Can I roll back a schema change in MySQL?

Not inside a transaction, no. MySQL `8.4` makes each schema statement atomic, but its manual says atomic DDL is not transactional DDL and that the statement ends any open transaction. PostgreSQL can run DDL inside a transaction.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Copying data out for analytics (part 2)
text:
Q7. Does MySQL have materialized views?

No. The MySQL `8.4` manual's views FAQ answers this question with a plain "No." PostgreSQL does support them, and you refresh one with the `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` command.

Q8. Which handles JSON better?

Both store and validate JSON. PostgreSQL has a binary `jsonb` type that supports indexing directly. MySQL indexes a JSON value through a generated column, and InnoDB supports multi-valued indexes on JSON arrays. Test your own queries.

Q9. Which is more popular?

PostgreSQL, in the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey: 55.6% of all respondents reported extensive development work with it, against 40.5% for MySQL. The survey measures use among respondents and says nothing about quality or speed.

title: Compare: Postgres vs MySQL: Differences and How to Choose | OLake > Conclusion
text:
Starting fresh: choose PostgreSQL if you want rollback-safe schema changes and a full outer join.

Already live on MySQL with tooling built around it: stay, unless the switch would save you more than it costs.

Check your version first. MySQL `8.0` is in Sustaining Support and PostgreSQL `14` reaches its final release on November 12, 2026, so an upgrade plan comes first. Then test your own queries, because no linked benchmark we found will decide it for you.

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

The big Snowflake competitors are Databricks, Google BigQuery, Amazon Redshift and Microsoft Fabric, and the right one mostly follows the cloud and the skills you already have. Pick Databricks if your team writes code and trains models. Pick BigQuery if you live on Google Cloud, Redshift if you live on AWS, and Fabric if Power BI (Microsoft's reporting tool) runs your reporting.

ClickHouse, MotherDuck, Dremio and Amazon Athena are aimed at narrower jobs. Prices don't line up one to one because the billing units differ.

- The options bill in different units. Snowflake sells credits, Databricks sells Databricks Units (DBU), BigQuery bills per tebibyte (TiB) scanned, Redshift Serverless per Redshift Processing Unit (RPU) hour, and Dremio per Dremio Compute Unit.
- Apache Iceberg lowers the cost of leaving. Most of these options document a way to read Iceberg tables in your own storage, each with limits.
- OLake Go can fill the tables. It copies database data into Iceberg tables that several of these engines read, and into Snowflake itself through the Snowflake Horizon Catalog. See Where OLake Go fits.

Every price below comes from the vendor's own page. We link the page next to the number and mark it "(checked Oct 2026)". If a vendor doesn't publish a price, we say "not published" and leave it there.

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > Why teams look past Snowflake
text:
Snowflake is a cloud data warehouse that runs on Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, according to its Service Consumption Table. Its pricing page describes consumption-based pricing, and that's where most of the friction starts.

You pay in credits, and what a credit costs depends on your edition and region. On AWS US East (Northern Virginia) a credit costs $2.00 on Standard, $3.00 on Enterprise and $4.00 on Business Critical. That is per Snowflake's Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026), effective October 15, 2026. In AWS EU Frankfurt the same editions cost $2.60 and $3.90 for Standard and Enterprise.

Then there's the warehouse size. It sets how many credits you burn per hour. Per the same table (checked Oct 2026), that is 1 for an X-Small, 4 for a Medium and 8 for a Large on a Standard warehouse.

A Medium warehouse (4 credits an hour) running 8 hours a day for 22 working days is 176 hours. That costs $1,408 on Standard at $2.00 a credit and $2,112 on Enterprise at $3.00. The hours are our assumption, and the credit prices are Snowflake's.

Two other things push teams to look around. Some features sit in higher editions. Per Snowflake's editions page and Time Travel docs (checked Oct 2026), multi-cluster warehouses and Time Travel beyond one day need Enterprise or above. And Snowflake's Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026) warn that reading or writing across regions or clouds can add egress charges. Egress means fees for moving data out of a cloud.

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 1. Databricks: for teams that write code and train models
text:
At a glance: proprietary platform on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, SQL Serverless $0.70 per Databricks Unit (DBU) on the Premium plan (AWS US East), pay-as-you-go per second, per its SQL pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

Databricks calls itself a "unified, open analytics platform" in its introduction docs. Its notebooks support Python, R and Scala as well as SQL, and it lists machine learning tools such as MLflow.

On its SQL pricing page (checked Oct 2026), SQL Classic is $0.22 per DBU, SQL Pro $0.55 and SQL Serverless $0.70. These are Premium plan rates on AWS US East. The Serverless rate includes the cloud machines. Classic and Pro are self-managed warehouses that run in your own cloud account, so that machine bill is separate.

What's good

- One platform for SQL, pipelines and model training. Its introduction docs list Delta Lake, Apache Spark, MLflow and Unity Catalog among the open source projects Databricks employees created, and notebooks support Python, R and Scala as well as SQL.
- Its Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026) say it supports Iceberg tables on Parquet at specification `v1`, `v2` and `v3`, managed by Unity Catalog or by foreign catalogs such as AWS Glue, Hive metastore or Snowflake Horizon Catalog.
- Outside engines can use the same tables: the Iceberg docs say the Iceberg REST Catalog API "supports read and write operations from external Iceberg engines", and managed tables can be created by engines such as Apache Spark, Flink, Trino or Kafka.
- Serverless SQL warehouses start in typically 2 to 6 seconds, per its warehouse docs (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 1. Databricks: for teams that write code and train models (part 2)
text:
- DBUs used per hour by warehouse size aren't on the sizing docs page we read (checked Oct 2026), so check the vendor calculator to forecast a bill.
- Managed Iceberg tables need Unity Catalog, Databricks Runtime `16.4` LTS or above and serverless compute, and they can only be created when predictive optimization is enabled for table maintenance, per its Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Foreign Iceberg tables are read-only in Databricks, per the same docs (checked Oct 2026). They don't support partition evolution, and only the `main` branch is accessible, because branching and tagging aren't supported.
- On Iceberg `v2`, position deletes and equality-based deletes aren't supported, per the same docs (checked Oct 2026). Databricks uses Iceberg `v3` deletion vectors for row-level deletes instead.
- External Iceberg engines can't read views through the REST catalog, per the same docs (checked Oct 2026). Partition evolution on managed tables works through external engines but not through Databricks SQL.
- Classic and Pro warehouses take about 4 minutes to start, against 2 to 6 seconds for Serverless, per its warehouse docs (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 2. Google BigQuery: for Google Cloud teams that want no servers
text:
At a glance: serverless, run by Google Cloud, $6.25 per TiB scanned after the first free TiB each month, or slot pricing under editions, per its pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

Google describes BigQuery as a "fully managed serverless data warehouse" in its introduction docs.

On-demand pricing charges for the bytes your queries read, per its pricing page (checked Oct 2026), and the first `1 TiB` each month is free.

A team that scans 10 TiB in a month pays for 9 TiB, which is $56.25 by our arithmetic.

Capacity pricing is the other model. The Standard edition shows $0.04 per slot-hour on the pricing page (checked Oct 2026). It has no commitment and is billed per second after a one-minute minimum (a slot is a unit of query compute).

What's good

- No cluster to size or pause: the introduction docs describe "zero infrastructure management" and say the BigQuery engineering team handles updates and maintenance.
- Its Iceberg docs say managed tables live in storage buckets you own, accept GoogleSQL data changes (DML) and support schema changes such as adding, dropping and renaming columns.
- Those tables also offer automatic storage optimization (adaptive file sizing, automatic clustering, garbage collection and metadata optimization), per the Iceberg docs.
- The Iceberg docs list export of an Iceberg `v2` snapshot for direct reads by open source engines such as Spark.
- The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) gives a monthly free tier of `1 TiB` of queries and the first `10 GiB` of storage. Storage not modified for `90 consecutive days` drops about 50 percent in price.
- Enterprise and Enterprise Plus list a 1-year capacity commitment at a 20 percent discount or a 3-year commitment at 40 percent, per the editions table (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 2. Google BigQuery: for Google Cloud teams that want no servers (part 2)
text:
- On-demand billing follows bytes scanned, and the pricing page (checked Oct 2026) says you are charged for the columns you select even with an explicit `LIMIT`, so one careless query over a whole large table costs real money.
- On-demand queries get "up to 2,000 concurrent slots, shared among all queries in a single project", per its pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- The Standard edition has no column-level access control, row-level security, data masking, BigQuery ML or VPC Service Controls, and it has no access to capacity commitments, per the editions table (checked Oct 2026).
- On Iceberg managed tables only one mutating DML statement (`UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `MERGE`) runs at a time per table, and the others queue, per its Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Iceberg managed tables don't support renaming, table copies, table clones or table snapshots, per the same docs (checked Oct 2026).
- It's a Google Cloud service, and a self-hosted option isn't stated.

What users say: Praise on PeerSpot (2025 to 2026): "BigQuery allows for very fast access, and it is efficient in handling large datasets compared to other SQL databases". Complaint on SoftwareReviews (June 2025): "What I dislike most is the lack of real-time cost visibility and predictability".

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 3. Amazon Redshift: for teams that already live on AWS
text:
At a glance: managed AWS data warehouse, Provisioned from $0.543 per hour or Serverless from $1.50 per hour, per its pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

AWS calls Redshift a "fully managed, petabyte-scale data warehouse service in the cloud" on its product page. Serverless is billed at $0.375 per Redshift Processing Unit (RPU) hour (RPU is its unit of compute). That is the rate in the US East examples on its pricing page (checked Oct 2026). One example there prices 128 RPUs for 8,190 seconds at $109.20.

New Serverless users can claim a $300 credit that expires after 90 days, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026). AWS also says its zero-ETL (no extract, transform, load pipeline for you to build) integrations copy data into Redshift. Sources include Aurora, RDS (managed databases) and DynamoDB, per its zero-ETL docs.

What's good

- Serverless compute is billed per second with no charges during idle periods, and base capacity can be set from `4` to `1024` RPUs, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Serverless Reservations reduce compute costs by up to 45 percent for a 3-year term or up to 24 percent for a 1-year term, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Each Redshift cluster earns up to one hour of free Concurrency Scaling credits per day, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Its zero-ETL docs list sources such as Aurora MySQL and PostgreSQL, DynamoDB, and RDS for MySQL, PostgreSQL and Oracle, plus applications such as Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow and Zendesk.
- The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) says Redshift adds no extra fee for zero-ETL. You still pay for storage, compute and cross-AZ transfer, and the source may add fees.
- Its Iceberg query docs (checked Oct 2026) say it queries Iceberg tables in the Glue catalog, `v1` to `v3`, and `INSERT INTO` or `CREATE TABLE AS` can copy an Iceberg table into a local Redshift table.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 3. Amazon Redshift: for teams that already live on AWS (part 2)
text:
- Writing new Iceberg tables from Redshift itself isn't stated on the Iceberg query page (checked Oct 2026), which says to create them in the Glue Data Catalog with a service such as Athena or Amazon EMR.
- AWS's docs (checked Oct 2026) say Redshift will no longer support Python user-defined functions after June 30, 2026, and AWS says it's enforcing this in phases. That date has passed, so check any you rely on.
- Zero-ETL tables need a primary key, data is replicated as-is with no transformation, and the destination database is read-only in Redshift, per its zero-ETL limits page (checked Oct 2026).
- Zero-ETL is capped at `50` integrations per Redshift target, per the same limits page (checked Oct 2026). The minimum latency is 15 minutes for DynamoDB and 1 hour for application sources.
- The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) gives a Provisioned example: four RG instances for 730 hours come to $8,884.60 a month on demand.
- It's an AWS service with no self-hosted option stated.

What users say: Praise on PeerSpot (June 2025). A reviewer wrote: "Amazon Redshift handles scalability automatically, so we do not need to scale up or down; it is all managed by Redshift". Complaint on PeerSpot (April 2024): "Amazon Redshift could work on reducing its costs, as they tend to increase significantly".

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 4. Microsoft Fabric: for Power BI and Azure estates
text:
At a glance: Microsoft's analytics platform, capacity-based, F SKUs billed per second, with an optional yearly reservation.

You buy Fabric as capacity. Per Microsoft's licensing page (checked Oct 2026), F capacities are billed per second with a one-minute minimum and no commitment. Microsoft's Fabric pricing page (checked Oct 2026) says a 1 or 3 year reservation can save about 41 percent against pay-as-you-go.

Its storage layer, OneLake, stores tables in Delta Parquet or Iceberg format, per Microsoft's OneLake overview. Fabric's engines store data in the open Delta Parquet format, and metadata virtualization bridges Iceberg to it.

What's good

- Free-licence users can view Power BI content when the capacity is `F64` or larger, per the licensing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Shortcuts reference data in OneLake, Azure Data Lake Storage, Azure Blob storage, Amazon S3 and S3-compatible stores, Iceberg-compatible sources and more, and unify data across clouds without copying it, per the OneLake overview.
- One OneLake per tenant keeps storage in a single place, per the OneLake overview. It supports Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 APIs and SDKs, so existing applications for that service can be used.
- The OneLake overview says you can write Iceberg tables directly to OneLake or create shortcuts to Iceberg tables stored elsewhere. Metadata virtualization lets Iceberg tables be read as Delta Lake tables inside Fabric, and Delta Lake tables be read by external Iceberg readers.
- The same overview says database mirroring continuously replicates data from an operational database into OneLake as Delta tables.
- Power BI reports can be built on top of OneLake with Direct Lake mode in the Analysis Services engine, per the OneLake overview.

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 4. Microsoft Fabric: for Power BI and Azure estates (part 2)
text:
- The dollar rates for each F SKU didn't load in the pricing page text we read (checked Oct 2026), so use the Azure calculator.
- On capacities smaller than `F64`, each person viewing Power BI content needs a Pro or Premium Per User licence, or an individual trial, per the licensing page (checked Oct 2026).
- The roughly 41 percent saving needs a yearly commitment, per the Fabric pricing page (checked Oct 2026). The per-second option has none, so the two suit different loads.
- Delta Lake to Iceberg conversion produces Iceberg `v2` metadata, per Microsoft's Iceberg conversion docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Iceberg `v3` source tables are only partially supported, equality deletes make conversion fail, and Parquet is the only underlying file format, per the same docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Source tables must have fewer than `5,000` commits for conversion to happen. Generating the metadata can take 5 seconds to 2 minutes, and conversion isn't supported on tenants or workspaces with private links enabled, per the same docs (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 5. ClickHouse: for fast scans of event data
text:
At a glance: open source under Apache 2.0, plus ClickHouse Cloud. compute is $0.2181 per unit-hour on Basic, $0.2985 on Scale and $0.3903 on Enterprise, plus $25.30 per TB of storage a month (N. Virginia), per its pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

ClickHouse describes itself in its docs as a "column-oriented SQL database management system (DBMS) for online analytical processing (OLAP)". OLAP just means questions that sum or count across many rows, like dashboards.

You can run the open source server yourself or pay for the cloud service. It meters compute and storage separately and offers $300 in credits for 30 days, per its pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

What's good

- You can self-host it: the intro docs say it is available as both open source software and a cloud offering, and the repository licence is Apache 2.0 (checked Oct 2026).
- Compute and storage are metered separately and scale to zero when idle in the cloud service. Compute is metered per minute in units of `8 GiB` of RAM and `2 vCPUs`, and storage is $25.30 per TB per month in the N. Virginia view of its pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- In N. Virginia, a compute unit costs $0.2181 an hour on Basic, $0.2985 on Scale and $0.3903 on Enterprise, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- The Iceberg table engine docs (checked Oct 2026) say ClickHouse reads tables that use position deletes, equality deletes (from version `25.8`) and deletion vectors.
- Its distinctive features page says "No locks are taken when new data is ingested."
- The Enterprise plan lists SAML single sign-on, private regions, transparent data encryption (CMEK), and "HIPAA and PCI compliance" on its pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 5. ClickHouse: for fast scans of event data (part 2)
text:
- Its Iceberg table engine page (checked Oct 2026) says it "is available but may have limitations", and that ClickHouse "wasn't originally designed to support tables with externally changing schemas".
- Deletion vector support is read-only, `ALTER TABLE ... DELETE` and `UPDATE` aren't supported on Iceberg `format-version 3` tables, and ClickHouse cannot create an Iceberg schema with `Bool`, `Decimal`, `FixedString`, `Int8`, `UInt8`, `Int16` or `UInt16` columns, per the same page (checked Oct 2026).
- The distinctive features page (checked Oct 2026) lists "No full-fledged transactions" and no ability to modify or delete inserted data "with a high rate and low latency" among the features that can be disadvantages.
- The same list (checked Oct 2026) says the sparse index makes ClickHouse "not so efficient for point queries retrieving single rows by their keys".
- Its ClickPipes docs (checked Oct 2026) describe change data capture (copying database changes) through ClickPipes for ClickHouse Cloud, and its MongoDB pipe is in public beta.
- Enterprise compute is $0.3903 per unit-hour against $0.2181 on Basic (N. Virginia), per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026), so the tier you need changes the bill.

What users say: Praise on Hacker News, "ClickHouse gets lazier and faster" thread (April 2025). One commenter wrote: "We migrated some analytics workloads from postgres to clickhouse last year, it's crazy how fast it is". Complaint on PeerSpot (December 2025): "Too many issues exist for beginners to set up ClickHouse".

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 6. MotherDuck: for small teams and embedded analytics
text:
At a glance: managed cloud service built on DuckDB. Lite is $0; Business is $250 per org per month plus usage, per its pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

DuckDB is an open source database that runs inside your own program, with no server to install. It's under the MIT (permissive open source) licence, per DuckDB's own page. MotherDuck sells a hosted version for sharing and scale.

Lite includes up to `3` internal active users, `10 GB` of storage and `10 hours` of Pulse compute per month, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026). Standard compute is $2.40 per hour billed per second, and storage is $0.04 per GB per month. Business adds up to `10` internal users and read-scaling replicas, and it offers a 7-day free trial.

What's good

- A free Lite plan, and Business at $250 per org per month, per its pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Hosted by MotherDuck, so there is no cluster for you to run. The pricing page says the plans fit "customer-facing analytics and internal data warehousing use cases".
- Pulse compute is $0.60 per compute unit hour, metered per query with a minimum of one compute unit second, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- You can pay MotherDuck directly or through an AWS Marketplace private offer on your AWS invoice, per the pricing page.
- Its Iceberg docs say you can attach an Iceberg REST catalog as a MotherDuck database. The catalog table shows read and write for Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Polaris, AWS Glue, Cloudflare R2, Databricks Unity Catalog and Snowflake Horizon (Unity and Horizon tables must be backed by external storage).

Where it falls short

- Lite caps internal users at `3`, and Business at `10`, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026). Enterprise pricing is custom.
- Iceberg updates, deletes and merges write small delete files (merge-on-read), per the Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026). Copy-on-write isn't supported, and a `DELETE` against a copy-on-write table fails.
- Per the Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026), `INSERT` and `UPDATE` fail on a table that declares a sort order. Reading from REST catalogs is limited to S3, S3-compatible storage including Cloudflare R2, S3 Tables and GCS backends.
- The larger Jumbo, Mega and Giga instances cost $4.80, $12.00 and $24.00 per hour, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 7. Dremio: for an Iceberg lakehouse
text:
At a glance: Dremio Cloud at $0.20 per Dremio Compute Unit (DCU), on AWS, with Azure listed as coming soon. Dremio Enterprise is by quote, per its pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

Dremio sells a lakehouse query platform. Its pricing page (checked Oct 2026) lists Apache Iceberg as an open source technology and an Iceberg lakehouse use case. Enterprise can be self-managed on cloud, Kubernetes or on-premises, and the page also lists a free Community Edition query engine for local machines or servers.

The pricing page also says "Query your data in minutes, no manual configuration required". That is Dremio's claim.

Ownership just changed. SAP (the business software company) lists its completed acquisition of Dremio on its news site, dated July 6, 2026. The Dremio pricing page banner reads "Dremio is now part of SAP". The page we read doesn't say what happens to Dremio Cloud's pricing or products.

What's good

- Lists an Iceberg lakehouse as a use case on its pricing page.
- Its Iceberg docs say connected sources use default Iceberg catalogs that support both read and write commands, and the built-in Iceberg catalog is based on Apache Polaris (incubating).
- Its data sources docs list lakehouse catalogs (including AWS Glue, Hive, Iceberg REST, Nessie and Unity Catalog), object storage (Amazon S3, Azure Storage, Google Cloud Storage, HDFS and NAS) and databases such as MongoDB, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQL Server.
- A published cloud rate of $0.20 per DCU, with a 30-day trial that includes $400 in credits and needs no credit card, per the pricing page FAQ (checked Oct 2026).
- A self-managed Enterprise option, and a free Community Edition query engine, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

Where it falls short

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 7. Dremio: for an Iceberg lakehouse (part 2)
text:
- The Enterprise price is not published ("Contact Sales") on its pricing page (checked Oct 2026), so you can't budget for it from the page.
- The cloud service is on AWS today, with Azure only listed as coming soon, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- On Iceberg, the docs (checked Oct 2026) say only Parquet file formats are currently supported and Amazon DynamoDB and JDBC catalogs are not supported. They also say Dremio does not support reading global equality deletes for Iceberg `v2` tables in one described case, and the page doesn't mention Iceberg `v3`.
- Relational sources must use a collation equivalent to `LATIN1_GENERAL_BIN2`, and case-sensitive source file and table names are not supported, per its data sources docs (checked Oct 2026).
- The SAP deal is new, and the plans after it aren't stated on the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 8. Amazon Athena: for occasional queries on files in S3
text:
At a glance: serverless SQL on files in Amazon S3, $5 per TB scanned (US East Ohio example), `10 MB` minimum per query. Both figures are per its pricing page and the AWS price list for US East (Ohio) (checked Oct 2026).

Athena is a query service. It reads files in S3 and bills for the data each query scans.

AWS's own example on the pricing page (checked Oct 2026) shows a 3 TB scan costing $15 on text files. Converted to compressed Parquet (a compact column file format), the same one-column query costs $1.25. For steady load it also sells Capacity Reservations, and its example uses $0.30 per Data Processing Unit (DPU) hour.

What's good

- Serverless per AWS, so there is no server to run. You can use SQL or Apache Spark, and the default bill follows the data each query scans.
- It queries data directly in Amazon S3, with no additional storage charges for querying, per the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).
- Its Iceberg docs say it can read, time travel, write and run DDL queries on Iceberg tables, and engine version `3` supports the Parquet, ORC and Avro file formats.
- Converting to Parquet cuts the scan bill sharply, per AWS's pricing example (checked Oct 2026).
- Spark use is billed per DPU-hour: AWS's pricing example (checked Oct 2026) prices 3.0 DPU-hours at $0.35 each, or $1.05.
- AWS's price list (checked Oct 2026) shows DDL, failed queries and statements that create or load partitions as free query types.

Where it falls short

- Its Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026) say only tables created against the AWS Glue catalog are supported, and that Athena operates on Iceberg `v2` tables only.
- Table definition commands (DDL) are not supported on Iceberg tables registered with Lake Formation, and timestamps are limited to millisecond precision, per the same docs (checked Oct 2026).
- Athena supports AWS Glue optimistic locking only, per the Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026). Using it to modify an Iceberg table with any other lock implementation can cause data loss and break transactions.
- It doesn't support `ALTER TABLE SET LOCATION` on Iceberg tables or partitioning them by nested fields, per the Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026).
- The bill follows bytes scanned, with a `10 MB` minimum per query per the AWS price list (checked Oct 2026), so large text files are the costly case, as AWS's own 3 TB example shows.

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > The 8 best Snowflake alternatives > 8. Amazon Athena: for occasional queries on files in S3 (part 2)
text: What users say: Praise on Hacker News, "Apache iceberg the Hadoop of the modern-data-stack?" thread (March 2025): "I never found Athena expensive. Compared to employment cost it will be miniscule". Complaint on PeerSpot (2025 to 2026): "Since the pricing is $5 per TB, large queries on big datasets can result in substantial bills".

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > Other Snowflake competitors worth knowing
text: - Trino is an open source query engine (Apache 2.0 repository licence). Its docs say it's not a replacement for databases such as MySQL or PostgreSQL, and that it wasn't designed for online transaction processing, the many small writes an app makes. Its Iceberg connector docs (checked Oct 2026) say it supports table versions `v1` and `v2`, with `v3` experimental.

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > Billing units side by side
text:
Snowflake, Databricks and Redshift Serverless meter compute over time, BigQuery on-demand and Athena meter data scanned, and Fabric and BigQuery slots reserve capacity. A workload with many small queries behaves very differently under each, so price your own query log.

Our summary of the vendor pricing pages cited above (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > Apache Iceberg and the cost of leaving
text:
Apache Iceberg is an open table format: a set of metadata files that tells any engine which Parquet files make up a table. If your tables sit in your own bucket in Iceberg format, several engines can read them. Trying a competitor gets cheaper because you don't copy the data first.

Snowflake's Iceberg docs (checked Oct 2026) say it supports Iceberg tables with Parquet files and externally managed writes on `v2` or `v3` of the spec. Its release notes list partition evolution for Iceberg tables as generally available on September 18, 2026. When the account and the storage sit in different regions or clouds, egress charges can apply.

Most options above document Iceberg support, but the depth varies.

Databricks, BigQuery and Fabric document managed or bridged tables. Redshift and Athena lean on the Glue catalog, and ClickHouse warns about limits. Test your exact table, catalog and engine pair before you promise anyone a quick move.

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > Where Snowflake fits
text:
Choose Snowflake if you need one of these, per its own docs.

- Sharing data between accounts. Snowflake's data sharing docs say that with Secure Data Sharing, no actual data is copied or transferred between accounts.
- AI functions inside the warehouse. Its Cortex AI functions offer models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral AI, DeepSeek and xAI, and its Cortex docs say the models are deployed within the Snowflake Service perimeter.
- Three clouds. It lists AWS, Azure and Google Cloud in its Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026). BigQuery, Redshift and Fabric each come from one cloud owner.

On cost, Select's run (a single third party's test; Select sells cost tools for Snowflake and Databricks) used 22 queries on a standard benchmark data set at scale factor `1000`. At $2 per credit, Snowflake was 34 percent faster and 17 percent cheaper than Databricks at $0.70 per DBU. At $3 per credit, Databricks was 20 percent cheaper in that same sequential test, per Select, April 10, 2026. The result followed the credit price.

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > What usually needs rework when you move
text:
The table data is the easy part. The work sits in the Snowflake-specific code and settings on top.

- Semi-structured columns. Snowflake's `VARIANT` type stores a value of any other type, including objects and arrays, up to `128 MB` uncompressed, per its data types docs (checked Oct 2026). Every target has its own JSON or struct type, so list the queries that read `VARIANT` columns first.
- SQL dialect. Databricks tells migrating teams to convert SQL "from dialects such as T-SQL, Snowflake, and Oracle" with its agentic code converter, per its migration docs. Treat any converter output as a first draft.
- History and recovery. Snowflake keeps one day of Time Travel by default, and Enterprise can raise it up to `90 days` on permanent tables, per its docs (checked Oct 2026). Check what each target offers for recovering a dropped table.
- Scheduling and permissions. We did not find a vendor page that maps these across tools, so plan a manual review. We found no standard migration time either, so we won't quote one.

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > What to test before you switch
text:
- Run your real queries. Take a week of your actual query log and price it in each vendor's unit.
- Check your SQL. Dialects differ, so run your ten most important queries and compare the results.
- Test Iceberg on your own tables. Use your catalog and your engine, and try an update and a delete as well as a read.
- Read the exit costs. Look for egress fees between regions or clouds, and for minimum commitments.
- Run both side by side for one billing cycle. Compare the invoices before you cancel anything.

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > Where OLake Go fits
text:
OLake Go is an open-source tool (Apache 2.0) that copies data from databases such as Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, SQL Server, Oracle and Db2 into Apache Iceberg tables or Parquet files on storage you control. You run it yourself, and the quickstart shows how.

Change data capture covers Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB, MongoDB and SQL Server. Snowflake has two routes. From v0.11.0, OLake Go can write Iceberg tables into a Snowflake database through the Snowflake Horizon Catalog, using a programmatic access token, key-pair authentication or External OAuth. Or OLake Go writes to another catalog, such as AWS Glue, and Snowflake reads those tables from an external catalog as read-only. Our compatibility page also lists Databricks, BigQuery, Redshift, Athena, Trino and Dremio among the engines that query the tables OLake Go writes. OLake Go's destinations are Iceberg and Parquet.

title: Compare: Snowflake Alternatives and Competitors in 2026 | OLake > FAQs
text:
Q1. Who are Snowflake's biggest competitors?

The large platforms covered above are Databricks, Google BigQuery, Amazon Redshift and Microsoft Fabric. We didn't measure market share, so we won't rank them. Pick by your cloud, your team's skills and how you'd like to be billed.

Q2. Is there a cheaper alternative to Snowflake?

It depends on your workload and your credit price. In Select's April 2026 sequential test, Snowflake was cheaper at $2 per credit and Databricks at $3 per credit. Price your own queries first.

Q3. What is an open-source alternative to Snowflake?

ClickHouse and Trino use the Apache 2.0 licence, and DuckDB uses the MIT licence (checked Oct 2026). They cover narrower jobs than a full warehouse, so check them against your workload.

Q4. Can Apache Iceberg help me avoid lock-in?

Partly. Several engines document how to read Iceberg tables in your own storage, which lowers the cost of switching, but support depth differs and cross-region reads can add egress fees.

Q5. Why can't I compare Snowflake and Databricks prices directly?

Because the units don't match. Snowflake bills credits, which depend on warehouse size, edition and region. Databricks bills DBUs, which depend on the compute type, the plan and the cloud.

Q6. What is hardest to move off Snowflake?

Usually the code around the data. Semi-structured JSON columns, Snowflake-specific SQL and recovery settings such as Time Travel need rework on any target.

Q7. How do I get my database data into a warehouse like these?

You need a pipeline tool that copies tables or changes from your databases. Our guides to best data pipeline tools and best data replication tools compare the main options and which ones write Apache Iceberg. OLake Go is one: it writes Iceberg tables or Parquet files that engines such as Databricks, BigQuery and Redshift can query, per our compatibility page. For Snowflake it can write Iceberg tables through the Snowflake Horizon Catalog from v0.11.0, and Snowflake reads tables in other catalogs as read-only.

title: Compare: Best ETL Tools for Snowflake: 10 Options, Real Costs | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

The best ETL (extract, transform, load) tool for Snowflake depends on where your data starts. Every load sends you two bills, one from the tool vendor and one from Snowflake for the compute the load uses. If your data already lands as files or rows, Snowflake's own loading features (Snowpipe, Snowpipe Streaming) add no second vendor fee, so price them first.

For lots of SaaS apps, look at Fivetran, Hevo or Airbyte.

For live database changes, look at Estuary, Fivetran or Snowflake's Openflow. For open-source database replication into Iceberg tables in Snowflake, look at OLake Go.

For the transform step, think dbt, Matillion or dynamic tables.

- Two bills. The tool vendor bills by rows, events, credits or gigabytes. Then Snowflake bills you separately for the warehouse time or loading service the data uses.
- Freshness costs real money on the Snowflake side. In our worked example below, syncing every 5 minutes uses 12 times the warehouse credits of syncing every hour. Same tool, same data.
- Snowflake already loads data.`COPY INTO` (a command that loads files from cloud storage), Snowpipe, Snowpipe Streaming, a Kafka connector and Openflow are all built in, so a third-party tool is optional.
- Transform tools don't load data. dbt and Snowflake dynamic tables transform data that is already in Snowflake.
- For Iceberg, check early. Several options below document Iceberg tables that Snowflake reads or hosts, and some are Beta, Preview or Early Access. OLake Go (v0.11.0+) creates them in Snowflake through the Horizon Catalog.

Every price below comes from the vendor's own page, checked in October 2026 and quoted with the date. Plans change often, so double-check before you decide.

Where a vendor does not publish a price, we say "not published".

This is the third guide in our series, after AWS ETL tools and Azure ETL tools.

title: Compare: Best ETL Tools for Snowflake: 10 Options, Real Costs | OLake > How we picked these ten
text:
The rules were simple. Each tool had to load data into Snowflake or transform it there, and have a public pricing or documentation page.

Vendor facts come from each vendor's own pricing and documentation pages. We did not run the other tools.

The two user opinions come from PeerSpot reviews of dbt, opened in October 2026 and quoted word for word with a month.

The ten entries are grouped by what they do, and the order inside a group means nothing.

title: Compare: Best ETL Tools for Snowflake: 10 Options, Real Costs | OLake > ETL, ELT and Snowflake, in plain words
text:
ETL means extract, transform, load: copy data out of a source, reshape it, then store it. ELT (extract, load, transform) flips the last two steps, so the raw data lands first and gets reshaped inside the warehouse with SQL (the standard database query language).

Snowflake can run that reshaping itself, so ELT is a common fit. Most tools below are loaders (the "E" and "L"), and a smaller group does the "T" inside Snowflake. A full pipeline is usually one tool from each group, or one tool that does both.

For a longer walk-through, see our ETL pipelines guide.
