title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

Fivetran is a paid, managed service that copies data from apps, databases, files and event streams into a data warehouse or data lake, then keeps that copy fresh. You pick a source, a destination and a schedule, and Fivetran runs the rest. Billing is by monthly active rows (MAR), meaning the distinct rows synced in a calendar month.

Teams that want hands-off pipelines (Fivetran's own pitch) are the likeliest fit. The bill follows usage, so you cannot know it until you estimate your changed rows. A fixed bill, self-hosting or open source code points elsewhere, and its lake output comes with rules to check first.

- Fivetran is an ELT service. ELT means extract, load, then transform: it drops raw data into your destination, and you reshape it there.
- A new connection copies everything once (the initial sync). After that, it moves only the changes, on a schedule.
- Pricing is per connection, by monthly active rows (MAR). The pricing page prints no per-row rate, but the Service Consumption Table does (checked Oct 2026).
- The bill is usage-based, so it is hard to predict: it depends on how many distinct rows change in each connection each month. Estimate that before you sign.
- For a lake, Fivetran writes and maintains the Iceberg tables. Its catalog docs say not to change them from other tools, and its lake docs list gaps worth testing: position deletes, upkeep and transformations.

Every Fivetran fact below comes from Fivetran's own pages, read between October 1 and October 7, 2026, with the page linked beside the claim. The rows for other tools carry their own sources.

Where a number isn't published, we say "not published". We did not run Fivetran, so this is a read of its documents, not a hands-on test. Claims about ease, speed or reliability are Fivetran's claims, and we did not test them.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > What is Fivetran?
text:
Fivetran describes its connectors as pre-built, and says they sync data from applications, databases, event streams and files to a data warehouse or data lake. A connector is a ready-made piece of software for one kind of source, such as a customer relationship management (CRM) tool like Salesforce, or a database like PostgreSQL. The pricing page calls them "fully managed". Taken at its word, that means Fivetran runs them, not you.

Two words will come up again and again. A source is where your data starts, such as a database or a business app. The destination is where Fivetran puts the copy, such as a data warehouse or a lake on cloud storage.

Per its transformations docs, Fivetran uses the extract, load, transform (ELT) model, so raw data stays available alongside transformed data. Fivetran loads the raw tables into a destination schema (a named folder inside the destination), and the transformations run in your destination.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > How a Fivetran sync works
text:
A sync is one run that moves data from a source to a destination. Fivetran's sync overview gives the order of events, and it's short.

- Initial sync. You have to run a historical sync before a connection is usable. The first one is the initial sync, and it copies all the data from the tables you selected.
- Incremental sync. Once the first run succeeds, the connection switches to incremental mode. Only data that was modified or added gets extracted, processed and loaded on schedule.
- Re-sync. Found a data integrity error? You can run a historical sync again. That's called a re-sync.

Fivetran uses cursors, markers of what it has already processed, so the next run can resume from that point. Its database docs say it also records the time of each row's last sync in a column called `_fivetran_synced`.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > How a Fivetran sync works > How often does it sync?
text:
Per the sync overview page (checked Oct 2026), you can pick a fixed interval or manual runs through its API. A cron schedule, a standard way to write timed schedules, is for Enterprise and Business Critical plans only. Every six hours is the default, and you can't schedule syncs less often than once every 24 hours.

Database connectors skip that default. Per the database connector docs, they sync new and changed data every 15 minutes. The pricing page (checked Oct 2026), covered below, lists 15-minute syncs on Standard and 1-minute syncs on Enterprise.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > How a Fivetran sync works > How does it catch database changes?
text:
So how does it spot changes in a database?

Fivetran uses the database's own change data capture (CDC) feature or a method of its own, depending on the database. CDC means reading the log where a database writes down every change, so you copy only what changed.

The database docs go database by database. The native routes are the binary log (MySQL's record of changes) for MySQL and MariaDB, logical replication (PostgreSQL's built-in way to stream changes) for PostgreSQL, and change streams (MongoDB's feed of changes) for MongoDB. For SQL Server, they are its Change Data Capture or Change Tracking features.

Teleport Sync is a separate, Fivetran-made method that doesn't read the change log. The database docs (checked Oct 2026) recommend it when you can't or don't want to give Fivetran access to your change logs. Their stated limit: if you update large parts of a table between syncs, Teleport Sync may be unable to find the changes, and the connection re-syncs the entire table.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > How a Fivetran sync works > A documented failure: when the change log runs out
text:
The database docs (checked Oct 2026) say where this breaks. Change logs expire, either by time or when the storage set aside for them fills up. If Fivetran falls behind for longer than the log is kept, the progress point is gone.

Fivetran's database docs say: "Expired change logs require a full source re-sync, because we cannot perform our usual incremental syncs without them" (checked Oct 2026). For SQL databases, that page names schema changes in the source as the most common trigger for a full table re-sync. On a big table, plan for the extra load and the extra wait.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > How a Fivetran sync works > A worked example: one orders table
text:
Sometimes a tiny example beats a page of docs. The tables below are an illustration, not a test run: we built them from the columns Fivetran documents, and we did not run Fivetran.

Per Fivetran's PostgreSQL connector docs, with logical replication a `DELETE` in the source table updates the destination row with `_fivetran_deleted = TRUE`. The database docs say `_fivetran_synced` records when each row last synced.

Source `orders` table at the first sync (T0), then at the next sync (T1):

| Time | id | status |
| T0 | 1 | new |
| T0 | 2 | new |
| T0 | 3 | new |
| T1 | 1 | new |
| T1 | 2 | shipped |
| T1 | 3 | (deleted in the source) |
| T1 | 4 | new (inserted after T0) |

Destination `orders` table after the T1 sync:

| id | status | _fivetran_deleted | _fivetran_synced |
| 1 | new | false | T0 |
| 2 | shipped | false | T1 |
| 3 | new | true | T1 |
| 4 | new | false | T1 |

Order 3 is still in the destination. It's just flagged.

So your queries have to filter it out. `SELECT count(*) FROM orders` returns 4 here, and adding `WHERE _fivetran_deleted = false` returns 3, which matches the source. Skip the filter and deleted orders show up in your reports.

Now the billing angle. Fivetran's usage-based pricing docs say a row is counted once per month, even if it syncs many times. And deletes count toward paid MAR like any changed row, from January 1, 2026 on pay-as-you-go plans and at renewal on annual contracts signed after March 1, 2025 (checked Oct 2026).

If the T1 changes all land in the same month after the initial sync, rows 2, 3 and 4 count as active that month, so that is 3 MAR. Row 1 doesn't count, because it never changed.

Now picture the log window running out between T0 and T1. The changes could not be read, and per the database docs a full source re-sync is then needed. So plan for a full re-copy.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Fivetran connectors, by type
text:
How big is the catalog? Fivetran's connector directory says it moves data from 750+ sources and activates back into 200+ destinations. That 200+ figure counts activation targets, such as CRMs and marketing tools (see Activations below), not warehouses or lakes.

The connectors docs title and the pricing page both say 700+ (checked Oct 2026), so quote the page you used.

The connectors docs sort connectors into six groups: Applications, Databases, Events, Files, Functions and Logs. Database connectors read changes from the source database, so they need setup on your side, such as log retention and permissions.

Source missing from the list? The docs describe a Connector SDK, which lets you write a custom connector in Python and run it on Fivetran's infrastructure. They also list a By Request Program for connectors not yet in the catalog.

High-Volume Agent (HVA) connectors are a database group of their own. Fivetran's HVA docs list Db2 for i, Oracle, SQL Server and SAP (business software). The pricing page lists "enterprise database connectors" from the Enterprise plan up (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Transformations and the dbt merger
text:
Raw tables are rarely what your analysts want to query. Fivetran's transformations page lists two options. One is pre-built data models that turn raw tables into analytics-ready ones, and the other is a Fivetran-hosted dbt integration, plus dbt Cloud and Coalesce connections.

(dbt, in case you're new to it, is a popular tool for writing SQL transformations.)

All these jobs run in your destination. Up to 5,000 model runs a month are free. One limit to flag: the same page (checked Oct 2026) says "Fivetran-hosted Transformations for dbt do not support Managed Data Lake Service destinations", a point we return to below.

On June 1, 2026, Fivetran announced the completion of its merger with dbt Labs. It was an all-stock deal first announced on October 13, 2025, and the combined company initially operates as Fivetran + dbt Labs.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Activations: sending data back out
text:
Most of this post is about data flowing in. Activations flips it: it sends data from the warehouse back out into business tools, such as a CRM. This is often called reverse ETL (ETL means extract, transform, load).

Fivetran's pricing page lists 200+ managed activation destinations (checked Oct 2026). Activations bill on monthly active rows too, with their own Free-plan allowance.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Managed Data Lake Service and Apache Iceberg
text:
Not everyone wants a warehouse. With Managed Data Lake Service, Fivetran writes your data to cloud storage you own: Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage or Google Cloud Storage. It writes Parquet files there and manages the table metadata and upkeep.

Apache Iceberg is an open table format. The short version: it lets several query engines read the same files as ordinary tables.

On the format, the lake docs say Fivetran always creates Iceberg metadata for these tables, and can optionally add Delta Lake metadata. The default catalog (the service that tracks your tables) is the Fivetran Catalog, built on Apache Polaris. Per the catalog docs, you can also connect AWS Glue and BigLake metastore for Iceberg tables, and Databricks Unity Catalog and OneLake for Delta Lake metadata.

The lake docs list 11 example query engines, including Amazon Athena, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks and DuckDB. So, per its docs, reading the tables from other tools is the intended use.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Managed Data Lake Service and Apache Iceberg > What to check before you pick the lake destination
text:
Fivetran says it writes the files, keeps the catalog and runs table upkeep, so you don't build that yourself. We did not test how well it does this. The trade is control: you own the storage bucket, but Fivetran manages the tables in it.

Fivetran's catalog docs (checked Oct 2026) are direct: "Do not modify these tables manually or by using any external catalog, as doing so may lead to data integrity issues." Read-only credentials are the default. The same page also offers write credentials. Its warning: "Modifying Fivetran-delivered tables directly can corrupt the tables and disrupt downstream workflows." So ask what your other tools can still do with these tables, using the documented limits below.

| Topic | What the docs state | What to ask Fivetran |
| Deletes | "Fivetran does not support position deletes for Iceberg tables." The docs recommend avoiding any query that generates them ( lake docs (checked Oct 2026)). Position deletes are a way to record removed rows without rewriting files | Which queries in my engine create position deletes, and what happens to a source delete in the lake table? |
| Other tools | Tables should not be changed from external catalogs, though Fivetran Catalog offers write credentials with a warning that direct changes can corrupt the tables, and the docs recommend against deleting metadata files ( catalog docs (checked Oct 2026)) | Can my tools write to these tables, or only read? |
| Table upkeep | Table snapshots past the retention period are deleted, and at least the last 2 are kept (a snapshot is a saved table version). Orphan files, which no table points to, are moved on the second and fourth Saturdays of each month. The page does not mention compaction ( lake docs (checked Oct 2026)) | Is compaction, which merges many small files into fewer large ones, done at all, and how often? |
| Transformations | Fivetran-hosted dbt transformations do not support these destinations. The lake docs list Quickstart data models (Beta) and dbt projects on Lake Compute, a DuckDB-based engine ( transformations page and lake docs (checked Oct 2026)) | Which of these will run on my tables, and is Quickstart out of beta? |

A missing upkeep task in the docs isn't proof the service lacks it. So treat the right-hand column as questions to put to Fivetran in a trial, using your own sync interval.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Deployment, security and compliance
text:
Where does your data actually get processed?

The deployment models page describes two options. With SaaS, "data processing is handled entirely within the Fivetran cloud". Hybrid is for teams that "need to keep their data local for security or compliance reasons but still want to benefit from Fivetran managed service".

The pricing page lists hybrid deployment as an Enterprise plan feature (checked Oct 2026). We found no published source licence for the core service.

For a security questionnaire, Fivetran's security page lists System and Organization Controls (SOC) 1 and 2, plus International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 27001. It also lists a commitment to GDPR (EU privacy law) and CCPA (California privacy law). A business associate agreement signed by Fivetran covers HIPAA (US health privacy law).

The security page (checked Oct 2026) says Health Information Trust Alliance (HITRUST) certification, a healthcare security framework, comes with the Business Critical plan.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > What does Fivetran cost?
text:
Fivetran counts MAR per connection. That one detail drives the examples below.

A row counts once in a month however many times it changes. Some re-syncs are free, but re-synced rows that changed count toward paid MAR, per the usage-based pricing docs.

The pricing page lists four plans: Free, Standard, Enterprise and Business Critical (checked Oct 2026).

| Plan | What the pricing page lists | List rate for the first million MAR |
| Free | Up to 500,000 MAR for connections, 3,500 MAR for activations, 5,000 model runs | $0 |
| Standard | 15-minute syncs, 700+ connectors, unlimited users, dbt Core integration | $495 per million, plus a $5 base |
| Enterprise | Adds 1-minute syncs, enterprise database connectors, hybrid deployment | $661.67 per million, plus a $5 base |
| Business Critical | Adds customer-managed keys, PCI DSS Level 1, private networking | $1,061.67 per million, plus a $5 base |

Sources: plans and features from the pricing page, rates from the Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026).

One thing to flag: Fivetran publishes no single monthly price, and your bill follows usage. The pricing page prints no per-row rate for the paid plans, but Fivetran's Service Consumption Table does (checked Oct 2026), in version 10, effective February 1, 2026.

Those are list prices, before any annual-contract discount.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > What does Fivetran cost? > How a bill is worked out
text:
The table prints one formula, and it's simple enough. Monthly spend for a connection is the base spend, plus your MAR above the threshold, times the incremental spend per million MAR. Partial millions are prorated, and each connection is priced on its own curve.

For one Standard connection, the tiers in the Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026) are:

- Up to 1 million MAR: $5 base, plus $495 per million.
- From 1 million MAR: $500 base, plus $170 per extra million.
- From 4 million MAR: $1,010 base, plus $58 per extra million.
- From 16 million MAR: $19.70 per extra million.

Let's put numbers on it. Here are three Standard-plan examples, with the arithmetic ours, from the rates above. They are illustrations at list price, not quotes.

| One connection, one month | Calculation | List price |
| 100,000 MAR | $5 + 0.1 x $495 | $54.50 |
| 1 million MAR | $5 + 1 x $495 | $500 |
| 5 million MAR | $1,010 + 1 x $58 | $1,068 |

Sources: Fivetran Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026), version 10, with the arithmetic ours.

The orders table above is far too small to bill like this, so take a separate, made-up workload. One connection has 109,000 distinct rows inserted, updated or deleted in a month, with no discount and no free re-syncs involved.

On Standard that is $5 + 0.109 x $495, or about $59 (the exact figure is $58.955). On Enterprise, at $661.67 per million, it is $5 + 0.109 x $661.67, or about $77.

Rates fall as volume grows, so cost per row drops with size. But each connection has its own curve, and you can't pool MAR across connections for a better rate.

Now two more made-up setups with the same 4 million changed rows in total. One connection costs $1,010. Four connections with 1 million MAR each cost 4 x $500, or $2,000.

There's more fine print: annual contracts, pay-as-you-go and the 2025 and 2026 billing changes each have dated rules.

Your warehouse also sends its own invoice. Fivetran's destination docs say your provider may charge for the compute used when Fivetran loads data, and that sync frequency and data volume drive that cost.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Limits to know before you buy
text:
- The bill depends on your change rates. The rates are published, but the meter counts distinct rows changed, per connection, so you need to know those rates first. The pricing page offers a pricing estimator, which we did not use, and your order form is what binds you.
- Re-copies cost time. For SQL databases, the database docs name schema changes as the most common trigger for an automatic full table re-sync. An expired change log means a full source re-sync.
- No published source licence or self-run version. We found no published source licence. Even the Hybrid model is described as a Fivetran managed service on its deployment models page (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Who Fivetran suits, and who should look elsewhere
text:
So, should you pick it?

Fivetran is a reasonable choice when you have many SaaS and database sources and want someone else to run the connectors, and you have a budget for usage-based billing. That bill can swing with your change rates. Its pages also list things some other tools do not: the compliance items on its security page, the Oracle and SAP connectors, or one vendor for loading, dbt and reverse ETL. We did not audit those claims.

Look elsewhere if you need a fixed monthly bill, want open source code, or need a destination Fivetran doesn't list. For a lake, check the write-credential limits first if your other tools need to modify the tables Fivetran manages. OLake Go writes Iceberg or Parquet to storage you choose, and several query engines read its tables (see the engine compatibility page).

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Who Fivetran suits, and who should look elsewhere > Test it against your own needs
text:
A trial or a quote call is the best check. Put these questions to Fivetran, and write down the answers.

- Capture method. Which method does it use for each of your databases, and what must you switch on at the source?
- Recovery time. How long would a full re-sync of your largest table take, and what does it do to your source database?
- Freshness. A sync interval isn't a delivery promise, so ask how Fivetran measures the gap between a source change and a row you can query. The pricing page ties 1-minute syncs to Enterprise (checked Oct 2026).
- Usage quote. Work out monthly active rows per connection from your own change rates, price them with the Service Consumption Table, and ask Fivetran to check the result.
- Lake rules. Run the lake table above past your query engine and transformation tool.
- Support. Which response times apply to your plan? We did not test support.
- Where it runs. Do rules force your data to stay in your network? Then Hybrid deployment is the one to look at.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Who Fivetran suits, and who should look elsewhere > Fivetran against five other options
text:
Maybe Fivetran isn't your tool. The table sets it beside five common options on one axis, how each bills, using each vendor's own pricing page. For a fuller comparison, see the head-to-head posts below.

| Option | How it bills | Source |
| Airbyte | Core is self-managed and free to self-host under the Elastic License 2.0 (you pay for servers and staff). Cloud bills in credits | airbyte.com/pricing , licence FAQ (checked Oct 2026) |
| Hevo | Events: each record inserted, updated or deleted in the destination is 1 event. Free plan up to 1 million events a month | hevodata.com/pricing (checked Oct 2026) |
| OLake Go | No licence fee: open source under Apache 2.0. You pay for your own servers and storage | github.com/datazip-inc/olake (checked Oct 2026) |
| Matillion | Credits by task hour, not rows. Dollar prices not published | matillion.com/pricing (checked Oct 2026) |
| Estuary Flow | $0.50 per GB moved, plus connector instances | estuary.dev/pricing (checked Oct 2026) |

Debezium, an open source change data capture project under the Apache License 2.0, has no vendor price, and the real cost is the servers and staff you run it with, per its license page (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Conclusion
text:
By its own description, Fivetran is a managed copy service, with dbt, reverse ETL and an Iceberg lake destination around it. Before you sign, run the checklist above against your largest database table and your lake tools. Then get one quote from another option, so you have a price to compare.

Want to check what you picked up? Try this quick quiz.

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > Conclusion > Test your Fivetran basics
text:
Question 1 of 5

In plain words, what does Fivetran do for you?

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > FAQs
text:
Q1. What is Fivetran in simple words?

Per Fivetran's connectors docs, it is a managed service that copies data from apps, databases, files and event streams into a data warehouse or lake, and keeps it current. You choose a source and a destination, and Fivetran runs the connector. The transformations then run in your destination, using pre-built data models or dbt.

Q2. Is Fivetran an ETL or an ELT tool?

ELT. Fivetran's transformations docs say it uses the ELT model, so your raw data is always available alongside your transformed data.

Q3. Is Fivetran free?

Partly. There's a Free plan, and per Fivetran's pricing page (checked Oct 2026) it covers up to 500,000 monthly active rows for connections, 3,500 for activations and 5,000 model runs a month. Paid plans bill on usage, with rates in the Service Consumption Table (checked Oct 2026), for example $495 per million MAR on Standard for the first million. Because the bill follows monthly active rows, estimate yours before you sign.

Q4. How many connectors does Fivetran have?

The connector directory says 750+ sources, and the connectors docs and pricing page say 700+ (checked Oct 2026). Quote the page you used. The 200+ destinations in the directory are activation targets, not warehouses or lakes.

Q5. Does Fivetran support change data capture?

Per its database docs, yes, for many databases. They list native routes such as the MySQL binary log, PostgreSQL logical replication, MongoDB change streams and SQL Server Change Data Capture, plus its own Teleport Sync. Its High-Volume Agent connectors cover Db2 for i, Oracle, SQL Server and SAP.

Q6. Did Fivetran merge with dbt Labs?

Yes. Fivetran announced the completion of the merger on June 1, 2026, and the combined company initially operates as Fivetran + dbt Labs. The all-stock deal was first announced on October 13, 2025.

Q7. Is Fivetran open source?

We found no published source licence for the core platform, so we cannot call it open source. Hybrid deployment lets data processing stay in your own network, but the deployment models page (checked Oct 2026) describes it as a Fivetran managed service.

Q8. Can Fivetran write Apache Iceberg tables?

title: Compare: What Is Fivetran? How It Works, Cost and Fit (2026) | OLake > FAQs (part 2)
text:
Yes, through Managed Data Lake Service on Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage or Google Cloud Storage. Fivetran always creates Iceberg metadata for these tables. The lake docs say it does not support Iceberg position deletes, and the catalog docs warn that modifying the tables directly can corrupt them. The lake page does not mention compaction, so ask Fivetran about it (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake
text:
Key takeaways

Matillion is a paid platform that loads your data into a cloud data warehouse, reshapes it with SQL that runs inside the warehouse, and schedules the whole job.

The catch is that you pay in credits, not dollars. Matillion publishes the credit rules, but its pricing page (checked Oct 2026) shows no price per credit and no dollar price for any plan. It does offer a 14-day trial with 500 free credits (checked Oct 2026).

Matillion's pages position it for teams that build and transform pipelines in a warehouse. Want open source code, a public price list or Apache Iceberg tables as output? Look elsewhere.

- Matillion does three jobs on one platform: it loads data, transforms it, and schedules the work. The transforms run as SQL inside your warehouse, which is called push-down.
- "Matillion" is now a family of products, not one thing. Maia Foundation is the current platform (formerly Data Productivity Cloud). Matillion ETL is an older product you run in your own cloud account. Each has its own credit meter.
- Maia Foundation uses credits per task hour (checked Oct 2026): 1 for orchestration pipelines (which load data), 3 for transformation pipelines, and 1 or 2 for streaming change capture. Extra developers cost 70 credits a month each.
- Matillion ETL uses 1 credit per virtual core hour (checked Oct 2026) while the software is switched on, plus 50 credits a month per extra active user.
- Maia's docs say new accounts get a 14-day free trial with 500 credits (checked Oct 2026). What you won't find on the pricing page (checked Oct 2026): any dollar price or the price of a credit. The connector page gives no connector count either.
- Budgets and alerts only warn. Maia's docs say budgets "do not restrict or block usage" (checked Oct 2026), so a runaway job can overspend a credit pack.

Every fact below comes from Matillion's own pages, with the page linked beside the claim. Prices, plans and limits end with a "(checked Oct 2026)" note.

When Matillion doesn't publish a number, we say "not published". We did not run Matillion. This is a careful read of its documents, not a hands-on test.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > What is Matillion?
text:
Matillion describes itself as born in Manchester, with headquarters in Denver and Manchester. Its about page lists Matthew Scullion as a founder and says "Empowering data teams since 2011".

These days the lead message is Maia. The home page calls Matillion "the company behind Maia, the agentic data team", and the Maia docs call Maia "the AI Data Automation platform by Matillion".

The short version: Matillion is software that moves data into a cloud data warehouse and gets it ready for analysis. Snowflake and Amazon Redshift are two examples of a data warehouse, a database built for reports. Teams save their steps as a pipeline, a series of steps that moves or reshapes data.

You'll often hear this kind of tool called ETL, short for extract, transform, load. Extract means read data from a source. Load means write it to a destination, and transform means clean it up and reshape it along the way.

Matillion's own comparison post describes the same idea: load data into a cloud data platform, then run the transformations there as SQL.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > The four names you will meet
text:
The product names overlap, and they changed in 2026.

| Name | What it is | Where it runs | Billing meter |
| Maia Foundation | The current platform, with pipelines, connectors and streaming change capture | Full SaaS (Matillion runs it) or Hybrid SaaS (you run the runner) | Credits per task hour, plus extra developers |
| Data Productivity Cloud | The old name of Maia Foundation | Same as above | Same as above |
| Matillion ETL | An older, separate product with its own docs | Instances in your own AWS, Google Cloud or Azure account | Credits per virtual core hour, plus extra active users |
| Matillion Data Loader | A loading tool, billed on rows, for customers not on Maia Foundation | Not stated in the pages we read | Credits per band of rows per month |

Sources: deployment options, credit terms, Matillion ETL docs.

Matillion's terminology page says that in early 2026 it decided to rebrand Data Productivity Cloud as Maia. It also renamed "agents" to "runners" and the "Enterprise edition" to the "Scale plan". The pricing page still says Data Productivity Cloud in places, so expect to see both names.

The Matillion ETL docs now say they only host Matillion ETL documentation, because the Maia docs moved. They have Create Project pages for Snowflake, Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery, Azure Synapse Analytics and Delta Lake on Databricks. For Maia Foundation, the home page says its connectors span Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery and Redshift.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > How Matillion works
text:
So what does a Matillion pipeline actually do? It has up to three parts, and Matillion bills them differently.

- Load. Pre-built connectors copy data from a source into your warehouse. In Matillion's words, these sit in orchestration pipelines, meaning the load-and-flow-control kind, which "handle the loading of data from source systems to a target data warehouse" (docs). A connector is just a ready-made piece of software for one kind of source. The Matillion ETL product page says "over 150 pre-built connectors".
- Transform. Transformation pipelines work on tables already in the warehouse, with steps such as Table Input, Filter, Aggregate and Rank (docs). You build them on a visual canvas, or in SQL or Python. Matillion's own comparison post says Maia Foundation runs transformations as native SQL pushed down into Snowflake, Databricks or AWS Redshift. So the warehouse does the heavy lifting, and yes, your warehouse bill grows with it.
- Chain and schedule. A pipeline can run on a schedule and call other pipelines. Each component has green, gray and red paths, so you can branch on success or failure. And a transformation pipeline slots into a load pipeline through a Run Transformation component.

On top of that, Matillion says Maia has an AI helper that builds pipelines from plain-language requests. We did not test it, and the next line matters.

Per the credit terms (checked Oct 2026), the Maia AI product is an add-on, priced as a separate annual fixed fee.

What about the free trial? The pricing page (checked Oct 2026) calls it "time-bound, fair-use" and gives no length.

Matillion's free trial doc (checked Oct 2026) says new accounts get 14 days and 500 complimentary credits, with every feature open.

When the trial ends, the runner is suspended until you subscribe. If you started from a marketplace or added payment details, a Pay-Go plan kicks in instead (free trial doc (checked Oct 2026)).

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > How Matillion works > Connector counts do not agree
text:
Count the connectors and you get different answers. The home page says Maia Foundation has 150+ connectors and the ETL product page claims over 150. Matillion's comparison post, dated July 16, 2025, says 130+ in its table and 150+ in its text, and its connector page states no count in the text we read.

Our advice: quote the page you used, with its date. And if one source matters to you, check that it's on the live list before you plan around it.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > How Matillion works > Change data capture and its limits
text:
Change data capture (CDC) means reading the log where a database records every change, so you copy only what changed instead of the whole table.

Matillion calls its CDC feature streaming pipelines. Per the streaming docs (checked Oct 2026), they only support relational databases: the International Business Machines (IBM) database Db2 for IBM i, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle and PostgreSQL. The pages say nothing about MongoDB or other non-relational sources, so don't assume.

Streaming is near-real-time, and change records are written in batches as Avro files (checked Oct 2026) to Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage, or loaded to Snowflake. Each streaming pipeline needs its own runner. One more catch: the pricing page lists streaming change data capture only under the Scale plan (checked Oct 2026).

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > How Matillion is priced
text:
Matillion sells annual packages of credits. A credit is its smallest unit of charge, and the pricing page (checked Oct 2026) says credits are used up by pipeline run time (called task hours) and by extra developer users. The page lists three plans and shows no dollar amount for any of them.

| Plan | Developer users included | What the page lists | Price |
| Developer | 1 | Unlimited projects, pre-built connectors, low-code canvas with SQL and Python, built-in Git | Not published |
| Teams | 5 | Audit log, standard support, Service Level Agreement (with an annual subscription), plus all Developer features | Not published |
| Scale | 5 | Custom single sign-on, hybrid cloud deployment, data lineage, streaming change data capture, 180+ day log retention, premium support available | Not published |

Source: Matillion pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

An account can hold one active subscription (checked Oct 2026), so you're on one plan at a time. You can buy directly or through the AWS, Azure or Snowflake marketplace. (A Service Level Agreement is a written promise about uptime or response times.)

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > How Matillion is priced > The Maia Foundation meter
text:
The credit consumption terms (checked Oct 2026) set the rates for Maia Foundation. A task hour is the combined run time of each task, counted in 2-second steps, and only while a pipeline runs. Per the terms, validation and sampling are not billed.

| What you run | Credits per task hour |
| Orchestration pipelines (loading and flow control) | 1 |
| Transformation pipelines | 3 |
| Streaming change capture, "essential" | 1 |
| Streaming change capture, "premium" | 2 |
| Each developer user beyond those included | 70 credits a month |

The terms (checked Oct 2026) say these rates are "fixed across the customer base and non-negotiable". But they don't define "essential" and "premium", and they don't say how an always-on streaming pipeline is counted. Ask Matillion both questions before you plan a streaming budget.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > How Matillion is priced > The Matillion ETL meter
text:
Now flip to the older product. The same terms page (checked Oct 2026) sets a different meter for Matillion ETL: one credit equals one virtual core for one hour, counted while the software is switched on in your cloud account. Each subscription includes 5 active users, and each extra one costs 50 credits in any month they log in.

Matillion ETL editions are listed (checked Oct 2026) as Basic, Advanced and Enterprise.

Data Loader is metered by rows (checked Oct 2026): in its first band, 1 to 5,000,000 rows a month, one credit buys 20,000 batch rows or 7,000 CDC rows. Matillion's own comparison post says "There's no per-user charge", yet the terms charge developer users. Our read: trust the terms over the blog post.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > How Matillion is priced > A worked example, with invented usage
text:
These numbers are illustrative: the usage is our own pick, while the rates come straight from the terms. No dollar value appears, because Matillion doesn't publish one.

Maia Foundation. Say a team on Teams has 7 developers, so 2 are beyond the 5 included. Their nightly load pipelines run 1.5 task hours a day, and their transformation pipelines run 0.5 task hours a day, for 30 days.

- Load (orchestration): 1.5 hours x 1 credit x 30 days = 45 credits.
- Transformation: 0.5 hours x 3 credits x 30 days = 45 credits.
- Extra developers: 2 x 70 credits = 140 credits.
- Total: 230 credits for the month.

The seats are the biggest slice, and a transformation hour costs 3 times a load hour.

For a 14-day trial, scale the run time: (45 + 45) x 14 / 30 = 42 credits. Even if the seat credits were also scaled, 230 x 14 / 30 is about 107. Both are far under the 500 trial credits, so they can cover a real test.

Matillion ETL. Say one instance has 4 virtual cores. Left on all month, it uses 4 x 24 hours x 30 days = 2,880 credits. Switched off outside 8 working hours a day, it uses 4 x 8 x 30 = 960 credits.

Same software, 3 times the bill. Matillion ETL bills for time switched on, not for work done.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > How Matillion is priced > Costs outside the credits
text:
Credits are not the whole bill. Because transformations are pushed into your warehouse, the warehouse provider bills you for that compute too. Then add any marketplace terms and the Order Form overage rate (checked Oct 2026).

Maia has a Budgets and alerts page. Its docs say budgets "do not restrict or block usage", so pipelines keep running past a threshold and you only get an alert (docs (checked Oct 2026)). A runaway job can overspend a credit pack and nothing stops it.

And watch the end of the contract. The terms (checked Oct 2026) allow Pay-Go for up to 60 days with no support, then access is lost unless you sign a new term.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > Where Matillion fits and its limits > What's good
text:
- One canvas, three ways to build. The Developer plan lists (checked Oct 2026) a low-code canvas with SQL and Python, pre-built connectors, unlimited projects and a built-in Git repository, and Scale adds bring-your-own Git. Matillion says a no-code designer builds custom REST API connectors.
- Scheduling and error handling are built in. Basic mode sets schedules in a graphical screen, and advanced mode takes Quartz cron expressions. The Retry component reruns a step until it succeeds or hits a maximum number of attempts, with no delay by default or a delay of about 2 seconds.
- You choose where the runner lives. In Hybrid SaaS you deploy the runner inside your own private cloud, and the docs recommend TLS 1.2 or higher between Matillion and your runners. The pricing page lists hybrid deployment under Scale.
- Usage is metered in small steps and is easy to see. The credit terms count task time in 2-second steps, and validation and sampling are not billed. The usage dashboard (checked Oct 2026) refreshes every 3 hours, splits credits by Orchestration, Transformation, Streaming and Additional Users, and exports to CSV. Budgets (checked Oct 2026) take up to two percentage thresholds and send alerts by email, Slack or webhook.
- Streaming change capture is near-real-time. The PostgreSQL source uses the Debezium PostgreSQL connector and supports versions 12 to 16 (checked Oct 2026). The streaming docs call the pipelines "self-healing" because they adapt to source schema changes.
- Audited security. The security page lists SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II and SOC 3 accreditation with ISO 27001 certification,.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > Where Matillion fits and its limits > Where it falls short
text:
- Streaming change capture is narrow and plan-gated. The docs (checked Oct 2026) say streaming pipelines "only currently support relational databases as sources": Db2 for IBM i, SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle and PostgreSQL. They are "only available to customers on specific Maia plans" and the pricing page lists them under Scale (checked Oct 2026). Each pipeline needs its own runner, and a MySQL source needs a driver you provide.
- Schema changes follow the data, not the source DDL. Per the same docs (checked Oct 2026), a source schema change does not reach the target until the data changes, a dropped column stays in the target with NULL values, and an incompatible type change renames the column with a timestamp suffix (`_yyyymmddhhmmss`). A new source table needs a new streaming pipeline.
- Output is warehouse tables or files, and the platform is closed source. The connectors page says its connectors are "built to load into Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Databricks or Redshift", and streaming writes Avro files to Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage, or loads to Snowflake. No Apache Iceberg destination appears in the Maia docs index or the 2026 changelog (checked Oct 2026), and Matillion publishes no open-source licence (checked Oct 2026) for its platform.
- Spend is hard to predict and hard to cap. A transformation hour costs 3 credits against 1 for a load hour, the warehouse bills you separately for push-down compute, and the Retry component's backoff delays can add to billable task time. Budgets only alert, the price per credit is not public, and the overage rate is on the Order Form only (credit terms (checked Oct 2026)).
- Names and components keep changing. Early 2026 brought the Maia rebrand, the Enterprise edition became Scale and agents became runners. The 2026 changelog renames the Runner role to Operator and deprecates the Google Cloud Storage Load component. The MongoDB Query component is deprecated too: it "can no longer be added to new pipelines" (checked Oct 2026), and each run drops and recreates its target table.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > Where Matillion fits and its limits > What practitioners say
text:
Independent talk about Matillion lives mostly on review sites. We found no substantive Reddit thread, and G2, Capterra and Gartner Peer Insights block automated readers, so we didn't use them directly. Each quote below is verbatim. Each quote is one person's view, with its date and link.

A reviewer on the AWS Marketplace review list, which republishes G2 reviews, wrote in June 2026: "My main concern is around pricing. I'd really like more transparency and predictability on cost".

On PeerSpot, one reviewer wrote (page read October 2026): "We frequently engage with them, and the documentation is top-notch."

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > Where Matillion fits and its limits > Security and deployment
text:
Matillion's security page lists System and Organization Controls (SOC) 1 and SOC 2 audit reports, both Type 2, plus International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 27001, an information security standard. It says it meets the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The text doesn't mention the US health privacy law, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), so ask if you need it.

Maia runs in two modes (docs). In Full SaaS, Matillion manages the runner for you. In Hybrid SaaS, you run it in your own private cloud, which gives you control over network isolation.

One catch: the runner still needs outbound internet access to Matillion's control plane.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > Who Matillion suits, and who should look elsewhere
text:
Matillion fits teams that:

- Want load, transform and schedule on one canvas, with transformations running as SQL pushed down into Snowflake, Databricks or Amazon Redshift.
- Need an audit log and a Service Level Agreement (checked Oct 2026) (Teams), or custom single sign-on, data lineage tracking and 180+ day log retention (Scale).
- Must keep the runner inside their own private cloud, which the pricing page lists as hybrid deployment under Scale (checked Oct 2026).
- Want change capture from Db2 for IBM i, SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle or PostgreSQL into cloud storage or Snowflake, and can budget for the Scale plan.

Look elsewhere if you need:

- Apache Iceberg tables as output. No Iceberg destination appears in Matillion's docs index (checked Oct 2026).
- Change capture from MongoDB or other non-relational sources. The streaming docs list five relational databases only (checked Oct 2026).
- A hard spending cap. Matillion's budgets only alert, and the price per credit is not public (checked Oct 2026).
- A vendor-run loader: Fivetran describes its service as managed.
- Software you run yourself: Airbyte Core, free to self-host under the Elastic License 2.0 (licence file (checked Oct 2026), which restricts offering it as a hosted or managed service) or Debezium (Apache License 2.0 (checked Oct 2026)), per their own pages.
- A published price list: compare each vendor's own pricing page.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > Who Matillion suits, and who should look elsewhere > Questions to ask Matillion before you sign
text:
- Plan. Is streaming change capture in my plan, and what do "essential" and "premium" mean?
- Trial. Can I test streaming and my real sources inside the 500 trial credits, and can the trial be extended?
- Credits. What is my price per credit, my overage rate, and how are always-on pipelines counted?
- Sources. Is each of my sources on the live connector list today?
- Version. If I use Matillion ETL, when does support for my version end?
- Exit. What happens at renewal, and how long does Pay-Go last?

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > Conclusion
text:
Matillion is a warehouse-focused platform for loading, transforming and scheduling data, sold by credit. Before you sign, get the price per credit in writing, run your real usage through the meter tables above, and compare at least one other quote.

title: Compare: What Is Matillion? Plans, Credits and Fit (2026) | OLake > FAQs
text:
Q1. What is Matillion in simple words?

Think of it as a paid platform that loads data into a cloud data warehouse, transforms it with SQL that runs in the warehouse, and schedules the jobs. It comes in two flavours: Maia Foundation, the current cloud platform, and Matillion ETL, an older product you run in your own cloud account.

Q2. Is Matillion an ETL or an ELT tool?

Both, really. Matillion's own comparison post says Maia Foundation runs transformations as native SQL pushed down into the warehouse, which is the ELT pattern. The older product is named Matillion ETL.

Q3. How does Matillion pricing work?

You buy annual credit packages, and then the meter runs. On Maia Foundation, credits go for task hours (1 for load pipelines, 3 for transformation, 1 or 2 for streaming) and 70 a month per extra developer. Matillion ETL uses 1 credit per virtual core hour and 50 per extra active user, per the credit terms (checked Oct 2026). Dollar prices? Not on the pricing page (checked Oct 2026).

Q4. Is Matillion free?

Not really, no. Matillion's free trial doc says a new account gets a 14-day trial with 500 complimentary credits and all features open, after which you need a paid plan (checked Oct 2026). The pricing page itself gives no trial length, and the Developer price is not published (checked Oct 2026).

Q5. What happened to Data Productivity Cloud?

Matillion's terminology page says it decided in early 2026 to rebrand Data Productivity Cloud as Maia, and the credit terms call Maia Foundation the former Data Productivity Cloud. The pricing page still uses the old name in places.

Q6. Does Matillion support change data capture?

Yes, through streaming pipelines, but for Db2 for IBM i, SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle and PostgreSQL only, per the streaming docs, which say nothing about MongoDB (checked Oct 2026). The pricing page lists streaming change data capture under Scale (checked Oct 2026).

Q7. Can Matillion write Apache Iceberg tables?

We found no Iceberg destination in the Maia docs index or the 2026 changelog (checked Oct 2026). Streaming to object storage writes Avro change files, not Iceberg tables. If Iceberg matters to you, ask Matillion before you plan around it.

title: Overview: Welcome to OLake Go > What is OLake Go?
text:
Fastest open-source tool for replicating Databases to Apache Iceberg or Data Lakehouse.

Efficient, quick and scalable data ingestion for real-time analytics.

QuickstartGitHub

What is OLake Go?
OLake Go is a high-performance, open-source EL (Extract–Load) platform that bridges operational databases and open lakehouse storage - writing Apache Iceberg tables or Parquet files on Amazon S3 , enabling organizations to replicate data at scale with minimal overhead. Supporting Incremental Sync, Change Data Capture (CDC), and stateful, resumable syncs, OLake Go ensures your tables remain fresh, organized, and optimized for analytics.

title: Overview: Welcome to OLake Go > Supported Sources
text:
OLake Go supports ingestion from the following sources:

| Source | Full Refresh | Full Refresh + Incremental | Full Refresh + CDC | CDC Only |
| PostgreSQL | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| MySQL | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| MongoDB | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Oracle Database | ✅ | ✅ | — | — |
| Apache Kafka | — | — | — | ✅ |
| DB2 | ✅ | ✅ | — | — |
| MSSQL | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| S3 | ✅ | ✅ | — | — |

title: Overview: Welcome to OLake Go > Destinations
text:
OLake Go writes data to open lakehouse storage:

-

Parquet files on object storage such as Amazon S3, MinIO, and Google Cloud Storage

-

Apache Iceberg tables with support for multiple catalog integrations including:

- AWS Glue Data Catalog
- Apache Hive Metastore
- REST catalogs such as Nessie, Polaris and Unity Catalog
- JDBC catalogs

To know more, read OLake Go Catalog Integration.

title: Overview: Welcome to OLake Go > Capabilities > 1. Parallelised Chunking
text:
Parallel chunking is a technique that splits large datasets or collections into smaller virtual chunks, allowing them to be read and processed simultaneously. It is used in sync modes such as Full Refresh, Full Refresh + CDC, and Full Refresh + Incremental.

What it does:

- Splits big collections into manageable pieces without altering the underlying data.
- Each chunk can be processed parallely & independently.

Benefit:

- Enables parallel reads, dramatically reducing the time needed to perform full snapshots or scans of large datasets.
- Improves ingestion speed, scalability, and overall system performance.

title: Overview: Welcome to OLake Go > Capabilities > 2. Stateful, Resumable Syncs
text:
It ensures that data syncs resume automatically from the last checkpoint after interruptions. Applicable for Full Refresh + CDC and Full Refresh + Incremental & Strict CDC sync modes.

What it does:

- Maintains state of in-progress syncs.
- Automatically resumes after crashes, network failures, or manual pauses.
- Eliminates the need to resync data from the beginning. Interrupted runs resume from the last checkpoint instead.

Benefit:

- Reduces data duplication and processing time.
- Ensures reliable, fault-tolerant pipelines.
- Minimizes manual intervention for operational teams.

title: Overview: Welcome to OLake Go > Capabilities > 3. Configurable Max Connections
text: Each job can set its own maximum number of database connections to the source. This limit is per job, not shared across jobs—even when several jobs use the same source, each job’s setting applies only to that job. Helps prevent overload and ensures stable performance on the source system.

title: Overview: Welcome to OLake Go > Capabilities > 4. Data Deduplication
text:
Data Deduplication ensures that only unique records are stored and processed in Upsert ingestion mode: saving space, reducing costs, and improving data quality. OLake Go automatically deduplicates data using the primary key from the source tables, guaranteeing that each primary key maps to a single row in the destination along with its corresponding olake_id.

**note:**

For Kafka sources, deduplication uses the dedup keys configured in the streams section rather than source primary keys.

title: Overview: Welcome to OLake Go > Capabilities > 5. Hive Style Partitioning
text:
Partitioning is the process of dividing large datasets into smaller, more manageable segments based on specific column values (e.g., date, region, or category), improving query performance, scalability, and data organization.

- Iceberg partitioning → Metadata-driven, no need for directory-based partitioning; enables efficient pruning and schema evolution.
- S3-style partitioning → Traditional folder-based layout (e.g., `year=2025/month=08/day=22/`) for compatibility with external tools.
- Normalization → Automatically expands level-1 nested JSON fields into top-level columns.

What it does:

- Converts nested JSON objects into flat columns for easier querying.
- Preserves all data while simplifying structure.

Benefit:

- Makes SQL queries simpler and faster.
- Reduces the need for complex JSON parsing in queries.
- Improves readability and downstream analytics efficiency.

title: Overview: Welcome to OLake Go > Capabilities > 6. Schema Evolution & Data Types Changes
text:
OLake Go automatically handles changes in your table's schema without breaking downstream jobs. Read More Schema Evolution in OLake Go

Capabilities > 7. Dead Letter Queue Columns (Coming soon)
The DLQ column handles values with data type changes not supported by Iceberg / Parquet destinations type promotions, safely storing them without loss. This prevents sync failures and ensures downstream models remain stable. By isolating incompatible values, it allows users to continue syncing data seamlessly while addressing type mismatches at their convenience, improving reliability and reducing manual intervention.

title: Overview: Welcome to OLake Go > Capabilities > 8. Two Phase Commit
text: OLake Go uses this mechanism for the Iceberg destination during full refresh, incremental, and CDC (MongoDB, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MSSQL), so per-chunk commit status is tracked via destination state making sure the syncs avoid inconsistencies and duplicate writes.

title: Overview: Welcome to OLake Go > Capabilities > 9. Query Engine Interoperability
text:
Query engines that read Apache Iceberg tables support different formats for row-level deletes. Some use equality deletes, others positional deletes, and Iceberg v3 adds deletion vectors. In Upsert mode, OLake Go can write any of these three formats, so ingestion is compatible with the engines we use to query the data.

What it does:

- Commits upsert and CDC updates as equality deletes, positional deletes, or deletion vectors.
- Lets you choose the delete format in job or stream settings. See Upsert for how each option works.

**note:**

For Kafka sources, Upsert uses positional deletes only.

Benefit:

- Improves interoperability with multiple query engines (for example, Spark, Trino, Databricks, Snowflake and Athena), each with its own delete-format support.

See OLake Go Compatibility with Query Engines for the full list of supported query engines and which delete formats each one supports.

title: OLake UI API > Accessing the OLake UI API
text:
This page contains the official Swagger documentation for the OLake UI API, including endpoint reference details, authentication instructions, and guidance for testing requests.

Accessing the OLake UI API
- OLake UI API: http://localhost:8000/swagger

title: OLake UI API > Authentication
text:
This API uses Session-based Authentication (Cookies).

To access protected endpoints:

- Login: Send a POST request to `/login` with your credentials.
- Cookie: A session cookie will be set in your browser automatically upon successful login.
- Requests: Subsequent requests will automatically include this cookie.

There is no need to manually handle tokens or headers.

title: OLake UI API > Authentication > Using cURL with Cookies
text:
When using cURL, you must explicitly save and send cookies between requests:

Step 1: Login and save the cookie

bash

```
curl -L 'http://localhost:8000/login' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -c cookies.txt \
  -d '{"username": "admin", "password": "password"}'
```

Step 2: Use the saved cookie for subsequent requests

bash

```
curl -L 'http://localhost:8000/api/v1/project/123/jobs' \
  -H 'Accept: */*' \
  -b cookies.txt
```

The `-c cookies.txt` flag saves the session cookie, and `-b cookies.txt` sends it with subsequent requests.

title: OLake UI API > Response Format
text:
The API uses standard HTTP response codes to indicate success or failure:

- 200 OK: Request was successful.
- 400 Bad Request: The request was invalid.
- 401 Unauthorized: Authentication failed or session expired.
- 500 Internal Server Error: Something went wrong on the server side.

title: Setup OLake Sync as a Kubernetes CronJob
text:
**note:**

This guide uses `selected_streams.json` and `available_streams.json`. See streams configuration. If you use the legacy `streams.json`, see the streams migration guide or the Streams v1 reference.

This guide details the process for deploying and managing an OLake data synchronization task as a scheduled Kubernetes CronJob. This configuration uses standard Kubernetes resources (ConfigMaps, PVC, CronJob) to automate recurring OLake `sync` operations using pre-generated streams files.

title: Setup OLake Sync as a Kubernetes CronJob > Prerequisites
text:
Ensure the following requirements are met before proceeding:

- Kubernetes Cluster Access: Administrative access to a Kubernetes cluster.
- `kubectl`: Configured `kubectl` command-line tool. Installation Guide.
- Pre-generated OLake streams files (`selected_streams.json` and `available_streams.json`): This setup requires both files, generated beforehand using the OLake `discover` command against your source database.

- Streams Generation Guides:

- Streams config

- The content of each file will be placed within the `cm_olake-streams-config.yaml` ConfigMap.

- Kubernetes Namespace: The manifests default to the `olake` namespace. Create it (`kubectl create namespace olake`) or update the `namespace` fields in all YAML files if using a different target.
- Node Labels (Optional): If using `nodeAffinity` in `cronjob_olake.yaml`, ensure target nodes possess the specified labels.

title: Setup OLake Sync as a Kubernetes CronJob > Configuration Steps
text:
This setup requires several Kubernetes manifest files. Download these files first, then customize them for your specific environment.

1. Download Manifest Files

Use the links below (or `curl`) to download the necessary YAML files:

-

Source ConfigMap:

- Download `cm_olake-source-config.yaml`bash

```
curl -Lo cm_olake-source-config.yaml https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-docs/refs/heads/master/kubernetes/cm_olake-source-config.yaml
```

-

Destination ConfigMap:

- Download `cm_olake-destination-config.yaml`bash

```
curl -Lo cm_olake-destination-config.yaml https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-docs/refs/heads/master/kubernetes/cm_olake-destination-config.yaml
```

-

Streams ConfigMap:

- Download `cm_olake-streams-config.yaml`bash

```
curl -Lo cm_olake-streams-config.yaml https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-docs/refs/heads/master/kubernetes/cm_olake-streams-config.yaml
```

-

CronJob & PVC Manifest:

- Download `cronjob_olake.yaml`bash

```
curl -Lo cronjob_olake.yaml https://raw.githubusercontent.com/datazip-inc/olake-docs/refs/heads/master/kubernetes/cronjob_olake.yaml
```

2. Customize Downloaded Files

Edit the downloaded files with your specific configurations:

- `cm_olake-source-config.yaml`: Update `source.json` with your source connection parameters.
- `cm_olake-destination-config.yaml`: Update `destination.json` with your destination configuration.
- `cm_olake-streams-config.yaml`: Replace the content under `selected_streams.json` with your own stream selection. Replace the content under `available_streams.json` with the file generated by `discover` (do not edit it).
- `cronjob_olake.yaml`:

title: Setup OLake Sync as a Kubernetes CronJob > Configuration Steps (part 2)
text:
- Set `metadata.namespace` / `spec.jobTemplate.metadata.namespace` / PVC `metadata.namespace` (default `olake`).
- Configure `spec.schedule`. Refer for schedule syntax: CronTab Guru
- Set `spec.suspend` to `false` to enable the schedule.
- Update `spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image` with the correct OLake source image (e.g., `olakego/source-mongodb:latest`). See OLake Docker Hub Images.
- Configure `nodeAffinity` (optional) under `spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.affinity`.
- Adjust `resources.requests` and `resources.limits` for the main OLake container.
- Crucially, set the correct `storageClassName` in the `PersistentVolumeClaim` definition at the end of the file. This StorageClass must support the `ReadWriteMany` access mode specified in the PVC.

title: Setup OLake Sync as a Kubernetes CronJob > Deployment Procedure
text:
Apply the configured manifests to your Kubernetes cluster:

-

Apply ConfigMaps:

bash

```
kubectl apply -f cm_olake-source-config.yaml -n olake
kubectl apply -f cm_olake-destination-config.yaml -n olake
kubectl apply -f cm_olake-streams-config.yaml -n olake
```

-

Apply CronJob and PVC:

bash

```
kubectl apply -f cronjob_olake.yaml -n olake
```

-

Verify PVC Status:

bash

```
kubectl get pvc olake-config-pvc -n olake
```

(Ensure `STATUS` is `Bound`. Troubleshoot StorageClass or provisioner if `Pending`).

-

Verify CronJob Status:

bash

```
kubectl get cronjob olake-mongodb-sync -n olake
```

title: Setup OLake Sync as a Kubernetes CronJob > Manual Job Execution and Control
text:
-

Trigger Manually: Create a Job instance immediately from the CronJob template. This is useful for testing or running outside the defined schedule.

bash

```
kubectl create job --from=cronjob/olake-mongodb-sync manual-olake-sync-$(date +%s) -n olake
```

Monitor the manually created job using the commands in the Monitoring section below.

-

Suspend CronJob: Prevent the CronJob from creating new jobs based on the schedule. Does not affect running jobs.

bash

```
kubectl patch cronjob olake-mongodb-sync -n olake -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'
```

-

Unsuspend CronJob: Re-enable the CronJob's schedule.

bash

```
kubectl patch cronjob olake-mongodb-sync -n olake -p '{"spec":{"suspend":false}}'
```

title: Setup OLake Sync as a Kubernetes CronJob > Cleanup
text:
To remove the deployed resources:

- Delete CronJob: `kubectl delete cronjob olake-mongodb-sync -n olake`
- Delete PVC: `kubectl delete pvc olake-config-pvc -n olake` (Caution: Deletes persisted data).
- Delete ConfigMaps:bash

```
kubectl delete configmap olake-source-config -n olake
kubectl delete configmap olake-destination-config -n olake
kubectl delete configmap olake-streams-config -n olake
```

title: Benchmarks / Ingestion Benchmarks > MSSQL → Apache Iceberg Connector Benchmark
text:
Benchmark Environment

- This benchmark uses standard NYC Taxi Data`trips` and `fhv_trips` tables.
- Since the original repo supports only PostgreSQL, we first ingested the NYC Taxi Data in the cloud PostgreSQL database (Azure Flexible DB), and then transferred the tables from there to our MSSQL database.
- Total rows 4,008,587,913 rows including both tables.
- The average row size is 215 bytes for `trips` and 177 bytes for `fhv_trips`.
- OLake Go was run on GCP Custom N2 VM (64 vCPUs, 128 GiB memory)
- Database instance: GCP Standard N2 VM (32 vCPUs, 128 GiB memory)

**note:**

We used AWS Glue as Iceberg catalog and AWS S3 as the storage layer on the destination side for this benchmarks.

title: Code of Conduct > Our Standards

- Using welcoming and inclusive language
- Being respectful of differing viewpoints and experiences
- Gracefully accepting constructive criticism
- Focusing on what is best for the community
- Showing empathy towards other community members

Examples of unacceptable behavior by participants include:

- The use of sexualized language or imagery and unwelcome sexual attention or advances
- Trolling, insulting/derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
- Public or private harassment
- Publishing others’ private information, such as a physical or electronic address, without explicit permission

Project maintainers have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, or to ban temporarily or permanently any contributor for other behaviors that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

text: This Code of Conduct applies within all project spaces, and it also applies when an individual is representing the project or its community in public spaces. title: Code of Conduct > Attribution
