title: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide
text:
This guide walks you through setting up Change Data Capture (CDC) for Amazon RDS PostgreSQL instances using logical replication with the native pgoutput plugin and a PostgreSQL publication for real-time data replication with OLake.

Prerequisites:

- An Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance (PostgreSQL 10+).
- A custom DB parameter group for this instance (the default parameter group cannot be modified).
- The RDS master user or another user with the `rds_superuser` and `rds_replication` roles.
- Automated backups enabled (backup retention > 0) – this is needed for long-term WAL retention on RDS

Steps:

title: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide > 1. Create and Configure a Parameter Group
text:
In the AWS RDS console, go to `Parameter Groups` and create a new parameter group for your PostgreSQL version (if you don’t already have one).

Associate the parameter group with your database instance and configure:

| Parameter | Value | Purpose |
| rds.logical_replication | 1 | Enables logical replication (required for pgoutput) |
| wal_level | logical | Usually set automatically by above |
| max_replication_slots | ≥5 | Number of concurrent CDC connections |
| max_wal_senders | ≥7 | Should exceed replication slots |
| wal_sender_timeout | 0 | Prevents snapshot timeouts |

Save the parameter group changes.

**caution:**

`rds.logical_replication` can only be turned on for read-replica instances that are running PostgreSQL 16 or later. If your replica is on an earlier major version the parameter will be ignored and logical decoding will NOT be available on that replica. Either upgrade the replica to v16+ or enable logical decoding only on the primary.

title: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide > 2. Reboot the RDS Instance
text:
Reboot the database instance so that the static parameters take effect. After reboot, confirm the settings:

sql

```
SELECT name, setting
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('rds.logical_replication','wal_level');
```

The query should show `rds.logical_replication` = on, and `wal_level` = logical.

title: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide > 3. Set Up a Replication User
Amazon RDS PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide > 4. Create Publication
text:
Publications define which tables will be replicated. Create a publication for the tables you want to monitor:

- Publication Name Configuration:

**Publication Name Configuration:**

Use the exact publication name that you configure in OLake UI or CLI. The publication name must match the `publication` parameter in your OLake source configuration.

sql

```
-- Create publication for all tables in the database
CREATE PUBLICATION olake_publication FOR ALL TABLES;

-- Or create publication for specific tables
CREATE PUBLICATION olake_publication FOR TABLE public.table1, public.table2, public.table3;

-- Or create publication for all tables in a specific schema
CREATE PUBLICATION olake_publication FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA public;
```

Enable `publish_via_partition_root` for partitioned tables:

The `publish_via_partition_root` setting MUST be enabled to ensure data integrity when replicating partitioned tables. Without this setting, changes to partitioned tables will not be properly captured, resulting in data loss or inconsistency.

sql

```
ALTER PUBLICATION olake_publication SET (publish_via_partition_root = true);
```

Publication Options:

sql

```
-- Customize what operations are published
CREATE PUBLICATION olake_publication FOR ALL TABLES
WITH (publish = 'insert,update,delete,truncate');

-- Only publish INSERT and UPDATE operations
CREATE PUBLICATION olake_publication FOR ALL TABLES
WITH (publish = 'insert,update');

-- For partitioned tables (PostgreSQL 13+): publish changes via the partition root
CREATE PUBLICATION olake_publication FOR ALL TABLES
WITH (publish = 'insert,update,delete,truncate', publish_via_partition_root = true);
```

Verify Publication:

sql

```
-- List all publications
SELECT * FROM pg_publication;

-- View tables in a publication
SELECT * FROM pg_publication_tables WHERE pubname = 'olake_publication';
```

Add Tables to Existing Publication:

sql

```
-- Add a single table
ALTER PUBLICATION olake_publication ADD TABLE public.new_table;

-- Add multiple tables
ALTER PUBLICATION olake_publication ADD TABLE public.table4, public.table5;

-- Remove a table
ALTER PUBLICATION olake_publication DROP TABLE public.old_table;
```

title: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide > 5. Create Replication Slot
text:
Set up the replication slot for OLake to consume changes:

**Slot Name Configuration:**

Use the exact replication slot name that you configure in OLake UI or CLI. The slot name must match the `replication_slot` parameter in your OLake source configuration.

Best practices:

- Create the publication before creating the replication slot
- Create the slot in the same database that OLake will connect to (slots are per-database)
- Use a unique slot name per OLake connection; slot names cannot start with a number

sql

```
-- Replace 'your_olake_slot_name' with the slot name from your OLake configuration
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('your_olake_slot_name', 'pgoutput');
```

Example with common slot names:

sql

```
-- If your OLake source config uses "olake_slot"
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('olake_slot', 'pgoutput');

-- If your OLake source config uses "postgres_slot"
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('postgres_slot', 'pgoutput');
```

Verify Slot Creation:

sql

```
SELECT * FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE slot_name = 'your_olake_slot_name';
```

title: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide > 6. Test Logical Decoding
text:
Verify that CDC is working correctly with pgoutput:

sql

```
-- Create test data
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS test_table (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    data TEXT,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Set replica identity
ALTER TABLE test_table REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT;

-- Add table to publication
ALTER PUBLICATION olake_publication ADD TABLE test_table;

-- Insert test data
INSERT INTO test_table (data) VALUES ('PostgreSQL pgoutput CDC test - INSERT');
```

**Delete records and full row values:**

By default, WAL only includes the primary key on deletes. In OLake, delete records (`_op_type = 'd'`) will therefore only retain the primary key and OLake metadata columns — other columns appear blank or null. To retain the full deleted row run the following query:

sql

```
ALTER TABLE test_table REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;
```

Check for changes using pg_logical_slot_peek_binary_changes:

sql

```
SELECT *
FROM pg_logical_slot_peek_binary_changes(
  'olake_slot', NULL, NULL,
  'proto_version','1',
  'publication_names','olake_publication'
);
```

Expected Results:

✅ Success: Returns binary change records from pgoutput

❌ Permission denied: Check user has REPLICATION role

❌ Publication not found: Verify publication exists and contains tables

❌ Slot not found: Check replication slot was created with pgoutput plugin

❌ No changes returned: Verify table has replica identity configured and is in the publication

**important:**

- Use the RDS endpoint, database name, and the replication user (`cdc_user` or master) in your OLake configuration. Ensure your source configuration includes `replication_slot` and `publication` names. OLake will stream changes via the pgoutput logical slot.
- Make sure the network setup allows the connector to reach the RDS instance (RDS must be publicly accessible or your connector is in the same VPC/network).
- Now that you have configured the database and created the CDC user, you can add the PostgreSQL source in OLake to build an ELT pipeline to Iceberg or Parquet. See the PostgreSQL connector overview for a high-level walkthrough.

title: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide > Troubleshooting
text:
-

Parameter Group Not Applying: If `rds.logical_replication` remains off after reboot, check that:

- The instance is actually using your custom parameter group (in the RDS console, on the Configuration tab, verify the parameter group name).
- The parameter group family matches your engine version (e.g., “postgres12”). If not, some parameters might be ignored.
- You saved the changes and rebooted. Static parameters won’t apply without a reboot.

-

Access Issues: If the OLake reports `ERROR: permission denied for relation/sequence ...` or "permission denied for schema" during snapshot or streaming, the replication user might lack SELECT privileges on those tables/schemas. Logical decoding itself does not check table ACLs for emitting changes. Grant the necessary privileges or use the master user for the initial snapshot. Also, ensure the user has the `rds_replication` role to use the slot.

-

Slot or Plugin Errors:

- If creating a slot yields `ERROR: permission denied to create replication slot`, use the master user or a user with `rds_superuser` role to create it.
- If you see `ERROR: logical decoding requires wal_level "logical"`, it means wal_level is not logical – double-check the parameter group (maybe the DB is still running with the old param group).
- If the error is about `pgoutput` not found, ensure PostgreSQL is version 10+ and `rds.logical_replication` is enabled.

-

WAL buildup / Disk-Full: Similar to Aurora, an inactive logical slot on RDS will prevent WAL files from being purged. Monitor the WAL storage on RDS (CloudWatch metric "TransactionLogsDiskUsage"). If your CDC connector falls behind or is stopped for a while, the disk usage can grow. In extreme cases, you might get RDS events complaining that “The transaction logs have consumed XX% of storage”. To fix, either restart the CDC process to consume the backlog or drop the slot if you no longer need it. For example:

sql

```
SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('cdc_slot');
```

Do this only if you are okay with re-snapshotting, as dropping the slot means you’ll lose the record of changes.

-

title: Amazon RDS PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide > Troubleshooting (part 2)
text:
Replication Role Setup: On RDS, you cannot simply do `ALTER ROLE ... WITH REPLICATION` (superuser required). Instead, AWS uses the predefined roles. The master user automatically has `rds_superuser` and `rds_replication`. If you create a new user, you can grant `rds_replication` to it. If that grant fails, it may require you to be master user (try as master). If using the master user for CDC, no action needed. In summary, many users choose the master user for CDC on RDS to avoid role issues.

-

Network and Connectivity: Ensure your RDS instance is reachable:

- If it’s in a private subnet, your CDC application must have network access (consider running the CDC connector on an EC2 in the same VPC).
- If it’s publicly accessible, open the security group to the connector's IP (or corporate network) on port 5432.
- RDS may enforce SSL; use the SSL connection if required (check the parameter `rds.force_ssl`).

-

Schema and Publication: Ensure new tables are added to your publication when needed. For tables without primary keys, set appropriate replica identity:

sql

```
ALTER TABLE my_table REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;
```

By following these steps, CDC should be active on your RDS PostgreSQL instance, streaming changes through pgoutput.

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin:
text:
This guide covers setting up Change Data Capture (CDC) for PostgreSQL running on any server infrastructure including EC2 instances, virtual machines, bare metal servers, or on-premises installations. The setup uses logical replication with the wal2json plugin for real-time data streaming.

Prerequisites:

- PostgreSQL version 9.4+ (version 10+ recommended for full logical replication support)
- Superuser access or ability to modify `postgresql.conf` and `pg_hba.conf`
- The `wal2json` plugin installed (or ability to install it)
- TLS/SSL enabled for secure connections (recommended)
- Sufficient disk space for WAL retention

**Read Replica Support:**

PostgreSQL 16+: Logical replication on read replicas is supported but may have limitations. Row deletions and vacuum operations on the primary can affect replication slot stability.

PostgreSQL 15 and earlier: Read replicas cannot act as publishers for logical replication. Connect OLake to the primary instance for CDC functionality.

Recommendation: Use the primary instance for production CDC workloads to ensure reliability.

Steps:

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin: > 1. Install wal2json Plugin
text:
The `wal2json` plugin is required for logical decoding. Installation varies by system:

Ubuntu/Debian:

bash

```
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install postgresql-15-wal2json  # Replace 15 with your version
```

CentOS/RHEL/Amazon Linux:

bash

```
sudo yum install postgresql15-wal2json  # Replace 15 with your version
# Or for newer versions:
sudo dnf install postgresql15-wal2json
```

From Source (if package not available):

bash

```
git clone https://github.com/eulerto/wal2json.git
cd wal2json
make USE_PGXS=1
sudo make USE_PGXS=1 install
```

Verify Installation:

sql

```
SELECT * FROM pg_available_extensions WHERE name = 'wal2json';
```

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin: > 2. Configure PostgreSQL Parameters
text:
Edit `postgresql.conf` (usually in `/etc/postgresql/15/main/` or `/var/lib/pgsql/15/data/`):

conf

```
# Enable logical replication
wal_level = logical

# Set replication limits
max_replication_slots = 10
max_wal_senders = 10

# Optional: Prevent timeouts during long snapshots
wal_sender_timeout = 0

# Optional: Control WAL retention
max_slot_wal_keep_size = 1GB

# Performance tuning (adjust based on your workload)
checkpoint_timeout = 15min
max_wal_size = 2GB
```

| Parameter | Recommended Value | Purpose |
| wal_level | logical | Enable logical decoding |
| max_replication_slots | ≥5 | Number of concurrent CDC connections |
| max_wal_senders | ≥7 | Should exceed replication slots |
| wal_sender_timeout | 0 | Prevents snapshot timeouts |
| max_slot_wal_keep_size | 1GB+ | Prevents WAL accumulation |

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin: > 3. Configure Client Authentication
text:
Edit `pg_hba.conf` to allow replication connections. Add entries for your OLake client:

conf

```
# Allow replication connections from OLake
host    replication     cdc_user        10.0.0.0/16         md5
host    all             cdc_user        10.0.0.0/16         md5

# For SSL connections (recommended)
hostssl replication     cdc_user        10.0.0.0/16         md5
hostssl all             cdc_user        10.0.0.0/16         md5
```

Replace `10.0.0.0/16` with your actual network range or specific IP addresses.

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin: > 4. Restart PostgreSQL
text:
Apply configuration changes by restarting PostgreSQL:

bash

```
# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo systemctl restart postgresql

# CentOS/RHEL
sudo systemctl restart postgresql-15  # Replace with your version

# Or using pg_ctl
sudo -u postgres pg_ctl restart -D /var/lib/pgsql/15/data/
```

Verify Configuration:

sql

```
SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('wal_level', 'max_replication_slots', 'max_wal_senders');
```

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin: > 5. Create Replication User
text:
Connect as a superuser (usually `postgres`) and create a dedicated CDC user:

sql

```
-- Create user with replication privileges
CREATE USER cdc_user WITH PASSWORD 'strongpassword';
ALTER ROLE cdc_user WITH REPLICATION;
```

Grant Database Access:

sql

```
-- Grant connection to specific database
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE mydb TO cdc_user;
```

Optional: Read-only Access for Initial Snapshot

For stricter security, grant explicit read permissions:

sql

```
-- Example for the "public" schema in database mydb
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO cdc_user;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO cdc_user;
-- Ensure future tables are covered automatically
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO cdc_user;
```

Multiple Schema Access:

sql

```
-- Repeat for each schema you want to sync
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA schema1 TO cdc_user;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA schema1 TO cdc_user;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA schema1 GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO cdc_user;
```

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin: > 6. Create Logical Replication Slot
text:
Set up the replication slot for OLake to consume changes:

**Slot Name Configuration:**

Use the exact replication slot name that you configure in OLake UI or CLI. The slot name must match the `replication_slot` parameter in your OLake source configuration.

sql

```
-- Replace 'your_olake_slot_name' with the slot name from your OLake configuration
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('your_olake_slot_name', 'wal2json');
```

Example with common slot names:

sql

```
-- If your OLake source config uses "olake_slot"
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('olake_slot', 'wal2json');

-- If your OLake source config uses "postgres_slot"
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('postgres_slot', 'wal2json');
```

Verify Slot Creation:

sql

```
SELECT * FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE slot_name = 'your_olake_slot_name';
```

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin: > 7. Test Logical Decoding
text:
Verify that CDC is working correctly:

sql

```
-- Create test data
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS test_table (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, data TEXT);
INSERT INTO test_table (data) VALUES ('Generic PostgreSQL CDC test');

-- Check for changes (replace 'your_olake_slot_name' with your actual slot name)
SELECT data FROM pg_logical_slot_get_changes(
    'your_olake_slot_name', null, null,
    'pretty-print', '1'
);
```

✅ Success: Returns JSON change records from wal2json
❌ Permission denied: Check user has `REPLICATION` role
❌ Plugin not found: Verify wal2json installation and wal_level setting

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin: > Troubleshooting > Configuration Issues
text:
-

wal2json Plugin Not Found:

sql

```
ERROR: could not access file "wal2json": No such file or directory
```

Solution: Install the wal2json package for your PostgreSQL version or compile from source.

-

WAL Level Not Logical:

sql

```
ERROR: logical decoding requires wal_level >= logical
```

Solution: Set `wal_level = logical` in `postgresql.conf` and restart PostgreSQL.

-

Configuration Not Applied: If settings don't take effect:

- Verify you edited the correct `postgresql.conf` file: `SHOW config_file;`
- Ensure PostgreSQL was restarted after changes
- Check PostgreSQL logs for configuration errors

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin: > Troubleshooting > Permission Issues
text:
-

Replication Slot Creation Failed:

sql

```
ERROR: permission denied to create replication slot
```

Solution: Ensure the user has `REPLICATION` role: `ALTER ROLE cdc_user WITH REPLICATION;`

-

Table Access Denied:

sql

```
ERROR: permission denied for table "some_table"
```

Solution: Grant SELECT privileges on the schema and tables the user needs to access.

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin: > Troubleshooting > Performance and Monitoring
text:
-

WAL Accumulation: Monitor disk usage as inactive slots retain WAL files:

sql

```
SELECT slot_name, active, restart_lsn, confirmed_flush_lsn
FROM pg_replication_slots;
```

Solution: Drop unused slots or ensure CDC consumers are actively reading.

-

High CPU/Memory Usage: Tune checkpoint settings:

conf

```
checkpoint_timeout = 15min
checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9
max_wal_size = 2GB
```

-

Slow Snapshots: For large tables, consider:

- Increasing `work_mem` for the CDC session
- Using `wal_sender_timeout = 0` to prevent timeouts
- Running snapshots during low-activity periods

title: PostgreSQL CDC Setup Guide using wal2json plugin: > Troubleshooting > Schema and Data Issues
text:
-

Missing Changes for Updates/Deletes: Ensure tables have primary keys or set replica identity:

sql

```
ALTER TABLE my_table REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;  -- For tables without PK
```

-

DDL Changes Not Captured: wal2json captures DDL in WAL, but OLake may need schema refresh for structural changes.

-

Large Transaction Handling: For very large transactions, monitor:

- WAL disk space usage
- Replication slot lag
- Memory usage during decoding

title: Sources / S3: Overview
text: The OLake Go S3 Source connector ingests data from Amazon S3 or S3-compatible storage (MinIO, LocalStack). It offers features like parallel chunking, checkpointing, and automatic resume for failed full loads. This connector can be used within the OLake UI or run locally via Docker for open-source workflows.

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Key Features
text:
-

Multi-Format Support: CSV files (`.csv`, `.csv.gz`), JSON files in JSONL and Array formats (`.json`, `.jsonl`, `.json.gz`), XML files (`.xml`, `.xml.gz`) and Parquet files

-

Automatic Compression Handling: Transparent gzip decompression (`.gz` files)

-

Folder-Based Streams: Groups files by top-level folder into logical streams. Files are automatically grouped into streams based on folder structure. An example of bucket structure is provided below:

```
s3://my-bucket/data/
├── users/
│   ├── 2024-01-01/users.parquet
│   └── 2024-01-02/users.parquet
├── orders/
│   ├── 2024-01-01/orders.parquet
│   └── 2024-01-02/orders.parquet
└── products/
    └── products.csv.gz
```

In the above example, as a result we get 3 streams created - `users`, `orders`, `products`.

-

S3-Compatible Services: AWS S3, MinIO, LocalStack, and other S3 APIs

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Sync Modes Supported
text:
- Full Refresh
- Full Refresh + Incremental

How Incremental Sync Works

The S3 connector uses S3's `LastModified` timestamp as a cursor for incremental syncs:

How it works:

- Discovery phase adds `_last_modified_time` field to each stream
- During sync, each record is injected with the file's LastModified timestamp
- State file tracks the latest `_last_modified_time` per stream
- Subsequent syncs only process files with `LastModified > last_synced_timestamp`

State Example:

json

```
{
  "users": {
    "_last_modified_time": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z"
  },
  "orders": {
    "_last_modified_time": "2024-01-15T11:45:00Z"
  }
}
```

**File Modifications:**

If a file's content changes and is re-uploaded to S3, it will be re-synced in incremental mode because S3 updates the LastModified timestamp.

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Prerequisites > Version Prerequisites
text:
- AWS S3 (any version) or S3-compatible service (MinIO 2020+, LocalStack 0.12+)

Prerequisites > Connection Prerequisites
-

Read access to S3 bucket (`s3:ListBucket`, `s3:GetObject`)

-

AWS Authentication: IAM roles, environment variables, instance profiles (recommended), or static access key and secret key credentials

-

Network connectivity to S3 endpoint

-

IAM policy for S3 source access:

s3-source-iam-policy.json

```
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:ListBucket"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::<YOUR_S3_BUCKET>"
      ]
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::<YOUR_S3_BUCKET>/*"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

- Replace `<YOUR_S3_BUCKET>` with your actual S3 bucket name.
- This policy provides read-only access required for the OLake Go S3 source connector.

After initial Prerequisites are fulfilled, the configurations for S3 can be configured.

title: Sources / S3: Overview > XML File Handling
text:
The following behavior applies when XML is selected as the file format.

XML File Handling > 1. Normalization OFF
When normalization is set to OFF in the Streams section, Row Identifier is ignored. OLake Go parses the XML into a JSON tree and stores it as a JSON string in the data column. Nested elements are stored as stringified JSON within that structure.

**note:**

If the Row Identifier entered in the source configuration is not present in the XML file, stream discovery will fail.

Example input:

xml

```
<orders>
  <order id="1001" status="NEW">
    <order_date>2024-08-01</order_date>
    <customer>
      <id>CUST_55</id>
      <name>Alice</name>
    </customer>
  </order>
</orders>
```

Output:

json

```
{"_last_modified_time":"2026-08-19T11:17:30Z","orders":{"order":"{\"_id\":\"1001\",\"_status\":\"NEW\",\"customer\":\"{\\\"id\\\":\\\"CUST_55\\\",\\\"name\\\":\\\"Alice\\\"}\",\"order_date\":\"2024-08-01\"}"}}
```

title: Sources / S3: Overview > XML File Handling > 2. Normalization ON
text:
When normalization is set to ON in the Streams section, OLake Go performs level 0 flattening and stores the data as a table. You must also set Row Identifier in the source configuration to the tag that encloses each record.

**note:**

If the Row Identifier is invalid (not present in the XML file), stream discovery will fail.

Example input (with `row_identifier = order`):

xml

```
<orders>
  <order id="1001" status="NEW">
    <order_date>2024-08-01</order_date>
    <customer>
      <id>CUST_55</id>
      <name>Alice</name>
    </customer>
  </order>
</orders>
```

Output table:

| _id | _status | order_date | customer |
| 1001 | NEW | 2024-08-01 | {"id":"CUST_55","name":"Alice"} |

title: Sources / S3: Overview > XML File Handling > 3. Level 0 Flattening Rules
text:
When normalization is ON, OLake Go applies level 0 flattening only. Using the example above:

- Attributes on the row identifier element become columns prefixed with `_`. For `<order id="1001" status="NEW">`, `id` and `status` become columns `_id` and `_status`.
- Direct child elements become columns using their tag name as-is. For example, `order_date` becomes column `order_date`.
- Nested child elements become columns using their tag name, but their contents are not flattened further. The value is stored as a JSON string. For example, `customer` becomes column `customer` with value `{"id":"CUST_55","name":"Alice"}`.

title: Sources / S3: Overview > XML File Handling > 4. Repeated Elements and Row Identifier
text:
Choosing the correct Row Identifier matters when XML contains repeated elements.

Example input:

xml

```
<items>
  <item>Apple</item>
  <item>Banana</item>
</items>
```

| Row Identifier | Result |
| item | Table with column item and two rows: Apple, Banana |
| items | Table with column item and one row: Banana (Apple gets overwritten) |

**Row Identifier Selection:**

Always set Row Identifier to the tag that encloses each individual record, not the parent wrapper element. An incorrect value can cause data loss from overwrites.

title: Sources / S3: Overview > XML File Handling > 5. Namespaced Elements
text:
When XML elements use namespaces, column names include the namespace prefix.

Example input (with normalization ON):

xml

```
<h:order id="1">
  <h:price>10</h:price>
  <f:price xmlns:f="http://f.ns">20</f:price>
</h:order>
```

Output table columns:`_id`, `h_price`, `f_price`

The namespace prefix is included in the column name to avoid collisions between elements that share the same local name (for example, `h:price` and `f:price`).

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Configuration
text:
**Use OLake UI for S3:**

Configuration > 1. Navigate to the Source Configuration Page
- Complete the OLake UI Setup Guide
- After logging in to the OLake UI, select the `Sources` tab from the left sidebar
- Click `Create Source` on the top right corner
- Select S3 from the connector dropdown

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Configuration > 2. Provide Configuration Details
text:
-

Enter S3 credentials.

**Connection details**

| Field | Description | Example Value |
| S3 Bucket Name required | Name of the S3 bucket that contains the files to sync. | dz-olake-testing |
| AWS Region | AWS Region where the bucket exists. Required so OLake Go calls the correct regional S3 endpoint. | us-east-1 |
| Access Key ID | AWS access key ID for authentication. Optional if using IAM roles or instance profiles. | <YOUR_KEY> |
| Secret Access Key | AWS secret access key for authentication. Optional if using IAM roles or instance profiles. | <YOUR_SECRET> |
| Path Prefix | Optional key prefix to limit discovery and sync to objects under this path. | data/ |
| Custom Endpoint | S3 API endpoint URL. Optional for AWS S3; required for S3-compatible storage such as MinIO. | https://minio.example.com |
| File Pattern | Regular expression to filter object keys by name. | .*\.csv$ |
| File Format required | Format of files in the bucket. OLake Go uses this to determine how to read and process files during sync. Additional format-specific fields appear in this section when applicable. | CSV JSON Parquet XML |
| Compression Type | Compression applied to files in the bucket. | none gzip zip |
| Delimiter | Field separator for CSV files. Shown when File Format is CSV . | , |
| Has Header | Whether CSV files include a header row. Shown when File Format is CSV . | Enabled |
| Skip Rows | Number of rows to skip at the start of each CSV file. Shown when File Format is CSV . | 0 |
| Quote Character | Quote character used in CSV files. Shown when File Format is CSV . | " |

**Additional configuration**

| Field | Description | Example Value |
| Retry Count | Number of retry attempts for failures. | 3 |
| Max Threads | Maximum number of worker threads the connector can spin up for parallel tasks. | 3 |

**AWS Authentication:**

- Access Key ID and Secret Access Key are optional for AWS S3. If omitted, the driver uses AWS default credential chain (IAM roles, environment variables, instance profiles, ECS task roles). This is the recommended approach for production deployments. If you provide one credential, you must provide both.
- Access Key ID, Secret Access Key and Endpoint is required for non AWS S3 services.

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Configuration > 3. Format-Specific Configuration
text:
**CSV Configuration:**

Additional fields for CSV files:

| Field | Description | Default |
| Delimiter | Field separator character | , |

| Quote Character | Quote character for CSV files | " |

Compression: Automatically detected from file extension (`.csv.gz` = gzipped)

Additional fields for JSON files:

Features:

- Efficient columnar reading
- Streaming support for large files
- Native type preservation

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Configuration > 1. Create Configuration File
text:
- Once the OLake CLI is setup, create a folder to store configuration files such as `source.json` and `destination.json`.

The `source.json` file for postgres must contain these mandatory fields.

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Configuration > 2. Provide Configuration Details
text:
An example `source.json` file will look like this:

**AWS S3 (IAM Role):**

source.json

```
{
  "bucket_name": "my-data-warehouse",
  "region": "us-east-1",
  "path_prefix": "data/",
  "file_format": "parquet",
  "max_threads": 10,
  "retry_count": 3
}
```

**AWS S3 (Static Keys):**

source.json

```
{
  "bucket_name": "my-data-warehouse",
  "region": "us-east-1",
  "path_prefix": "data/",
  "access_key_id": "<YOUR_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID>",
  "secret_access_key": "<YOUR_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY>",
  "file_format": "parquet",
  "max_threads": 10,
  "retry_count": 3
}
```

| Field | Description | Example Value | Type |
| bucket_name required | S3 bucket name where Iceberg table data and metadata files will be stored. | "my-data-warehouse" | String |
| region required | AWS Region where your S3 bucket exists. Required so OLake Go calls the correct regional S3 endpoint. | "us-east-1" | String |
| path_prefix | Optional path prefix to filter files | "data" | String |
| access_key_id | AWS access key ID for authentication. Optional if using IAM roles or instance profiles. | "<YOUR_KEY>" | String |
| secret_access_key | AWS secret access key for authentication. Optional if using IAM roles or instance profiles. | "<YOUR_SECRET>" | String |
| endpoint | Custom S3 endpoint for MinIO/LocalStack (required for non-AWS) | "http://localhost:9000" | String |
| file_format required | Select the format of files in the bucket to sync. OLake Go uses this to determine how to read and process files during sync. | Parquet XML JSON CSV | String |
| max_threads | Maximum number of worker threads the connector can spin up for parallel tasks. | 10 | Integer |
| retry_count | Number of retry attempts for failures. | 3 | Integer |
| compression | Compression format of the files. | none gzip zip | String |
| file_pattern | Regular expression to filter files by name. | .*\.csv$ | String |

**AWS Authentication:**

- Access Key ID and Secret Access Key are optional for AWS S3. If omitted, the driver uses AWS default credential chain (IAM roles, environment variables, instance profiles, ECS task roles). This is the recommended approach for production deployments. If you provide one credential, you must provide both.
- Access Key ID, Secret Access Key and Endpoint is required for non AWS S3 services.

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Configuration > 3. Format-Specific Configuration Examples
text:
**CSV Format:**

source.json - CSV Format

```
{
  "bucket_name": "source-data",
  "region": "us-east-1",
  "path_prefix": "csv/",
  "access_key_id": "minioadmin",
  "secret_access_key": "minioadmin",
  "endpoint": "http://localhost:9000",
  "file_format": "csv",
  "max_threads": 5,
  "retry_count": 3,
  "csv": {
    "has_header": true,
    "delimiter": ",",
    "skip_rows": 0,
    "quote_character": "\""
  }
}
```

CSV Configuration Fields:

| Field | Description | Default |
| delimiter | Field separator character | "," |
| has_header | Whether CSV files contain a header row | true |
| skip_rows | Number of rows to skip at the beginning of CSV files | 0 |
| quote_character | Quote character for CSV files | "\"" |

Note: Gzip compression is automatically detected for `.csv.gz` files.

**JSON Format:**

source.json - JSON Format

```
{
  "bucket_name": "source-data",
  "region": "us-east-1",
  "path_prefix": "json/",
  "access_key_id": "minioadmin",
  "secret_access_key": "minioadmin",
  "endpoint": "http://localhost:9000",
  "file_format": "json",
  "max_threads": 5,
  "retry_count": 3,
  "json": {
    "line_delimited": true
  }
}
```

JSON Configuration Fields:

| Field | Description | Default |
| line_delimited | Use line-delimited JSON (JSONL) format instead of JSON array | true |

Supported JSON Formats:

- JSONL: `{"id": 1}\n{"id": 2}\n`
- JSON Array: `[{"id": 1}, {"id": 2}]`
- Single Object: `{"data": [...]}`

Format is auto-detected if `line_delimited` is not specified.

Note: Gzip compression is automatically detected for `.json.gz` and `.jsonl.gz` files.

**Parquet Format:**

source.json - Parquet Format

```
{
  "bucket_name": "source-data",
  "region": "us-east-1",
  "path_prefix": "parquet/",
  "access_key_id": "minioadmin",
  "secret_access_key": "minioadmin",
  "endpoint": "http://localhost:9000",
  "file_format": "parquet",
  "max_threads": 5,
  "retry_count": 3
}
```

Parquet Configuration Fields:

| Field | Description | Default |
| streaming_enabled | Use S3 range requests for memory-efficient streaming (recommended for large files) | true |

Parquet Features:

- Schema automatically read from Parquet file metadata
- No additional configuration required
- Supports all Parquet data types
- Efficient streaming for large files using S3 range requests
- Native columnar reading preserves type information

**XML Format:**

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Configuration > 3. Format-Specific Configuration Examples (part 2)
text: source.json - XML Format

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Configuration > 3. Format-Specific Configuration Examples (part 3)
text:
```
{
  "bucket_name": "your-bucket",
  "region": "us-east-1",
  "path_prefix": "data/xml/",
  "file_format": "xml",
  "xml": { "row_identifier": "order" },
  "compression": "none",
  "max_threads": 5,
  "retry_count": 3
}
```

XML Configuration Fields:

| Field | Description | Example Value |
| row_identifier | XML tag that encloses each record | record |

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Configuration > 4. Check Source Connection
text:
To verify the database connection following command needs to be run:

check command

```
docker run --pull=always \
-v "[PATH_OF_CONFIG_FOLDER]:/mnt/config" \
olakego/source-s3:latest \
check \
--config /mnt/config/source.json
```

-

In case of connection failure, refer to the Troubleshooting section.

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Data Type Mapping
text:
| File Format | Source Data Type | Destination Data Type | Notes |
| CSV | Inferred from data | string | All CSV fields initially treated as strings |
| CSV | Numeric patterns | int, bigint, double | Integer and floating-point numbers auto-detected |
| CSV | ISO 8601 dates | timestamptz | Date/datetime strings converted to timestamp |
| CSV | Boolean values | boolean | true / false strings converted to boolean |
| JSON | string | string | JSON string fields |
| JSON | number (integer) | bigint | JSON integer values |
| JSON | number (float) | double | JSON floating-point values |
| JSON | boolean | boolean | JSON boolean values |
| JSON | object, array | string | Nested objects/arrays serialized to JSON strings |
| JSON | null | string | Null values converted to empty strings |
| Parquet | STRING, BINARY | string | Parquet string types |
| Parquet | INT32, INT64 | int, bigint | Parquet integer types |
| Parquet | FLOAT, DOUBLE | float, double | Parquet floating-point types |
| Parquet | BOOLEAN | boolean | Parquet boolean type |
| Parquet | TIMESTAMP_MILLIS | timestamptz | Parquet timestamp types |
| Parquet | DATE | date | Parquet date type |
| Parquet | DECIMAL | float | Parquet decimal types converted to float64 |
| XML | text content, attributes | string | All scalar element text and attribute values treated as strings |
| XML | nested elements | string | Nested elements serialized to JSON strings |
| XML | empty or null | string | Empty or null values treated as nullable string |
| All Formats | _last_modified_time | timestamptz | S3 LastModified metadata (added by connector) |

**Schema Inference:**

- CSV: Uses AND logic - examines all sampled rows to determine most restrictive type
- JSON: Auto-detects types from JSON primitives
- Parquet: Schema read directly from file metadata (no inference needed)
- XML: All values treated as strings; no datatype inference. Nested elements stored as JSON strings.

**timestamptz timezone:**

OLake Go always ingests timestamp data in UTC format, independent of the source timezone.

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Date and Time Handling
text:
During transfer, values in date, time, and timestamp columns are modified to ensure valid calendar ranges and destination compatibility.

- Case I (Year 0000):
Source dates with year `0000` are not valid in most destinations, so we change them to the epoch start date.
Example: `0000-05-10 → 1970-01-01`
- Case II (Year > 9999):
Extremely large years are capped at `9999`. The month and date are not affected.
Examples: `10000-03-12 → 9999-03-12`
-  Case III (Invalid month/day):
When the month or day exceeds valid ranges (i.e. month > 12 or day > 31), or the combined date is invalid, the value is replaced with the epoch start date.
Examples: `2024-13-15 → 1970-01-01`,` 2023-04-31 → 1970-01-01`

**Note:**

These rules apply to date, time, and timestamp columns during transfer.

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Troubleshooting > 1. Connection Failed - Access Denied
text:
logs

```
ERROR failed to list objects: AccessDenied: Access Denied
```

Cause: Insufficient IAM permissions or incorrect credentials

Solution:

- If using static credentials: Verify access key and secret key are correct
- If using IAM roles: Ensure the IAM role has proper S3 permissions attached
- Check IAM policy includes:json

```
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetObject"],
  "Resource": [
    "arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name",
    "arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/*"
  ]
}
```

- AWS Credential Chain Order:

- Static credentials in config (access_key_id, secret_access_key)
- Environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY)
- IAM role attached to EC2 instance/ECS task
- AWS credentials file (~/.aws/credentials)

- For MinIO/LocalStack: Ensure credentials match server configuration

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Troubleshooting > 2. No Streams Discovered
text:
Cause: Files not organized in folders or incorrect path_prefix

Solution:

- S3 connector requires folder structure: `bucket/prefix/stream_name/files`
- Check path_prefix matches your structure
- Verify file extensions match format (`.csv`, `.json`, `.parquet`)
- Example command to verify:bash

```
aws s3 ls s3://bucket-name/prefix/ --recursive
```

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Troubleshooting > 3. Schema Inference Failed - CSV
text:
logs

```
ERROR failed to infer schema: invalid delimiter or header configuration
```

Cause: Incorrect CSV configuration

Solution:

- Verify `has_header` matches file (check first row)
- Check `delimiter` is correct (`,` vs `;` vs `\t`)
- Ensure all rows have same column count
- Test with a small sample file first

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Troubleshooting > 4. JSON Format Not Detected
text:
Cause: Mixed JSON formats in same folder or invalid JSON

Solution:

- Keep JSONL and JSON Array formats in separate folders/streams
- Validate JSON syntax: `jq . < file.json`
- Ensure consistent field names across records
- Check for trailing commas or syntax errors

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Troubleshooting > 5. Parquet File Cannot Be Read
text:
logs

```
ERROR failed to read parquet schema: not a parquet file
```

Cause: Corrupted file or invalid Parquet format

Solution:

- Verify file with parquet-tools: `parquet-tools schema file.parquet`
- Check file wasn't corrupted during upload
- Ensure file extension is `.parquet` (not `.pq` or other)
- Re-upload file from source

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Troubleshooting > 6. Incremental Sync Not Working
text:
Cause: State file not persisted or incorrect sync_mode

Solution:

- Verify `state.json` file location is writable
- Check the stream in `selected_streams.json` has `sync_mode: "incremental"`
- Ensure `cursor_field: "_last_modified_time"` is set
- Confirm state file is being passed to sync command:bash

```
--state /path/to/state.json
```

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Troubleshooting > 7. MinIO Connection Timeout
text:
logs

```
ERROR dial tcp: i/o timeout
```

Cause: Network connectivity or incorrect endpoint

Solution:

- Check MinIO is running: `docker ps | grep minio`
- Test endpoint: `curl http://localhost:9000/minio/health/live`
- Verify endpoint format: `http://hostname:9000` (include protocol)
- For Docker: Use container name instead of localhost

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Troubleshooting > 8. Files Not Syncing Despite Being Present
text:
Cause: File extension mismatch or compression not detected

Solution:

- Ensure file extensions match format:

- CSV: `.csv` or `.csv.gz`
- JSON: `.json`, `.jsonl`, `.json.gz`, `.jsonl.gz`
- Parquet: `.parquet`

- Check file size is non-zero: `aws s3 ls s3://bucket/prefix/ --recursive --human-readable`
- Verify files are in correct folder structure

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Troubleshooting > 9. Out of Memory Errors
text:
logs

```
FATAL runtime: out of memory
```

Cause: Too many large files processed concurrently

Solution:

- Reduce `max_threads` in configuration (try 3-5)
- Process fewer streams at once
- Split very large files (>5GB) before upload
- Increase container memory limits

title: Sources / S3: Overview > Troubleshooting > 10. Permission Denied - LocalStack
text:
Cause: LocalStack IAM policy simulator

Solution:

- LocalStack accepts any credentials by default (`test`/`test`)
- Ensure endpoint is correct: `http://localhost:4566`
- Check LocalStack is running: `docker ps | grep localstack`
- Verify bucket exists: `awslocal s3 ls`

If the issue is not listed here, post the query on Slack to get it resolved within a few hours.

text:
**Deprecated: streams.json:**

The single-file `streams.json` format is deprecated. It still works, and OLake Go logs a warning when you use it. This will be removed in a future release. To move to Streams v2, read the migration guide. For Streams v2, see the streams reference.

title: Docker CLI / Streams v1 (legacy): Streams v1 (legacy streams.json) reference > Discover Command
text:
-

To discover the available streams from the source, run the following command:

discover command

```
docker run --pull=always \
-v "[PATH_OF_CONFIG_FOLDER]:/mnt/config" \
olakego/source-[SOURCE-TYPE]:latest \
discover \
--config /mnt/config/source.json
```

Running this command generates a `streams.json` file, which contains the list of available streams along with their metadata.

title: Docker CLI / Streams v1 (legacy): Streams v1 (legacy streams.json) reference > Discover Command > Re-discover and keep your edits
text:
Pass `--streams` with your existing `streams.json` to refresh stream metadata from the source. OLake Go keeps your `selected_streams` entries in that file.

re-discover command

```
docker run --pull=always \
-v "[PATH_OF_CONFIG_FOLDER]:/mnt/config" \
olakego/source-[SOURCE-TYPE]:latest \
discover \
--config /mnt/config/source.json \
--streams /mnt/config/streams.json \
```

New tables are not selected automatically. Add them to `selected_streams` in `streams.json` by hand.

**Available flags**

`--config`required

bash

```
--config /mnt/config/source.json
```

Description:

- Specifies the path to the source configuration file.
- For details about configuration files for different sources, see:

- MongoDB Config file
- MySQL Config file
- Oracle Config file
- PostgreSQL Config file
- S3 Config file
- DB2 Config file
- MSSQL Config file
- Kafka Config file

`--streams`optional

bash

```
--streams /mnt/config/streams.json
```

Description:

Specifies the path to the streams.json file. This file is generated after the discover command. When used during discovery, this flag updates the existing streams.json:

- Keeps prior manual changes.
- Adds new streams detected in the source database.
- Allows selecting which columns should be synced for each table.
- Allows updating the destination database name for each stream.

➡️ You must learn about `streams.json` configuration. Refer to the Streams Config guide.

`--destination-database-prefix`optional

bash

```
--destination-database-prefix olake
```

Description:

- Adds a custom prefix to the database name created in the destination.
- Example:

If the source database is `sales-db` and the driver is `mysql`:

- Default (Normalized) → `mysql_sales_db`
- With prefix (Normalized) → `olake_sales_db`

`--timeout`optional

bash

```
--timeout 600
```

Description:

- Applies only to the discover command.
- Overrides the default timeout of 300 seconds (5 minutes).
- This is helpful when working with large datasets or slower networks where the operation may need extra time to complete.

`--max-discover-threads`optional

bash

```
--max-discover-threads 100
```

Description:

title: Docker CLI / Streams v1 (legacy): Streams v1 (legacy streams.json) reference > Discover Command > Re-discover and keep your edits (part 2)
text:
- Applies only to the discover command.
- Sets the maximum number of parallel threads used for discovering table schemas in the database.
- Value: Integer (mandatory when the flag is used). Minimum value is 1 (must be greater than 0).
- Default: If the flag is not provided, the value defaults to 50.

`--target-query-engines`optional

bash

```
--target-query-engines trino,databricks,spark
```

Description:

- Applies only to the discover command.
- Comma-separated list of query engines you plan to use to read synced Iceberg tables (for example `trino`, `databricks`, `spark`).
- Discover limits each stream's `available_update_types` in `available_streams.json` to delete formats those engines can read. With multiple engines, only formats supported by all listed engines are included (the intersection).
- Use this when editing `selected_streams.json` so `update_type` choices match your query engines.
- To know more about the behavior of this flag, see Target Query Engines.

`--difference`optional

bash

```
--streams /path/old_streams.json \
--difference /path/new_streams.json
```

Description:

- Used with the discover command to compare differences between two streams, specifically an old stream and a new stream.
- Must be used together with `--streams /path/old_streams.json` to specify the path to the old streams file.
- The `--difference` flag specifies the path to the new streams file that will be compared against the old one.
- Running this command generates a `difference_streams.json` file containing the differences between the old and new streams.

**Internal testing command**

This command is primarily used internally for testing purposes to compare differences between old and new streams. It is not typically required for production use. However, if you want to check the differences between streams, you can use this command.

**Use version specific command:**

Using a version specific image is recommended instead of using latest in the commands for production use case.

What's Next : Understanding the streams config file for stream/table level modifications

title: Docker CLI / Streams v1 (legacy): Streams v1 (legacy streams.json) reference > Streams Config
text:
The `streams.json` file is organized into two main sections:

- `selected_streams`: Lists the streams that have been chosen for processing. These are grouped by namespace.
- `streams`: Contains an array of stream definitions. Each stream holds details about its schema, supported synchronization modes, primary keys, and other metadata.

title: Docker CLI / Streams v1 (legacy): Streams v1 (legacy streams.json) reference > Streams Config > 1. Selected Streams
text:
The `selected_streams` section groups streams by their namespace. For example, the configuration might look like this:

streams.json

```
"selected_streams": {
  "my_db": [
    {
      "partition_regex": "/{dropoff_datetime, year}",
      "stream_name": "table1",
      "normalization": true,
      "update_type": "eq",
      "append_mode": false,
      "selected_columns": {
                    "columns": [
                        "_cdc_timestamp",
                        "_olake_id",
                        "_cdc_lsn",
                        "_op_type",
                        "id",
                        "updated_at",
                        "dropoff_datetime",
                        "_olake_timestamp"
                    ],
                    "sync_new_columns": true
                },
      "filter": "UPDATED_AT >= \"08-JUN-25 07.19.23.690870000 AM\""
    },
    {
      "partition_regex": "",
      "stream_name": "table2",
      "normalization": false,
      "append_mode": false,
      "selected_columns": {
                    "columns": [
                        "_cdc_timestamp",
                        "_olake_id",
                        "_cdc_lsn",
                        "_op_type",
                        "id",
                        "city",
                        "_olake_timestamp"
                    ],
                    "sync_new_columns": true
                },
      "filter": "city = \"London\""
    }
  ]
}
```

**Kafka-specific configuration:**

For Kafka sources with Upsert ingestion mode, the following configuration is required:

- `append_mode` must be set to `false`
- `update_type` must be set to `"pos"` (Positional Deletes only)
- An additional field `"dedup_keys"` (array) must be added to specify deduplication keys, for example: `"dedup_keys": ["customer_id"]`

**Details about all the fields mentioned in selected streams**

title: Docker CLI / Streams v1 (legacy): Streams v1 (legacy streams.json) reference > Streams Config > 1. Selected Streams (part 2)
text:
| Component | Type | Example Value | Description |
| namespace | string | my_db | Groups streams that belong to a specific database or logical category |
| stream_name | string | "table1" , "table2" | Identifier for the stream. Must match the stream name defined in the Streams configurations. |
| partition_regex | string | "/{dropoff_datetime, year}" | A pattern defining how to partition the data. To read more, refer the Partition Regex for S3 or Partition Regex for iceberg |
| normalization | boolean | true | Converts top-level JSON fields into columns, while nested JSON objects are stored as string values. |
| update_type | string | "eq" or "pos" or "dv" | Specifies the format in which delete files are written during sync. "eq" writes equality delete files. "pos" writes positional delete files. "dv" writes deletion vector files. |
| append_mode | boolean | false | Disables upserts in Iceberg when set to true . (In upsert mode dedupe happens via equality delete) |
| dedup_keys | array | ["customer_id"] | Required when Upsert ingestion mode is selected for Kafka source. Specifies the columns used to identify unique records for deduplication. |
| selected_columns.columns | array | ["_cdc_timestamp", "id", "updated_at"] | List of columns to be included in the sync for each stream. |
| selected_columns.sync_new_columns | boolean | true | If true , newly discovered columns are automatically included in future syncs. If false , new columns must be manually added to selected_columns.columns to be synced. |
| filter | string | "UPDATED_AT >= \"08-JUN-25 07.19.23.690870000 AM\"" | Ensures that only data matching the specified condition is synced. |

title: Docker CLI / Streams v1 (legacy): Streams v1 (legacy streams.json) reference > Streams Config > 2. Streams
Docker CLI / Streams v1 (legacy): Streams v1 (legacy streams.json) reference > Streams Config > 2. Streams (part 2)
text:
| Component | Example Value | Description & Possible Values |
| name | "stream_8" | Unique identifier for the stream. Each stream must have a unique name. |
| namespace | "olake_db" | The grouping or database name that the stream belongs to. |
| type_schema | (JSON object with properties) | Defines the columns in streams or tables, including the destination column name. The source column name is normalized by replacing special characters and spaces with underscores ( _ ) and is used as the final column name in the destination table. |
| supported_sync_modes | ["full_refresh", "cdc", "incremental","strict_cdc"] | Lists the sync modes the stream supports. Includes "full_refresh" , "cdc" , "strict_cdc" and "incremental" . To read more about sync modes read |
| source_defined_primary_key | ["_id"] | Specifies the field(s) that is set as a primary key in the source. |
| available_cursor_fields | ["_id", "name", "marks", "updated_at"] | Lists fields that can be used to track synchronization progress in incremental sync mode. |
| sync_mode | "incremental" | Indicates the active sync mode. Possible values are defined in supported_sync_modes . |
| cursor_field | "updated_at" | Defines the cursor field used to track incremental sync. To read more about incremental sync read this |
| destination_database | "prefix:my_db" | Specifies the destination database name where data will be stored. By default, the driver name is used as the prefix, but you can override it using the --destination-database-prefix flag. The source namespace is always appended to the database name. All special characters and spaces are replaced with ( _ ), and the database is automatically created if it doesn’t exist. |
| destination_table | "table1" | Specifies the name of the destination table where the data will be stored. The table name is derived from the source stream name and normalized by replacing special characters and spaces with underscores ( _ ). |

Whats's Next: Once the streams.json file is configured as required, sync can be initiated.

text:

sync command

```
docker run --pull=always \
-v "[PATH_OF_CONFIG_FOLDER]:/mnt/config" \
olakego/source-[SOURCE-TYPE]:latest \
sync \
--config /mnt/config/source.json \
--streams /mnt/config/streams.json \
--destination /mnt/config/destination.json
```

**Available flags**

`--config`required

--config /mnt/config/source.json

Description:

- For details about configuration files for different sources, see:

- S3 Config file
- DB2 Config file

`--streams`required

bash

```
--streams /mnt/config/streams.json
```

Description:

Specifies the path to the streams.json file. This file is generated after the discover command. When used during discovery, this flag updates the existing streams.json:

- Keeps prior manual changes.
- Adds new streams detected in the source database.
- Allows selecting which columns should be synced for each table.
- Allows updating the destination database name for each stream.

➡️ You must learn about `streams.json` configuration. Refer to the Streams Config guide.

`--destination`required

bash

```
--destination /mnt/config/destination.json
```

Description:

- S3 Tables Catalog configuration
- Unity Catalog configuration
- Apache Polaris Catalog configuration
- BigLake Catalog configuration

`--state`optional

bash

```
--state /mnt/config/state.json
```

Description:

- Specifies the path to the state file.
- The state file contains metadata (such as offsets and positions) that enables:

- Resuming interrupted syncs.
- Continuing incremental or CDC syncs without restarting from scratch.
- Storing the version in the state file for maintaining backward compatibility.

The `state.json` file is organized into two main sections:

**1. Global State**

title: Docker CLI / Streams v1 (legacy): Streams v1 (legacy streams.json) reference > Sync > Sync command (part 2)
Docker CLI / Streams v1 (legacy): Streams v1 (legacy streams.json) reference > Sync > Sync command (part 3)

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2
text:
**Streams v2 is here:**

-

Streams config now uses two files: `selected_streams.json` (the file you edit) and `available_streams.json` (read-only, written by discover).

-

Streams v2 and the new CLI flags are supported from OLake Go v1.0.0 or later.

-

See the migration guide to migrate to Streams v2 from Streams v1 or the Streams v1 reference for more details on the legacy format.

Streams v2 replaces the single Streams v1 file, `streams.json`, with two files: one that you maintain and one that OLake Go writes during discovery. Migration is optional; existing workflows that use `streams.json` continue to work until Streams v1 is removed. This page describes what changed and how to switch to Streams v2.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 1. Do I Need to Migrate?
text:
No, not immediately. Legacy `streams.json` remains supported for `discover`, `sync`, and `clear-destination`. OLake Go logs a deprecation warning when you use it.

`streams.json` is deprecated and will be removed in a future release. Plan to migrate on your own schedule, and complete migration before upgrading past the release that drops Streams v1 support. For most CLI deployments, migration consists of updating command flags; OLake UI migrates jobs automatically.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 2. Why the Change
text:
The legacy `streams.json` combined two types of data:

- A large, machine-written schema (`streams[]`).
- A smaller set of user-defined settings (`selected_streams`).

Editable settings were distributed across both structures. For example, `sync_mode` and `destination_table` appeared in `streams[]`.

Streams v2 separates these concerns:

| File | Who writes it | What it holds | Do you edit it? |
| selected_streams.json | You (discover writes the first copy) | Streams to sync and every per-stream setting | Yes |
| available_streams.json | discover | Every stream OLake Go found: schema, supported sync modes, primary keys, cursor candidates, defaults | No, read-only |

This yields a single file to edit, smaller diffs, clearer reviews, and safer re-discover operations.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 3. Before and After
Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 3. Before and After > Precedence Rule
text:
A value in `selected_streams.json` takes precedence. If a field is not set there, OLake Go uses the value in `available_streams.json` (or the stream's `default_stream_properties`).

When you next edit a stream, move `sync_mode`, `cursor_field`, `destination_database`, and `destination_table` into `selected_streams.json`.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 4. Flag Mapping
text:
| Command | Legacy flag | New flags |
| discover (re-run, keep edits) | --streams <path> | --selected-streams <path> and --available-streams <path> |
| discover (compare) | --streams <old> and --difference <new> | --selected-streams , --available-streams , --difference-selected-streams , --difference-available-streams |
| sync | --streams <path> (or --catalog ) | --selected-streams <path> and --available-streams <path> |
| clear-destination | --streams <path> | --selected-streams <path> and --available-streams <path> |

`--streams`, `--catalog`, and `--difference` remain supported. `--streams` and `--catalog` log this warning:

```
--streams is deprecated and will be removed in a future release; use --available-streams and --selected-streams instead
```

`--difference` logs this warning:

```
--difference is deprecated and will be removed in a future release; use --difference-available-streams and --difference-selected-streams instead
```

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 5. Migrate the OLake Go CLI
text:
Each `discover` run on a Streams v2 writes three files in sync: `streams.json`, `selected_streams.json`, and `available_streams.json`. For most setups, migration therefore requires only a flag change.

All examples assume your files are in `/mnt/config`.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 5. Migrate the OLake Go CLI > Step 1. Make Sure You Have the Two New Files
text:
After you run `discover` command, the two new files should already exist alongside `streams.json` with equivalent settings. Proceed to Step 2.

If your `streams.json` was produced by an older version, run re-discover to generate the two files. This connects to the source and preserves your existing edits.

bash

```
discover --config /mnt/config/source.json \
  --streams /mnt/config/streams.json
```

OLake Go writes all three files. New tables are not selected automatically.

Open `selected_streams.json` and verify that every stream you sync is listed. Do not edit `available_streams.json`.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 5. Migrate the OLake Go CLI > Step 2. Change the Flags
text:
Replace `--streams` (or `--catalog`) with `--selected-streams` and `--available-streams` in every command, script, and scheduler definition.

sync

```
sync --config /mnt/config/source.json \
  --destination /mnt/config/destination.json \
  --selected-streams /mnt/config/selected_streams.json \
  --available-streams /mnt/config/available_streams.json \
  --state /mnt/config/state.json
```

clear-destination

```
clear-destination --destination /mnt/config/destination.json \
  --selected-streams /mnt/config/selected_streams.json \
  --available-streams /mnt/config/available_streams.json \
  --state /mnt/config/state.json
```

discover (re-run and keep edits)

```
discover --config /mnt/config/source.json \
  --selected-streams /mnt/config/selected_streams.json \
  --available-streams /mnt/config/available_streams.json
```

Do not pass `--streams` together with the new flags. `state.json` requires no changes.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 5. Migrate the OLake Go CLI > Step 3. Edit Only selected_streams.json From Now On
text:
After you switch, apply every stream configuration change in `selected_streams.json`.

**Migration is one-way:**

After you switch, do not revert to `--streams`. Downgrade to Streams v1 is not supported. For example, if `selected_streams.json` sets `sync_mode` to `full_refresh` while the stream was `incremental` in the legacy file, `streams.json` may still record `incremental`. Reverting would change how those streams sync without an explicit configuration update.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 6. OLake UI Users
text:
No manual action is required. OLake UI migrates jobs automatically:

- When OLake UI starts, it converts every job whose source connector version supports Streams v2.
- When you upgrade a source's version in the UI, it converts that source's jobs.
- A job that cannot be converted remains on `streams.json` and continues to run as before.

After a source runs a version that supports Streams v2, you cannot downgrade that source below that version. The UI blocks the change and returns an error similar to:

```
invalid streams format: source version <version> is below <minimum version> and job_id[<id>] uses the split format
```

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 7. What Stays the Same
text:
- `state.json` is unchanged; no state migration is required.
- `source.json`, `destination.json`, and the `check` and `spec` commands are unchanged.
- Scripts that still pass `--streams` continue to work until Streams v1 is removed.

8. Common Mistakes
| Mistake | Error code | Message |
| Pass only one of --available-streams or --selected-streams | config.incomplete_catalog_flag_pair | --available-streams and --selected-streams must be passed |
| Pass --streams together with both --available-streams and --selected-streams | config.conflicting_catalog_flags | --streams cannot be combined with --available-streams/--selected-streams |
| Run sync or clear-destination with no streams flags | config.flag_missing | --streams or --available-streams and --selected-streams not passed |
| Pass only one flag of the difference pair | config.incomplete_difference_flag_pair | --difference-available-streams and --difference-selected-streams must be passed together |
| Use --difference with the new difference pair | config.conflicting_difference_flags | --difference cannot be combined with --difference-available-streams/--difference-selected-streams |
| available_streams.json has no streams | catalog.available_streams_empty | available_streams file <path> has no streams[] |

Additional considerations:

- A stream in `selected_streams.json` with no match in `available_streams.json` is skipped with a warning: `Skipping; selected stream <ns>.<name> has no matching entry in streams[]. Rediscover or check the streams file.`
- Re-discover does not add new tables to `selected_streams.json`. Add them manually.
- Re-discover removes entries for tables that no longer exist in the source.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 9. FAQ > 1. What Are Streams v1 and v2?
text:
Streams v1 is the legacy single file, `streams.json`. Streams v2 is the pair `selected_streams.json` + `available_streams.json`. Streams v1 is deprecated; use Streams v2 for new setups.

9. FAQ > 2. I Use the OLake UI. Do I Need to Do Anything?
No. OLake UI converts your jobs at startup and when you upgrade a source version. See OLake UI Users.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 9. FAQ > 3. Can I Downgrade a Source After the UI Migrates Its Jobs?
text:
No. The UI prevents downgrade below the first version that supports Streams v2.

9. FAQ > 4. Can I Go Back to streams.json ?
No. Migration is one-way. `streams.json` does not reflect `sync_mode`, `cursor_field`, `destination_database`, and `destination_table` values set in `selected_streams.json`, so reverting would change how those streams sync.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 9. FAQ > 5. Is Migration Just a Flag Change?
text:
Yes, if you already ran `discover` on a Streams v2 capable release (OLake Go Version 1.0.0 or later). Those runs already wrote the two new files in sync with `streams.json`.

9. FAQ > 6. When Is streams.json Removed?
In a future release. OLake Go has not announced a removal date. It logs a deprecation warning until removal.

title: Docker CLI / Migrate to Streams v2: Migrate from Streams v1 ( streams.json ) to Streams v2 > 9. FAQ > 7. Do I Need to Migrate My State File?
text:
No. `state.json` is unchanged.

9. FAQ > 8. Where Is the Old Format Documented?
See the legacy `streams.json` reference. For Streams v2, see the streams reference.

title: Use Cases: Use Cases for OLake Go > 1. Offloading OLTP Databases for Analytics
text:
Running complex analytical queries directly on production OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) databases can degrade performance and affect transactional workloads.

OLake Go addresses this by replicating data from MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and MongoDB into an Apache Iceberg based data lake.

This approach provides:

-

Workload separation → Keep analytics independent from production databases.

-

Faster performance → Run queries on Iceberg tables optimized for analytics.

-

Efficient bootstrapping → Use full-load sync for initial data migration.

-

Resilience → Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) ensures schema changes don’t break pipelines.

With OLake Go, you can maintain stable transactional systems while enabling scalable and reliable analytics on Apache Iceberg.

title: Use Cases: Use Cases for OLake Go > 2. Building Open Data Stacks and Scaling Data Engineering
text:
Organizations looking to reduce reliance on proprietary ETL and data warehousing tools can use OLake Go as part of an open-source data stack. By standardizing on Apache Iceberg as the table format, OLake Go ensures broad compatibility with query engines like Trino, Presto, Spark, Dremio, and DuckDB.

With its open-source approach, OLake Go helps teams:

-

Replace managed ETL/replication services with a community-driven alternative.

-

Customize and extend the platform through its open codebase.

-

Standardize data lake storage on Apache Iceberg.

-

Avoid vendor lock-in tied to closed formats and tools.

Support multiple query engines across different use cases and teams.

This enables a flexible, scalable, and future-proof data architecture built on open standards.

title: Use Cases: Use Cases for OLake Go > 3. Enabling Near-Real-Time Analytics
text:
Modern applications need fresh data within minutes, not hours. OLake Go enables near-real-time analytics by continuously replicating data from transactional databases using CDC, often achieving sub-minute latency for updates to appear in Iceberg.

Key benefits:

-

Low-latency ingestion with log-based CDC.

-

Incremental processing powered by Apache Iceberg.

-

Efficient queries using Iceberg optimizations like hidden partitioning, metadata pruning,

This allows teams to run fast, cost-efficient analytics on frequently updated data.

title: Use Cases: Use Cases for OLake Go > 4. Cost-Effective Data Retention and Compliance
text:
Storing historical data for compliance, audits, or analysis can be costly in traditional data warehouses. OLake Go addresses this by replicating data into Apache Iceberg, which stores it on cost-efficient object storage (e.g., S3, GCS).

With Iceberg, data remains immediately queryable across compatible engines—no rehydration needed. Its built-in schema evolution ensures that structural changes over time don’t break access to historical data.

Key benefits:

-

Store large historical datasets at lower cost.

-

Keep retained data instantly queryable.

-

Meet compliance and auditing needs with long-term retention.

Adapt to schema changes seamlessly with Iceberg.

title: Use Cases: Use Cases for OLake Go > 5. Powering AI and ML Data Pipelines
text:
Building effective AI and ML models requires fresh, reliable, and structured data. OLake Go automates the ingestion of transactional data into an Iceberg-based lakehouse, ensuring that pipelines always have access to the latest information.

With continuous updates, ML feature stores and training datasets stay current, while Iceberg's compatibility with engines like PySpark and DuckDB makes it easy to plug into existing data science workflows. This supports faster model development and iteration.

Key benefits:

-

Automate ingestion of transactional data for ML feature stores.

-

Provide consistent, up-to-date data for training and evaluation.

-

Seamlessly integrate with ML processing engines (e.g., PySpark, DuckDB).

title: Use Cases: Use Cases for OLake Go > 6. Simplifying Change Data Capture
text:
Setting up scalable CDC pipelines is often complex. OLake Go makes this easier by providing an open-source solution purpose-built for database-to-Iceberg replication.

It uses log-based CDC for minimal impact on source databases, supports schema evolution to handle structural changes, and includes a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) for reliable error handling. The design aligns with open-source streaming concepts, ensuring flexibility and robustness.

Key benefits:

-

Log-based CDC with low impact on source systems.

-

Automatic handling of schema changes.

-

Dead Letter Queue for dependable error management.

title: Use Cases: Use Cases for OLake Go > 7. Reducing Cloud Data Warehouse Costs
text:
Cloud data warehouses can become expensive due to storage and compute costs. OLake Go helps reduce these expenses by offloading raw, historical, or less frequently used data into an Iceberg lakehouse on cost-effective object storage.

This lets teams keep their warehouse optimized for active data, while still retaining full access to complete datasets in Iceberg.

Key benefits:

-

Lower costs by storing large datasets in Iceberg on object storage.

-

Optimize warehouse usage for critical, high-value data.

title: Benchmarks / AWS DMS vs OLake Go: OLake Go vs AWS DMS Benchmark
text:
In today's data-driven world, organizations are migrating massive datasets from traditional databases to cloud storage. But here's the million-dollar question: Which tool can handle multi billion records efficiently without breaking the bank?

The following benchmark evaluates performance, environment configuration, and cost considerations for migrating PostgreSQL data to Parquet (AWS S3) using AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) and OLake Go.

title: Benchmarks / AWS DMS vs OLake Go: OLake Go vs AWS DMS Benchmark > Workload
text:
- Dataset: This benchmark uses two large tables from NYC Taxi Data`trips2` and `fhv_trips`. For details on how the data is generated, check here: How the data is generated!
- Total rows:4,008,587,913 rows including both tables
- Modes evaluated: We are performing Full Refresh and CDC workload (50 million rows)

title: Benchmarks / AWS DMS vs OLake Go: OLake Go vs AWS DMS Benchmark > Environment
text:
- Source database: Azure PostgreSQL (32 vCores, 128 GB RAM)
- Destination: Amazon S3 (Parquet)
- Migration compute: c6i.16xlarge (64 vCPU, 128 GB RAM)
- Reference compute price: ~$3.07/hour

**note:**

The same dataset and compute were used for both the tools.

title: Benchmarks / AWS DMS vs OLake Go: OLake Go vs AWS DMS Benchmark > Full Refresh Results
text:
The full-load test evaluates the time and throughput required to transfer the complete dataset from the source PostgreSQL database to Parquet files in S3, establishing a baseline for bulk data movement under sustained load conditions.

| Tool | Rows Processed | Total Time | Avg Throughput (rows/sec) |
| OLake Go | 4,008,587,913 | 1 h 59 m | 558,765 |
| AWS DMS | 4,008,587,913 | 9 h 8 m | 122,000 |

Key observations:

- OLake Go achieved a 4.6× faster full refresh performance compared to AWS DMS.
- OLake Go eliminates the need for manual partition-boundary scripting, while DMS relies on manual boundary generation to achieve PostgreSQL parallelization.

Parallelism used:

- OLake Go ran with 32 threads.
- DMS ran with: 40 parallel tasks.

title: Benchmarks / AWS DMS vs OLake Go: OLake Go vs AWS DMS Benchmark > CDC Results (Insert-only; 50M rows)
text:
The CDC test evaluates the sustained ingestion of incremental changes from PostgreSQL into Parquet, validating plugin configuration, replication slots, and overall throughput. Each of the tables `trips2` and `fhv_trips` will ingest 25 million records.

| Tool | Rows Processed | Total Time | Avg Throughput (rows/sec) |
| AWS DMS | 50,000,000 | 22 m 41 s | 36,738 |
| OLake Go | 50,000,000 | 16 m 24 s | 50,812 |

Key Observations:

- OLake Go performed the CDC workload approximately 1.38× faster than AWS DMS.
- OLake Go requires minimal configuration , selecting the Full Refresh + CDC Sync Mode option is sufficient, whereas DMS requires enabling pglogical via Azure extensions, performing a detailed pglogical setup, and specifying the starting LSN for replication tasks.

Parallelism used:

- OLake Go ran with 32 threads.
- DMS ran with: 40 parallel tasks.

title: Benchmarks / AWS DMS vs OLake Go: OLake Go vs AWS DMS Benchmark > Resource Utilization
text:
We’re focusing on resource utilization for the Full Refresh process, as it’s significantly more resource-intensive than CDC.

The memory utilization shown corresponds to a transfer of ~4 billion records. As the data volumes increase, being memory efficiency becomes highly crucial — an area where OLake Go excels.

| Memory Stats | OLake Go | DMS |
| Min | 4.19 GB | 20 GB |
| Max | 50.55 GB | 40 GB |
| Mean | 31.76 GB | 30 GB |

OLake Go's memory usage ranged from 4.19 GB to 50.55 GB, averaging 31.76 GB throughout the transfer. For DMS, the memory usage ranged from 20 GB to 40 GB, averaging 30 GB throughout the transfer.

title: Benchmarks / AWS DMS vs OLake Go: OLake Go vs AWS DMS Benchmark > Cost Comparison (Compute Only)
text:
Compute costs scale linearly with runtime at a given instance class for both OLake Go and DMS.

Here is the cost comparison for Full Refresh process.

| Scenario | Instance | Runtime | Approx. Cost |
| DMS Full Refresh | c6i.16xlarge | 9h 08m | ~$28.03 |
| OLake Go Full Refresh | c6i.16xlarge | 1h 59m | ~$6.08 |

Important-

OLake Go is delivering 4.61x cost savings as compared to DMS on compute alone. When you're moving terabytes monthly, those savings add up fast!

Scaling Impact-

Let us take a closer look at how the costs evolve over time for both the tools.

Assume that the same dataset is migrated "once daily" for the durations specified below.

| OLake Go | ~$182 | ~$364 | ~$1094 |

The cost trends over time make it evident which tool is more cost-efficient. Considering, typical workflows involve more than one daily sync, so the costs would increase from the baseline shown here.

OLake Go is open source and incurs no licensing fees ; costs depend solely on the user’s infrastructure and storage consumption
